mammals.name: Reindeer
mammals.summary: The reindeer or caribou (Rangifer tarandus) is a species of deer with circumpolar distribution, native to the Arctic, subarctic, tundra, boreal, and mountainous regions of Northern Europe, Siberia, and North America. It is the only representative of the genus Rangifer.
facts: Their eyes physically change color with the seasons, shifting from golden-yellow in the continuous summer sun to deep blue in the dark Arctic winter to capture more light.
They are the only known mammals capable of seeing ultraviolet light, which makes white fur and urine-soaked snow glow brightly against the winter landscape.
Walking reindeer produce an audible 'click-click' sound from tendons snapping over small bones in their feet, allowing herds to stay together during blinding blizzards.
Unlike every other species of deer, female reindeer grow antlers right alongside the males, and keep theirs through winter while males shed theirs in late autumn.
Their specialized nasal passages contain scrolled bones that warm icy air before it hits the lungs and condense moisture on the way out, sometimes making their noses glow red on thermal cameras.
Reindeer hair is completely hollow and filled with trapped air, acting like a natural life jacket that lets them float effortlessly across frigid rivers.

mammals.name: Beluga whale
mammals.summary: The beluga whale () or the white whale (Delphinapterus leucas) is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean. It is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae, along with the narwhal, and the only member of the genus Delphinapterus.
facts: Earned the nickname 'canaries of the sea' from early whalers who could hear their repertoire of chirps, whistles, trills, and clicks right through wooden ship hulls.
Unlike almost all other whales, the seven vertebrae in a beluga's neck are not fused together, allowing them to nod and turn their heads side to side.
That squishy, bulbous forehead, called a melon, is filled with specialized oil that the whale can intentionally reshape using facial muscles to focus echolocation beams like a flashlight.
Calves are born dark slate-gray or brownish-pink to blend into murky estuary waters and don't turn completely snow-white until they are up to eight years old.
Every summer, thousands of belugas gather in shallow arctic river mouths to rub against coarse gravel and molt their yellowed top layer of skin like a giant sunburn.

A captive beluga named NOC once startled Navy divers in San Diego by spontaneously mimicking the rhythm and pitch of human speech so convincingly that a diver surfaced to ask who was telling him to get out of the water.

mammals.name: Cheetah
mammals.summary: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx. The cheetah is a pursuit predator and the fastest land animal, capable of running at 93–104 km/h (58–65 mph); it has evolved for speed, having powerful hindlimb muscles and a long lumbar spine.
facts: At top speed, a cheetah spends more than half of its time completely airborne, covering up to 23 feet in a single stride and going from 0 to 60 mph in just three seconds.
Unlike lions and leopards, cheetahs cannot roar; instead, they purr loudly on both the inhale and exhale and communicate with high-pitched bird-like chirps that carry for a mile.
Their claws are only semi-retractable and stay exposed like the cleats on a track runner's spikes, giving them explosive traction during hairpin turns.
The black 'tear marks' running from the inside corners of their eyes down to their mouths act like a football player's eye-black, absorbing harsh glare from the midday sun.
An oversized heart, giant nostrils, and enlarged lungs let a sprinting cheetah jump its breathing rate from 60 to 150 breaths per minute in seconds.

Modern cheetahs survived such a severe ice-age genetic bottleneck about 10,000 years ago that unrelated cheetahs today are practically clones and can accept skin grafts from one another without rejection.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth, capable of accelerating from 0 to 60 mph in just three seconds.
Unlike big cats in the genus Panthera, cheetahs cannot roar; instead they purr, chirp, and stutter.
Black 'tear marks' running from a cheetah's eyes down its cheeks help reflect the glare of the midday sun.
Cheetahs have semi-retractable claws that grip the ground like track cleats during high-speed sprints.

mammals.name: Domestic dog
mammals.summary: The dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves. Also called the domestic dog, it was selectively bred during the Late Pleistocene by hunter-gatherers.
facts: Every dog's wet nose print is formed by a unique pattern of ridges and dimples, making it as reliable for identification as a human fingerprint.

Unlike wolves, domestic dogs evolved a specialized facial muscle, the levator anguli oculi medialis, specifically to raise their inner eyebrows into an irresistible 'puppy-dog eyes' expression for humans.
When dogs kick up dirt after going to the bathroom, they aren't trying to bury anything; they are using pheromones secreted by glands in their paw pads to leave a pungent scent signpost.

A dog's sense of smell is so layered that it can detect the equivalent of half a teaspoon of sugar dissolved in an Olympic-sized swimming pool, and its nostrils sample air separately to pinpoint which direction an odor came from.
The Basenji is famous as the world's only 'barkless' dog; because of its uniquely shaped larynx, it produces a melodic yodel called a 'barroo' when excited.
During the domestication process, dogs gained extra copies of the AMY2B gene for digesting starch, allowing them to thrive on human agricultural scraps that would upset a wolf's stomach.

mammals.name: Dingo
mammals.summary: The dingo is a lineage of dog found in Australia. It is a medium-sized canine that possesses a lean, hardy body adapted for speed, agility, and stamina.
facts: Dingoes have remarkably flexible wrists that can rotate in ways domestic dogs' cannot, allowing them to turn doorknobs, unlatch gates, and climb trees or vertical chain-link fences.
To keep them out of southeastern Australia's sheep pastures, humans built the Dingo Fence, the longest fence on Earth, stretching 3,488 miles across the continent.
Unlike domestic dogs that bark at anything, dingoes almost never bark, relying instead on eerie, harmonized pack howls and chortles to coordinate across the Outback.
Female dingoes only come into heat once a year, just like wolves, whereas domestic dogs can breed two or three times annually.
A dingo can turn its head nearly 180 degrees in either direction thanks to extra-supple neck joints.
Archaeological burials show that Indigenous Australians welcomed dingoes into their camps around 3,500 years ago, often wrapping deceased dingoes in paperbark and burying them alongside people.

mammals.name: Coyote
mammals.summary: The coyote (/kaɪ(j)oʊt(i)/, KY-(y)oh-t(ee)) (Canis latrans) is a species of canine also known as the American jackal, prairie wolf, and brush wolf. It is native to North America, and it is smaller than its close relative, the gray wolf, and slightly smaller than the closely related eastern wolf and red wolf.
facts: Coyotes and American badgers sometimes team up into an unlikely hunting duo: the badger digs into ground-squirrel burrows while the coyote waits at the escape tunnels, making both predators roughly 30% more successful.

Because of a quirk of female reproductive biology called litter-size compensation, when humans try to cull coyote populations, the surviving females respond by having larger litters of up to a dozen pups.
Known as 'song dogs,' a single pair of coyotes can use rapid yips, barks, and overlapping frequency shifts called the 'beau geste effect' to trick listeners into thinking a whole pack surrounds them.
Despite the cartoon myth that roadrunners leave them in the dust, a real coyote can sprint at 40 miles per hour, nearly twice as fast as a running Greater Roadrunner.
Urban coyotes in cities like Chicago have been filmed patiently waiting at crosswalks for traffic lights to turn red and looking both ways before trotting across multi-lane avenues.
In many Native American traditions, Coyote is the ultimate trickster-creator hero who stole fire for humanity and scattered the stars across the night sky.

mammals.name: Tiger
mammals.summary: The tiger (Panthera tigris) is a large cat and a member of the genus Panthera native to Asia. It has a powerful, muscular body with a large head and paws, a long tail and orange fur that fades to white in parts, with black, mostly vertical stripes.
facts: If you shaved a tiger completely bald, its stripes would still be visible; the dark bands are pigmented directly into the skin underneath the fur, and no two tigers share the same pattern.
The white circular spots on the backs of a tiger's ears, called ocelli, act as 'false eyes' to deter ambush attacks from behind and help cubs follow their mother through tall grass.
Unlike almost all house cats, tigers love water and are powerhouse swimmers capable of crossing four-mile-wide rivers or lounging neck-deep in forest pools to beat the heat.
A tiger's roar is so loud and contains such low-frequency infrasound (below 20 Hz) that it can travel nearly two miles and momentarily rattle or paralyze prey with fear.
Tiger saliva contains natural antiseptic compounds, which is why they furiously lick their wounds with their sandpaper-rough tongues to prevent infection.
Because most of their ambushes fail, tigers are masters of patience that will mimic the mating call of sambar deer to lure curious targets straight into striking range.
Tigers are the largest extant cat species, and no two tigers have the exact same pattern of stripes.
A tiger's stripe pattern is pigmented directly into its skin as well as its fur.
Unlike most cats, tigers are avid swimmers and frequently bathe in rivers and lakes to cool off.
Tigers have white circular spots called ocelli on the backs of their ears that act as false eyes.

mammals.name: Domestic cat
mammals.summary: The cat (Felis catus), also called domestic cat and house cat, is a small domesticated carnivorous mammal. It is a member of Felidae, the family of mammals in the order Carnivora also colloquially referred to as cats.
facts: Adult cats almost never meow at other adult cats; they reserve that vocalization almost exclusively to manipulate and converse with humans, often matching the frequency of a crying human baby.
A cat's purr vibrates at a steady frequency between 25 and 150 Hertz, the exact range shown in orthopedic medicine to stimulate bone density and accelerate tissue repair.
Cats lack the functional TAS1R2 gene receptor on their tongues, meaning they are completely blind to the taste of sweetness and have zero interest in sugar.
Roughly 70% to 80% of all orange tabby cats are male because the gene for orange fur resides on the X chromosome, so a female needs two orange copies while a male needs only one.
Because a cat's collarbone (clavicle) floats freely in muscle rather than attaching to other bones, the animal can squeeze its entire body through any gap wide enough for its skull.
Cats walk with a 'direct register' gait; their hind paws step into the exact footprints just vacated by their front paws, minimizing noise and ensuring solid footing in the dark.

mammals.name: Orca
mammals.summary: The orca (Orcinus orca), or killer whale, is a toothed whale and the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family. The only extant species in the genus Orcinus, it is recognizable by its distinct pigmentation, being mostly black on top, white on the bottom, and having recognizable white eye patches.
facts: Despite being called 'killer whales,' orcas are actually the largest members of the oceanic dolphin family; the name is a flipped translation of old Spanish sailors calling them 'asesina de ballenas' (whale killers).
Each matrilineal pod speaks its own distinct vocal dialect of clicks and whistles passed down through generations, and calves learn their mother's accent just like human babies.

In the summer of 1987, a single female orca in Puget Sound started balancing a dead salmon on her nose like a hat; within weeks, the 'dead salmon hat' fashion fad spread across three pods before vanishing completely the next year.
Antarctic 'wave-washing' orcas swim in tight formation toward an ice floe and dive at the last second to generate a synchronized wall of water that washes resting seals right off the ice.

Female orcas are one of only a handful of mammals on Earth, alongside humans and a few other toothed whales, that go through menopause, living for decades after they stop reproducing to lead the pod as wise grandmothers.

A group of orcas off the coast of South Africa known as Port and Starboard learned to flip great white sharks upside down to induce tonic immobility, dining solely on the sharks' nutrient-rich livers with surgical precision.
Despite the nickname 'killer whale', the orca is actually the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family.
Orca pods pass down distinct regional dialects and specialized hunting traditions across generations in matrilineal families.
Wild orcas have been observed creating synchronized waves to wash seals off floating ice floes.
Female orcas undergo menopause and can live into their 80s or 90s as matriarchs guiding their pods.

mammals.name: Lion
mammals.summary: The lion (Panthera leo) is a large cat of the genus Panthera, currently ranging only in sub-Saharan Africa and India. It has a muscular, broad-chested body; a short, rounded head; round ears; and a dark, hairy tuft at the tip of its tail.
facts: A lion's roar can reach an ear-splitting 114 decibels, loud enough to be heard five miles away across the open savanna, thanks to flat, square-shaped vocal cords that vibrate under minimal lung pressure.
In the scorching heat of the Serengeti, lions spend up to 20 hours a day sleeping or lounging in the shade, doing the vast majority of their hunting under cover of darkness.

Research shows that dark, thick manes come with a heavy thermal cost, making male lions significantly hotter, yet females strongly prefer dark-maned mates and rival males are more intimidated by them.

During the 1898 construction of a railway bridge over the Tsavo River in Kenya, two maneless male lions terrorized the work camps for nine months, dragging workers from tents before being stopped by Lt. Col. John Henry Patterson.
Lionesses in the same pride often synchronize their reproductive cycles and nurse one another's cubs indiscriminately in a communal 'crèche,' protecting the young from nomadic males.

In Tanzania's Lake Manyara and Uganda's Ishasha sector, entire prides of lions have developed the unusual cultural habit of climbing high into sprawling acacia and fig trees to escape biting tsetse flies.
Lions are the only wild cats that live in large cooperative social prides.
A lion's roar can reach 114 decibels and be heard up to five miles away across the savanna.
Female lions do 85 to 90 percent of the pride's hunting, working in coordinated formations.
A small remnant population of wild Asiatic lions still survives in India's Gir Forest.

mammals.name: Sperm whale
mammals.summary: The sperm whale or cachalot (Physeter macrocephalus) is the largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator. It is the only living member of the genus Physeter and one of three extant species in the sperm whale superfamily Physeteroidea, along with the pygmy sperm whale and dwarf sperm whale of the genus Kogia.
facts: Their clicking vocalizations can reach 230 decibels underwater, making them the loudest animal on Earth, powerful enough to rupture human eardrums and vibrate a diver's body from yards away.

Up to a third of a sperm whale's massive block-shaped head is occupied by the 'spermaceti organ,' a chamber holding up to 500 gallons of liquid wax that the whale may cool or warm with blood flow to adjust its buoyancy during mile-deep dives.
Sperm whales sleep vertically in small groups, bobbing motionless near the surface like a forest of giant floating logs for 10 to 15 minutes at a time in the shortest sleep cycle of any mammal.

When irritable squid beaks get stuck in a sperm whale's intestines, the whale coats them in a fatty secretion that hardens into ambergris, a rare, sweet-smelling 'floating gold' prized for centuries by high-end perfumers.
Their brains weigh around 18 pounds (roughly five times heavier than a human brain), making the sperm whale's brain the largest of any animal that has ever lived on Earth.
Old bulls often bear circular sucker scars, and sometimes deep gouges, around their heads from pitch-black battles with giant and colossal squid more than 3,000 feet beneath the ocean surface.

mammals.name: Horse
mammals.summary: The horse (Equus ferus caballus) is a domesticated, one-toed, hoofed mammal. It belongs to the taxonomic family Equidae and is one of two extant subspecies of Equus ferus.
facts: Thanks to the 'stay apparatus', a clever system of ligaments and tendons that locks the major joints of their limbs without muscular effort, horses can doze lightly on their feet without collapsing.

Horses are obligate nasal breathers; a flap of tissue called the soft palate blocks off the trachea from the mouth except when swallowing, making it physically impossible for a horse to breathe through its mouth or vomit.
With eyes set on the sides of their heads, horses enjoy a nearly 350-degree panoramic view of the world with only two tiny blind spots: directly in front of their noses and right behind their tails.

A horse's teeth take up more volume inside its skull than its brain does, and because those teeth continuously erupt throughout life to compensate for abrasive grass, you really can tell a horse's age by looking in its mouth.

When a horse curls its upper lip back and inhales with its head raised, looking like it's laughing at a joke, it is performing the 'flehmen response' to trap airborne pheromones in a specialized scent organ in the roof of its mouth.

A horse's hooves are not solid blocks; each foot contains a spongy, V-shaped structure called the 'frog' that acts like a hydraulic pump with every step, squeezing blood back up the leg toward the heart.

mammals.name: Moose
mammals.summary: The moose or elk (Alces alces) is the world's tallest, largest and heaviest extant species of deer and the only extant species in the genus Alces. It is also the tallest, and the second-largest, land animal in North America, falling short only to the American bison in body mass.
facts: Despite their towering, ungainly frames, moose are extraordinary divers that can hold their breath for a full minute and plunge up to 20 feet underwater to graze on sodium-rich aquatic plants.

A bull moose regrows its massive palmate antlers from scratch every single spring; during peak summer growth, the antlers add up to a pound of bone per day, making them the fastest-growing animal tissue on Earth.

Those wide, parabolic antlers act as giant satellite dishes; tests show that a bull moose with antlers has noticeably sharper directional hearing than a moose without them, helping him pinpoint a cow's distant mating call.
In winter, a moose's sensitive muzzle can detect the faint heat and carbon dioxide escaping through a foot of snow from tiny green shoots buried underneath.

The flap of skin dangling beneath a moose's throat is called a 'bell' or 'dewlap'; during the autumn rut, bulls splash in urine-soaked wallows so their bells waft a musky perfume to prospective mates.

When Swedish king Karl XI tried in the 17th century to train cavalry regiments mounted on moose to terrify enemy horses, the project failed partly because moose were too smart to charge into gunfire and easily caught livestock diseases.

mammals.name: Sheep
mammals.summary: Sheep (pl.: sheep) or domestic sheep  (Ovis aries) are a domesticated ruminant mammal typically kept as livestock. Although the term sheep can apply to other species in the genus Ovis, in everyday usage it almost always refers to domesticated sheep.
facts: Sheep have horizontal, rectangular pupils that give them a sharp, wide-angle field of vision spanning nearly 300 degrees, allowing them to scan the horizon for predators without lifting their heads while grazing.
Far from being mindless flock-followers, sheep can recognize up to 50 different sheep faces and human faces from photographs and still remember them after two years apart.

In 2004, a runaway Merino wether in New Zealand named Shrek became a national celebrity after hiding in mountain caves for six years to avoid shearing; when finally caught, his single fleece weighed a staggering 60 pounds.
Wild ancestors of sheep naturally shed their coats every spring, but centuries of selective breeding for wool created domestic breeds whose fleece never stops growing without human intervention.

When sheep are sick or suffering from intestinal parasites, they have been observed self-medicating by seeking out specific bitter plants containing tannins and saponins that healthy sheep normally ignore.
In 1996, a Finnish Dorset sheep named Dolly became the first mammal ever cloned from an adult somatic cell, proving that specialized adult DNA could be reprogrammed to create an entire new organism.

mammals.name: Red fox
mammals.summary: The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is the largest of the true foxes, and the most widely distributed member of the order Carnivora. It is present across the entire Northern Hemisphere, including most of Europe, Asia, and North America, as well as parts of North Africa.
facts: When pouncing on rodents hidden beneath deep snow, red foxes align their leaps with Earth's magnetic field; jumping toward the northeast produces a nearly 73% success rate compared to less than 18% in all other directions.

Although classified as canids, red foxes behave remarkably like cats: they have vertical slit pupils for night vision, walk on their toes, pounce with forepaws pinned together, and can even retract their claws halfway to climb trees.

Starting in 1959 in Siberia, geneticist Dmitri Belyaev selectively bred wild silver-morph red foxes strictly for tameness; within just a few decades, the foxes spontaneously developed floppy ears, curly tails, spotted coats, and dog-like tail wagging.
A red fox's bushy tail, known as a 'brush', is up to a third of its total body length and serves as a warm fur blanket wrapped over its nose during subzero winter nights.
During the springtime breeding season, female red foxes let out a blood-curdling, raspy scream in the dead of night that has terrified campers and inspired ghost folklore for centuries.

Rather than eating a windfall of prey all at once, a red fox will dig dozens of shallow 'cache' holes, tamp the dirt back down with its snout, and use spatial memory to retrieve the buried snacks weeks later.

mammals.name: Chimpanzee
mammals.summary: The chimpanzee (; Pan troglodytes), commonly abbreviated to chimp, is a medium-sized great ape species found in the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa. It has four confirmed subspecies and a fifth proposed one.
facts: Chimpanzees have far faster photographic working memory than adult humans; in famous Kyoto University experiments, a chimp named Ayumu routinely glanced at scrambled numbers 1 through 9 for a fraction of a second and tapped their hidden locations in order without error.
Wild chimpanzees in West Africa fashion wooden spears using their teeth to sharpen the tips, then jab them into hollow tree trunks to hunt sleeping bushbabies.

Just like humans, chimpanzees are ticklish; when tickled on their armpits or bellies during play, they produce breathy, rhythmic panting chuckles that evolutionary biologists consider the direct ancestor of human laughter.

To treat painful intestinal parasites, wild chimps fold and swallow rough, bristly leaves whole without chewing them; the Velcro-like leaves scour worms right out of their digestive tracts on the way through.
In Gabon, chimpanzees have been observed catching beetles and crushing specific insects to dab onto their own open wounds, as well as the wounds of injured troop members, as a topical medicine.

Despite being smaller than an average adult human man, a chimpanzee's muscles contain roughly twice the proportion of fast-twitch fibers, giving it pound-for-pound pulling and jumping power about 1.35 times greater than a human's.

mammals.name: Raccoon
mammals.summary: The raccoon ( or US:  , Procyon lotor), sometimes called the North American, northern or common raccoon (also spelled racoon) to distinguish it from other species of raccoon, is a mammal native to North America. It is the largest of the procyonid family, having a body length of 40 to 70 cm (16 to 28 in), and a body weight of 5 to 26 kg (11 to 57 lb).
facts: A raccoon's scientific species name, 'lotor,' translates from Latin as 'the washer,' inspired by its habit of dunking food in water, though they aren't actually washing dirt off; wetting their forepaws softens the tough outer skin and dramatically boosts nerve sensitivity so they can 'see' with their hands.
Nearly two-thirds of the sensory processing area of a raccoon's cerebral cortex is dedicated solely to interpreting tactile signals from its hyper-dexterous front paws.
Thanks to ankle joints that can rotate 180 degrees, raccoons are one of the few mammals that can climb straight down a tree trunk headfirst at full speed.

In early 20th-century intelligence tests, raccoons frustrated behavioral psychologists by picking the locks on their puzzle boxes faster than cats and dogs, and even opening latches while hanging upside down.
President Calvin Coolidge kept a beloved pet raccoon named Rebecca at the White House, walking her around the grounds on a custom embroidered leash and letting her join the annual Easter Egg Roll.
The black fur mask around a raccoon's eyes reduces glare to sharpen night vision, much like a bandit's mask built for nocturnal foraging.

mammals.name: Rabbit
mammals.summary: The European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) or coney is a species of rabbit native to the Iberian Peninsula and southwestern France. It has been introduced to hundreds of locations around the world.
facts: To squeeze every drop of nutrition out of tough grass, rabbits ferment plant fiber in their cecum and produce soft, vitamin-packed droppings called cecotropes, which they immediately eat straight from their own bottoms before producing normal hard pellets.
When a rabbit is overjoyed, it performs a 'binky', leaping straight into the air, twisting its head and body in opposite directions, and kicking its feet mid-flight.
A rabbit's four front incisor teeth grow continuously at a rate of about three to five inches per year, stayed in check only by constant grinding against hay, bark, and opposing teeth.

Because their eyes sit high on the sides of their skulls, rabbits can see almost 360 degrees around them, including straight above for diving hawks, leaving only a tiny blind spot right in front of their noses.
Rabbits cannot sweat or pant effectively; instead, they regulate their body temperature by dilating or constricting a dense network of blood vessels inside their oversized ears.

In 1859, an English settler named Thomas Austin released just 24 European rabbits onto his estate in Victoria, Australia, for sport hunting; within a few decades, their descendants numbered in the hundreds of millions across the continent.

mammals.name: Giraffe
mammals.summary: Giraffes (genus Giraffa) are large African hoofed mammals. They are the tallest living terrestrial animals and the largest ruminants on Earth.
facts: Despite having a neck that can stretch over six feet long, a giraffe has the exact same number of neck vertebrae as a human or a tiny mouse: just seven, each one up to ten inches long and connected by flexible ball-and-socket joints.

To prevent a giraffe's brain from exploding with blood Pressure every time it bends down to drink, or fainting when it lifts its head, its jugular veins have one-way valves and a sponge-like network of blood vessels at the base of the skull called the rete mirabile.

A giraffe's prehensile tongue is a whopping 18 to 20 inches long and colored dark purplish-black with melanin, which acts as natural sunscreen while the animal spends up to 12 hours a day stripping leaves under the equatorial sun.

Giraffes have the shortest sleep requirement of almost any land mammal, getting by on as little as 30 minutes of fragmented sleep per day, often in five-minute power naps with their necks curled onto their rumps.
For decades, people assumed giraffes were nearly mute, but researchers discovered they hum to one another at night in a rich, eerie harmony combined with low-frequency infrasound.

Newborn calves enter the world with a literal six-foot drop straight to the hard ground as their mothers give birth standing up, a jolt that snaps the umbilical cord and shocks the calf into taking its first breath.
Despite having a six-foot-long neck, a giraffe has the exact same number of neck vertebrae as a human: seven.
A giraffe's prehensile tongue is 18 to 20 inches long and purplish-black to prevent sunburn while browsing treetops.
Giraffes only sleep for about 30 minutes a day, often in quick five-minute power naps while standing up.
A giraffe's heart is two feet long and generates double the blood pressure of other mammals to pump blood up to its brain.

mammals.name: Bonobo
mammals.summary: The bonobo (; Pan paniscus), also historically called the pygmy chimpanzee, is the smallest species of great ape and one of the two making up the genus Pan (the other being the chimpanzee, Pan troglodytes). While bonobos are today recognized as a distinct species, they were initially thought to be a subspecies of Pan troglodytes, because of the physical similarities between the two species.
facts: Unlike male-dominated chimpanzee troops, bonobo societies are strictly matriarchal: a coalition of females sits at the top of the hierarchy, and a male's social rank depends heavily on how influential his mother is.

Bonobos are famous for resolving almost every social tension, from fighting over a fig tree to greeting strangers, through affectionate grooming, hugging, and non-reproductive sexual contact rather than lethal violence.

They are the only great apes that never overlap in the wild with chimpanzees or gorillas, kept completely isolated for over a million years on the south bank of the massive Congo River, which apes cannot swim across.

A celebrated bonobo named Kanzi stunned linguists by learning hundreds of geometric symbols on a lexigram keyboard simply by watching researchers try (and fail) to teach his adoptive mother, eventually understanding thousands of spoken English sentences.
Every single bonobo tested to date has the exact same blood type (human ABO group A) and could theoretically receive a blood transfusion from a type-A human without immediate rejection.
Bonobos are born with pitch-black faces and bright pink lips that stand out sharply against their dark fur, along with a distinctive center-parted hairstyle on top of their heads.

mammals.name: Wild boar
mammals.summary: The wild boar (Sus scrofa), also known as the wild swine, common wild pig, Eurasian wild pig, or simply wild pig, is a suid native to much of Eurasia and North Africa and has been introduced to the Americas and Oceania. The species is now one of the widest-ranging mammals in the world as well as the most widespread suiform.
facts: Before giving birth, a female wild boar builds a remarkably elaborate 'farrowing nest', digging a shallow crater, lining it with soft grass, and weaving a weatherproof dome of branches overhead that can stay warm inside even in freezing snow.
A wild boar's disc-shaped snout is reinforced with a unique bone called the 'os rostri' right at the tip, allowing it to plow through frozen turf and lift heavy rocks like a living bulldozer.
Their lower canine tusks grow continuously and rub against the shorter upper tusks every time the boar opens and closes its mouth, honing the edges to razor sharpness.
Piglets arrive in the world wearing coats of pale longitudinal stripes over dark brown fur, a woodland camouflage pattern known as 'pajamas' that fades away after about four months.

Mature males develop a thick, fibrous layer of cartilage and tough hide over their shoulders and ribcage called a 'shield,' which can reach up to two inches thick to block rival tusks during mating duels.
Because wild boars completely lack functional sweat glands, rolling in thick mud wallows is not dirty behavior; it provides a cooling evaporative coat and suffocates ticks and lice.

mammals.name: Sea otter
mammals.summary: The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is a marine mammal native to the coasts of the northern and eastern North Pacific Ocean. Adult sea otters typically weigh between 14 and 45 kg (30–100 lb), making them the heaviest members of the weasel family, but among the smallest marine mammals.
facts: Because sea otters lack the insulating blubber layer that seals and whales rely on, they survive icy Pacific waters with the densest fur in the animal kingdom, up to one million hairs per square inch, or more hair on a single square inch than on an entire human head.
Each sea otter has a loose pouch of skin under its forearms, especially on the left side, which it uses like a built-in pocket to stash extra clams and its favorite rock hammer while diving.
To keep from drifting apart on ocean currents while sleeping, sea otters wrap themselves in anchored kelp fronds like seatbelts or float on their backs in 'rafts' while holding paws.
When sea otters feast heavily on purple sea urchins, a natural pigment in the urchins called echinochrome stains the otter's teeth and entire skeleton a striking violet-purple color.
A mother sea otter's pup has fur so buoyant and filled with trapped air that the baby physically cannot sink, leaving it bobbing on the surface like a furry cork while Mom dives for dinner.
To stay warm without blubber, a sea otter must burn calories at three times the rate of land mammals its size, eating roughly 25% of its entire body weight in shellfish every single day.
Sea otters have the densest fur in the animal kingdom, with up to one million hairs per square inch.
Unlike other marine mammals, sea otters have no blubber layer and rely entirely on air trapped in their fur for warmth.
Sleeping sea otters wrap themselves in giant kelp or hold paws in floating 'rafts' so they don't drift apart.
Sea otters have a loose pouch of skin under each forearm where they store their favorite rock for cracking shellfish.

mammals.name: Brown bear
mammals.summary: The brown bear (Ursus arctos) is a large bear native to Eurasia and North America. Of the land carnivorans, it is rivaled in size only by its closest relative, the polar bear, which is much less variable in size and slightly bigger on average.
facts: During up to seven months of winter hibernation, a brown bear does not eat, drink, urinate, or defecate once; instead, its body recycles toxic urea from its bladder back into amino acids to rebuild muscle so it emerges in spring with almost no loss of strength.

Female brown bears experience 'delayed implantation': after mating in May or June, the fertilized egg floats dormant in the uterus until November, implanting only if the mother has packed on enough autumn fat to survive nursing in her den.
A brown bear's iconic shoulder hump is not a store of fat like a camel's; it is a massive slab of solid muscle that powers the front legs to flip 300-pound boulders and dig out marmot burrows.

During the summer salmon run in Alaska, coastal brown bears often practice 'high-grading', catching fish after fish and eating only the calorie-dense brains, skin, and roe while leaving the fillets behind for gulls and eagles.
Despite weighing as much as a grand piano, an adult brown bear can sprint at 35 miles per hour, fast enough to easily outrun an Olympic sprinter uphill or downhill.

During World War II, soldiers of the Polish II Corps adopted an orphaned Syrian brown bear cub in Iran named Wojtek, officially enlisting him as a private (and later corporal) who helped carry heavy artillery crates during the Battle of Monte Cassino.

mammals.name: Jaguar
mammals.summary: The jaguar (Panthera onca) is a large cat species and the only living member of the genus Panthera that is native to the Americas. Its coat features pale yellow to tan colored fur covered with spots that transition to rosettes on the sides; some individuals have a melanistic spotted coat.
facts: Unlike all other big cats, which suffocate prey by clamping onto the throat or windpipe, a jaguar kills by driving its thick canine teeth directly through the skull between the ears to pierce the brain.
Pound for pound, the jaguar has the strongest bite force of any felid on Earth, powerful enough to crack open the armored shells of river turtles and crush the skulls of caimans.
Its name comes from the Indigenous Tupi-Guarani word 'yaguara,' which translates to 'a beast that overcomes its prey in a single bound.'

You can tell a jaguar coat apart from a leopard's at a glance: a jaguar's black ring-shaped rosettes have small dark spots dotted inside the center of the rings, whereas a leopard's rosettes are empty inside.

About 6% to 10% of jaguars are born with a dominant gene for melanism, making them appear jet-black ('black panthers'), though their signature rosettes are still clearly visible when sunlight catches their fur at an angle.
Jaguars are so comfortable in flooded rainforests that they regularly hunt underwater, lunging off riverbanks to wrestle anacondas and giant river otters.
Pound for pound, the jaguar has the strongest bite force of any big cat, able to pierce turtle shells and caiman skulls.
Unlike most felines, jaguars deliver a fatal bite directly through the skull between the prey's ears rather than the throat.
The word 'jaguar' comes from the Indigenous Tupi-Guarani word 'yaguara', meaning 'he who kills with one leap'.
Jaguars are the largest cat native to the Americas and are strong swimmers that hunt fish and caimans in rivers.

mammals.name: Spotted hyena
mammals.summary: The spotted hyena (Crocuta crocuta), also known as the laughing hyena, is a hyena species, currently classed as the sole extant member of the genus Crocuta, native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is listed as being of least concern by the IUCN due to its widespread range and large numbers estimated between 27,000 and 47,000 individuals.
facts: Despite looking and acting much like big dogs, spotted hyenas belong to the suborder Feliformia, making them far more closely related to cats, civets, and mongooses than to wolves.
Female spotted hyenas are larger, heavier, and far more aggressive than males, in their strict matriarchal clans, even the lowest-ranking female outranks the highest-ranking adult male.

Because females possess an elongated, muscular external birth canal that resembles male anatomy, spotted hyenas are the only mammals without a distinct vaginal opening, making mating and birth extraordinarily challenging.

Their jaws and conical premolar teeth are engineered like industrial bone-crushers, allowing them to pulverize and digest giraffe femurs, hooves, and horns, leaving behind chalk-white droppings packed with calcium.

The eerie, high-pitched 'giggle' that earned them the nickname 'laughing hyena' is actually a sound of extreme frustration, fear, or excitement emitted when squabbling over a carcass, and its pitch reveals the hyena's age and social rank.

Far from being lazy scavengers that just steal from lions, spotted hyenas actively hunt and kill up to 90% of their own food, and lions actually steal more kills from hyenas than the other way around.

mammals.name: Leopard
mammals.summary: The leopard (Panthera pardus) is one of the five extant cat species in the genus Panthera. It has a pale yellowish to dark golden fur with dark spots grouped in rosettes.
facts: To keep hard-won meals away from marauding lions and hyena packs, a leopard can hoist a carcass weighing more than its own body weight, such as a young giraffe or impala, straight up a vertical tree trunk to wedge it in the branches.
Rather than roaring like a lion, a leopard announces its territory with a raspy, rhythmic 'sawing' call that sounds uncannily like someone cutting through a thick plank of wood with a coarse handsaw.
In Asia and Africa, a 'black panther' is simply a regular leopard with a recessive genetic mutation for melanism that turns its coat midnight-black while preserving hidden spots underneath.

Leopards are the most adaptable of all big cats, thriving everywhere from parched deserts and snow-dusted mountains to the bustling parks inside Mumbai, India, where urban leopards quietly hunt stray dogs at night.
When hunting in dense brush, a leopard uses extra-long, ultra-sensitive white whiskers on its muzzle and eyebrows to feel out obstacles in pitch darkness without rustling a single leaf.
A leopard's long, muscular tail is nearly as long as its entire body, acting as a high-speed rudder and counterweight when leaping across rocky cliffs or chasing monkeys through the treetops.
Leopards are pound-for-pound climbers strong enough to haul prey heavier than themselves 20 feet up into a tree.
Melanistic leopards, commonly called black panthers, still have visible rosettes when viewed in bright sunlight.
The leopard has the largest natural geographic distribution of any wild cat across Africa and Asia.
Leopards stash their kills high in forked tree branches to keep them away from lions and hyenas.

mammals.name: American black bear
mammals.summary: The American black bear (Ursus americanus), or simply black bear, is a species of medium-sized bear which is endemic to North America. It is the continent's smallest and most widely distributed bear species.
facts: Despite their name, American black bears come in a surprising rainbow of colors: depending on regional genetics, a 'black' bear can be cinnamon-red, chocolate brown, honey-blonde, blue-gray (the 'glacier bear' of Alaska), or stark creamy white.

On the islands of coastal British Columbia, a double-recessive gene produces the white 'Kermode bear' or 'Spirit Bear', and research shows these white bears are 30% better at catching salmon during the day because fish looking up see their white fur blend into the bright sky.

Cubs are born blind and hairless in the middle of winter while their mother is hibernating, weighing less than a can of soda, giving black bears one of the highest mother-to-newborn weight ratios of any placental mammal.

Unlike grizzly bears, whose long, straight digging claws make tree-climbing clumsy in adulthood, black bears have short, curved, cat-like claws that let them shimmy up a tree trunk at startling speed.

In 1950, firefighters in New Mexico rescued a badly burned black bear cub clinging to a charred pine tree after the Capitan Gap fire; named Smokey Bear, he lived at the National Zoo for 26 years and received so much fan mail the U.S. Postal Service gave him his own ZIP code (20252).
During autumn 'hyperphagia,' a black bear preparing for winter enters a non-stop eating frenzy, consuming up to 20,000 calories a day in acorns and berries to gain up to five pounds every 24 hours.

mammals.name: Gray wolf
mammals.summary: The wolf (Canis lupus; pl.: wolves), also known as the grey wolf or gray wolf, is a canine native to Eurasia and North America. More than thirty subspecies of Canis lupus have been recognized, including the dog and dingo, though grey wolves, as popularly understood, include only naturally occurring wild subspecies.
facts: When a wolf pack howls together, no two wolves stay on the exact same pitch; they intentionally shift into discordant harmonies so the acoustic reverberation makes a small pack of four sound like a dozen to rival intruders.

A wolf's huge paws are partially webbed between the toes and feature a specialized blood-vessel heat-exchanger that keeps their paw pads just one degree above freezing so they never get frostbite or melt snow into ice balls on their fur.

The famous concept of a tyrannical 'alpha wolf' battling packmates for supremacy was actually a mistake based on unrelated captive wolves forced into enclosures; in the wild, a wolf pack is simply a nuclear family led by Mom and Dad.

After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 following a 70-year absence, their presence kept elk moving out of river valleys, allowing willow and aspen groves to rebound and bringing beavers and songbirds back to the streams.
Wolves have two distinct layers of fur: a dense, waterproof undercoat and long outer guard hairs that shed snow and dirt, so warm that snow falling on a sleeping wolf won't even melt.

In 1921, a lone wild female wolf known as 'Lobo's mate' or later the famous disperser 'OR-7' in Oregon proved just how far wolves travel; wolves routinely trot 30 to 50 miles in a single night and have been tracked crossing over 1,000 miles in search of a mate.

mammals.name: Orangutan
mammals.summary: The Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) is an orangutan species endemic to the island of Borneo. It belongs to the only genus of great apes native to Asia and is the largest of the three Pongo species.
facts: Their name comes directly from the Malay and Indonesian words 'orang' (person) and 'hutan' (forest), literally translating to 'person of the forest', and local folklore once held that they could speak perfectly well but stayed silent so humans wouldn't put them to work.

Every single evening before dark, an orangutan weaves a brand-new, engineering-grade treetop bed up to 100 feet in the air, complete with a springy mattress, woven branch support, a leafy pillow, and sometimes a rain roof overhead.

Orangutan mothers have the longest child-rearing period of any land mammal other than humans: a baby clings to and learns from its mother for seven to eight years, and females only give birth once every eight or nine years.

Mature males come in two radically different body types ('bimaturism'): dominant males grow wide cheek pads called flanges and a throat sac for booming 'long calls,' while subordinate males stay smaller and unflanged, until the dominant male disappears, triggering a hormonal surge that grows their cheek pads.

In 2024, researchers in Sumatra documented a wild male orangutan named Rakus chewing the pain-relieving, antibacterial leaves of the liana plant Fibraurea tinctoria into a paste and repeatedly applying the poultice to a deep facial wound until it healed without a scar.

Because they spend over 90% of their lives in the forest canopy, an orangutan's arms span more than seven feet from fingertip to fingertip, far longer than its five-foot standing height, and its curved fingers and toes lock onto branches like suspension hooks.

mammals.name: Gray whale
mammals.summary: The gray whale (Eschrichtius robustus), also known as the grey whale, is a baleen whale that migrates between feeding and breeding grounds yearly. It reaches a length of 14.9–15.2 m (49–50 ft), a weight of  up to 41 to 45 tonnes (45 to 50 short tons; 40 to 44 long tons) and lives between 55 and 70 years, although one female was estimated to be 75–80 years of age.
facts: Gray whales undertake one of the longest annual migrations of any mammal on Earth, swimming up to 12,000 miles round-trip between their icy summer feeding grounds in the Bering and Chukchi Seas and warm winter birthing lagoons in Baja California.

Unlike filter-feeding whales that gulp krill in open water, gray whales are bottom-feeders that dive to the seafloor, roll onto their sides, and plow trenches through the mud to vacuum up amphipod crustaceans.

Wait, just like humans are mostly right-handed, almost all gray whales are 'right-sided,' preferentially rolling onto their right flanks to scrape the seabed so often that the baleen plates on the right side of their mouths wear down noticeably shorter than the left.
A single adult gray whale can carry up to 400 pounds of hitchhiking whale barnacles and whale lice encrusted on its skin, giving the dark whale its mottled, rock-like gray patchwork appearance.

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, commercial whalers gave gray whales the nickname 'devil fish' for the ferocity with which mothers rammed wooden harpoon boats to defend their calves, yet today in Baja's San Ignacio Lagoon, those same mothers actively nudge their calves up to small tourist skiffs to be petted on the nose.

Newborn gray whale calves drink up to 50 gallons of their mother's thick, toothpaste-consistent milk every day, which is 53% fat, more than ten times richer than cow's milk, allowing them to double their weight before heading north to the Arctic.

mammals.name: Cougar
mammals.summary: The cougar ( KOO-gər; Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large small cat native to the Americas. It inhabits North, Central and South America, making it the most widely distributed wild, terrestrial mammal in the Western Hemisphere, and one of the most widespread in the world.
facts: Because its range stretches all the way from the Yukon in Canada to the tip of Patagonia in Chile, the widest latitudinal range of any wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere, the cougar holds the Guinness World Record for the animal with the most names, with over 40 in English alone including puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther.

Although it is as large as a leopard, the cougar is not a 'big cat' of the genus Panthera; genetically, its closest living relatives are the cheetah and the tiny jaguarundi, which means a cougar cannot roar and instead purrs like a giant housecat.

Cougars are the undisputed high-jump champions of the cat world: their oversized hind legs allow them to leap 18 feet straight up into a tree from a standstill and bound 40 feet horizontally across a canyon.
During the mating season, female cougars emit a piercing, human-like wail known as a 'caterwaul' that echoes through mountain valleys and has fueled countless frontier ghost stories.
Cougar kittens are born with bright blue eyes, ringed tails, and coats covered in dark camouflage spots that completely fade into a uniform tawny coat by the time they are a year old.
A solitary cougar will conceal a large elk or deer kill under a mound of pine needles, sticks, and snow called a 'cache,' returning night after night for up to two weeks to finish the meal.
The cougar holds the Guinness World Record for the animal with the most common names, including puma, mountain lion, and catamount.
Cougars have the largest north-to-south range of any wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere, from Yukon to Patagonia.
Despite its size, the cougar is more closely related to small domestic cats and cheetahs than to lions or tigers.
A cougar can leap 18 feet vertically into a tree from a standing start.

mammals.name: Cattle
mammals.summary: Cattle (Bos taurus) are large, domesticated, bovid ungulates widely kept as livestock. They are prominent modern members of the subfamily Bovinae and the most widespread species of the genus Bos.
facts: High-resolution satellite imagery of thousands of pastures worldwide revealed that grazing and resting cattle naturally align their bodies along a north-south axis with Earth's magnetic field, unless they are standing under high-voltage power lines that scramble the magnetic signal.

Contrary to the popular myth that cows have four separate stomachs, cattle actually have just one stomach divided into four specialized fermentation chambers: the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum.

The largest chamber, the rumen, acts as a 40-gallon living fermentation vat teeming with trillions of microbes that break down tough cellulose while the cow spends up to eight hours a day re-chewing its cud.

Studies tracking heart rates and cortisol levels show that cows form lifelong 'best friend' pairs within a herd; when separated from their preferred companion, their heart rates spike and their milk yield drops.
In bullfighting, bulls do not charge the matador's cape because it is red; cattle are red-green colorblind (dichromats) and are reacting strictly to the taunting motion of the fabric.
A cow has no upper front incisor teeth; instead, it has a tough, leathery dental pad on the roof of its mouth and wraps its muscular, sandpaper-rough tongue around tufts of grass to rip them upwards.

mammals.name: Golden jackal
mammals.summary: The golden jackal (Canis aureus), also called the common jackal, is a wolf-like canid that is native to Eurasia. The golden jackal's coat varies in color from a pale creamy yellow in summer to a dark tawny beige in winter.
facts: Golden jackals are among the rare mammals that form lifelong monogamous pairs; mated partners hunt synchronously, share food by regurgitating meals for one another, and perform affectionate greeting ceremonies.

In India and Sri Lanka, some golden jackals develop a tiny bony cone on the back of their skulls covered by a tuft of hair known as the 'jackal's horn' (narricombu), which local folklore long revered as a magical talisman that grants wishes to its owner.

For over a century, biologists assumed the golden jackal lived across both Eurasia and Africa, until a 2015 DNA study shocked zoologists by revealing that 'African golden jackals' were actually an entirely separate species, the African golden wolf, that had evolved to look identical.

In Serengeti ecosystems and parts of Asia, golden jackals frequently trail tigers or lions at a polite distance to clean up scraps, earning the Sanskrit nickname 'srigala' (the howler) and inspiring the character Tabaqui in Rudyard Kipling's 'The Jungle Book.'
At dusk, a family of golden jackals begins a chorus of undulating wails punctuated by three quick yips, a vocal roll call used to establish boundaries without wasting energy in physical fights.
Though part of the carnivore order, golden jackals have a surprisingly sweet tooth and will gorge on fallen figs, watermelons, grapes, and sugarcane whenever fruit is in season.

mammals.name: Tasmanian devil
mammals.summary: The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii; palawa kani: purinina) is a carnivorous marsupial of the family Dasyuridae. It was formerly present across mainland Australia, but became extinct there around 3,500 years ago; it is now confined to the island of Tasmania.
facts: Pound for pound, the Tasmanian devil delivers the strongest bite force of any living mammal on Earth, capable of exerting enough pressure to bite clean through thick metal wire traps and devour every bone and tooth of a carcass.
When a Tasmanian devil gets agitated or fights over food, its body rushes blood directly into its hairless ears, making them glow a bright, fiery crimson red as a visual warning to rivals.

Excess fat isn't stored around a devil's belly; instead, the animal packs its fat reserves straight into its thick tail, so a plump, sausage-like tail is the ultimate sign of a healthy, well-fed devil.

A mother Tasmanian devil gives birth to up to 40 tiny, rice-grain-sized joeys at once, but she only has four teats inside her backward-facing pouch, sparking a frantic survival race where only the first four newborns to latch on survive.

Since 1996, devils have battled Devil Facial Tumour Disease, one of the few known contagious cancers in nature where living cancer cells physically jump from one animal to another when they bite each other's faces during noisy communal feasts.

Their spine-chilling nocturnal screeches, guttural coughs, and sneezing growls terrified early European settlers in Tasmania into naming them 'devils' and inspired the whirling Looney Tunes character Taz.

mammals.name: Dugong
mammals.summary: The dugong (; Dugong dugon) is a marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
facts: Along with manatees, dugongs inspired centuries of sailors' mermaid legends; their scientific order, Sirenia, is named directly after the mythical Sirens of Homer's Odyssey, though up close their whiskered, vacuum-like snouts look nothing like half-fish maidens.
Despite looking like plump marine seals, dugongs are actually ‘ungulates’ whose closest living land relatives are elephants and tiny rock hyraxes.
Even the males of some populations sprout short, ivory-like incisor tusks that erupt when they hit puberty, which they use to spar over territory and leave rake marks on seagrass beds.

Wait; how do you tell a dugong from a manatee? Look at the tail: a manatee has a rounded, paddle-shaped tail like a beaver, whereas a dugong has a deeply notched, V-shaped fluke just like a whale or dolphin.

Because their lungs run nearly the entire length of their backs for buoyancy and their bones are solid and marrow-less (pachyostotic) like a diver's weight belt, dugongs can effortlessly walk along the seafloor on their front flippers while grazing on seagrass.

When a mother dugong nurses her calf, the baby suckles from mammary glands located right under the mother's flippers, essentially in her armpits, creating a silhouette that looks remarkably human from a ship's deck.

mammals.name: Giant panda
mammals.summary: The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China. It is characterised by its white coat with black patches around the eyes, ears, legs and shoulders.
facts: To hold bamboo stalks securely without opposable thumbs, the giant panda evolved a 'sixth finger', an enlarged radial sesamoid wrist bone that works like a movable thumb to strip leaves and peel shoots.

Although 99% of a giant panda's diet consists of tough bamboo, its digestive tract is still built like a meat-eating bear's, meaning it digests less than a fifth of what it eats and has to spend up to 14 hours a day munching 40 pounds of bamboo, and defecating up to 40 times a day.
Why doesn't meat appeal to them anymore? Around four million years ago, giant pandas suffered a mutation that deactivated their T1R1 umami taste-receptor gene, making meat taste completely bland.

A newborn giant panda cub weighs only about 3.5 ounces, the weight of a stick of butter, making it roughly 1/900th the size of its mother, the smallest newborn relative to maternal size of any placental mammal.
To make prospective mates notice their scent marks at eye level, male giant pandas frequently walk backward up to a tree trunk and do a full handstand to pee as high up the bark as possible.

In winter across China's Qinling Mountains, wild giant pandas have been filmed rolling enthusiastically in fresh horse manure, not by accident, but because compounds in the dung block cold-sensing TRP channels in their skin, acting like a chemical warming blanket.
Although classified in the order Carnivora, a giant panda's diet is 99 percent bamboo.
Because bamboo is so low in nutrients, an adult giant panda spends up to 14 hours a day eating 25 to 80 pounds of shoots and leaves.
Newborn giant panda cubs are pink, blind, and weigh only 3.5 ounces, about 1/900th the size of their mother.
Giant pandas have an elongated radial sesamoid wrist bone that functions as a sixth opposable 'thumb' for stripping bamboo.

mammals.name: Blue whale
mammals.summary: The blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus) is a species of baleen whale and the largest marine mammal in the rorqual family Balaenopteridae. Reaching a maximum confirmed length of 29.9–30.5 m (98–100 ft) and weighing up to 190–200 t (190–200 long tons; 210–220 short tons), it is the largest animal known to have ever existed.
facts: The blue whale is not merely the largest animal alive today, weighing up to 190 tons and stretching nearly 100 feet long, it is the heaviest animal known to have ever lived on Earth, outweighing even the largest sauropod dinosaurs.
A blue whale's heart is the size of a Volkswagen Beetle and weighs roughly 400 pounds; when the whale dives into the frigid deep, that colossal heart slows down to as few as two beats per minute.

Its tongue alone weighs as much as an entire adult Asian elephant, and when it lunges into a swarm of krill, its pleated throat pouch balloons outward to hold up to 100 tons of water and food in a single gulp.

Despite having a mouth big enough to park a minivan inside, a blue whale's esophagus is only about four to eight inches wide, meaning it physically cannot swallow anything larger than a grapefruit or a beach ball.

Blue whale calls reach 188 decibels at ultra-low frequencies around 10 to 40 Hertz (mostly below the range of human hearing), allowing two blue whales to hear each other across an entire ocean basin hundreds of miles apart.

Fueled by milk as thick as cottage cheese, a nursing blue whale calf packs on an astonishing 200 pounds of weight every single day, nearly nine pounds every hour, during its first seven months of life.
The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have lived on Earth, even heavier than the largest sauropod dinosaurs.
A blue whale's heart is the size of a small golf cart and beats only 4 to 8 times per minute during deep dives.
Despite weighing up to 190 tons, blue whales feed almost exclusively on tiny shrimp-like krill.
A blue whale's tongue alone can weigh as much as an entire adult elephant.

mammals.name: Dhole
mammals.summary: The dhole ( dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia. The sole member of the genus Cuon, it is anatomically distinguished from members of the genus Canis in several aspects: its skull is convex rather than concave in profile, it lacks a third lower molar, and the upper molars possess only a single cusp as opposed to between two and four.
facts: Often called the 'whistling dog' of Asia, dholes communicate through dense jungle vegetation using an eerie, bird-like 'coo-coo' whistle made by blowing air across their lower incisors.

Unlike wolves and domestic dogs, which have 42 teeth, the dhole has only 40 teeth; it lacks the last pair of lower molars, trading bone-crushing power for razor-sharp shearing teeth that allow packs to eat quickly before tigers arrive.
Dholes are astonishingly athletic jumpers that can leap over 7 feet straight into the air to spot prey above tall elephant grass or bound 20 feet horizontally across mountain streams.

Inside a dhole pack, there is no rigid dominance fighting over food; instead, adults step back at a fresh kill to let the youngest pups eat first, and packmates regurgitate meat at the den for the nursing mother and designated 'babysitter' dogs.
To mark their territory or deter rival predators, dholes sometimes perform a handstand on their front paws and spray urine high onto bushes with uncanny accuracy.

In Rudyard Kipling's 'Second Jungle Book,' the fearsome 'Red Dogs of the Dekkan' that drive even tigers and wolves into hiding are modeled directly on real-life dhole super-packs, which historically numbered up to 40 animals.

mammals.name: White-tailed deer
mammals.summary: The white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), also known commonly as the whitetail and the Virginia deer, is a medium-sized species of deer native to North and South America. It is the most widely distributed mainland ungulate herbivore in the Americas; coupled with its natural predator, the mountain lion (Puma concolor), it is one of the most widely distributed terrestrial mammal species in the Americas and the world.
facts: When startled, a white-tailed deer flips up its broad tail like a warning flag to expose the bright white underside, releasing alarm pheromones from glands between its toes at the exact same moment so the whole herd knows to bolt.
In winter, white-tailed deer have hollow guard hairs packed with microscopic air cells that trap body heat so effectively that snow can pile up inches deep on a deer's back without melting.

Fawns are born covered in roughly 300 white spots that mimic sunbeams filtering through forest leaves, and for their first week of life they produce almost zero body scent, so a coyote can walk within feet of a curled-up fawn without smelling it.
Before a fawn can urinate or defecate on its own, its mother must lick its belly to stimulate digestion, and she consumes all the waste so no odor ever gives away the baby's hiding spot.

While a buck's antlers are growing in spring and summer, they are wrapped in 'velvet', a warm, fuzzy skin rich with blood vessels and nerves that makes the growing antlers sensitive enough to feel a fly land on them.

Because their eyes contain a dense ring of horizontal photoreceptors and almost triple the blue-light cones of humans, white-tailed deer have razor-sharp vision at dawn and dusk, the exact crepuscular hours when predators prowl.

mammals.name: Koala
mammals.summary: The koala (Phascolarctos cinereus), sometimes inaccurately called the koala bear, is an arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia. It is the only extant representative of the family Phascolarctidae.
facts: Koalas have fingerprints with loops, whorls, and arches so shockingly identical to human fingerprints that even under a scanning electron microscope, forensics experts have trouble telling them apart.

Because eucalyptus leaves are tough, fibrous, and laced with cyanide-like phenolic toxins that would poison almost any other mammal, a koala's liver carries specialized cytochrome P450 enzymes and a six-foot-long cecum packed with detoxifying microbes.

Due to their low-calorie diet, koalas sleep or doze wedged in tree forks for 18 to 22 hours every day, and their brains have evolved to be unusually small and smooth, filling only about 60% of their cranial cavity to save metabolic energy.

Newborn koala joeys are born without the gut bacteria needed to digest toxic eucalyptus; to inoculate the baby's stomach before weaning, the mother produces a special green microbial paste from her cecum called 'pap' that the joey eats like baby food.

During the Australian breeding season, male koalas produce a shockingly deep, resonant bellow that sounds like a cross between a revving motorcycle and a snoring giant; made possible by an extra pair of oversized vocal cords situated outside the larynx.

A koala's hands have two opposable thumbs alongside three fingers, giving them a vise-like double grip on slick eucalyptus bark, while a thick cartilage pad on their rumps acts like a built-in seat cushion.

mammals.name: Dromedary
mammals.summary: The dromedary (Camelus dromedarius), also known as the dromedary camel, Arabian camel and one-humped camel, is a large camel of the genus Camelus with one hump on its back. It is the tallest of the three camel species; adult males stand 1.8–2.4 m (5.9–7.9 ft) at the shoulder, while females are 1.7–1.9 m (5.6–6.2 ft) tall.
facts: Contrary to cartoon legend, a dromedary camel's hump does not store sloshing water; it holds up to 80 pounds of solid fat, which concentrates body heat insulation in one spot on the back so the rest of the camel's body can radiate heat freely.

When a dromedary goes weeks without drinking, it can lose up to 30% of its body water without dying (humans suffer fatal heart failure at 12–15%) because its red blood cells are oval-shaped instead of round, allowing them to keep flowing smoothly through thickened, dehydrated blood.
Once it finally reaches an oasis, a thirsty dromedary can guzzle 30 gallons of water in just 10 minutes, a feat that would cause most mammals' red blood cells to burst from osmotic shock.

To survive swirling Sahara sandstorms, a dromedary has three eyelids on each eye, including a translucent third eyelid that wipes sideways like a windshield wiper so it can still see while blinking, plus muscular nostrils that pinch completely shut.

During the mating season, a bull dromedary inflates a bizarre, pink, balloon-like sac from the roof of its mouth called a 'dulla,' letting it dangle out the side of its lips while gurgling loudly to impress females.

There are no longer any truly wild dromedaries living in their native Middle Eastern and North African homelands, yet central Australia is home to the world's largest feral population, nearly a million dromedaries descended from pack animals released after automobiles arrived in the 1920s.

mammals.name: Bottlenose dolphin
mammals.summary: The common bottlenose dolphin or Atlantic bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) is one of three species of bottlenose dolphin in the genus Tursiops. While formerly known simply as the bottlenose dolphin, this term is now applied to the genus Tursiops as a whole.
facts: Every bottlenose dolphin invents its own unique 'signature whistle' in the first months of life, which functions just like a spoken first name; dolphins call out a friend's specific whistle to get their attention and remember those names even after 20 years apart.

Because dolphins are conscious breathers that must actively decide to take every breath at the surface, they sleep with only one half of their brain at a time (unihemispheric slow-wave sleep), keeping the opposite eye open to watch for sharks and podmates.

In Shark Bay, Western Australia, female bottlenose dolphins pluck cone-shaped marine sponges off the seafloor and wear them over their snouts like protective work gloves while rooting through sharp rocks and venomous stonefish for prey, a cultural skill mothers teach their daughters.

In Florida Bay, pods use a dazzling team tactic called 'mud-ring feeding': one dolphin swims in a tight circle beating its tail against the shallow bottom to stir up a circular curtain of mud, trapping panicked mullet that leap into the air right into the waiting mouths of the pod.

The U.S. Navy Marine Mammal Program has trained bottlenose dolphins since the 1960s to use their biological sonar, far more sensitive than any human-made metal detector in cluttered shallow water, to locate buried sea mines and attach marker buoys.

Dolphins have extraordinarily rapid wound healing: even after suffering deep shark bites the size of dinner plates, natural antimicrobial compounds in their blubber prevent infection and regenerate tissue in weeks without apparent pain behavior.

mammals.name: Gorilla
mammals.summary: The western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is a great ape found in Africa, one of two species of the hominine genus Gorilla. Large and robust with males weighing around 168 kilograms (370 lb), the species is found in a region of midwest Africa, geographically isolated from the eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei).
facts: Just as humans have unique fingerprints and dogs have unique nose prints, every gorilla has a unique pattern of wrinkles and creases right above its nostrils, a 'nose print' that conservationists use to identify individuals from photos.

When a silverback gorilla beats his chest, he doesn't use clenched fists like King Kong; he cups his hands to strike inflated air sacs inside his chest, producing a resonant, low-pitched drum roll that announces his exact body size to rivals over half a mile away.

Even though a mature silverback can weigh over 400 pounds and bend iron bars, wild gorillas are almost purely vegetarian gentle giants that spend their days munching bamboo shoots, wild celery, and stinging nettles.
Every single night at dusk, every adult and juvenile gorilla in a troop weaves a fresh leafy nest on the ground or in low branches, never sleeping in the same bed twice to avoid parasites.

When gorillas are happily gorging on their favorite foods, they often sing and hum improvised little food songs of contentment; soft, melodic rumbles and purrs that stop immediately if someone interrupts their meal.

Only about 17% of human infectious diseases leave gorillas untouched; because they share over 98% of our DNA, gorillas can catch the common cold, flu, or pneumonia from tourists, which is why mountain gorilla trekkers now wear surgical masks.

mammals.name: European bison
mammals.summary: The European bison (pl.: bison) (Bison bonasus) or the European wood bison, also known as the wisent ( or ), the zubr (), or sometimes colloquially as the European buffalo, is a European species of bison. It is one of two extant species of bison, alongside the American bison.
facts: Known across Europe as the 'wisent,' the European bison was hunted to total extinction in the wild when the last free-roaming animal was shot in the Caucasus in 1927; every single one of the roughly 10,000 wisents alive today descends from just 12 zoo survivors.

Wait; how does a European bison differ from its American cousin? The European bison is actually taller at the shoulder, has longer legs and a less pronounced hump, holds its head higher, and browses on tree twigs and acorns in forests rather than grazing endless open prairies.

For centuries, Polish kings treated the Białowieża Forest as a royal hunting preserve where poaching a wisent was punishable by death, inadvertently preserving the ancient primeval forest that later served as the species' reintroduction cradle.
Unlike cattle herds led by bulls or solo wanderers, European bison herds are guided by an experienced older matriarch cow who decides when and where the group moves through the snow.
During the autumn rut, bulls roll vigorously in sandy pits soaked in their own urine and bellow with a deep, guttural grunt rather than a cow-like moo.
In winter, European bison strip up to 70 pounds of tree bark and woody shoots per day, acting as ecological landscapers that open up sunlit clearings in dense European woodlands.

mammals.name: Asian elephant
mammals.summary: The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus), also known as the Asiatic elephant, is the only living species in the genus Elephas. It is the largest living land animal in Asia and the second largest living elephantid in the world.
facts: You can tell an Asian elephant from an African elephant in a split second by looking at their ears and trunks: an Asian elephant's smaller ears are shaped like the map of India, and the tip of its trunk has just one finger-like projection instead of two.

An elephant's trunk contains roughly 40,000 individual muscles, compared to fewer than 650 in the entire human body, giving it the strength to uproot a tree and the finesse to pick up a single tortilla chip without cracking it.
Asian elephants can 'hear' through their feet: fatty pads in their heels pick up low-frequency seismic rumbles traveling through the ground from other elephant herds up to 10 miles away.

Although they weigh up to five tons, elephants walk almost completely silently because they walk on their tiptoes, cushioned by a thick, shock-absorbing sponge of fibrous fat underneath their heel bones.

Asian elephants have the longest pregnancy of any mammal on Earth, carrying a single calf in the womb for an astonishing 22 months, nearly two full years, so the baby's massive brain has time to wire up before birth.

Why do elephants almost never get cancer despite having 100 times more cells than humans? They carry roughly 20 copies of the tumor-suppressor gene TP53 (humans have just one), which immediately destroys damaged cells before they can turn malignant.

mammals.name: American bison
mammals.summary: The American bison (Bison bison; pl.: bison), commonly known as the American buffalo, or simply buffalo (not to be confused with true buffalo), is a species of bison that is endemic to North America. It is one of two extant species of bison, along with the European bison.
facts: Unlike domestic cattle, which walk away from approaching blizzards and risk freezing along fences, American bison instinctively turn and walk directly into the teeth of a snowstorm, knowing they will pass through the weather front faster while their thick head coats shield them.

Despite weighing up to 2,000 pounds, an American bison can sprint at 35 miles per hour, pivot on its front hooves vs. its hind feet like a sports car, and jump vertically clear over a six-foot fence from a standstill.
A bison's massive winter coat is so heavily insulated that on infrared thermal cameras, the animal appears almost completely cold and invisible from the outside except for its eyes and nostrils.
In winter, bison use their massive heads and muscular shoulder humps like snowplows, swinging their muzzles side to side to sweep aside three feet of packed snow to reach buried prairie grass.

By the late 1880s, commercial hide hunters had reduced an estimated 30 to 60 million North American bison down to fewer than 1,000 survivors, before a handful of ranchers and the Bronx Zoo bred the last remnants to rescue the species.

Bison wallows, shallow depressions in the prairie where bison roll to coat themselves in dust and shed their winter fur, collect rainwater in spring and create essential seasonal vernal pools for prairie frogs and wildflowers.

mammals.name: Domestic pig
mammals.summary: The pig (Sus domesticus), also called swine (pl.: swine) or hog, is an omnivorous, domesticated, even-toed, hoofed mammal. It is named the domestic pig when distinguishing it from other members of the genus Sus.
facts: In comparative cognition labs at Penn State, pigs learned to use a joystick with their snouts to move a cursor on a computer monitor, mastering the video game faster than dogs and performing on par with chimpanzees.

The phrase 'sweating like a pig' is a total biological falsehood: pigs have almost no functional sweat glands anywhere on their bodies, which is why they must wallow in cool mud to keep from overheating.

A pig's disk-like snout contains more tactile nerve receptors than the human hand, paired with an olfactory system so acute that French truffiers have used pigs for centuries to sniff out underground black truffles three feet deep.
Mother sows 'sing' to their nursing piglets with a rhythmic series of low grunts that accelerates just before milk let-down, telling the litter the exact 20-second window when milk is flowing.

Because a pig's heart valves, skin thickness, and organ sizes are remarkably close to human anatomy, porcine heart valves have been surgically implanted to save human cardiac patients for over 50 years.

When given a mirror in an enclosure, pigs quickly figure out how reflections work; instead of grunting at the 'stranger' in the glass, they use the mirror's angle to locate a hidden bowl of treats behind a barrier.

mammals.name: Slow loris
mammals.summary: Slow lorises are a group of several species of nocturnal strepsirrhine primates that make up the genus Nycticebus. Found in Southeast Asia and nearby areas, they range from Bangladesh and Northeast India in the west to the Sulu Archipelago in the Philippines in the east, and from Yunnan province in China in the north to the island of Java in the south.
facts: The slow loris is the world's only venomous primate: before biting, it raises its arms over its head to lick a specialized brachial gland near its elbow, mixing the pungent secretion with saliva to create an allergen potent enough to cause anaphylactic shock.

Notice those viral videos where a slow loris raises both arms like it wants its armpits tickled? That is actually a terrified defensive posture; the animal is reaching for its elbow venom glands to prepare a toxic bite.
