How can a slow loris hang upside down from a branch by its feet for hours without its muscles cramping? Its limbs contain a dense web of blood vessels called a 'rete mirabile' that flushes oxygen in and lactic acid out without effort.

A mother slow loris 'parks' her infant on a twig while she forages at night, first licking the baby from head to toe with her venom-laced saliva to wrap it in an invisible chemical shield that repels leopards, sun bears, and orangutans.

Inside its mouth, a slow loris actually has two tongues: a normal fleshy tongue on top and a jagged, cartilaginous 'sublingua' underneath used specifically as a built-in toothcomb to scrape matted fur and tree gum from its front teeth.

Despite its giant, cartoonish eyes built for pitch-black rainforest nights, the slow loris completely lacks the gene for short-wavelength cones, making it entirely colorblind and able to see only in shades of monochrome.

mammals.name: Elk
mammals.summary: The elk (pl.: elk or elks; Cervus canadensis) or wapiti (pronounced ) is the second largest species within the deer family, Cervidae, and one of the largest terrestrial mammals in its native range of North America and Central and East Asia. The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose, Alces alces, but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.
facts: What Europeans call an 'elk' is actually what North Americans call a moose; early English colonists in Virginia used the word 'elk' for this giant deer before learning the Shawnee name 'wapiti,' which literally means 'white rump.'

Why does an enormous 700-pound bull elk produce a high-pitched, whistling 'bugle' instead of a deep roar? A bull forces air through a tiny gap in its vocal folds while simultaneously roaring, creating an eerie dual-pitched whistle that carries for miles across mountain meadows.

Elk have peculiar ivory teeth; two upper canine teeth that are evolutionary remnants of the long curved saber-tusks carried by their prehistoric deer ancestors, which bulls flash by curling their lips at rivals.

Every spring, bull elk shed their old antlers and grow a brand-new set at a blistering pace of up to an inch per day, fueled by intense summer sunlight and minerals pulled straight from their own skeleton.
Dropped elk antlers rarely last long on the forest floor because porcupines, squirrels, and mice immediately gnaw them down to nubs for their concentrated calcium and phosphorus.

During the autumn rut, a dominant harem master bull gets so busy bugling, herding cows, and sparring with challengers that he barely eats for weeks, losing up to 20% of his entire body weight before winter even starts.

mammals.name: Platypus
mammals.summary: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus), sometimes referred to as the duck-billed platypus, is a semiaquatic, egg-laying mammal endemic to eastern Australia, including Tasmania. The platypus is the sole living representative of the family Ornithorhynchidae and genus Ornithorhynchus, though a number of related species appear in the fossil record.
facts: When the first preserved platypus skin arrived at the British Museum in 1799, zoologist George Shaw was so convinced someone had sewn a duck's beak onto a beaver's body as a taxidermy hoax that he took a pair of scissors to the pelt looking for stitches, and the scissor marks are still visible on the specimen today.

When a platypus dives underwater, it shuts its eyes, ears, and nostrils completely tight, hunting blind by using 40,000 electroreceptors in its rubbery bill to detect the tiny electrical signals fired by a shrimp's contracting tail muscles.
The platypus has no stomach at all; hundreds of millions of years ago its ancestors lost the genes for stomach acid and pepsin, so its esophagus connects directly to its intestines.

Male platypuses carry a hollow calcaneus spur on the inside of each hind ankle wired to a crural venom gland; during the breeding season, it pumps out a cocktail of 80 toxins that causes excruciating, morphine-resistant pain in humans for weeks.
Under ultraviolet blacklight, a platypus's dark brown fur glows a spooky, neon bluish-green, making it one of the first biofluorescent monotremes ever discovered.

Although female platypuses lay leathery eggs like reptiles, they hatch their babies after ten days and nurse them without nipples; instead, milk oozes like sweat from mammary patches on the mother's belly for the puggles to lap off her fur.
The platypus is one of only five living species of egg-laying mammals known as monotremes.
A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears, and nostrils shut, detecting prey via 40,000 electroreceptors in its bill.
Male platypuses have hollow ankle spurs connected to venom glands that are potent enough to cause excruciating pain.
Platypuses have no stomach; their gullet connects directly to their intestines.

mammals.name: Nutria
mammals.summary:
The nutria () or coypu () (Myocastor coypus) is an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent native to South America.
Classified for a long time as the only member of the family Myocastoridae, Myocastor has since been included within Echimyidae, the family of the spiny rats.
facts: Look inside a nutria's mouth and you'll spot four startlingly bright, neon-orange incisor teeth; the enamel is infused with iron oxide (literally rust), which makes the front of the teeth harder than the back so they self-sharpen into chisels as the nutria chews.

Why are a female nutria's nipples located high up on her sides, almost on her back? That clever placement lets her swim and float in the marsh while her kits sit on her back and nurse without having to hold their breath underwater.

Nutrias have special valvular lips that seal tightly shut right behind their protruding orange front teeth, allowing them to gnaw through tough plant roots completely underwater without swallowing a drop of muddy marsh water.

In the 1930s, eccentric Tabasco sauce heir E.A. McIlhenny imported nutrias from South America to Avery Island, Louisiana, for fur farming; when a 1940 hurricane breached the pens (along with deliberate releases), they multiplied into millions that now devour thousands of acres of coastal wetlands a year.

In the 1960s, the Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office in Louisiana tried to combat the nutria invasion by holding charity shooting contests and publishing 'nutria gourmet' cookbooks featuring nutria gumbo and nutria jambalaya.
A nutria's giant webbed hind feet propel it through water like scuba fins, while its nimble, unwebbed front paws work like human hands to peel water hyacinths and groom its velvety underfur.

mammals.name: Beaver
mammals.summary: The North American beaver (Castor canadensis) is one of two extant beaver species, along with the Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber). It is native to North America and has been introduced in South America (Patagonia) and Europe (primarily Finland and Karelia).
facts: Scientists running field experiments found that beavers don't even need to see water to build a dam; when researchers placed a loudspeaker playing the sound of trickling water on dry land, beavers immediately buried the speaker under mud and sticks until the 'leak' went quiet.
Like nutrias, beavers have bright orange front teeth fortified with iron on the outer enamel layer, allowing them to fell a five-inch-thick willow tree in less than three minutes.
Beavers have a set of transparent third eyelids called nictitating membranes that slide across their eyes like built-in swimming goggles whenever they submerge.

The world's longest beaver dam, discovered via satellite imagery in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park in 2007, stretches an astonishing 2,790 feet (more than half a mile) long and is clearly visible from space.

For centuries, perfumers and food makers harvested 'castoreum,' a vanilla- and raspberry-scented secretion from a beaver's castor sacs used to waterproof its fur, and medieval Catholic church authorities officially classified the scaly-tailed swimmer as a 'fish' so people could eat it on Fridays during Lent.

Inside a winter beaver lodge, the underwater entrances stay completely ice-free below the frozen pond surface, and the family often shares its cozy, wood-insulated living room with peaceful winter houseguests like muskrats.

mammals.name: Polar bear
mammals.summary: The polar bear (Ursus maritimus) is a large bear native to the Arctic and nearby areas. It is closely related to the brown bear, and the two species can interbreed.
facts: A polar bear's fur is not actually white, and its skin is not pale: every single hair is a transparent, hollow tube that scatters visible light like fresh snow, while the bear's skin underneath is jet-black to soak up every ray of Arctic sunshine.

Because a polar bear's outer coat radiates almost zero body heat through its thick blubber and hollow guard hairs, wildlife biologists trying to count polar bears from airplanes using infrared thermal cameras found the bears were nearly invisible, only their eyes and exhaled breath lit up.

A polar bear's liver is so concentrated with stored Vitamin A from eating bearded and ringed seals that consuming just a few ounces of it causes severe hypervitaminosis A in humans, making skin peel and hair fall out.
Polar bears are marathon open-ocean swimmers; satellite-collared bears have been tracked swimming nonstop for nine days straight across more than 400 miles of frigid Arctic sea.

To keep from slipping on glare ice, a polar bear's massive 12-inch-wide paws are covered on the bottom with tiny, soft dermal bumps called papillae that create suction and friction like winter snow tires.

After catching a fat seal, a fastidious polar bear immediately washes itself by rubbing its face and chest in clean, dry snow for up to 20 minutes because matted, bloody fur loses its insulating power.

mammals.name: Pangolin
mammals.summary: The Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica), also known as the Malayan or Javan pangolin, is a species of pangolin. It is a member of the Manidae family.
facts: Pangolins are the only mammals on Earth completely covered in overlapping protective scales; made of keratin (the exact same protein as human fingernails), those razor-edged armor plates account for 20% of the animal's body weight.

When threatened by a lion or hyena, a pangolin tucks its head between its front legs and curls into an impenetrable armored sphere; its name comes from the Malay word 'pengguling,' meaning 'one that rolls up.'

A pangolin's sticky tongue is sometimes longer than its head and body combined; because no normal mouth could hold a tongue that long, its root attaches all the way back near the animal's pelvis and last pair of ribs.

Pangolins have zero teeth in their jaws; instead, they swallow small pebbles and coarse sand that sit inside a muscular, horny-walled gizzard-like stomach to grind up 70 million ants and termites a year.
While raiding an aggressive ant colony, a pangolin seals its nostrils and ear openings completely shut with muscular valves so biting soldiers can't crawl inside its head.

Baby pangolins are born with soft, pink scales that harden on their second day, and for their first few months they commute through the forest by riding on the base of their mother's tail like tiny armored backpackers.
Pangolins are the only known mammals in the world covered from head to tail in overlapping keratin scales.
When threatened, a pangolin curls into an impenetrable armored ball whose sharp scales can cut a lion's paws.
A pangolin's tongue is anchored near its pelvis and is longer than its head and body combined when fully extended.
Because pangolins have no teeth, they swallow small pebbles and sand that grind up ants inside their muscular gizzard-like stomachs.

mammals.name: Flying fox
mammals.summary: The large flying fox (Pteropus vampyrus), also known as the greater flying fox, Malayan flying fox, Malaysian flying fox, large fruit bat, kalang, or kalong, is a southeast Asian species of megabat in the family Pteropodidae. Despite its scientific name, it feeds exclusively on fruits, nectar, and flowers, like the other flying foxes of the genus Pteropus.
facts: With a wingspan stretching up to five feet seven inches across, wider than many adult humans are tall, the giant golden-crowned and large flying foxes are the biggest bats on Earth, though they weigh only about three pounds.

Unlike microbats that navigate the night with ultrasonic echolocation, flying foxes cannot echolocate at all; instead, they rely on oversized, dog-like eyes with night vision far sharper than a cat's and a keen nose to find ripe rainforest fruit.

Why doesn't all the blood rush to a flying fox's head while it hangs upside down all day? Its veins have specialized one-way valves, and its tendons lock into place under its own body weight, so hanging upside down requires zero muscular effort, even after death.

Flying foxes are the unsung farmers of tropical islands: because they spit out heavy fruit pulp and swallow tiny seeds that pass through their gut in 20 minutes while flying 30 miles a night, they regenerate whole rainforest canopies and pollinate durian and baobab trees.

On hot Australian afternoons when temperatures top 100°F, thousands of flying foxes fan themselves with their leathery wing membranes and lick their wrists and bellies to cool their blood via evaporation.

Wait; if a flying fox needs to go to the bathroom while roosting upside down, how does it avoid making a mess on itself? It deftly unhooks its feet, flips right-side up to hang by its thumbs for a few seconds to do its business, and gives a quick shake before flipping back upside down.

mammals.name: Hippopotamus
mammals.summary: The hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius; ; pl.: hippopotamuses or hippopotami), often shortened to hippo (pl.: hippos), further qualified as the common hippopotamus, Nile hippopotamus and river hippopotamus, is a large semiaquatic mammal native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is one of only two extant species in the family Hippopotamidae, the other being the pygmy hippopotamus (Choeropsis liberiensis or Hexaprotodon liberiensis).
facts: A hippopotamus doesn't actually swim; its bones are so dense and solid that it sinks straight to the riverbed, where it propels itself through deep water by bouncing and galloping in slow motion off the bottom.

For centuries, explorers thought hippos 'sweated blood,' til chemists discovered the reddish-orange fluid oozing from their skin is a combination of two unique pigments, hipposudoric acid and norhipposudoric acid, that act as a natural waterproof sunscreen and potent antibiotic.

Wait; what is a hippo's closest living relative in the animal kingdom? DNA analysis proved that despite looking like giant pigs, hippos are the closest living land cousins of whales and dolphins, having split from a common semi-aquatic ancestor about 55 million years ago.
A hippo can unhinge its massive jaws to a nearly 180-degree yawn, revealing self-sharpening lower canine tusks up to 20 inches long that can snap a ten-foot crocodile in half.

To mark territory and impress females, a dominant bull hippo backs up to a riverbank or rival and spins his paddle-shaped tail like a high-speed propeller while defecating, flinging dung in a 10-foot radius.

Sleeping hippos can rest completely submerged at the bottom of a river; every few minutes, an automatic subconscious reflex makes them push off the bottom, rise to the surface to take a breath through top-mounted nostrils, and sink right back down without ever waking up.
Hippos cannot actually swim or float; instead, their dense bones let them sink and bounce-gallop along riverbeds.
Hippos secrete a reddish oily fluid called 'blood sweat' that acts as both a natural sunscreen and an antibiotic.
Genetic studies show that hippos are the closest living land-dwelling relatives of whales and dolphins.
A hippo can open its jaws a full 150 degrees and has four-foot-wide canines that sharpen themselves whenever it closes its mouth.

mammals.name: Golden lion tamarin
mammals.summary: The golden lion tamarin (Leontopithecus rosalia; Portuguese: mico-leão-dourado [ˈmiku leˈɐ̃w do(w)ˈɾadu, - liˈɐ̃w -]), less commonly known as the golden lion marmoset, is a small New World monkey of the family Callitrichidae. Endemic to the Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil, the golden lion tamarin is an endangered species.
facts: In a golden lion tamarin family, about 80% of all births produce fraternal twins, and because carrying two babies that weigh 20% of the mother's body weight is exhausting, the father does almost all the heavy lifting, carrying the twins on his back all day and handing them to Mom only to nurse.

Their long, spider-like fingers and claw-like nails (tegulae) are specialized for 'micromanipulation,' allowing them to reach deep inside bromeliad plants and narrow tree bark crevices to snatch hidden tree frogs and katydids.

By the late 1960s, deforestation in Brazil's Atlantic coastal rainforest had pushed golden lion tamarins down to roughly 150 individuals in the wild, before a global zoo breeding and forest-corridor program brought their numbers back over 3,500.

Within a family troop of up to eight tamarins, only the dominant alpha female is biologically capable of getting pregnant; she emits chemical pheromones that completely suppress ovulation in all her daughters until they leave to start their own families.

Where does that shimmering, fiery reddish-gold mane get its brilliance? Wild tamarins get carotenoids from tropical fruits and insects combined with sunlight reflection across microscopic ridges in their hair shafts.

Golden lion tamarins share their food generously with family members, even using a distinct high-pitched 'food transfer call' to invite young siblings over whenever an adult finds a particularly juicy fruit.

mammals.name: Narwhal
mammals.summary: The narwhal (Monodon monoceros) is a species of toothed whale native to the Arctic. It is the only member of the genus Monodon and one of two living representatives of the family Monodontidae.
facts: A narwhal's famous spiral 'horn' is actually an overgrown left upper canine tooth that pierces right through the whale's upper lip and twists in a counterclockwise helix for up to ten feet.

Unlike our teeth, which have hard enamel on the outside and soft nerves on the inside, a narwhal's tusk is built inside-out: it is flexible enough to bend a foot in any direction without snapping and is perforated by 10 million microscopic nerve pathways that sense water salinity and temperature.
Around 1 in every 500 male narwhals grows two full-sized spiral tusks side by side when the right canine tooth also decides to erupt through the lip.

During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, Viking traders sold narwhal tusks across Europe as genuine 'unicorn horns' said to neutralize poison; queen Elizabeth I once paid 10,000 pounds (the price of an entire castle) for a single carved narwhal tusk.

Drone footage captured in Tremblay Sound, Canada, finally solved the mystery of how narwhals hunt with their tusks: they use the tusk like a rapid-fire fencing foil to tap and stun Arctic cod before gulping the immobilized fish whole.

Because narwhals spend their winters beneath solid pack ice in Baffin Bay, they have completely lost their dorsal fin over evolutionary time so their smooth backs can glide directly under jagged ice sheets without snagging.
A narwhal's iconic spiral 'horn' is actually an overgrown upper left canine tooth that grows right through its upper lip.
The narwhal tusk is packed with up to 10 million nerve endings that sense changes in water salinity and temperature.
Unlike most toothed whales, adult narwhals have no functional teeth inside their mouths and swallow squid and fish whole.
Narwhals can dive nearly a mile deep beneath dense Arctic pack ice in search of Greenland halibut.

mammals.name: Guinea pig
mammals.summary: The guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), also known as the domestic guinea pig, cavy or domestic cavy ( KAY-vee), is a species of rodent. It belongs to the genus Cavia, family Caviidae, and its closest wild relatives include the montane guinea pig.
facts: Guinea pigs aren't from Guinea and aren't pigs at all; they are Andean rodents domesticated by Indigenous peoples of Peru and Bolivia over 5,000 years ago, and their English name likely arose from confusion with 'Guiana' or the old British guinea coin.

When a guinea pig is thrilled, it performs an explosive little jump-and-twist in midair called 'popcorning,' often accompanied by a high-pitched 'wheek-wheek' whistle reserved solely for begging humans for snacks.

Unlike mice or hamsters that are born blind, hairless, and helpless, baby guinea pigs arrive after a long 68-day pregnancy fully furred, eyes wide open, with a full set of teeth, and capable of running and nibbling solid hay within hours of birth.

Just like humans and great apes, guinea pigs carry a mutated GULO gene that makes it impossible for their livers to synthesize Vitamin C, which is why they played a pivotal role in discovering the cure for scurvy.

In Switzerland, animal welfare laws strictly forbid owning just a single guinea pig because they are such deeply social herd creatures that solitary confinement causes severe depression; there is even a Swiss rent-a-guinea-pig service to provide a temporary companion when one of a pair passes away.

Across the Andes mountains of Peru and Ecuador, folk healers known as curanderos still practice 'shoqma', rubbing a live black guinea pig over a sick patient's body, believing the sensitive rodent absorbs the illness and reveals the diagnosis.

mammals.name: Humpback whale
mammals.summary: The humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) is a species of baleen whale. It is a rorqual (a member of the family Balaenopteridae) and is the only species in the genus Megaptera.
facts: Every breeding season, all the male humpback whales in an entire ocean basin sing the exact same complex, 20-minute haunting song, and as the months pass, they collaboratively remix and evolve the verses together like a planetary jazz band.

Humpback whales are the only baleen whales that hunt using 'bubble-net feeding': a pod swims in a tight spiral beneath a school of herring while blowing curtains of air from their blowholes, trapping the fish inside a rising cylinder of bubbles before lunging upward with mouths wide open.

Why wasn't a sailboat captain ever crushed when a 40-ton humpback breached nearby? Their 16-foot pectoral fins, the longest appendages of any animal on Earth, have bumpy leading edges called tubercles that channel water to prevent stalling, a bio-engineering marvel now copied onto wind turbine blades.

Marine biologists have documented dozens of cases across the globe of humpback whales charging in from miles away to rescue seals, sea lions, gray whale calves, and even sunfish from attacking pods of orcas, swatting the killer whales with their barnacle-crusted fins.

The black-and-white pigment pattern on the underside of each humpback's tail fluke is as distinct as a fingerprint, allowing researchers to track individual whales like 'Migaloo' (a famous all-white albino humpback) for decades.

In 1985, a lost humpback whale nicknamed 'Humphrey' swam through the Golden Gate Bridge and spent weeks 68 miles up the freshwater Sacramento River before rescuers lured him back to the Pacific by playing recordings of humpback feeding sounds from a boat.

mammals.name: Zebra
mammals.summary: The plains zebra (Equus quagga, formerly Equus burchellii) is the most common and geographically widespread species of zebra. Its range is fragmented, but spans much of southern and eastern Africa south of the Sahara.
facts: After more than a century of debate over why zebras have stripes, camouflage, cooling eddies, or social ID, scientists putting striped horse coats on domestic horses proved the primary superpower: the high-contrast dazzle pattern scrambles the landing vision of disease-carrying tsetse flies and horseflies, reducing bites by over 75%.

Wait; is a zebra white with black stripes, or black with white stripes? Embryological studies show that every zebra fetus starts out with completely jet-black skin and dark fur, and the white stripes only appear in the final stage of development where pigment production is switched off.

No two zebras have the exact same stripe pattern, and right after giving birth, a mother zebra isolates her newborn foal from the herd for two days so the baby can memorize her unique hindquarter stripe 'barcode' before meeting anyone else.

Why were zebras never domesticated to pull chariots or ride into battle like horses? Having evolved alongside lions, hyenas, and crocodiles for millions of years, zebras have a hair-trigger fight-or-flight reflex, no hierarchical family structure for humans to take over (in Grevy's zebras), and a vicious habit of biting and refusing to let go.

Even so, eccentric British aristocrat Lord Walter Rothschild famously broke in four plains zebras in 1898 and drove a zebra-drawn carriage right through the streets of London to Buckingham Palace to prove a point.
Plains zebras don't neigh like horses; instead, they bark with a cheerful, high-pitched 'kwa-ha-ha' call that inspired the indigenous Khoikhoi name 'quagga.'

mammals.name: Walrus
mammals.summary: The walrus (Odobenus rosmarus; plural walrus or walruses) is a large pinniped marine mammal with  discontinuous distribution about the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean and subarctic seas of the Northern Hemisphere. It is the only extant species in the family Odobenidae and genus Odobenus.
facts: The scientific name of the walrus, Odobenus rosmarus, translates from Greek and Latin as 'tooth-walking sea-horse', because walruses literally jam their yard-long ivory tusks into ice floes and haul their 3,000-pound bodies out of the water by their teeth.

That bushy mustache on a walrus's snout isn't hairs at all: it consists of 400 to 700 individual muscular whiskers called vibrissae, each wired directly to blood vessels and nerves so sensitive the walrus can distinguish a tiny clam from a pebble in pitch-black mud.

Wait; how does a walrus actually eat 5,000 clams in a single dive without crushing the shells with its teeth? It seals its rubbery lips over the edge of the shell and pulls its tongue back like a high-powered bicycle pump, creating vacuum suction strong enough to pop the clam meat right out of the shell.

A walrus can sleep floating vertically in the middle of the icy ocean thanks to two inflatable pharyngeal air pouches in its neck that puff out like twin neck pillows and hold up to 13 gallons of air.

During the mating season, those same inflatable throat pouches act as acoustic resonance chambers, allowing bulls to produce underwater 'bell-ringing' chimes and knocks that sound like church bells echoing beneath the ice.

When a walrus rests on land or ice in warm weather, it turns bright bubblegum pink as blood vessels dilate in its two-inch-thick skin to shed excess heat; then turns ghostly pale white as soon as it plunges back into freezing water.

mammals.name: Bobcat
mammals.summary: The bobcat (Lynx rufus), also known as the wildcat, bay lynx, or red lynx, is one of the four extant species within the medium-sized wild cat genus Lynx. Native to North America, it ranges from southern Canada through most of the contiguous United States to Oaxaca in Mexico.
facts: Why is it called a 'bobcat'? Its stubby 4- to 6-inch tail looks 'bobbed' (docked short), with a black tip on top and stark white underneath that flashes to kittens walking behind Mom in dense brush.

Although only about twice the size of a housecat, a bobcat is a fearless ambush hunter capable of leaping 10 feet onto the back of an adult white-tailed deer eight times its own weight while the deer is bedded down in winter snow.
A bobcat's hind legs are noticeably longer than its front legs, giving it a slightly raised rump and the spring-loaded power to bound 12 feet horizontally in a single pounce.

Look closely at the pointed black tufts of hair sprouting from the tips of a bobcat's ears; research shows these tufts act like acoustic antennas that funnel faint rustling sounds from mice directly into the ear canal.

In Indigenous Shawnee, Potawatomi, and Mohican folklore, the bobcat got its spotted coat and short tail after getting tricked by a rabbit trapped inside a hollow tree who tossed hot campfire embers onto the cat's fur.
Bobcats rarely vocalize except during the late-winter mating season, when their eerie yowls, hisses, and demonic-sounding shrieks sound startlingly like a person screaming in the woods.

mammals.name: Asian black bear
mammals.summary: The Asian black bear (Ursus thibetanus), also known as the Asiatic black bear, moon bear and white-chested bear, is a medium-sized bear species native to Asia that is largely adapted to an arboreal lifestyle. It is distributed from southeastern Iran, Pakistan, India and the Himalayas to mainland Southeast Asia, the Korean Peninsula, Taiwan, China and the Russian Far East to the islands of Honshū and Shikoku in Japan.
facts: Often called the 'moon bear' because of the brilliant creamy-white V-shaped or crescent moon marking splashed across its jet-black chest, which it flashes by standing upright on its hind legs to warn tigers away.

Asian black bears spend up to half their lives high in the forest canopy, snapping leafy oak and beech branches to weave giant, bowl-shaped 'bear nests' 50 feet up in the treetops where they nap and dine on acorns.

Unlike any other bear species, an Asian black bear walks on its hind legs for remarkable distances; researchers have filmed wild moon bears strolling bipedal for over a quarter of a mile just to carry armfuls of fruit.

Why did the Asian black bear evolve such a shaggy mane of long hair around its neck and shoulders? Because unlike American black bears, it shares its forests with Bengal and Siberian tigers, and that thick ruff helps prevent a tiger from getting a clean throat bite.

Wait; does Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer have competition in children's literature? 'Winnie-the-Pooh' was inspired by an American black bear cub named Winnipeg, while Rudyard Kipling's laid-back 'Baloo' is often associated with Asian bears like the sloth bear and Himalayan moon bear.

In northern parts of their range like Siberia and Japan, moon bears hibernate through winter in hollow trees or rock caves, whereas moon bears in warm tropical forests of Thailand and Taiwan stay wide awake all year long.

mammals.name: Manatee
mammals.summary: The West Indian manatee (Trichechus manatus), also known as the North American manatee, is a large, aquatic mammal native to warm coastal areas of the Caribbean, from the Eastern United States to northern Brazil. Living alone or in herds, it feeds on underwater plants and uses its whiskers to navigate.
facts: Unlike almost all other mammals on Earth, including giraffes and whales, which all have seven neck vertebrae, the manatee has only six cervical vertebrae, which means it cannot turn its head sideways and must pivot its entire tubby body to look around.

Because seagrass is packed with abrasive silica sand that quickly grinds teeth down to the roots, manatees evolved 'marching molars': new teeth continuously sprout at the very back of the jaw and slowly march forward like a conveyor belt all their lives as worn front teeth fall out.

Wait, how does a manatee rise to the surface or sink to the bottom without paddling its flippers? It controls its buoyancy internally by contracting its ribcage and using flat, horizontally split diaphragms, and yes, by holding in or releasing digestive gas from its 145-foot-long intestines.

Despite looking blubbery and round, a manatee actually has less than an inch of fat under its skin; most of its barrel-shaped torso is gigantic intestines, leaving it so susceptible to 'cold stress' that it must seek out warm 70°F natural springs or power plant outflows whenever winter temperatures dip.
A manatee's upper lip is split right down the middle into two independent halves that move like a pair of prehensile fingers to pluck aquatic plants and tuck them into its mouth.

On the outside of its skin, a manatee has about 3,000 tiny tactile hairs spread across its body that work like a fish's lateral line, letting it feel the faint water pressure ripples of an approaching boat or fish in zero-visibility water.

mammals.name: Brown rat
mammals.summary: The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), also known as the common rat, street rat, sewer rat, wharf rat, Hanover rat, Norway rat and Norwegian rat, is a widespread, common species of rat. One of the largest muroids, it is a brown or grey rodent with a body length of up to 28 cm (11 in) long, and a tail slightly shorter than that.
facts: Why was the brown rat given the scientific name Rattus norvegicus ('Norwegian rat') when it actually originated on the plains of northern China and Mongolia? In 1769, English naturalist John Berkenhout mistakenly thought they had arrived in Britain aboard timber ships from Norway, and the geographic misnomer stuck forever.

When neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp tickled brown rats on the nape of their necks, ultrasonic microphones revealed the rats were emitting exuberant 50-kilohertz 'chirps' of pure joy, the rodent equivalent of giggling, and the rats eagerly chased his hand begging to be tickled again.

In empathy experiments at the University of Chicago, brown rats consistently chose to unlock a plastic door to rescue a trapped cage-mate before opening a second container filled with chocolate chips, and then saved half the chocolate for their freed friend.

A brown rat's skeleton is so collapsible and its ribs so hinged on its spine that it can flatten its torso to wriggle through any pipe or hole the size of a U.S. quarter (about 0.9 inches), as well as tread water for three days straight and swim up through toilet S-bends.

Because brown rats are physically incapable of vomiting or burping due to a muscular barrier at the top of their stomachs, they practice extreme 'neophobia', taking a tiny, cautious nibble of any unfamiliar food and waiting hours to see if they feel sick before eating a full meal.
Selective breeding of gentle albino brown rats in the 19th century created the modern laboratory rat, the very first mammal species ever domesticated specifically for scientific research.

mammals.name: Red panda
mammals.summary: The red panda (Ailurus fulgens), also known as the lesser panda, is a small mammal native to the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China. It has dense reddish-brown fur with a black belly and legs, white-lined ears, a mostly white muzzle and a ringed tail.
facts: Notice the name: the red panda was actually named 'panda' in 1825 by French zoologist Frédéric Cuvier, nearly 45 years before Western science ever discovered the black-and-white giant panda, which borrowed its name from the little red original.

Wait; what family does the red panda belong to? After baffling scientists who grouped it first with raccoons and then with bears, DNA sequencing revealed it is the sole living survivor of its own ancient family (Ailuridae), a living fossil whose closest distant cousins include skunks, weasels, and raccoons.

In one of evolution's strangest cases of convergence, both the red panda and the unrelated giant panda independently evolved a 'false thumb', an elongated wrist bone used specifically to grip slippery bamboo stalks.

When a red panda feels cornered or wants to look intimidating, it stands straight up on its hind legs and throws both front paws high over its head in an adorable 'stick-'em-up' pose that makes it look twice as tall before it pounces.

Despite having a digestive tract built for meat and eating mostly low-calorie bamboo, the red panda survived by developing the ability to detect artificial sweeteners like aspartame, the only non-primate mammal known to do so.
In Mandarin Chinese, the red panda is called 'hun-ho' or 'huo-hu,' which literally translates to 'fire fox', inspiring the name and logo of the Mozilla Firefox web browser.
The red panda was described by Western science 48 years before the giant panda and is the original 'panda'.
Although it eats mostly bamboo like the giant panda, the red panda belongs to its own unique taxonomic family, Ailuridae.
Both red pandas and giant pandas independently evolved a 'false thumb', an enlarged wrist bone used to grip bamboo stems.
Red pandas descend tree trunks headfirst by rotating their ankle joints 180 degrees.

mammals.name: Ring-tailed lemur
mammals.summary: The ring-tailed lemur (Lemur catta) is a medium- to larger-sized strepsirrhine (wet-nosed) primate and the most internationally recognized lemur species, owing to its long, black-and-white, ringed tail. It belongs to Lemuridae, one of five lemur families, and is the only member of the Lemur genus.
facts: When rival male ring-tailed lemurs clash during the breeding season, they settle disputes with 'stink fights': each male rubs his long striped tail across scent glands on his inner wrists and chest, then stands on all fours and waves the noxious, smelly plume right at his opponent's face until one backs down.

Ring-tailed lemur troops of up to 30 animals are strictly ruled by alpha females; even juvenile females outrank full-grown adult males and get first dibs on the best sleeping branches and ripe tamarind pods.

Every crisp morning in southern Madagascar, troop members sit upright on the ground facing the rising sun with their arms spread wide and palms resting on their knees in a serene, lotus-like yoga pose to warm their thinly furred white bellies.

Look at the black-and-white rings on a ring-tailed lemur's two-foot-long tail: there are almost always exactly 13 alternating black and white bands, always ending in a black tip, which the troop holds straight up in the air like periscopes while marching through tall grass.

Why is a lemur called a 'lemur'? Early European naturalists in Madagascar heard their eerie, wailing cries in the forest canopy at dusk and saw their glowing reflective eyes, naming them after the 'lemures'; the restless ghosts and spirits of ancient Roman mythology.

On the backs of their wrists, males possess a sharp horny spur right over their brachial scent gland, which they use like a carpenter's gouge to carve deep, smelly grooves into young tree saplings to mark troop borders.

mammals.name: Goat
mammals.summary: The goat or domestic goat (Capra hircus) is a species of caprine that is mostly kept as livestock. It was domesticated from the wild goat (C. aegagrus) of Southwest Asia and Eastern Europe.
facts: According to 9th-century Ethiopian legend, mankind owes its morning coffee to a goat herder named Kaldi, who noticed his goats dancing excitedly and refusing to sleep all night after nibbling the bright red berries of wild Coffea arabica bushes.

Why do 'fainting goats' (Myotonic goats) suddenly freeze stiff as a board and topple over sideways when startled? They don't actually lose consciousness; they carry a harmless hereditary mutation in the CLCN1 muscle chloride channel gene that delays muscle relaxation for ten seconds whenever they get excited.

In Morocco's Souss Valley, entire herds of nimble domestic goats climb 30 feet up into gnarled, thorny Argania spinosa trees, balancing on pencil-thin branches like acrobats to munch the bitter fruit and spit out the oil-rich nuts.

A goat's horizontal, slit-shaped pupils stay parallel to the horizon even when the goat tilts its head straight down to graze; the eyeballs physically rotate up to 50 degrees inside their sockets so their wide-angle predator radar never tilts.

During the mating season, a billy goat performs 'self-enurination': he curves his head down between his front legs and sprays his own face, chest, and beard with pheromone-loaded urine, creating a pungent cologne that brings females in the herd into synchronized heat.

Goats speak with regional accents! Researchers at Queen Mary University of London recorded kid goats as they moved between different social groups and found that their bleats subtly shifted pitch and tone to match their new peers, making them one of the few mammals outside humans, bats, and whales known to pick up local accents.

mammals.name: Przewalski's horse
mammals.summary: Przewalski's horse (Equus ferus przewalskii or Equus przewalskii), also called the takhi, Mongolian wild horse or Dzungarian horse, is a rare and endangered wild horse originally native to the steppes of Central Asia. It is named after Russian geographer and explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky.
facts: While every other 'wild' horse on Earth, from American mustangs to Australian brumbies, is actually a feral descendant of escaped domestic horses, Przewalski's horse is the world's only truly wild horse whose ancestors were never tamed or ridden by humans.
Przewalski's horse has 66 chromosomes in every cell compared to 64 chromosomes in all domestic horses, yet the two can still interbreed and produce fertile offspring with 65 chromosomes.

By 1969, hunting and harsh winters had wiped out Przewalski's horse in the Mongolian Gobi Desert, leaving the species completely extinct in the wild; every one of the roughly 2,500 living today descends from just 12 wild-caught horses kept in zoos in Prague and Munich before World War II.

Unlike domestic horses whose manes cascade softly down the side of their necks and stay year-round, a Przewalski's horse has a stiff, brush-like Mohawk mane that stands straight up without a forelock and sheds completely every spring.

In 2020, conservationists cloned a stallion named Kurt from skin cells that had been frozen in liquid nitrogen inside the San Diego Zoo's 'Frozen Zoo' for 40 years, restoring lost genetic diversity to the tiny surviving gene pool.

Their thick, stocky builds, yellowish-dun coats, and dark dorsal stripes down their spines match the prehistoric horses painted by Ice Age artists on the walls of France's Lascaux caves 17,000 years ago.

mammals.name: Ocelot
mammals.summary: The ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) is a medium-sized spotted wild cat that reaches 40–50 cm (16–20 in) at the shoulders and weighs between 7 and 15.5 kg (15 and 34 lb) on average. It is native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, Central and South America, and the Caribbean islands of Trinidad and Margarita.
facts: Why is an ocelot's coat so unlike any other cat's? Instead of simple dots or rosettes, its velvety fur features long, chain-like dark blotches bordered in black that flow horizontally down its sides, mimicking streaks of sunlight and shadow in tropical brush.

Twentieth-century surrealist painter Salvador Dalí famously kept a pet Colombian ocelot named Babou, taking the spotted cat on a jewel-studded leash aboard the ocean liner SS France and into upscale Manhattan restaurants, where he once assured a horrified diner that Babou was just 'a normal domestic cat painted over in an op-art design.'
Unlike almost all small wild cats, ocelots have no fear of water and are strong, eager swimmers that dive into jungle streams to catch fish, frogs, and land crabs.
When eating a captured bird, an ocelot methodically plucks off every large feather with its teeth before dining, whereas it swallows furry mice and lizards whole.
An ocelot's raspy tongue is covered in rear-facing, curved spines called papillae made of keratin that work like a miniature meat rasp, scraping every last shred of muscle clean off a prey bone.
In ancient Inca and Moche civilizations of Peru, the ocelot was revered as a sacred symbol of agricultural fertility and nocturnal vision, frequently depicted on ceramic vessels and gold masks.

mammals.name: Spectacled bear
mammals.summary: The spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), also known as the Andean bear, is a species of bear native to the Andes Mountains in northern and western South America. It is the only living species of bear native to South America, and the last remaining short-faced bear (subfamily Tremarctinae).
facts: The spectacled bear is the only bear species native to South America and the last living survivor of the ancient subfamily Tremarctinae; the short-faced bears whose giant Ice Age cousins once towered 11 feet tall across the Americas.
Wait, even its ribs are different from every other bear on Earth! All seven other bear species have 14 pairs of ribs, whereas the spectacled bear has only 13 pairs.

Named for the creamy-white or yellowish rings of fur that circle its eyes like a pair of eyeglasses, every bear's facial markings are completely unique and extend down onto its throat like a fingerprint.
Also known across the Andes as the 'ukumari' or Andean bear, it was the real-life inspiration for Michael Bond's beloved storybook character Paddington Bear from 'Darkest Peru.'

More than 90% of a spectacled bear's diet is pure plants: its massive jaw muscles and broad molars are built to tear open the spiky hearts of tough mountain bromeliads and crunch palm nuts up in the cloud forest.

Rather than retreating to caves to hibernate, spectacled bears build sturdy wooden platforms high in fruit trees where they camp out for days at a time waiting for crops of wild figs and avocados to ripen.

mammals.name: Donkey
mammals.summary: The donkey, ass, or burro is a domesticated equine. It derives from the African wild ass, Equus africanus, and may be classified either as a subspecies thereof, Equus africanus asinus, or as a separate species, Equus asinus.
facts: Why does a donkey get a bad rap for being 'stubborn' when you try to pull it into a scary situation? Unlike horses, which evolved on open plains where bolting in panic is the safest bet, donkeys evolved in rugged desert canyons where one panicked misstep means falling off a cliff, so a startled donkey freezes in place to calmly calculate the danger before moving.

Because donkeys are stoic desert survivors that rarely show pain or panic and despise wild canines on sight, ranchers across the world place a single 'guard donkey' inside sheep and goat pastures to chase off coyotes and feral dogs with flying hooves.

A donkey's oversized ears do double duty: they act as desert radiators packed with surface blood vessels to dump body heat, and they swivel like radar dishes to pick up the call of another donkey up to 60 miles away across flat desert air.

Unlike a horse's waterproof coat, a donkey's coat has almost no natural lanolin or oil because rain is rare in its ancestral African deserts, meaning a donkey left out in heavy, cold rain without shelter will soak right through to the skin and catch a chill.

When a male donkey (a jack) breeds with a female horse (a mare), the offspring is a mule, which has 63 chromosomes and is almost always sterile, yet carries the hybrid vigor of a horse's size and a donkey's legendary endurance and sure-footedness.

How does a donkey manage to make its two-tone 'hee-haw' bray? Donkeys are one of the few mammals capable of vocalizing loudly on both the inward breath ('hee') and the outward breath ('haw') in a single continuous call.

mammals.name: Wolverine
mammals.summary: The wolverine ( WUUL-və-reen, US also  WUUL-və-REEN; Gulo gulo), also called the carcajou or quickhatch (from East Cree, kwiihkwahaacheew), is the largest land-dwelling member of the family Mustelidae. It is a muscular carnivore and a solitary animal.
facts: The wolverine's scientific name, Gulo gulo, literally translates from Latin as 'glutton, glutton', earned because this 35-pound member of the weasel family will devour frozen carrion, bones, and teeth whole and fiercely drive bears and wolf packs off their own kills.

In winter, a wolverine's dense, oily, hydrophobic fur completely resists frost and ice crystallization, which is why Indigenous Arctic peoples have prized wolverine fur for centuries as the ultimate ruff trim around parka hoods where human breath freezes.

Look inside the back of a wolverine's mouth and you'll find a specialized pair of upper molar teeth rotated a full 90 degrees inward toward the throat, giving it the leverage to shear through meat frozen as hard as oak wood.

Despite weighing no more than a medium-sized dog, wolverines have been documented bringing down adult reindeer and caribou ten times their weight when the ungulates get bogged down in deep snowdrifts.

Because their enormous five-toed paws spread out to twice their normal width when stepping down, wolverines carry only a fraction of an ounce of pressure per square inch on snow, letting them sprint across soft powder where wolves sink to their bellies.

A male wolverine patrols a mountainous winter territory of up to 600 square miles, scaling sheer, ice-crusted peaks in Glacier National Park so effortlessly that biologists had to hire mountaineers just to check their camera traps.
Pound for pound, the wolverine is the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family Mustelidae.
A wolverine's upper molars are rotated 90 degrees inward, allowing it to shear through meat frozen solid in Arctic winters.
Wolverines have hydrophobic frost-resistant fur that was prized by Indigenous Arctic peoples for lining parka hoods.
A single wolverine can patrol a snowy mountain home range of over 500 square miles.

mammals.name: Opossum
mammals.summary: The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana), also known as the North American opossum, is a member of the opossum family found from southern Canada to northern Costa Rica, making it the northernmost marsupial in the world. Commonly referred to simply as the possum, it is a solitary nocturnal animal about the size of a domestic cat, and a successful opportunist.
facts: When an opossum 'plays possum' in front of a threat, it isn't putting on a conscious acting performance: extreme terror triggers an involuntary neurological faint (thanatosis) that drops its heart rate by half, makes its tongue loll out of a drooling mouth, and pumps a foul, corpse-smelling green fluid from its anal glands until the predator walks away.

Opossums carry a miraculous protein in their blood serum called LTNF (Lethal Toxin Neutralizing Factor) that makes them virtually immune to the venom of rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths, and even honeybees, allowing them to hunt pit vipers for dinner.

Why is it practically impossible for a wild opossum to catch and spread rabies? Their normal resting body temperature is unusually low for a mammal (around 94° to 97°F), which is too chilly for the rabies virus to replicate effectively.
The Virginia opossum is a walking tick vacuum: a single opossum grooming itself in the woods devours up to 5,000 disease-carrying ticks in a single season.

A newborn opossum is no bigger than a honeybee: after a remarkably short 12-day pregnancy, up to 20 tiny, embryonic joeys crawl blind through their mother's fur into her pouch, where a single litter of 16 babies can fit comfortably inside one metal teaspoon.

Wait; does an adult opossum actually sleep hanging upside down by its tail like in cartoons? While juveniles can briefly dangle by their prehensile tails, an adult is too heavy and uses its tail like a fifth hand to carry bundles of dry leaves and twigs to its nest while walking on all fours.

mammals.name: African wild dog
mammals.summary: The African wild dog (Lycaon pictus), also called painted dog and Cape hunting dog, is a wild canine native to sub-Saharan Africa. It is the largest wild canine in Africa and the only extant member of the genus Lycaon, which is distinguished from Canis by dentition highly specialised for a hypercarnivorous diet and by a lack of dewclaws.
facts: While lions succeed on only about 25% of their hunts and cheetahs around 50%, the African wild dog is the savanna's true persistence-hunting champion: by running in relay formations at 37 miles per hour, a pack brings down its quarry on more than 80% of all chases.

Before setting off on an evening hunt, a pack of African wild dogs gathers in a circle to rally, and biologists in Botswana discovered they actually vote on whether to depart by sneezing! If the dominant pair initiates a rally, three sneezes are enough to launch the hunt, whereas lower-ranking dogs need at least ten sneezes from the group to get everyone moving.
The African wild dog's scientific name, Lycaon pictus, means 'painted wolf,' and every individual's asymmetrical patchwork coat of black, yellow, brown, and white is completely unique.

Unlike every other member of the dog family, which has five toes on its front paws (including the dewclaw), the African wild dog has only four toes per foot, an evolutionary adaptation for longer strides and higher running speeds.

Instead of barking or howling, painted wolves communicate with high-pitched, bird-like 'chirps' and soft bell-like 'hoo' calls that can reunite lost packmates from over a mile away without alerting lions.

Pack loyalty runs so deep that if a member is crippled by a snare or broken leg, the rest of the pack will hunt, gorge on meat, and run miles back to the den to regurgitate fresh food for the injured adult for months on end.

mammals.name: American mink
mammals.summary: The American mink (Neogale vison) is a semiaquatic species of mustelid native to North America, though human introduction has expanded its range to many parts of Europe, Asia, and South America. Because of range expansion, the American mink is classed as a least-concern species by the IUCN. The American mink was formerly thought to be the only extant member of the genus Neovison following the extinction of the sea mink (N. macrodon), but recent studies, followed by taxonomic authorities, have reclassified it and the sea mink within the genus Neogale, which also contains a few New World weasel species.
facts: When an American mink spots prey underwater from a riverbank, how does it compensate for the way water bends light (refraction)? It bobs its head up and down to triangulate the exact angle before diving in like a furry torpedo.

Because a mink lacks the specialized low-light cones and vertical slit pupils of cats or owls, its vision drops sharply once it dives underwater, forcing it to rely on sensitive whiskers to track sculpin and crayfish along dark creek beds.

When startled or cornered, an American mink can fire a foul-smelling liquid from twin anal scent glands that rivals a skunk's spray, and unlike a skunk's, a mink's musk smells like burnt rubber and fermented garlic.
Although mink have only partially webbed toes, a thick coat of oil-soaked guard hairs traps an insulating layer of air next to their skin so they can dive 16 feet deep in icy midwinter rivers.

Rather than digging its own burrows from scratch, a solitary mink usually moves into an abandoned muskrat den or hollow waterside log, sometimes after eating the muskrat that built it, and lines the bedroom with soft mouse fur and duck feathers.
Like its cousin the stoat, a happy or excited mink performs a bouncing, sideways 'weasel war dance' complete with soft chuckling 'dook-dook' sounds.

mammals.name: Snow leopard
mammals.summary: The snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a felid species in the genus Panthera. It has a thick whitish to grey fur with black spots on the head and neck, with larger rosettes on the back, flanks and bushy tail.
facts: Why is a snow leopard's tail so absurdly long and thick? Measuring up to three feet long, nearly the entire length of its torso, that fluffy tail works both as a tightrope-walker's balancing pole during 50-foot cliff leaps and as a built-in fur scarf wrapped over its nose to warm subzero mountain air while sleeping.

Unlike lions, tigers, leopards, and jaguars, the snow leopard physically cannot roar; it lacks a thick pad of elastic tissue in its vocal folds, communicating instead with loud 'chuffs,' mews, and yowls.
When a snow leopard wants to greet or reassure another snow leopard, it makes a distinctive puffing sound called 'prusten' (also shared by tigers) by blowing air noisily through its closed nostrils.

Known across the Himalayas and Altai mountains as the 'ghost of the mountains,' its smoky-gray rosettes blend so seamlessly into jagged shale and snow patches that wildlife photographers can stare right at one from 30 feet away without seeing it.

To breathe thin, freezing oxygen at altitudes of 18,000 feet, a snow leopard has oversized nasal cavities that heat cold air before it hits the lungs and blood packed with tiny, numerous red blood cells.

Genetically, the snow leopard is not actually a close sibling of the common leopard; DNA analysis proved its closest living sister species is the tiger, having diverged from a common ancestor in central Asia over three million years ago.
Snow leopards use their thick, furry tails, which are nearly as long as their bodies, as a blanket to wrap around their faces in subzero winds.
Expanded nasal cavities warm frigid Himalayan air before it reaches a snow leopard's lungs.
Wide, fur-covered paws act as natural snowshoes to keep snow leopards from sinking into deep alpine drifts.
Because of modifications to their hyoid bone and larynx, snow leopards cannot roar.

mammals.name: Meerkat
mammals.summary: The meerkat (Suricata suricatta) or suricate is a small mongoose found in southern Africa. It is characterised by a broad head, large eyes, a pointed snout, long legs, a thin tapering tail, and a brindled coat pattern.
facts: Whenever a meerkat mob forages with their heads down in scorpion burrows, one volunteer stands bolt upright on a termite mound or bush as the 'sentinel,' scanning the sky for martial eagles and using dozens of distinct alarm calls that tell the group both whether the predator is in the air or on the ground and how urgently to bolt.

The black rings of fur around a meerkat's eyes work just like built-in wraparound sunglasses, cutting the blinding glare of the Kalahari Desert sun so the sentinel can look almost straight toward the sun to spot diving hawks.

Meerkats are completely immune to the neurotoxic venom of Kalahari thick-tailed scorpions, which can kill an adult human, and adult meerkats actively 'school' young pups by bringing them first dead scorpions, then live scorpions with the stingers bitten off, and finally fully armed scorpions until the youngsters master the kill.

How does a meerkat dig through sun-baked desert clay without getting dirt in its ears? Its crescent-shaped outer ears have muscular flaps that fold completely shut like little cellar doors while the animal excavates 15-entrance underground complexes.

Inside a meerkat clan of up to 40 individuals, the dominant female is a ruthless matriarch who accounts for 80% of all litters, and will banish or even kill the pups of any subordinate female who dares give birth without permission, after which those banished subordinates often start lactating to serve as wet nurses for the queen's babies.

A meerkat's belly is covered in only sparse, thin hair over dark skin; after chilly desert nights, the whole mob lines up standing on their hind legs using their stiff tails like tripods to solar-charge those dark belly patches in the morning sun.

mammals.name: Black rhinoceros
mammals.summary: The black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis), also called the black rhino or the hooked-lip rhinoceros, is a species of rhinoceros native to East and Southern Africa, including Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Although the species is referred to as black, its colours vary from brown to grey.
facts: Neither the black rhino nor the white rhino is actually black or white! Both are slate-gray; the 'white' rhino got its name when English settlers in South Africa misheard the Afrikaans word 'wyd' (meaning wide, for its square grazing lip) as 'white,' and then started calling the hook-lipped browsing species the 'black' rhino just to tell them apart.

Unlike an elephant's ivory tusks or a bull's bony horns, a black rhino's two horns have zero bone core; they are made entirely of densely compacted, glued-together fibers of keratin (hair and fingernail protein) that grow three inches a year and can even grow back if broken off.

Look at a black rhino's upper lip: it tapers into a pointed, prehensile finger that works like a garden pruner, grabbing thorny acacia twigs and stripping leaves off branches that would shred a normal mouth.

Black rhinos have a fiery, love-hate relationship with oxpecker birds, known in Swahili as 'Askari wa kifaru' (the rhino's guard), which ride on their backs eating ticks and hiss loudly whenever an approaching poacher enters their nearsighted host's blind spot, though the birds also mischievously peck at the rhino's healing scratches to drink blood.

Because a black rhino's eyesight is so poor that it can barely distinguish a motionless person from a tree trunk at 100 feet, its sense of smell and swivel-mounted ears do almost all the work, which is why a startled black rhino often charges tree trunks and boulders first and asks questions later.

To keep in touch across dusty scrubland, black rhinos use communal 'middens', shared dung piles where every passing rhino stops to sniff the news, add its own deposit, and kick the pile around with its hind feet to spread its personal scent on its soles.

mammals.name: European badger
mammals.summary: The European badger (Meles meles), also known as the Eurasian badger, is a species of badger in the family Mustelidae native to Europe and West Asia and parts of Central Asia. It is classified as least concern on the IUCN Red List due to its wide range and large, stable population size which is thought to be increasing in some regions.
facts: European badgers live in sprawling underground family mansions called 'setts' that are passed down and expanded for so many generations that several documented setts in England have been continuously occupied by the same badger clans for over 300 years, spanning half a mile of tunnels and up to 50 entrances.

Badgers are fanatical housekeepers: unlike foxes, which leave bones and food scraps rotting inside their dens, badgers refuse to bring food underground, regularly drag their dry grass bedding outside to air out in the morning sun, and dig designated communal toilet pits ('latrines') well away from their front doors.

Why does a European badger have such bold, high-contrast black-and-white stripes down its face? In dim moonlight, those stark stripes act as a visual warning badge, like a skunk's stripes, telling wolves and dogs from afar that this low-slung mustelid has a jaw that locks onto bone.

Speaking of its jaw: the hinge of a European badger's lower jaw wraps so tightly around the cheekbones of its skull that you literally cannot dislocate a badger's jaw from its socket without breaking the bone itself.

Although armed like a formidable carnivore, the European badger in Britain gets up to 80% of its calories from a single surprising food: ordinary earthworms, slurping up over 200 worms like spaghetti in a single damp night.
The English verb 'to badger', meaning to pester someone relentlessly, comes from the cruel medieval blood sport of badger-baiting, which was finally outlawed in the UK in 1835.

mammals.name: House mouse
mammals.summary: The house mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail. It is one of the most abundant species of the genus Mus.
facts: Male house mice sing intricate, multi-syllable courtship songs to females that sound strikingly like birdsong when slowed down; humans never hear them only because the mice sing at ultrasonic frequencies between 30 and 110 kilohertz.

Every time a house mouse scurries along a baseboard, it dribbles tiny micro-droplets of urine infused with 'major urinary proteins' that glow under UV light and act as scented breadcrumbs so the mouse can race back to its hole in total darkness without looking.
A house mouse can flatten its flexible ribcage to squeeze under a closed door through a gap just a quarter of an inch high, roughly the width of a standard wooden pencil.

Without its tail, a house mouse would quickly overheat and lose its balance: the nearly hairless tail acts both as a tightrope counterweight for walking along electrical wires and as a thermoregulator that dilates blood vessels to dump up to 20% of the mouse's excess body heat.

In 1900, a retired Massachusetts schoolteacher named Abbie Lathrop began breeding fancy pet mice on her farm in Granby and selling them to Harvard geneticists; her 'C57BL/6' black mouse strain became the ancestor of the vast majority of biomedical research mice used worldwide today, including mice that have flown aboard the International Space Station.

Because a female house mouse can get pregnant again within 24 hours of giving birth and her daughters hit puberty at just six weeks old, a single pair of house mice could theoretically produce over 5,000 descendants in a single year.

mammals.name: Rhesus macaque
mammals.summary: The rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), colloquially rhesus monkey, is a species of Old World monkey in the Macaca genus. There are between six and nine recognised subspecies split between two groups, the Chinese-derived and the Indian-derived.
facts: Why is your blood type listed as 'Rh positive' or 'Rh negative'? The 'Rh' stands directly for the Rhesus macaque, in whose red blood cells scientists Karl Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener first identified the Rhesus antigen factor in 1937.

Long before Neil Armstrong or even Yuri Gagarin reached space, a rhesus macaque named Albert II became the first primate in space on June 14, 1949, soaring 83 miles high aboard a U.S.-launched V-2 rocket, followed a decade later by Miss Able and Miss Baker, who safely returned from space in 1959.

Rhesus macaques have expandable cheek pouches inside their mouths that can stretch to hold as much food as their actual stomachs, letting them raid a farmer's fruit stand or temple offering in seconds and sprint to a safe rooftop before chewing.

In a female-led rhesus macaque troop, social class is strictly hereditary and matrilineal: daughters inherit their rank right below their mothers, and the youngest daughter in a family automatically outranks all of her older sisters!

During the breeding season, high surging levels of estrogen and testosterone cause the bare skin on both male and female rhesus macaques' faces and rumps to flush a vivid, glowing cherry red, and studies show females strongly prefer the reddest-faced males.
Unlike many forest monkeys that dread deep water, rhesus macaques are joyful recreational swimmers that dive off overhanging branches into rivers to cool off and swim half a mile between islands.

mammals.name: Groundhog
mammals.summary:
The groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots. 
A lowland creature of North America, it is found through much of the Eastern United States, across Canada and into Alaska.
facts: Every February 2nd in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, tens of thousands of spectators gather at Gobbler's Knob to watch 'Punxsutawney Phil' predict the weather, a tradition brought by Pennsylvania Dutch settlers who originally used a European badger ('Dachs') in Germany before switching to the abundant local groundhog.

Wait; how much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood? None at all! The nickname 'woodchuck' has nothing to do with trees or chucking; it is an English phonetic corruption of the Algonquian Cree name 'wuchak.'

Groundhogs are among the few true, deep hibernators on Earth: during winter in an underground chamber sealed behind a wall of dirt, a groundhog's body temperature plummets from 99°F down to 37°F, its breathing slows to once every six minutes, and its heart beats just four or five times a minute.

Why did the groundhog get the nickname 'whistle-pig'? Whenever a groundhog spots a hawk, coyote, or gardener, it stands up on its hind legs and lets out a piercing, single-note whistle that sends every squirrel and rabbit in the meadow diving for cover.

A single groundhog excavating its winter burrow moves up to 700 pounds of dirt and stones with its claws and teeth, building a multi-room underground bunker complete with a separate waterproof bathroom chamber so its sleeping nest stays spotless.
Even though groundhogs are stocky, heavy-bodied ground squirrels, they can climb straight up into mulberry and apple trees to gorge on summer fruit and effortlessly swim across farm ponds.

mammals.name: Stoat
mammals.summary: The stoat (Mustela erminea), also known as the Eurasian ermine or ermine, is a species of mustelid native to Eurasia and the northern regions of North America. Because of its wide circumpolar distribution, it is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
facts: In winter across snowy northern latitudes, a stoat sheds its brown summer coat and turns completely snow-white except for a jet-black tip on the end of its tail, in this royal winter outfit, it is known as 'ermine,' the luxurious fur trimmed with black dots worn for centuries on the ceremonial robes of British monarchs and European peers.

Why does the very tip of a stoat's tail stay pitch-black even when the rest of the animal turns white for winter camouflage? It acts as a life-saving decoy target: when a diving hawk or owl strikes at the conspicuous black spot against the snow, it grabs only a mouthful of tail hair while the stoat twists free and escapes.

To hunt rabbits up to five times its own weight, a stoat performs a mesmerizing, erratic 'weasel war dance', sommersaulting, zig-zagging, and twisting in midair right in front of the rabbit until the bewildered prey stands frozen long enough for the stoat to close the gap and deliver a precision bite to the base of the skull.

Female stoats have the most extreme reproductive schedule in the mammal world: through embryonic diapause (delayed implantation), newborn female kits are often mated in the nest while still blind, deaf, and less than three weeks old; meaning almost every female stoat is already pregnant before she even opens her eyes or stops nursing.
Because a stoat's long, tubular body loses heat rapidly, it must eat roughly a third of its own body weight every single day, hunting inside narrow mouse tunnels where larger predators cannot fit.

When New Zealand imported stoats from Britain in the 1880s to control invasive European rabbits, the stoats quickly realized that native flightless birds like kiwis and kakapos were far easier to catch than fast rabbits, turning the introduction into an ecological disaster.

mammals.name: Sloth
mammals.summary:
The brown-throated sloth (Bradypus variegatus)  is a species of three-toed sloth found in the Neotropical realm of Central and South America.
It is the most common of the five species of three-toed sloth, and is found in the forests of South and Central America  in countries such as Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, and Venezuela.
facts: Why does a sloth climb all the way down from the safety of the rainforest canopy to the forest floor once a week just to poop, where over half of all sloth predation deaths occur? Its shaggy fur hosts an entire ecosystem of symbiotic 'sloth moths' that lay their eggs exclusively in fresh sloth dung, and the moths in turn fertilize the green algae growing in microscopic cracks on the sloth's hairs, giving it camouflage and nutritious snacks.

Unlike almost every other mammal on Earth, which strictly maintains seven neck vertebrae, three-toed sloths have 8 to 10 cervical vertebrae, allowing them to turn their heads nearly 270 degrees in either direction like an owl without moving their bodies a millimeter.

Because a sloth hangs upside down for so much of its life, its internal organs, liver, stomach, and spleen, are tethered directly to its lower ribs and pelvic girdle by fibrinous adhesions so they don't press down on its lungs and suffocate it.

A sloth has only about half the muscle mass of a typical mammal its size, yet its grip strength is so tenacious, and its curved claws work like passive bone hooks, that sloths sometimes stay hanging from a branch even after dying of old age.

On land, a sloth crawls at a torturous 6 to 8 feet per minute, yet drop a sloth into a flooded Amazonian river and it transforms into a graceful freestyle swimmer moving three times faster than it can walk and capable of holding its breath underwater for up to 40 minutes by slowing its heart rate to a third of normal.
With the slowest metabolic rate of any non-hibernating mammal, it takes a sloth up to an entire month just to digest a single meal of tough cecropia leaves in its four-chambered stomach.

mammals.name: Bowhead whale
mammals.summary: The bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus), sometimes known as the Greenland right whale, Arctic whale, and polar whale, is a species of baleen whale belonging to the family Balaenidae and is the only living representative of the genus Balaena. It is the only baleen whale endemic to the Arctic and subarctic waters, and is named after its characteristic massive triangular skull, which it uses to break through Arctic ice.
facts: The bowhead whale is the longest-lived mammal on Earth: in 2007, Inupiat whalers in Alaska recovered the tip of a brass bomb-lance harpoon embedded in a bowhead's neck blubber that had been manufactured and patented in New Bedford, Massachusetts, around 1880, and amino-acid eye-lens dating proved another individual lived to an astonishing 211 years old.

How does a bowhead whale breathe when solid Arctic sea ice freezes over its head? Its colossal, triangular skull is arched upward like a battering ram and topped with a muscular blowhole cushion, allowing the whale to smash straight up through two feet of solid polar ice from below.

Bowhead whales grow the longest baleen plates of any whale in the ocean, over 600 fringed plates of flexible 'whalebone' hanging up to 14 feet long from their arched upper jaws, which 19th-century fashion designers harvested to make corsets, hoop skirts, and umbrella ribs.
To stay warm in freezing polar waters year-round without migrating south, a bowhead whale wears the thickest coat of blubber in the animal kingdom, measuring up to 20 inches (nearly two feet) thick.

During the 24-hour darkness of the Arctic winter in the Fram Strait, bowhead whales sing complex, two-voice polyphonic songs, simultaneously producing two completely independent pitches at once, changing their entire repertoire of dozens of different songs every single year.

Scientists sequencing the bowhead whale genome discovered duplicated genes linked to DNA repair (ERCC1) and cell-cycle regulation (PCNA), explaining how a 100-ton mammal can live for over two centuries without developing cancer.

mammals.name: Ferret
mammals.summary: The ferret (Mustela furo) is a small, domesticated species belonging to the family Mustelidae. The ferret is most likely a domesticated form of the wild European polecat (Mustela putorius), as evidenced by the ferret's ability to interbreed with European polecats and produce hybrid offspring.
facts: A group of ferrets is officially called a 'business', a collective noun that dates back to medieval English hunting books.
The word 'ferret' comes from the Latin 'furittus', which translates to 'little thief,' a nod to their compulsive habit of stealing shiny or rubbery objects and hiding them in secret stashes.
When excited, ferrets perform a frantic, sideways-hopping, arched-back routine known as the 'weasel war dance,' often colliding clumsily into furniture while making soft 'dook-dook' chuckling sounds.
Because their spines are extra-flexible and their ribs can flatten slightly, a ferret can squeeze through any hole big enough to fit its skull.

In 1999, technicians at London's Millennium Dome and event organizers in Auckland used trained ferrets wearing tiny harnesses to pull fiber-optic and electrical cables through long, narrow underground conduits.

Healthy ferrets sleep so deeply, up to 18 hours a day, that they occasionally enter a limp, unresponsive state known to owners as 'ferret dead sleep,' where they won't wake up even when picked up and shaken.
Unspayed female ferrets are induced ovulators; if they go into heat and do not mate, persistently high estrogen levels can cause fatal bone marrow suppression unless treated by a vet.

mammals.name: African elephant
mammals.summary: The African bush elephant (Loxodonta africana), also known as the African savanna elephant, is a species of elephant native to sub-Saharan Africa and the largest living terrestrial animal, with fully grown bulls reaching an average shoulder height of 3.04–3.36 m (10.0–11.0 ft) and a body mass of 5.2–6.9 t (5.7–7.6 short tons); the largest recorded specimen had a shoulder height of 3.96 m (13.0 ft) and an estimated body mass of 10.4 t (11.5 short tons). It is characterised by its long prehensile trunk with two finger-like processes; a concave back; large ears which help reduce body heat; and sturdy tusks that are noticeably curved.
facts: An African elephant's trunk contains around 40,000 individual muscles, compared to fewer than 700 in the entire human body, and is dexterous enough to pluck a single blade of grass or crack a peanut shell without crushing the seed.
Elephants can 'hear' with their feet: fatty pads in their soles and sensitive nerve endings pick up low-frequency seismic rumbles transmitted through the ground by other herds up to 20 miles away.

Look closely at an African elephant's massive ears and you'll notice they are shaped remarkably like the continent of Africa itself; packed with blood vessels, flapping them can cool the animal's blood by up to 9°F before it circulates back to the brain.

They are terrified of tiny honeybees and have evolved a specific, distinct alarm rumble exclusively to warn herd members to flee and shake their heads so bees don't sting the sensitive insides of their trunks.
At nearly 22 months, the African elephant has the longest pregnancy of any living mammal, giving birth to a calf that already weighs around 250 pounds.

Elephants go through six sets of massive, brick-sized molar teeth over their lifetimes; rather than growing up from the gums like human teeth, new molars emerge at the back of the jaw and push worn teeth forward like a conveyor belt.

mammals.name: African buffalo
mammals.summary: The African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) is a large bovine native to sub-Saharan Africa. First described in 1779 by Anders Sparrman, it is the only extant species of the genus Syncerus.
facts: In older bulls, the two massive curved horns fuse together across the forehead to form a solid, helmet-like shield of bone and keratin called a 'boss' that cannot be penetrated even by high-powered rifle rounds.

Herd members appear to 'vote' on which direction to travel: during rest stops, adult females stand up, stare intently in the direction they want to go, and lie back down, and the entire herd eventually marches in the direction chosen by the majority.
They are famous for holding grudges and actively mobbing predators, frequently circling back to trample or launch lions into the air if a herd member is attacked.
