African buffaloes engage in a mutually beneficial spa relationship with oxpecker birds, which ride on their backs eating ticks and earwax, though the birds also mischievously peck at healing wounds to drink the buffalo's blood.

Despite having no genetic overlap with domestic cattle strong enough to produce fertile hybrids, a single buffalo herd can form a stampeding wall of up to 1,000 animals that even whole lion prides refuse to challenge.
Nicknamed the 'Black Death' or 'Widowmaker' by safari guides, they have a reputation for circling back on human trackers and ambushing pursuers from dense brush.

mammals.name: Muskox
mammals.summary: The muskox (Ovibos moschatus) is a hoofed mammal of the family Bovidae. Native to the Arctic, it is noted for its thick coat and for the strong odor emitted by males during the seasonal rut, from which its name derives.
facts: Despite its name and appearance, the muskox is not an ox at all; DNA reveals it is much more closely related to sheep and mountain goats than to cattle.

Its undercoat, known by the Inuit name 'qiviut,' is eight times warmer than sheep's wool, finer than cashmere, does not shrink in hot water, and sells for up to $100 per ounce when combed from shedding animals.

When threatened by Arctic wolves, a muskox herd instantly forms an impenetrable defensive circle or crescent, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with their razor-sharp horns facing outward while calves shelter safely in the center.
During the autumn rut, rival bulls back up 50 yards and charge headfirst into each other at 30 miles per hour, producing a skull-cracking boom that can be heard nearly a mile away across the tundra.

To survive those high-speed headbutt collisions without brain damage, a bull's skull features four inches of solid horn and three inches of spongy, air-cushioned bone acting as a built-in football helmet.
Only the males produce the strong-smelling musk that gives the animal its name, secreting it from specialized facial glands near their eyes during mating season and rubbing it into their forelegs.

mammals.name: Maned wolf
mammals.summary: The maned wolf  (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America. It is found in Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, and Paraguay, and is almost locally extinct in Uruguay.
facts: Despite its name, the maned wolf is neither a fox nor a true wolf; it sits alone in its own distinct genus (*Chrysocyon*) and looks like a red fox walking around on a pair of black stilts.

Its famously stinky urine smells almost identical to cannabis because of chemical compounds called pyrazines; in 2006, Dutch police were called to the Rotterdam Zoo to investigate visitors allegedly smoking marijuana, only to discover the scent was coming from the maned wolf enclosure.

Up to half of its diet isn't meat at all, but a tomato-like fruit native to the South American savanna called the 'lobeira' or 'wolf apple,' which locals long believed protected the animal from giant kidney worms.
Rather than howling like a gray wolf, it communicates across the tall grasslands with a deep, booming 'roar-bark' that sounds like a giant guard dog.

Its disproportionately long legs are an evolutionary adaptation for peering over five-foot-tall savanna grass, and when it walks, it moves both legs on the same side of its body together in a pacing gait like a giraffe or camel.
Unlike pack-hunting wolves, mated maned wolves are fiercely solitary; they share a territory boundary and even sleep during the day, only crossing paths briefly during the breeding season.

mammals.name: Llama
mammals.summary:
The llama (; Spanish pronunciation: [ˈʎama] or [ˈʝama]; Lama glama) is a domesticated South American camelid, widely used as a meat and pack animal by Andean cultures since the pre-Columbian era.
Llamas are social animals and live with others as a herd.
facts: When a llama is deeply annoyed by another llama, or an intrusive human, it doesn't just spit saliva; it regurgitates foul-smelling, bright green, partially digested contents from the first of its three stomach compartments.

Llama blood is packed with unusually tiny, oval-shaped red blood cells and record-high concentrations of hemoglobin, allowing them to haul heavy packs effortlessly in the thin air of the Andes at 13,000 feet.
Because the ancient Incas had no written alphabet, they used spun cords of dyed llama and alpaca wool tied in intricate knots, called 'quipu', to record census data, taxes, and historical calendars.
Llamas make surprisingly fierce livestock guardians on North American ranches, where a single 'guard llama' will bond with a flock of sheep and aggressively charge, kick, and stomp coyotes to death.
Instead of hard hooves that tear up fragile mountain trails, a llama's two-toed foot has soft, leathery pads on the underside that give it goat-like traction on slick rocks.

Scientists actively study llama antibodies, known as 'nanobodies' because they are a fraction of the size of human antibodies, to develop treatments that can slip into microscopic crevices on viruses like influenza and COVID-19.

mammals.name: Pallas's cat
mammals.summary: Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul), also called manul, is a small wild cat with long and dense light grey fur, and rounded ears set low on the sides of the head. Its head-and-body length ranges from 46 to 65 cm (18 to 26 in) with a 21–31 cm (8.3–12.2 in) long bushy tail.
facts: Unlike almost all other small cats, whose pupils constrict into vertical slits in bright light, the Pallas's cat has round pupils just like humans and big roaring lions.
Because of its flat face, low-set ears, and ultra-dense coat, the longest and thickest fur of any wild cat, it has become an internet sensation known for looking perpetually grumpy and dramatic.
In the freezing steppes of Central Asia, a Pallas's cat keeps its sensitive paws off the snow by standing right on top of its own bushy, ringed tail like a built-in fur muff.
Despite looking wide and chubby, a Pallas's cat is mostly fluff; underneath that plush winter coat, its actual body is no heavier than a typical seven-pound housecat.

Its stubby legs make it a terrible sprinter, so instead of chasing prey across the open plains, it freezes flat against the ground to masquerade as a gray boulder or ambushes pikas right at their burrow entrances.
Its ears are set far down on the sides of its head rather than on top, allowing the cat to peek over rocky ledges at prey without revealing its silhouette.

mammals.name: Giant otter
mammals.summary: The giant otter or giant river otter (Pteronura brasiliensis) is a South American carnivorous mammal. It is the longest member of the weasel family, Mustelidae, reaching up to 1.8 m (5 ft 11 in).
facts: Known in South America as the 'lobo del río' (river wolf), the giant otter grows up to six feet long and hunts in noisy, tight-knit family packs that have been filmed killing and eating six-foot caimans and anacondas.
Every individual giant otter has a completely unique pattern of cream-colored blotches on its throat and chin, which researchers use like fingerprints to identify specific animals from afar.

They are the noisiest of all otter species, utilizing a vocabulary of at least nine distinct vocalizations, including submarine-like hums, barks, and ear-splitting 'hah!' alarm snorts that echo down Amazonian tributaries.

When hunting, a giant otter relies on thick, super-sensitive facial whiskers called vibrissae that can detect the tiniest changes in water pressure and turbulence left by fish swimming in pitch-black, muddy water.
Unlike most solitary carnivores, giant otter families dig communal riverside campsites where they clear away all vegetation, trample the mud flat, and maintain shared family latrines.

They consume up to nine pounds of fish and crustaceans every single day, grasping slippery piranhas and catfish in their webbed front paws and always eating them headfirst so the sharp fin spines go down smoothly.

mammals.name: Impala
mammals.summary: The impala or rooibok (Aepyceros melampus, lit. 'black-footed high-horn' in Ancient Greek) is a medium-sized antelope found in eastern and southern Africa.
facts: When startled, an impala can bound 10 feet straight up into the air and cover 33 feet in a single horizontal leap, often jumping purely for joy or to confuse predators by kicking its hind legs in midair.
The impala's name comes from the Zulu word 'im-pala,' and its athleticism is so iconic that Chevrolet named its flagship car after the antelope in 1958, complete with a leaping impala hood emblem.

Along each hind ankle, an impala has a distinctive black tuft of hair covering a specialized scent gland; when leaping over bushes, it kicks out a burst of airborne pheromones that acts as a chemical breadcrumb trail so the herd stays together in chaos.
Look at the rear end of a fleeing impala and you'll spot three vertical black stripes on a white background, a visual bullseye that scientists joke looks exactly like the McDonald's 'M' logo.
Impalas possess a unique dental tool called a 'toothcomb': their lower front incisors are arranged like a fine-toothed comb that rocks slightly in the jaw to scrape ticks and burrs out of their fur.
Female impalas can voluntarily delay giving birth for up to an extra month if the seasonal rains are late and the savanna grass hasn't turned green yet.

mammals.name: Pronghorn
mammals.summary: The pronghorn (UK: , US: ) (Antilocapra americana) is a species of artiodactyl (even-toed, hoofed) mammal indigenous to interior western and central North America. Though not an antelope, it is known colloquially in North America as the American antelope, prong buck, pronghorn antelope, and prairie antelope, because it closely resembles the antelopes of the Old World and fills a similar ecological niche due to parallel evolution.
facts: The pronghorn is a 'ghost of evolution': it can sprint at 55 miles per hour and sustain 30 mph for miles because it evolved to outrun the extinct American cheetah (*Miracinonyx*), which vanished at the end of the last Ice Age.
Although everyone in North America calls it an 'antelope,' it isn't related to true African antelopes; its closest living relatives on the evolutionary tree are actually giraffes and okapis.
It is the only horned mammal in the world that sheds its outer horn sheaths every single year, and the only one with branched ('pronged') horn sheaths growing over a permanent bony core.

Despite being able to outrun any living predator in North America, pronghorns are notoriously terrible jumpers and will almost always crawl awkwardly underneath barbed-wire fences rather than hop over a three-foot rail.

When alarmed, a pronghorn contracts specialized muscles to flare the bright white hairs on its rump into two giant, reflective rosettes visible to other herd members up to two miles away across the prairie.
To fuel its marathon running, a pronghorn has a windpipe nearly two inches wide and lungs and a heart three times larger than those of a domestic sheep of the same body weight.

mammals.name: Water buffalo
mammals.summary: The water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), also called domestic water buffalo, Asian water buffalo, and Asiatic water buffalo, is a large domesticated bovine originating in South and Southeast Asia descended from the wild water buffalo. Today, it is also kept in regions including Italy, the Balkans, Australia, the Americas, and parts of Africa.
facts: More human beings on Earth depend on the water buffalo than on any other domesticated animal, using them as 'living tractors' to plow flooded rice paddies where heavy mechanical tractors would sink into the mud.

Authentic Italian 'Mozzarella di Bufala' is made exclusively from water buffalo milk, which has twice the butterfat content of cow's milk and is bright white because buffaloes convert yellow beta-carotene into clear vitamin A.

A water buffalo's wide, splayed hooves have flexible joints that spread out like snowshoes when stepping into deep swamp muck and contract cleanly when pulled out so the animal never gets suctioned stuck.
Wild water buffaloes boast the widest horn span of any living bovid, with sweeping crescent horns that can measure more than six feet from tip to tip along the curve.

Because they have only one-tenth as many sweat glands per square inch as domestic cattle, water buffaloes can easily overheat in the tropical sun unless they submerge themselves nose-deep in muddy wallows.
Despite carrying two different numbers of chromosomes, river buffaloes have 50 while swamp buffaloes have 48, the two types can still interbreed and produce fertile offspring with 49 chromosomes.

mammals.name: Amazon river dolphin
mammals.summary: The Amazon river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis), also known as the boto, bufeo or pink river dolphin, is a species of toothed whale endemic to South America and is classified in the family Iniidae. Three subspecies are currently recognized: I. g.
facts: Also called the 'boto,' this freshwater dolphin starts life gray and gradually turns bubblegum pink as it ages, especially the males, whose skin flushes brighter pink from roughhousing scar tissue and excitement.

Unlike marine dolphins whose neck vertebrae are fused together for high-speed swimming, the Amazon river dolphin has unfused neck bones, allowing it to turn its head 90 degrees left and right to weave between flooded rainforest tree trunks.

In Amazonian folklore, the boto is believed to shapeshift at night into a handsome man in a white suit and straw hat who charms village women at riverside dances, wearing the hat to hide the blowhole on top of his head.
During the mating season, adult males try to impress females by swimming around carrying heavy props in their jaws, such as branches, clumps of clay, or even live river turtles.

Its long, forceps-like snout contains two different kinds of teeth; sharp cones in the front for grabbing armored catfish and flat, molar-like pegs in the back for crushing hard-shelled river crabs and turtles.
When swimming through shallow, tangled flooded forests, it often flips completely upside down so its bulbous forehead ('melon') doesn't block its downward view of the muddy river bottom.

mammals.name: Jaguarundi
mammals.summary: The jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi;  or ) is a wild cat native to the Americas. Its range extends from central Argentina in the south and much of South America east of the Andes, through Central America, and into northern Mexico.
facts: With its flattened head, tiny rounded ears, elongated body, and short legs, the jaguarundi looks so much like a giant weasel or otter that it is known in parts of Latin America as the 'otter cat' (*gato nutria*).

It has the largest vocal repertoire of almost any small wild cat, producing at least 13 distinct calls, including a bird-like chirp, whistle, purr, and chatter that sounds nothing like a normal housecat.
While nearly all other wild cats are strictly nocturnal or crepuscular, the jaguarundi does almost all of its hunting in broad daylight, resting at night in hollow logs.
Single litters can contain kittens of two completely different color morphs, some charcoal-black ('eyra') and others rusty chestnut-red, born to the exact same mother.
Genetic testing revealed a surprise: despite its tiny nine-pound size and bizarre weasel-like build, the jaguarundi's closest living relative is the 150-pound mountain lion (cougar).
It can leap six feet straight into the air from a standing start to snatch low-flying tinamous and quail right out of the air.

mammals.name: Alpaca
mammals.summary: The alpaca (Lama pacos) is a domesticated species of South American camelid. Traditionally, alpacas were kept in herds that grazed on the level heights of the Andes of Southern Peru, Western Bolivia, Ecuador, and Northern Chile.
facts: Unlike sheep's wool, alpaca fiber contains zero lanolin (grease), making it naturally hypoallergenic, water-repellent, and remarkably flame-resistant.

There are two distinct breeds of alpaca: the 'Huacaya,' which looks like a plush, fluffy teddy bear, and the 'Suri,' whose silky fleece grows in long, pencil-thin dreadlocks that hang nearly to the ground.

An entire herd of alpacas uses a single communal bathroom spot in their pasture, lining up to use the exact same dung pile, which keeps the rest of their grazing grass clean and free of intestinal parasites.

When contented or curious, alpacas communicate with a gentle, musical 'hmmm' humming sound, while danger triggers a high-pitched, warbling alarm call that sounds like a tropical bird or a squeaky toy.

During the height of the Inca Empire, alpaca garments were considered the 'cloth of gold', far more valuable than silver or gold bullion, and paying soldiers with spun alpaca cloth was a standard royal reward.
Alpacas only have lower front teeth and a tough, leathery dental pad on top, allowing them to snip off meadow grass neatly like garden shears without pulling up the roots and ruining the pasture.

mammals.name: Springbok
mammals.summary: The springbok or springbuck (Antidorcas marsupialis) is an antelope found mainly in south and southwest Africa. The sole living member of the genus Antidorcas, this bovid was first described by the German zoologist Eberhard August Wilhelm von Zimmermann in 1780.
facts: The springbok gets its Afrikaans name ('jumping buck') from a bizarre behavior called 'pronking,' in which it stiffens its legs, arches its back, points its head down, and bounces repeatedly six feet into the air like it has invisible pogo sticks for legs.

Running down the middle of its back is a hidden pocket of skin lined with snow-white hair; when the springbok pronks or gets startled, it flips this pocket inside-out into a dazzling white fan while releasing a sweet, honey-like scent.

Before fences cross-hatched southern Africa, springboks formed 'trekbokken'; mega-herds so gargantuan that an 1896 migration was estimated to be 15 miles wide and 100 miles long, taking days to pass a single town.

They can survive for years in the bone-dry Kalahari Desert without ever drinking a single drop of liquid water, extracting all the moisture they need by feeding at night when desert shrubs absorb damp air.
South Africa's national sports teams, most famously the world-champion national rugby team, are universally known as the 'Springboks' and wear the leaping antelope on their green-and-gold jerseys.
Both males and females grow black, lyre-shaped, ringed horns that hook inward at the tips.

mammals.name: Black-footed ferret
mammals.summary: The black-footed ferret (Mustela nigripes), also known as the American polecat or prairie dog hunter, is a mustelid species native to central North America. It is roughly the size of a mink and is similar in appearance to the European polecat and the Asian steppe polecat.
facts: Every single black-footed ferret alive today, around 300 in the wild, is descended from just seven founding individuals rescued from a ranch dog's discovery near Meeteetse, Wyoming, in 1981 after the species was declared extinct.

In 2020, a black-footed ferret named Elizabeth Ann became the first endangered species native to North America to be successfully cloned, using frozen cells preserved in a 'Frozen Zoo' since 1988 from a wild female named Willa.

Roughly 90 percent of a black-footed ferret's diet consists exclusively of prairie dogs, and a single ferret family eats about 250 prairie dogs a year while moving right into their empty underground burrows.
Like a comic-book burglar, it wears a natural black bandit mask across its eyes and four matching black 'boots' on its feet.

During conservation reintroduction programs, biologists have had to vaccinate wild prairie dogs against sylvatic plague using peanut-butter-flavored bait pellets dropped by drones so the ferrets' food supply doesn't vanish.
They spend up to 90 percent of their lives completely underground in pitch-dark prairie dog tunnels, emerging mainly at night when their eyes shine bright emerald-green in spotlights.

mammals.name: Capybara
mammals.summary: The capybara (  kap-ih-BAR-uh) or greater capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile. It is a semiaquatic herbivore that inhabits savannas and dense forests, living near and in bodies of freshwater and feeding mainly on grasses and aquatic plants.
facts: In the 16th century, the Vatican officially classified the capybara as a 'fish' after Venezuelan missionaries wrote to the Pope explaining the furry, webbed-footed rodent spent its life in water, making it legal for Catholics to eat during Lent.
Known across the internet as 'nature's ottoman,' capybaras are so famously chill and non-aggressive that wild birds, monkeys, rabbits, turtles, and even juvenile caimans routinely nap on their backs.
Like rabbits, capybaras practice 'coprophagy', eating their own nutrient-rich morning droppings so their gut bacteria have a second chance to break down tough wetland grasses.

Their eyes, ears, and nostrils are all positioned in a neat line along the very top of their rectangular heads, allowing them to stay 95 percent submerged like a hippo while watching for jaguars and anacondas.
A capybara can hold its breath underwater for up to five minutes and frequently takes full naps along muddy river bottoms with only the tip of its nose poking above the surface.
Dominant males have a large, dark, hairless bump right on top of their snouts called a 'morrillo,' which is a specialized scent gland they rub against trees and twigs to mark their territory.
The capybara is the largest living rodent in the world, weighing up to 140 pounds.
Capybaras have slightly webbed feet and can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes to evade predators.
Their eyes, ears, and nostrils sit aligned along the very top of their heads so they can see and breathe while almost fully submerged.
Like guinea pigs, capybaras cannot synthesize their own vitamin C and get it from fresh aquatic grasses.

mammals.name: Mandrill
mammals.summary: The mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx) is a large Old World monkey native to west central Africa. It is one of the most colorful mammals in the world, with red and blue skin on its face and posterior.
facts: Charles Darwin wrote in *The Descent of Man* that 'no other member in the whole class of mammals is colored in so extraordinary a manner as the adult male mandrill'; whose neon blue and scarlet face is matched by an equally bright rear end.

The vivid blue ridges on a male mandrill's snout aren't caused by blue pigment at all; they are produced by 'structural coloration,' where microscopically aligned collagen fibers scatter light in the exact same physical way a bluejay's feathers do.

When a mandrill bares its three-inch canine teeth in what looks like a huge, toothy grin while shaking its head, it isn't angry, in mandrill body language, that 'silent bared-teeth face' is actually a peaceful greeting.

A dominant alpha male's scarlet nose and rump literally glow brighter as his testosterone rises; if he is overthrown by a rival, his testosterone plummets and his bright facial colors fade into dull gray.
Mandrills gather in the largest hordes of any non-human primate on Earth, forming rainforest super-troops in Gabon that have been filmed numbering more than 800 individuals.
They have oversized cheek pouches equal in volume to their actual stomachs, allowing them to stuff two full meals of fruit and seeds into their faces before retreating up a tree to chew in safety.

mammals.name: Caracal
mammals.summary: The caracal (Caracal caracal) is a wild cat native to Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, and arid areas of Pakistan and northwestern India. It is characterised by a robust build, long legs, a short face, long tufted ears, relatively short tail, and long canine teeth.
facts: A caracal can leap 10 feet straight up into the air and bat down two or three flying pigeons in a single bound with its oversized paws, twisting its body like a gymnast to land on its feet.
The name 'caracal' comes from the Turkish word *karakulak*, meaning 'black ear,' referring to the dramatic, two-inch-long black feather-like tufts on the tips of its ears.

Each of a caracal's tufted ears is controlled by 20 independent muscles that swivel like twin radar dishes to pinpoint the rustle of a desert rodent, and flick in rapid patterns to signal moods to other caracals.

In ancient India and Persia, royalty kept trained caracals like hunting falcons and placed wagers on which cat could knock down the most birds from a flock of pigeons feeding in an arena, giving rise to the expression 'to put a cat among the pigeons.'
Despite its long, tufted ears, the caracal is not a true lynx; DNA shows its closest living relatives are the African golden cat and the serval.
It can survive for months in arid scrublands without drinking water, getting all the hydration it needs from the body fluids of its prey.

mammals.name: Wombat
mammals.summary:
The common wombat (Vombatus ursinus), also known as a bare-nosed wombat, is a marsupial, one of three extant species of wombats and the sole extant member of the genus Vombatus. It has three subspecies: Vombatus ursinus hirsutus, found on the Australian mainland;
Vombatus ursinus tasmaniensis (Tasmanian wombat), found in Tasmania; and Vombatus ursinus ursinus (Bass Strait wombat), found on Flinders Island and Maria Island in the Bass Strait.
facts: The wombat is the only animal on Earth that produces cube-shaped poop, up to 100 neat, two-centimeter dice every single night, which it stacks on top of rocks and fallen logs as territorial signposts that won't roll away.

In 2021, researchers won an Ig Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering *how* wombats make square poop: the last section of a wombat's 30-foot intestine has two stiff grooves and two flexible bands that mold the drying feces into sharp corners with every contraction.

A wombat's rear end is reinforced by a thick, armor-like shield of cartilage, bone, fat, and tough skin; when chased into its burrow by a dingo or Tasmanian devil, it plugs the tunnel with its butt and crushes the predator's skull against the tunnel roof.
Because wombats spend hours every day digging massive underground tunnel complexes, a female wombat's pouch faces backward toward her rear legs so she doesn't shovel dirt onto her baby.
Despite looking like a sleepy, stubby-legged barrel on paws, a startled wombat can sprint at 25 miles per hour, nearly as fast as Usain Bolt, for up to 90 seconds.
All 24 of a wombat's teeth, including its molars, not just its front incisors, never stop growing for its entire life to compensate for the grit and tough Australian grasses it grinds down.
Wombats are the only animals in the world that produce cube-shaped poop, which keeps their territorial markers from rolling away.
A female wombat's marsupial pouch faces backward toward her rear so it doesn't fill with dirt while she digs burrows.
Wombats have a tough shield of cartilage in their rump that they use to block tunnel entrances and crush predators' skulls against the burrow roof.
Like rodents, wombats have rootless teeth that grow continuously throughout their lives to compensate for chewing gritty roots.

mammals.name: Indian rhinoceros
mammals.summary: The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis), also known as the greater one-horned rhinoceros, great Indian rhinoceros or Indian rhino, is a rhinoceros species native to the Indian subcontinent. It is the second largest living rhinoceros and the largest in Asia, with adult males weighing 2.07–2.2 t (2.04–2.17 long tons; 2.28–2.43 short tons) and adult females 1.6 t (1.6 long tons; 1.8 short tons).
facts: When the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer drew his famous 1515 woodcut of a rhino, without ever seeing one in person, he based it on descriptions of an Indian rhinoceros sent to King Manuel I of Portugal, whose heavy skin folds really do look like medieval plate armor.
Along the edges of those thick, rivet-studded skin plates, an Indian rhino's hide is up to 1.5 inches thick, yet the skin tucked inside the creases is soft and sensitive enough to get sunburned.
Unlike African rhinos, which use their horns as primary weapons in fights, the Indian rhinoceros fights using razor-sharp, tusk-like lower incisor teeth that can slash deep wounds in rivals.
Despite weighing more than two tons, an Indian rhino is a fantastic swimmer that regularly dives underwater to pluck aquatic plants from the river bottom and can run at 34 miles per hour on land.
Its single black horn is not made of bone; it is composed entirely of densely packed keratin fibers, the exact same protein found in human fingernails and hair.

By the early 1900s, relentless hunting had reduced the wild population in India's Kaziranga region to fewer than two dozen individuals before strict protection helped rebound the species to over 4,000 today.

mammals.name: Sloth bear
mammals.summary: The sloth bear (Melursus ursinus), also known as the Indian bear, is a myrmecophagous bear species native to the Indian subcontinent. It feeds on fruits, ants and termites.
facts: When European naturalists first examined the skin and skull of a sloth bear in 1791, they were so baffled by its long curved claws and missing upper front teeth that they officially classified it as a giant species of tree sloth ('Bradypus ursinus').

That gap where its two upper front incisors should be is an evolutionary adaptation: the bear folds its long, flexible lips into a tube, seals its nostrils shut using muscular flaps, and sucks termites out of mounds like a high-powered vacuum cleaner.
A sloth bear vacuuming up termites makes such a loud, rhythmic sucking and blowing racket that human trackers can hear it from nearly 600 feet away through the Indian jungle.
Mother sloth bears are the only bears that routinely carry their cubs around on their shaggy backs for the first nine months of life, even while climbing trees or fighting off predators.

Because sloth bears share forests with ambush-hunting Bengal tigers and have poor eyesight, they have evolved an explosive, hyper-aggressive defensive reflex, often charging and mauling tigers (and startled humans) rather than backing down.
Rudyard Kipling's beloved character Baloo from *The Jungle Book* is a sloth bear, In Hindi, the word for this species is literally *bhalu*.

mammals.name: Sand cat
mammals.summary: The sand cat (Felis margarita) is a small wild cat that inhabits sandy and stony deserts far from water sources. With its sandy to light grey fur, it is well camouflaged in a desert environment.
facts: The bottoms of a sand cat's paws are covered in a dense mat of stiff, wiry hair that insulates its feet from 125°F desert sand and acts like snowshoes so the cat leaves almost zero footprints for predators or researchers to track.
Even when fully grown to adulthood, a sand cat retains the wide head, enormous eyes, and tiny four-pound stature of a three-month-old domestic kitten.
Instead of meowing during the breeding season, sand cats call out across the empty Sahara and Arabian deserts with a sharp, high-pitched bark that sounds remarkably like a small chihuahua.

Its giant ear canals and middle-ear chambers ('auditory bullae') are twice the size of a domestic cat's, tuned to amplify the faint vibrations of beetles and gerbils scurrying beneath the sand up to 1,500 feet away.
Because its sandy yellow coat reflects infrared heat and it spends daylight hours underground, a sand cat doesn't even show up on standard thermal-imaging cameras at night.
When it catches a venomous desert horned viper, the sand cat stuns the snake with lightning-fast blows to the head before biting through its neck.

mammals.name: Okapi
mammals.summary: The okapi (; Okapia johnstoni), also known as forest giraffe and zebra giraffe, is an artiodactyl mammal that is endemic to the northeast Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is the only species in the genus Okapia.
facts: Although its bold black-and-white striped hindquarters make it look like a cross between a zebra and a horse, the okapi is actually the only living relative of the giraffe.
Just like its giraffe cousin, an okapi has a dark blue-black prehensile tongue up to 18 inches long, long enough that it can lick its own eyeballs clean and flick insects right out of its ears.

For decades, Western scientists dismissed reports from the Mbuti people of the Congo Basin about a striped 'forest horse' as a mythical cryptid on par with the unicorn, until Sir Harry Johnston sent an intact skin and skull to London in 1901.
Between the toes of all four feet, an okapi has specialized scent glands that leave behind an invisible, tar-like smelly residue with every footstep to mark its territory on the rainforest floor.
To stay hidden from its primary predator, the leopard, a mother okapi and her calf communicate using infrasound; deep, rumbling vibrations below 20 hertz that humans and leopards cannot hear at all.
Newborn okapi calves have a remarkable survival trick: they do not defecate for the first four to eight weeks of life so that their scent never reveals their hiding spot in the undergrowth.
Although its zebra-striped hindquarters make it look like an equine, the okapi is the only living relative of the giraffe.
An okapi's prehensile tongue is so long, up to 18 inches, that it can lick its own eyelids and clean inside its ears.
Secretive and solitary in the Ituri Rainforest, the okapi remained unknown to Western science until 1901.
Okapis communicate with their calves using infrasound frequencies too low for human ears to detect.

mammals.name: Striped hyena
mammals.summary: The striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena) is a species of hyena native to North and East Africa, the Middle East, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It is the only extant species in the genus Hyaena.
facts: When threatened or trying to intimidate a rival, a striped hyena can erect the long, coarse hair along its spine into a dramatic mane that makes the animal look nearly 40 percent larger than it actually is.
Unlike its famous cousin the spotted ('laughing') hyena, the striped hyena is almost completely silent and solitary, foraging alone in the dead of night.

Its conical premolar teeth and massive jaw muscles exert enough crushing force to pulverize the thickest camel and ox femurs into powder, allowing it to digest bone mineral and marrow that no other predator can touch.

When cornered by larger predators like lions or packs of shepherd dogs, a striped hyena will sometimes drop limp to the ground and play dead with such commitment that it won't flinch even while being bitten and dragged.
Inside its anal pouch is a specialized scent gland that can flip inside-out like a pink flower to smear a pungent, creamy-yellow paste called 'hyena butter' onto grass stalks.
In ancient Egypt, striped hyenas were occasionally captured, tethered, and force-fed roasted duck and meat until they were plump enough to be hunted or eaten by the nobility.

mammals.name: Aardvark
mammals.summary: The aardvark ( ; Orycteropus afer) is a medium-sized, burrowing, nocturnal mammal native to Africa. The aardvark is the only living member of the genus Orycteropus, the family Orycteropodidae and the order Tubulidentata.
facts: The aardvark is the only surviving species in the entire mammalian order *Tubulidentata* ('tube-toothed'): instead of having pulp cavities or enamel, each flat-topped cheek tooth is made of up to 1,500 microscopic hexagonal tubes of dentin glued together.
Its name comes directly from Afrikaans and Dutch for 'earth pig,' and because it begins with a double 'A,' it sits first in almost every English dictionary.
An aardvark can dig through sun-baked, concrete-hard termite mounds at a rate of two feet in 15 seconds; faster than a team of several men digging with shovels.
While burrowing headfirst into dirt and swarming ants, an aardvark seals its nostrils shut with dense hair and muscular valves, and folds its long, rabbit-like ears backward to keep dirt out.

It is the sole pollinator and seed-disperser of the 'aardvark cucumber' (*Cucumis humifructus*), a bizarre African plant that grows its fruit underground specifically so aardvarks will dig it up for water and bury the seeds in their fertilized dung.
Its sticky, worm-like tongue measures up to 12 inches long and can lap up 50,000 ants and termites in a single night.
The name 'aardvark' comes from Afrikaans for 'earth pig', though it isn't related to pigs at all.
The aardvark is the sole surviving species in the entire mammalian order Tubulidentata.
An aardvark can dig a two-foot-deep burrow in under 30 seconds and eat up to 50,000 ants and termites in a single night.
Aardvark teeth have no enamel or roots; instead they are made of bundles of hexagonal tubes that grow continuously.

mammals.name: Binturong
mammals.summary: The binturong (Arctictis binturong) (; bin-TURE-ong, BIN-ture-ong), also known as the bearcat, is an arboreal viverrid native to South and Southeast Asia. It is the only species in the genus Arctictis, and it is divided into nine subspecies.
facts: The binturong smells unmistakably like hot, buttered movie-theater popcorn, a warm aroma caused by a chemical compound called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (the exact same molecule created when corn kernels pop or bread crusts bake) found in its urine and scent glands.

Along with the South American kinkajou, the binturong is one of only two carnivorans in the entire world equipped with a fully muscular, prehensile tail that acts like a fifth hand with a leathery grip pad at the tip.
Popularly called the 'bearcat,' it is neither a bear nor a cat, and it can rotate its hind ankles a full 180 degrees so its claws still grip tree bark when it climbs straight down a trunk headfirst.
When happy or feeling affectionate, a binturong makes a series of loud, rhythmic chuckling sounds and soft purrs, whereas an annoyed binturong lets out a high-pitched scream.
It is a crucial rainforest gardener because it is one of the very few animals with digestive enzymes strong enough to soften the tough outer coat of strangler fig seeds so they can sprout.
Female binturongs are one of the few mammals capable of embryonic diapause, pausing the development of fertilized embryos inside the womb until environmental conditions are ideal to give birth.
The binturong, also called the bearcat, smells unmistakably like hot buttered popcorn due to the compound 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline in its scent glands.
Along with the kinkajou, the binturong is one of only two carnivores in the world with a truly prehensile, muscular gripping tail.
Binturongs are crucial rainforest seed dispersers for strangler figs because their digestive enzymes soften the fig seeds' tough outer coats.

mammals.name: Porcupine
mammals.summary: The North American porcupine (Erethizon dorsatum), also known as the Canadian porcupine, is a large quill-covered rodent in the New World porcupine family. It is the second largest rodent in North America after the North American beaver (Castor canadensis).
facts: Contrary to cartoon myth, porcupines cannot shoot or throw their quills; the quills detach on contact because their tips are covered in up to 800 microscopic, backward-facing barbs that expand when warmed by a predator's body moisture.

Because porcupines frequently fall out of trees and accidentally impale themselves on their own 30,000 quills, their quills are coated in natural fatty acids with antibiotic properties that prevent self-inflicted punctures from getting infected.

Wait before popping a balloon near a North American porcupine: Those barbed quills slide into flesh with less than half the pressure of a hypodermic needle because the microscopic scales reduce friction on the way in.

Porcupines have an insatiable craving for salt and sodium; in campgrounds, they routinely chew up wooden canoe paddles, axe handles, plywood, and even rubber car brake lines just to lick up the salty residue of human sweat or road salt.

A female porcupine is fertile for only 8 to 12 hours once a year; to persuade her to lower her spiky quills, a male stands on his hind legs and sprays her from head to foot with a high-pressure stream of urine.

Baby porcupines, officially called 'porcupettes', are born with soft, flexible quills so they don't injure their mother in the birth canal, but the quills harden into sharp spines within an hour of hitting the air.

mammals.name: Mongoose
mammals.summary: The Indian grey mongoose or Asian grey mongoose (Urva edwardsii) is a mongoose species native to the Indian subcontinent and West Asia. It is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List.
facts: A mongoose can take a bite from a king cobra and keep fighting because its muscle receptors for acetylcholine have a mutated shape, complemented by sugar molecules that physically block neurotoxins from binding and paralyzing its nerves.

In 1883, Hawaiian sugar cane planters imported Indian mongooses to wipe out invasive rats; the plan backfired spectacularly because rats are nocturnal and mongooses are diurnal, so the two species barely crossed paths and the mongooses ate Hawaii's native birds instead.

To crack open hard-shelled bird eggs or giant millipedes, a mongoose stands on its hind legs, grips the prize in its front paws, and hikes it backward between its legs like an NFL center snapping a football against a rock.

Banded and dwarf mongooses live in matriarchal mobs where all the adult females synchronize their pregnancies to give birth on the exact same night, preventing the dominant female from killing anyone else's pups.
When mobbing a venomous snake, a mongoose fluffs every hair on its body to double its apparent width, forcing the snake to strike at empty fur rather than flesh.
Rudyard Kipling immortalized the Indian gray mongoose in his 1894 story *Rikki-Tikki-Tavi*, accurately describing how a mongoose's eyes turn bright red when its blood pressure spikes in battle.

mammals.name: Capuchin monkey
mammals.summary: The capuchin monkeys () are New World monkeys of the subfamily Cebinae. They are considered among the most intelligent primates and are known for their complex foraging skills, such as tool use to crack open nuts.
facts: White-throated capuchin monkeys receive their name from 16th-century Franciscan friars of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin, who wore brown robes with large white cowls that looked just like the monkey's fur markings, and the coffee drink 'cappuccino' gets its name from the exact same friars.

Wild bearded capuchins in Brazil have entered their own Stone Age: for at least 3,000 years, they have selected heavy quartz hammerstones weighing up to a third of their own body weight to smash open rock-hard palm nuts on flat stone anvils.

During the rainy season, capuchin monkeys rub toxic millipedes and crushed citrus leaves all over their fur, sharing the bug-juice 'lotion' in groups because the millipedes' defensive benzoquinones act as a potent natural mosquito and tick repellent.
To show romantic interest, a female capuchin raises her eyebrows, grins, and throws pebbles directly at the male she likes until he notices her.

Male capuchins engage in 'urine washing', peeing directly into their hands and rubbing it thoroughly into their palms and the soles of their feet, which cools them down, improves grip on branches, and signals calm confidence to troop mates.
When classic organ-grinders performed on Victorian street corners, the clever little monkey in a velvet vest tipping its hat to collect coins was almost always a capuchin.

mammals.name: Sun bear
mammals.summary: The sun bear (Helarctos malayanus) is a bear species in the family Ursidae found in the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. It is the only species in the genus Helarctos and the smallest bear species, standing nearly 70 cm (28 in) at the shoulder and weighing 25–65 kg (55–143 lb).
facts: The sun bear is the smallest of all eight bear species, yet it possesses the longest tongue of any bear, stretching a ridiculous 10 inches long to slurp honey and bee larvae out of deep tree cavities.

Its loose, saggy black skin is an intentional survival feature: if a tiger or leopard bites a sun bear by the scruff, the bear has enough slack skin to spin completely around inside its own hide and bite the predator back in the face.

Because sun bears love standing upright on their hind legs with their saggy skin pooled in wrinkles around their hips, a Chinese zoo in 2023 had to issue an official press statement proving its sun bear wasn't a human employee in a cheap bear costume.
It gets its name from the golden, crescent-shaped patch of fur on its chest, which Southeast Asian folklore says represents the rising sun, and no two sun bears have the exact same chest marking.

Mother sun bears have been photographed cradling their tiny cubs in their arms while walking upright on two legs and making human-like facial expressions that mimic each other with split-second precision.

Armed with four-inch sickle-shaped claws and powerful canine teeth, sun bears act as 'forest engineers' by ripping open solid hardwood trees, creating nesting hollows later used by hornbills and flying squirrels.

mammals.name: Sugar glider
mammals.summary: The sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps) is a small, omnivorous, arboreal, and nocturnal gliding possum. The common name refers to its predilection for sugary foods such as sap and nectar and its ability to glide through the air, much like a flying squirrel.
facts: A sugar glider can launch itself from a treetop and glide more than 150 feet, half the length of a football field, using a furry membrane called a 'patagium' that stretches from its fifth finger to its first ankle bone.
In flight, it steers by curving its bushy tail like a rudder and adjusting the tension of its wrist membranes to bank left, bank right, and swoop upward right before landing softly on all fours.

Male sugar gliders appear to go bald as they reach maturity, but that bare patch right on top of the forehead is actually a prominent scent gland used to rub pheromones onto the chests of every member in their family colony.
They get their name from a sweet tooth for sugary tree sap and eucalyptus gum, which they harvest by gouging bark open with their chisel-like lower incisor teeth.

When bitterly cold rain hits the Australian forest, a colony of up to 12 sugar gliders huddles in a tree hollow and enters 'torpor', dropping their body temperature to 50°F and slowing their heartbeats to survive without eating.
Despite looking almost identical to North America's flying squirrel, the sugar glider is a marsupial more closely related to kangaroos and koalas, a textbook case of convergent evolution.

mammals.name: Chital
mammals.summary: The chital (Axis axis; ), also called spotted deer and axis deer, is a deer species native to the Indian subcontinent. It was first described by Johann Christian Polycarp Erxleben in 1777.
facts: Also called the 'axis deer,' the chital has forged an extraordinary mutual alarm network with Northern plains gray langur monkeys: the deer have a superior sense of smell while the monkeys have a vantage point in the treetops, so both species eavesdrop on each other's tiger alarm calls.

Even better for the chital, langurs are notoriously messy eaters that drop tons of tender leaves and fruits from the high canopy, so herds of chital follow troops of monkeys through the forest like vacuum cleaners.
Unlike almost all other deer species, whose fawns lose their white spots as they grow up, the chital keeps its dappled white polka dots on a cinnamon coat for its entire life.
A chital's high-pitched alarm bark is one of the primary audio cues used by wildlife guides and filmmakers in India to track the stealthy movements of Bengal tigers.

Because chital live in tropical climates without harsh winters, bucks do not shed their three-pronged, three-foot antlers on a strict seasonal calendar; you can spot bucks with velvet antlers and hard antlers in the same herd any month of the year.
Introduced as an exotic gift to the island of Molokai in 1868 by King Kamehameha V, chital populations in Hawaii exploded without tigers or leopards to keep them in check.

mammals.name: Naked mole-rat
mammals.summary: The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber), also known as the sand puppy, is a burrowing rodent native to the Horn of Africa and parts of Kenya, notably in Somali regions. It is the only species in the genus Heterocephalus.
facts: The naked mole-rat is the only cold-blooded (thermoconforming) mammal known to science, and alongside the Damaraland mole-rat, the only mammal that lives in a 'eusocial' insect-like colony with a single breeding queen and sterile worker castes, just like bees or ants.
It can survive for up to 18 minutes in zero-oxygen environments without suffering any brain damage by switching its metabolism from glucose to fructose, the exact chemical pathway plants use.
Because their skin lacks a neurotransmitter called 'Substance P,' naked mole-rats feel zero pain when exposed to acid or fiery chili-pepper capsaicin.

While a normal house mouse lives about three years, naked mole-rats can live past 37 years without ever showing standard signs of mammalian aging, and their tissues produce an ultra-heavy form of hyaluronic acid that makes them nearly immune to cancer.
A naked mole-rat digs tunnels with its massive front incisor teeth, which actually grow right through its lips so the animal can gnaw through hard dirt with its mouth completely closed.
Twenty-five percent of a naked mole-rat's entire muscle mass is dedicated strictly to its jaws, and it can move its two lower front teeth independently like a pair of chopsticks.
Naked mole-rats are one of only two eusocial mammals, living in underground colonies ruled by a single breeding queen like bees or ants.
They are virtually insensitive to acid pain and can survive up to 18 minutes in zero-oxygen environments by metabolizing fructose like plants.
A naked mole-rat can move its prominent front incisors independently like a pair of chopsticks.
Despite being mouse-sized, naked mole-rats can live over 30 years and show extraordinary resistance to cancer.

mammals.name: Serval
mammals.summary: The serval (Leptailurus serval) is a wild small cat native to Africa. It is widespread in sub-Saharan countries, where it inhabits grasslands, wetlands, moorlands and bamboo thickets.
facts: Proportionally, the serval boasts the longest legs and the largest ears of any member of the cat family; if a domestic housecat had ears scaled like a serval's, they would be the size of dinner plates.

Those giant satellite-dish ears allow a serval to hunt almost entirely by sound in waist-high grass, pinpointing rodents tunneling underground before leaping up to nine feet into the air to pounce vertically.
With a hunting success rate of roughly 50 percent, catching prey on one out of every two pounces, the serval is far more accurate than a lion (around 25%) or a leopard (around 35%).

On the backs of its black ears are two bold, bright white oval spots called 'ocelli' (false eyes), which help kittens follow their mother through tall savanna grass and fool predators sneaking up from behind.
A serval's extra-long front leg bones and elongated foot bones ('metapodals') double as specialized fishing poles for reaching deep into rodent burrows or slapping frogs out of marsh water.
Unlike almost all other cats, a serval loves playing with its food, tossing captured mice, snakes, and birds into the air and batting them around for minutes before eating.

mammals.name: White rhinoceros
mammals.summary: The white rhinoceros, white rhino or square-lipped rhinoceros (Ceratotherium simum) is the largest extant species of rhinoceros. It has a wide mouth used for grazing and is the most social of all rhino species.
facts: The white rhinoceros isn't white at all; its name is a linguistic accident from the Afrikaans word 'wyd' (meaning 'wide'), referring to its wide, square, lawnmower-like upper lip, which early English settlers misheard as 'white.'
Because that wide mouth is built for grazing grass while the black rhino's hooked lip is built for browsing bushes, the two species can share the exact same territory without ever competing for food.
While other rhinos are famously grumpy loners, female white rhinos and their calves form affectionate social groups properly called a 'crash' of up to 14 individuals.

The northern white rhinoceros subspecies is functionally extinct, with only two females, a mother and daughter named Najin and Fatu, left on Earth under 24-hour armed guard at Kenya's Ol Pejeta Conservancy.

To keep cool and rid itself of ticks, a white rhino rolls in mud wallows that dry into a crust; when it rubs that mud off on a favorite tree stump or boulder, it polishes the wood or stone smooth over generations.

Dominant bulls mark the borders of their territory by backing up to communal dung heaps called 'middens' and kicking their hind legs through the pile so their feet track their scent for hundreds of yards.

mammals.name: Gibbon
mammals.summary: The lar gibbon (Hylobates lar), also known as the white-handed gibbon, is an endangered primate in the gibbon family, Hylobatidae. It is one of the better-known gibbons and is often kept in captivity.
facts: Swinging hand-over-hand through the rainforest canopy in a motion called 'brachiation,' a gibbon can rocket from branch to branch at up to 35 miles per hour and clear 50-foot gaps in a single fling.
To prevent its wrists from snapping or dislocating during those high-speed aerial swings, the gibbon evolved a unique ball-and-socket wrist joint that swivels freely like a human shoulder.

Every morning at dawn, mated pairs of gibbons sit in the highest treetops and belt out intricate, synchronized 'duet songs' that echo for up to two miles through the jungle to announce their marriage and territory.
Although most people call them monkeys, gibbons are tail-less 'lesser apes'; meaning they are more closely related to humans and gorillas than to any monkey.
When walking along a wide tree branch or across the ground, a gibbon walks completely upright on two legs while holding both long arms high above its head like a tightrope walker for balance.

In 2017, archeologists excavating the 2,200-year-old tomb of Lady Xia, the grandmother of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, discovered the skeleton of a royal pet gibbon belonging to a completely extinct species (*Junzi imperialis*).

mammals.name: Armadillo
mammals.summary: The nine-banded armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus), also called the nine-banded long-nosed armadillo or common armadillo, is a species of armadillo native to South America. The Mexican long-nosed armadillo of North America was formerly treated as a subspecies of the nine-banded armadillo.
facts: The nine-banded armadillo is the only mammal that gives birth to genetically identical quadruplets every single time: a single fertilized egg always splits into four identical embryos.

When a nine-banded armadillo needs to cross a narrow stream, it holds its breath, up to six minutes at a time, and simply walks underwater across the river bottom because its heavy armor makes it sink like a stone.
To swim across a wider river, that same armadillo swallows gulps of air to inflate its stomach and intestines to twice their normal size, turning its digestive tract into an internal pool float.

Despite cartoon depictions, only two species of armadillo, the three-banded armadillos of South America, can actually roll up into a completely sealed, basketball-like sphere; in 2014, FIFA named the Brazilian three-banded armadillo ('Fuleco') its official World Cup mascot.

When startled by an approaching car on a highway, a nine-banded armadillo has a reflex to jump three to four feet straight up into the air, which protects it from coyotes in the wild, but tragically launches it right into car bumpers.

Because their normal body temperature is unusually cool for a mammal (around 90°F), nine-banded armadillos are one of the only animals besides humans that can naturally contract and carry the bacteria that causes leprosy.

mammals.name: Tarsier
mammals.summary: The Philippine tarsier (Carlito syrichta) is a species of tarsier endemic to the Philippines. It is found in the southeastern part of the archipelago, particularly on the islands of Bohol, Samar and Leyte.
facts: Each of a tarsier's gigantic eyeballs is larger and heavier than its entire brain; if a human had eyes scaled to the same proportion, they would be the size of grapefruits.
Because those enormous eyes are wedged tightly into the skull and cannot move in their sockets at all, a tarsier can swivel its head nearly 180 degrees in either direction like an owl.
The tarsier is the only 100-percent carnivorous primate on Earth, refusing fruit and leaves entirely to feast exclusively on live insects, spiders, lizards, frogs, and even small bats.
It gets its name from its absurdly elongated 'tarsus' (ankle) bones, which act as spring-loaded levers to launch the fist-sized primate 40 times its own body length from tree trunk to tree trunk.

Philippine tarsiers communicate on a secret ultrasonic channel, sending out high-pitched alarm calls at 70 kilohertz, more than three times higher than the upper limit of human hearing and even higher than many bats.
Special effects makeup legend Stuart Freeborn modeled the wise, saucer-eyed face of Yoda in *The Empire Strikes Back* directly on a combination of Albert Einstein and a tarsier.

mammals.name: Clouded leopard
mammals.summary: The clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa), also called mainland clouded leopard, is a wild cat that has large dusky-grey blotches and irregular spots and stripes reminiscent of clouds. Its head-and-body length ranges from 68.6 to 108 cm (27.0 to 42.5 in) with a 61 to 91 cm (24 to 36 in) long tail, which it uses for balancing when moving in trees.
facts: Pound for pound, the clouded leopard has the longest canine teeth of any living cat, measuring two inches long, give or take, giving its skull the exact proportions of an extinct saber-toothed tiger.
To bite into large prey with those oversized fangs, it can open its jaws to a staggering 100-degree gape, compared to about 65 degrees in a lion.

Thanks to flexible ankle joints that rotate backward, a clouded leopard is one of the very few cats that can walk straight down a vertical tree trunk headfirst like a squirrel, and even hang upside down from a horizontal branch by its hind paws.
Its tail is almost as long as its entire head and body combined, acting as a heavy balancing pole as it sprints through the rainforest canopy at night.

Because it lacks a fully ossified hyoid bone in its throat, a clouded leopard cannot roar like a lion AND cannot purr like a housecat; instead, it greets friendly cats with a soft, breathy snort called a 'prusten.'

In 2006, DNA testing revealed that the clouded leopards living on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra had been reproductively isolated from mainland clouded leopards for over a million years, splitting them into two distinct species.

mammals.name: Arctic fox
mammals.summary: The Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus), also known as the white fox, polar fox, or snow fox, is a small species of fox native to the Arctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere and common throughout the Arctic tundra. It is well adapted to living in cold environments, and is known for its thick, warm fur that can be used as camouflage against snow in the winter.
facts: An Arctic fox does not even begin to shiver until the outside temperature plunges to -94°F (-70°C), thanks to the warmest pelage of any mammal on Earth and a network of counter-current blood vessels that keeps its paws just above freezing on solid ice.
It is one of the few mammals that undergoes a complete wardrobe change twice a year, shedding its snow-white winter coat for a smoky brown-and-charcoal summer coat as the tundra snow melts.

In 2018, a young female Arctic fox fitted with a satellite collar stunned scientists by walking 2,175 miles from Norway's Svalbard archipelago across sea ice all the way to Canada's Ellesmere Island in just 76 days.

When hunting lemmings buried under three feet of snow, the Arctic fox tilts its head like a radar dish, leaps high into the air, and nose-dives straight down through the crust, a study showed its pounces are most successful when aligned northeast with Earth's magnetic field!

During summer booms when seabirds and lemmings are abundant, an Arctic fox digs a deep hole straight down into the permafrost and stocks it with dozens of dead birds and eggs like a natural walk-in freezer.
In winter, lonely Arctic foxes frequently shadow polar bears across the sea ice to scavenge scraps from their seal kills, though they have to stay nimble so they don't become the bear's dessert.

mammals.name: Gelada
mammals.summary: The gelada (Theropithecus gelada, Amharic: ጭላዳ, romanized: č̣əlada, Oromo: Jaldeessa daabee), sometimes called the bleeding-heart monkey or the gelada baboon, is a species of Old World monkey found only in the Ethiopian Highlands, living at elevations of 1,800–4,400 m (5,900–14,400 ft) above sea level. It is the only living member of the genus Theropithecus, a name derived from the Greek root words for "beast-ape" (θηρο-πίθηκος : thēro-píthēkos).
facts: Often called the 'bleeding-heart monkey,' the gelada has a bright, hourglass-shaped patch of bare red skin on its chest; in females, this patch swells and necklaces itself with white, pearl-like fluid blisters when she is ready to mate.
Geladas are the last surviving species of prehistoric grazing primates and the only monkeys on Earth whose diet consists almost entirely (up to 90%) of grass blades and seeds.

Because they spend all day sitting on their rumps plucking grass on the Ethiopian plateau, they move from patch to patch using a unique 'shuffle gait', sliding forward in a squat without ever bothering to stand up, and have evolved thick, padded cushions on their butts.

To free up both hands for rapid-fire grass plucking, geladas possess the most dexterous opposable thumbs of any non-human primate, allowing them to pinch single blades of grass with index-finger precision.

When a male gelada flips his upper lip completely inside-out over his nostrils to expose bright pink gums and massive fangs, it looks terrifying, yet researchers found they often make this face when anxious or submitting.
In 2013, acoustic researchers discovered that geladas produce rapid, rhythmic lip-smacking calls called 'wobbles' that have the exact same syllable cadence and frequency range as spoken human speech.

mammals.name: Hedgehog
mammals.summary: The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus), also known as the West European hedgehog, Western European hedgehog or common hedgehog, is a hedgehog species native to Europe from Iberia and Italy northwards into Scandinavia and westwards into Ireland. It is a generally common and widely distributed species that can survive across a wide range of habitat types.
facts: Whenever a hedgehog encounters a strange, pungent new smell, like leather, cigar smoke, soap, or a toxic toad, it contorts its body and froths up mouthfuls of foamy saliva to lick all over its own spines in a bizarre ritual called 'self-anointing.'

Unlike porcupine quills, a hedgehog's 5,000 hollow keratin spines have no barbs and do not detach on contact; instead, each spine has a tiny bend near the base that acts like a shock absorber when the hedgehog falls out of a bush.

Hedgehogs have evolved significant natural resistance to European adder venom via blood proteins called 'erinacines,' allowing them to eat small vipers, and even chew up venomous toads to smear the toxins on their quills.

When threatened, a circular sheet of muscle along the hedgehog's back ('orbicularis panniculi') tightens like a drawstring purse, pulling its prickly mantle over its face, feet, and belly simultaneously.

In ancient Rome, before the invention of brushes, people used dried hedgehog skins to card wool and raise the nap on freshly woven cloth, so valuable that the Roman Senate actually passed laws regulating the hedgehog trade.
Before mating, a male hedgehog may circle a reluctant female for several hours while snorting, puffing, and sneezing rhythmically in a display British naturalists call 'the hedgehog carousel.'

mammals.name: Prairie dog
mammals.summary: The black-tailed prairie dog (Cynomys ludovicianus) is a rodent of the family Sciuridae (the squirrels) found in the Great Plains of North America from about the United States–Canada border to the United States–Mexico border. Unlike some other prairie dogs, these animals do not truly hibernate.
facts: Biologist Con Slobodchikoff spent 30 years recording prairie dog alarm calls and proved they have the most sophisticated grammatical language in the animal kingdom: in a single chirp, a prairie dog specifies whether an approaching human is tall or short, what color shirt they are wearing, and how fast they are walking.

When an entire town of prairie dogs wants to test if the coast is clear, one individual stands up on its hind legs, throws its front paws skyward, and shouts 'Yip!', triggering a stadium 'Mexican wave' called a jump-yip across the whole colony.

Wait until you hear how they greet family: two prairie dogs meet nose-to-nose, open their mouths, and touch their front incisor teeth together in what looks like a lingering French kiss to recognize whether they belong to the same clan.
In the late 1800s, a single colossal black-tailed prairie dog 'super-town' in Texas stretched 100 miles wide by 250 miles long and contained an estimated 400 million prairie dogs.

Their underground burrows are engineering marvels built on the 'Bernoulli principle': they sculpt one entrance into a tall volcano cone and leave the other entrance flat so passing prairie wind creates suction that pulls fresh air through the tunnels.
Despite their name, they aren't canines at all; they are ground squirrels named by early explorers and Lewis and Clark ('petit chien') for their dog-like warning bark.

mammals.name: Leopard seal
mammals.summary: The leopard seal (Hydrurga leptonyx), also referred to as the sea leopard, is a long and muscular seal native to the Southern Ocean of Antarctica and southern Patagonia. It is the second largest species of seal in the Antarctic (after the southern elephant seal).
facts: Wait until you look inside a leopard seal's mouth: while its front canines are built for tearing apart penguins and smaller seals, its back cheek teeth lock together into intricate, three-pronged sieves for straining tiny krill out of seawater, just like a baleen whale.

In 2006, National Geographic photographer Paul Nicklen dove into Antarctic waters where a massive female leopard seal spent four days trying to feed him live and pre-killed penguins, apparently convinced the clumsy human with a camera was a starving, helpless seal.
Unlike other true seals that wiggle on their bellies or use their hind flippers to swim, the leopard seal has huge, muscular front flippers that let it fly underwater like a sea lion.

During the Antarctic summer breeding season, leopard seals hang upside down under the ice and belt out eerie, haunting underwater trills at 300 hertz that vibrate right through the hulls of research ships.

Because a leopard seal cannot swallow large chunks of meat underwater without choking, it grabs a penguin or small seal in its jaws and thrashes it back and forth against the ocean surface with bone-shattering force to skin it before eating.

Its reptilian, S-curved neck, flat head, and black-spotted coat give it the silhouette of a mythical sea serpent, and unlike almost every other mammal, the females grow significantly larger than the males.

mammals.name: Japanese macaque
mammals.summary: The Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan. Colloquially, this macaque is referred to as the "snow monkey", because some live in areas where snow covers the ground for months each year.
facts: In 1963, a young female Japanese macaque named Mukubili at Jigokudani Monkey Park accidentally dropped some soybeans into a steaming volcanic hot spring, jumped in to retrieve them, and discovered how delightful the warm water felt, sparking a 'spa culture' that her entire troop passed down for generations.

Ten years earlier, on Koshima Island in 1953, another clever young female named Imo figured out how to wash sandy sweet potatoes in a stream and then dip them into the ocean after every bite to season them with salt, and soon the whole island troop was seasoning its food.

Imo didn't stop there: when researchers threw wheat grains onto the sandy beach, she scooped up a handful of sand and wheat and tossed it into a puddle; the sand sank and the clean wheat floated to the top, inventing 'placer mining' for monkeys.
In winter, juvenile Japanese macaques pack snow into giant snowballs and roll them down hills purely for the joy of playing.
Known as 'snow monkeys,' they hold the record as the farthest-north-living non-human primate on Earth, surviving blizzards where temperatures drop to 5°F (-15°C).
To avoid fights while soaking elbow-to-elbow in hot springs, snow monkeys purposely avert their eyes from one another because direct eye contact is considered an aggressive challenge.

mammals.name: Numbat
mammals.summary: The numbat (; binomen: Myrmecobius fasciatus), also known as the noombat or walpurti, is an insectivorous marsupial. It is diurnal and its diet consists almost exclusively of termites.
facts: The numbat eats an exclusively termite-based diet, up to 20,000 termites every single day, yet its peg-like jaws are so weak it cannot tear open a hard termite mound; instead, it waits until termites move into shallow surface galleries warmed by the sun and digs them out.
Because its schedule is strictly tied to the sun warming the soil enough for termites to become active, the numbat is the only 100-percent diurnal (day-active) marsupial in Australia.

Although it is a marsupial, a female numbat has no pouch at all; her four tiny, blind, bean-sized joeys simply clamp onto her nipples and dangle underneath her belly fur for the first five months of life.
Its slender, sticky pink tongue measures four inches long, nearly half the length of its head and body, and darts into narrow cracks in rotting eucalyptus logs where no claw can reach.
The numbat holds the record for the most teeth of any land mammal on Earth, sporting up to 52 tiny, mostly useless peg teeth that it rarely even chews with because it swallows termites whole.
At night, a numbat wedges itself inside a hollow log and plugs the entrance tightly with its rump, which consists of solid bone and skin nearly impossible for a predatory snake or fox to bite into.

mammals.name: Echidna
mammals.summary: The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus), also known as the common echidna, or short-nosed echidna, is one of four living species of echidna, and the only member of the genus Tachyglossus, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (takhús), meaning "fast", and γλῶσσα (glôssa), meaning "tongue". It is covered in fur and spines and has a distinctive snout and a specialised tongue, which it uses to catch its insect prey at a great speed.
facts: Along with the platypus, the echidna is one of the only mammals on Earth that lays eggs: the female lays a single, leathery, grape-sized egg directly into a temporary skin fold on her belly, where a baby called a 'puggle' hatches 10 days later.
Because a mother echidna has no nipples, she secretes thick, pink milk, rich in iron, directly through specialized skin pores ('milk patches') inside her pouch for the puggle to lap up off her fur.
During mating season, up to 11 male echidnas form a single-file conga line called an 'echidna train,' marching nose-to-tail behind a single female for up to six weeks until she chooses a suitor.
A male echidna has a four-headed penis, during mating, he shuts off blood flow to two of the heads and uses the other two, alternating which side he uses between mating sessions.
The tip of an echidna's rubbery snout contains up to 2,000 microscopic electroreceptors that detect the faint electrical impulses generated by the muscles of beetles and ants moving underground.

Named after Echidna, the half-woman, half-snake mother of monsters in Greek mythology, this spiny survivor has NO stomach acid and NO teeth; instead, it crushes insects between horny pads at the back of its tongue and the roof of its mouth.
Alongside the platypus, echidnas are the only living mammals that lay leathery eggs instead of giving birth to live young.
An echidna's body temperature is around 31°C (88°F), the lowest of any active mammal.
Baby echidnas are called puggles and hatch from a dime-sized egg into the mother's pouch after just 10 days.
Echidnas have a six-inch sticky tongue that darts in and out up to 100 times per minute to lap up ants and termites.

mammals.name: Red deer
mammals.summary: The red deer (Cervus elaphus) is a species of deer in the genus Cervus. It is one of the largest deer species.
facts: During the autumn rut, red deer stags engage in booming vocal shouting matches across the valleys before locking antlers: the deeper and faster a stag can roar (up to 3,000 times a day), the larger his body size, allowing weaker stags to back down without risking a fatal goring.
A red deer stag's branching antlers are the fastest-growing bone in the animal kingdom, sprouting up to an inch per day while covered in blood-rich 'velvet' skin before shedding every spring.

Because growing a new set of 30-pound bone antlers every spring drains so much calcium and phosphorus from a stag's own skeleton, stags actually suffer temporary osteoporosis each summer, and are frequently spotted chewing on shed antlers or old bones on the ground to replenish minerals.

Even when resting with its eyes open, a red deer can keep its pupils permanently horizontal relative to the ground as it lowers its head to graze, a trick called 'cyclovergence' that ensures a 300-degree panoramic view of stalking wolves at all times.
In medieval Britain, red deer were considered 'royal beasts of the forest,' and poaching a king's stag carried the penalty of being blinded or executed.
Newborn red deer calves have zero body odor for the first several days of life and freeze flat in the heather so predators can walk within three feet without smelling them.

mammals.name: Roe deer
mammals.summary: The roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), also known as the roe, western roe deer, or European roe, is a species of deer. The male of the species is sometimes referred to as a roebuck.
facts: The roe deer is the only hoofed mammal (ungulate) in the world that practices 'embryonic diapause': after mating in the warm days of July or August, the fertilized egg floats dormant inside the mother's uterus for five whole months before implanting in January so the fawn is born in lush May.

During summer courtship, a buck chases a doe around and around a favorite tree or bush for hours until their hooves wear raw, circular tracks into the forest floor known in European folklore as 'fairy rings' or 'witches' circles.'

When startled, a roe deer doesn't bound away silently; it flares the white hair on its rump into a bright heart-shaped or kidney-shaped patch and lets out a loud, hoarse bark that sounds exactly like a German Shepherd.

Female roe deer occasionally sprout full, velvet-covered antlers of their own due to hormone fluctuations, and in 19th-century Bavaria, collectors prized these rare 'horned does' and mistook them for mythical 'wolpertingers.'
Because a roe deer's tiny stomach cannot digest coarse meadow grass, it acts like a picky gourmet chef, nibbling only the most nutrient-dense buds, berries, mushrooms, and ivy shoots.
Unlike red deer stags, which gather large harems of females, a male roe buck defends a strict private territory during summer and courts one female at a time.

mammals.name: Giant anteater
mammals.summary: The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is a large insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America. It is the largest of the four living species of anteaters, which are classified with sloths in the order Pilosa.
facts: A giant anteater's two-foot-long, spaghetti-thin tongue is not attached to the back of its mouth at all; it anchors all the way down on the animal's sternum (breastbone) and can flick in and out 160 times per minute.

Because it has zero teeth, a giant anteater swallows pebbles, sand, and twigs along with 30,000 ants a day; its muscular stomach has hardened folds like a bird's gizzard that grind the ants against the swallowed stones.
Even wilder, a giant anteater's stomach does not produce hydrochloric acid of its own; instead, it uses the concentrated formic acid naturally inside the ants it swallows to digest its meal!

To keep its four-inch-long, scythe-like front claws razor-sharp for ripping open concrete-hard termite mounds, the giant anteater curls its claws inward into its palms and walks on its knuckles like a gorilla.
When it curls up to sleep on the open savanna, it drapes its massive, fan-like bushy tail completely over its head and body like a warm blanket that doubles as dead-grass camouflage.

At around 91°F (32.7°C), the giant anteater has one of the lowest normal body temperatures of any placental mammal, burning so few calories that it can survive strictly on tiny insects, yet if cornered by a jaguar, it rears up on its hind legs and can disembowel the big cat with a single swipe of its claws.

mammals.name: Hyrax
mammals.summary: The rock hyrax (; Procavia capensis), also called dassie, Rickaz, Cape hyrax, rock rabbit, or coney (in early English Bible translations), is a medium-sized terrestrial hyrax native to Africa and the Middle East. Commonly called the dassie in South Africa (; Afrikaans: klipdassie), it is one of the five living species of the order Hyracoidea, and the only one in the genus Procavia.
facts: Although it looks like an oversized guinea pig or furry potato, the rock hyrax's closest living relatives on Earth are the elephant and the manatee.

Take a peek inside a hyrax's mouth and you'll see the family resemblance: its two upper incisor teeth grow continuously into miniature elephant tusks, and its flattened nails look just like tiny elephant toenails.

When Phoenician sailors reached the coast of Iberia around 1000 BCE and saw millions of wild rabbits, they mistook them for the hyraxes back home and called the peninsula *I-Shaphan-im* ('Coast of Hyraxes'), which the Romans Latinized into *Hispania*, meaning the country of Spain literally means 'Land of the Hyraxes.'

For thousands of years, rock hyraxes have peed and pooped in the exact same rocky crevices, where their waste bakes into a dark, resinous, fossilized mass called 'hyraceum' that luxury French perfumers harvest as a prized musk fixative.
That fossilized hyrax urine preserves ancient pollen grains for up to 55,000 years, giving paleoclimatologists an unbroken timeline of African climate change.

The rubbery soles of a hyrax's feet are packed with sweat glands and retract downward in the middle like suction cups, allowing it to sprint straight up sheer granite cliffs and bounce between narrow rock ledges.

mammals.name: Baboon
