mammals.summary: The olive baboon (Papio anubis), also called the Anubis baboon, is a member of the family Cercopithecidae Old World monkeys. The species is the most wide-ranging of all baboons, being native to 25 countries throughout Africa, extending from Mali eastward to Ethiopia and Tanzania.
facts: In ancient Egypt, the hamadryas baboon was worshipped as the earthly manifestation of Thoth, the god of wisdom, science, and the moon, because baboons sit up on rocky cliffs at dawn and bark in chorus to 'greet' the rising sun as they warm up.

In the late 1800s, a disabled South African railway signalman named James 'Jumper' Wide bought a chacma baboon named Jack to push his wheelchair and operate the heavy train track levers; after passing an official railway inspection, Jack was given an employment number, paid 20 cents a day plus half a bottle of beer a week, and never made a single mistake in nine years on the job.

Wild baboons in Saudi Arabia and Ethiopia have been filmed kidnapping feral puppies, raising them gently as members of their troop, grooming them, and using the grown dogs as perimeter security guards.
A male baboon's upper canine teeth grow up to two inches long, longer than an adult lion's fangs, and sharpen themselves like scissors every time they slide against the lower premolars.
Female baboons inherit their mother's exact social rank for life in a strict 'matrilineal monarchy,' where even an infant daughter of the alpha female outranks every other adult female in the troop.

Despite spending their days foraging on the ground, baboons climb sheer rock cliffs or tall fever trees at dusk to sleep sitting upright, helped by thick, hairless butt calluses called 'ischial callosities' that prevent their bottoms from going numb on narrow branches.

mammals.name: Sea lion
mammals.summary: The California sea lion (Zalophus californianus) is a coastal eared seal native to western North America. It is one of six species of sea lions.
facts: Here is the easiest way to tell a sea lion apart from a true seal: sea lions have visible external ear flaps, can rotate their hind flippers forward to walk on all fours on land, and bark noisily, whereas true seals have tiny ear holes and wiggle on their bellies like caterpillars.

The U.S. Navy Marine Mammal Program trains California sea lions to recover sunken practice mines and attach leg cuffs to enemy frogmen; a sea lion carries the cuff in its mouth, snaps it onto a diver's ankle so handlers on the surface can reel them in, and swims away before the diver even knows what happened.

In 2013, a rescued California sea lion named Ronan became the first non-human mammal scientifically proven to keep a musical beat, bobbing her head in perfect rhythm to Earth, Wind & Fire's 'Boogie Wonderland' and the Backstreet Boys even when researchers secretly sped up or slowed down the tempo.
When diving up to 1,000 feet deep, a sea lion exhales before going under and voluntarily collapses its own lungs so nitrogen gas can't dissolve into its bloodstream and cause 'the bends.'

During deep dives, a sea lion can slow its heart rate from 95 beats per minute down to just 20 beats per minute, shutting off blood flow to its kidneys and muscles to save oxygen strictly for its brain and heart.

Since the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged San Francisco's Pier 39, hundreds of wild California sea lions have taken over the marina docks, drawing millions of tourists to watch their noisy king-of-the-raft shoving matches.

mammals.name: Blue wildebeest
mammals.summary: The blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), also called the common wildebeest, white-bearded gnu or brindled gnu, is a large antelope and one of the two species of wildebeest. It is placed in the genus Connochaetes and family Bovidae, and has a close taxonomic relationship with the black wildebeest.
facts: Every year, roughly 1.5 million blue wildebeests, accompanied by 200,000 zebras, complete a 1,800-mile clockwise loop across the Serengeti and Maasai Mara in the largest overland mammal migration on Earth.

Zebras and wildebeests travel as a tactical tag team: zebras go first to chomp down the tall, coarse, fibrous tops of the savanna grass, exposing the short, tender green shoots underneath that wildebeests need.

In February, half a million pregnant female wildebeests synchronize their deliveries so that 80 percent of all calves are born within the exact same three-week window, flooding the plains with so many babies at once that lions and hyenas quickly get too full to eat any more.
A newborn blue wildebeest calf can stand up within six minutes of hitting the ground and outrun a lioness before it is 24 hours old.

Scientists proved that an entire herd of wildebeests possesses 'swarm intelligence': even without a single leader, scent glands between their hooves leave a chemical trail that allows thousands of animals to navigate around obstacles as a single cohesive organism.
Its alternative name, 'gnu,' is an onomatopoeia coined by the Khoikhoi people of southern Africa to mimic the metallic, nasal *'g-nu!'* grunt that bulls belt out incessantly.

mammals.name: Saiga antelope
mammals.summary: The saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica, ), or simply saiga, is a species of antelope which during antiquity inhabited a vast area of the Eurasian steppe, spanning the foothills of the Carpathian Mountains in the northwest and Caucasus in the southwest into Mongolia in the northeast and Dzungaria in the southeast. During the Pleistocene, it ranged across the mammoth steppe from the British Isles to Beringia.
facts: The saiga antelope looks like a creature straight out of *Star Wars* thanks to its oversized, flexible, downward-pointing trunk ('proboscis') that hangs right over its mouth.

That bizarre, inflatable nose is a multi-season life-support system: in summer, mucous membranes inside the trunk filter out choking clouds of steppe dust kicked up by migrating herds, and in -40°F winters, it warms icy air before it reaches the lungs.

During the autumn rut, a male saiga's nose swells up like a balloon, and dominant bulls battle so violently for harems of up to 50 females that the mortality rate for adult males reaches 70 percent from exhaustion and horn wounds.

Saigas have existed virtually unchanged since the Pleistocene Ice Age, when they grazed alongside woolly mammoths and saber-toothed cats from England all the way across the Bering Land Bridge into Alaska.
To rebuild their numbers after harsh winters, 85 percent of adult female saigas give birth to twins, and even one-year-old females frequently have twins.

In May 2015, over 200,000 saigas, more than half the world's population, died across Kazakhstan in a single catastrophic week when unusual heat and humidity caused a normally harmless bacteria living in their noses (*Pasteurella multocida*) to invade their bloodstreams.

mammals.name: Peccary
mammals.summary: The collared peccary (Dicotyles tajacu) is a peccary, a species of artiodactyl (even-toed) mammal in the family Tayassuidae. It is the only extant member of the genus Dicotyles.
facts: Often called a 'javelina' (from the Spanish word for 'spear'), the peccary looks like a wild pig, yet it belongs to a completely separate New World family: a pig's upper canine tusks curve upward and outward, while a peccary's razor-sharp canines point straight down like daggers that interlock and sharpen each other.
Even more noticeably, while a pig has four toes on every foot and a visible curly tail, a collared peccary has only three toes on its hind feet and a vestigial tail hidden under its fur.

In the middle of a peccary's lower back sits a basketball-sized patch of raised skin covering a dorsal musk gland; herd members rub their cheeks against each other's back glands so the entire herd smells identical, and a frightened peccary releases a skunk-like stench you can smell 300 feet away.
A peccary's mouth and digestive tract are so tough that it routinely chomps and swallows whole prickly-pear cactus pads, four-inch spines and all, without flinching.

When a herd of peccaries is attacked by a jaguar or mountain lion, one individual often charges the predator head-on and clacks its teeth like castanets to buy time for the rest of the family to escape.

The largest species, the Chacoan peccary, was known to science only from Ice Age fossils and considered extinct for thousands of years until biologists stunned the world by finding live herds running around the Paraguayan Chaco in 1971!

mammals.name: Fishing cat
mammals.summary: The fishing cat (Prionailurus viverrinus) is a medium-sized wild cat of South and Southeast Asia. It has a deep yellowish-grey fur with black lines and spots.
facts: Unlike almost every other cat, the fishing cat loves diving headfirst into deep rivers and swamps, using partially webbed front toes and a thick, water-repellent double coat that stays dry at the skin like a wetsuit.

To lure curious fish within striking range, a fishing cat sits quietly on an overhanging riverbank and lightly taps the surface of the water with one paw, mimicking the ripples of a struggling insect that fish swim up to eat.

Wait until you examine its paws: a fishing cat's front claws are so long that they never fully retract into their fleshy sheaths, leaving the sharp tips permanently exposed like gaff hooks for snagging slippery carp and eels.
When swimming underwater, the cat can fold its small, rounded ears flat to seal its ear canals against water and uses its short, muscular tail as a rudder.
Its vocalizations sound so remarkably like the 'quack' of a wild duck or the 'chuck' of a frog that local fishermen in the mangroves of India and Bangladesh often mistake its calls for wetland birds.
In 2012, the Indian state of West Bengal officially declared the fishing cat (*baghrol*) its state animal to help protect the shrinking urban wetlands around Kolkata.

mammals.name: Quokka
mammals.summary: The quokka (; Setonix brachyurus) is a macropod native to Australia. It is about the size of a domestic cat.
facts: In 1696, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh landed on an island off Western Australia, saw hundreds of cat-sized marsupials hopping through the brush, mistook them for giant rats, and named the island *'t Eylandt 't Rottenest* ('Rats' Nest'), which is known today as Rottnest Island.

Because of the evolutionary geometry of its jaw muscles and protruding front teeth, when a quokka pants to cool down after hopping, its face pulls back into a giant, photogenic smile that earned it the title of 'the happiest animal in the world.'

On Rottnest Island, where quokkas have lived without foxes or dingoes for thousands of years, they have zero natural fear of humans, prompting a viral 'quokka selfie' craze with celebrities like Roger Federer, Margot Robbie, and Chris Hemsworth, though touching or feeding one carries an instant $300 fine.

Behind that adorable smile lies a ruthless survival reflex: if a predator chases a mother quokka, she can relax her pouch muscles to drop her joey onto the ground; the hissing baby distracts the predator while the mother escapes.

Better yet, female quokkas keep a 'backup baby' in waiting via embryonic diapause: if she loses or drops her current joey, a dormant second fertilized embryo waiting in her womb immediately resumes growing without her even needing to mate again.
A quokka can go for months without drinking fresh water by extracting moisture from succulent coastal shrubs and recycling urea through its kidneys.
Known as the 'world's happiest animal' for its upturned mouth, the quokka is a cat-sized macropod native to Rottnest Island off Western Australia.
Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh mistook quokkas for giant rats in 1696 and named their island 'Rottnest' ('rat's nest').
Like kangaroos, quokkas can pause the development of an embryo in a process called embryonic diapause.

mammals.name: Muskrat
mammals.summary:
The muskrat or common muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent. 
Adult muskrats weigh 0.6–2 kg (1+1⁄4–4+1⁄2 lb), with a body length (excluding the tail) of 20–35 cm (8–14 in).
facts: A muskrat can chew down cattail reeds and dig bank tunnels completely underwater for up to 17 minutes without inhaling a single drop of water because its furry lips close tightly *behind* its protruding front incisor teeth.

During the freezing winter months, muskrats construct dome-shaped wetland lodges out of mud and cattails, AND chew 'push-ups,' which are miniature breathing domes built over holes in the lake ice so they can stop for a breath of air halfway through a long under-ice swim.

In winter, up to a dozen muskrats huddle together inside a single cattail lodge to share body heat, yet if food gets scarce before spring, they can buy time by eating the edible cattail walls of their own house!

When diving into icy water, a muskrat experiences 'regional heterothermy': its internal organs stay warm at 99°F while blood flow to its scaly, flattened tail and webbed hind feet is throttled down so its extremities drop to near freezing without wasting heat.
To steer underwater, a muskrat uses its hairless, vertically flattened tail like a scull oar while paddling with its fringed hind feet, and it can swim backward just as fast as it swims forward.

In the Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit and down along the Detroit River, a centuries-old French-Canadian fur-trapper dispensation passed down from missionary priests still permits Catholics to eat muskrat dinners on Fridays during Lent.

mammals.name: Honey badger
mammals.summary: The honey badger (Mellivora capensis), also known as the ratel ( or ), is a mammal widely distributed across Africa, Southwest Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It is the sole living representative of the Mellivorinae subfamily of the Mustelidae.
facts: In 2002, the *Guinness Book of World Records* officially crowned the honey badger (ratel) the 'Most Fearless Animal in the World', a 25-pound dynamo regularly filmed chasing lions off kills, raiding beehives, and fighting off leopards and pythons.

The skin on the back of a honey badger's neck is a full quarter-inch (6 millimeters) thick, tough enough to deflect arrows, spears, and porcupine quills, and hangs so loosely on its frame that if a leopard grabs it by the scruff, the badger can twist 180 degrees inside its own skin to bite the predator's face.

Like the mongoose, a honey badger has evolved mutated nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that prevent cobra and puff adder neurotoxins from binding to its nerves; if bitten in the face by a puff adder while eating it, the badger simply passes out for two hours, wakes up, and finishes eating the snake.

In South Africa, a captive honey badger named Stoffel became a legendary escape artist after repeatedly unlocking bolts on his enclosure gate, stacking rocks, rolling mud balls into a ladder, and using a rake and tree branches to climb over concrete walls.

Look under its tail and you'll find a reversible anal pouch that can turn inside-out to release a suffocating, skunk-like stench; keepers report the smell helps calm angry bees when a honey badger tears open a hive.
Female honey badgers spend up to 18 months teaching their cubs how to hunt in the Kalahari Desert, including how to dig scorpions and deadly barking geckos out of three-foot burrows.
A honey badger's skin is so thick and loose around its body that it can twist 180 degrees inside its own hide to bite an attacker holding it.
Honey badgers have evolved molecular mutations in their acetylcholine receptors that make them largely immune to cobra venom.
Despite its name, the honey badger is actually a giant weasel relative in the family Mustelidae.
Honey badgers have a reversible anal pouch that releases a suffocating stench used to calm bees while raiding hives.

mammals.name: Aardwolf
mammals.summary: The aardwolf (Proteles cristatus) is an insectivorous hyaenid species, native to East and Southern Africa. Its name means "earth-wolf" in Afrikaans and Dutch.
facts: Although it belongs to the bone-crushing hyena family (*Hyaenidae*) and looks like a miniature striped hyena, the aardwolf's cheek teeth have shrunk into tiny, weak pegs because it eats almost nothing except harvester termites.

Unlike the aardvark, which rips open termite mounds with giant claws, the aardwolf gently laps termites straight off the desert soil using a broad, sticky tongue covered in tough papillae, consuming up to 300,000 termites in a single night without destroying the nest so the colony rebuilds for future meals!

Harvester termites defend themselves by squirting toxic terpenes from nozzle-shaped heads, yet the aardwolf's oversized salivary glands pump out neutralizing saliva that detoxifies the chemical spray on contact.

To find termites without digging, an aardwolf swivels its large, pointed ears toward the ground and listens for the faint clicking and rustling of thousands of tiny insect legs marching across the dry grass.
When threatened by a jackal or dog, a 20-pound aardwolf erects the seven-inch hair along its spine from forehead to tail tip, instantly puffing itself up to look twice its real size while roaring.
Its name comes directly from Afrikaans and Dutch for 'earth wolf,' referring to its habit of sleeping through the scorching African heat inside abandoned aardvark and springhare burrows.

mammals.name: Yak
mammals.summary: The wild yak (Bos mutus) is a large, wild bovine native to the Himalayas. It is the ancestor of the domestic yak (Bos grunniens).
facts: The yak has evolved the ultimate high-altitude toolkit to thrive on the Tibetan Plateau up to 20,000 feet above sea level: its chest holds an extra pair of ribs (14 pairs instead of 12 or 13 in cattle) to make room for lungs and a heart nearly twice the size of a lowland cow's.

Even wilder, a yak lacks the genetic mechanism that causes blood vessels in the lungs of lowland mammals to constrict when oxygen drops; meaning yaks are completely immune to high-altitude pulmonary edema ('mountain sickness').
Unlike domestic cows that moo, yaks never moo; instead, both wild and domestic yaks communicate with low, rhythmic pig-like grunts, leading to their scientific name *Bos grunniens* ('grunting ox').

On the treeless Tibetan plateau, dried yak dung is not waste; it is the primary fuel used by nomadic families for cooking and heating, and it burns cleanly with a mild, herbal scent rather than a foul odor.

Fresh yak milk is naturally pale golden-pink at first and contains up to 10 percent butterfat; Tibetans churn it into rich 'yak butter' to mix into salted brick tea and to fuel thousands of flickering butter lamps inside Buddhist monasteries.

A yak survives -40°F blizzards thanks to a floor-length outer skirt of coarse hair hanging over a dense, cashmere-soft winter undercoat, combined with virtually zero active sweat glands so no body heat escapes through damp skin.

mammals.name: Kinkajou
mammals.summary: The kinkajou (/ˈkɪŋkədʒuː/ KING-kə-joo; Potos flavus) is a mammal of the family Procyonidae, a relative to olingos, coatis, raccoons, and the ringtail and cacomistle. It is the only member of the genus Potos and is also known as the honey bear (a name shared with several unrelated species).
facts: Although Amazonian locals call it the 'honey bear' (*oso mielero*) and early naturalists thought it was a lemur or monkey, the kinkajou is actually a tropical tree-dwelling member of the raccoon family (*Procyonidae*).

To lap sweet nectar out of night-blooming rainforest flowers and raid wild beehives, a kinkajou unrolls a skinny, five-inch-long tongue, making it one of the world's only carnivorans that acts as a major flower pollinator as pollen dusts its golden face.

Along with the Asian binturong, the kinkajou is one of only two carnivores on Earth with a truly prehensile tail: it grips branches like a fifth hand and even doubles as a cozy blanket wrapped around its nose while sleeping in tree holes.

Just like its raccoon cousin the margay and binturong, a kinkajou can rotate its hind ankles a full 180 degrees backward, enabling it to run straight down vertical tree trunks headfirst or hang upside down by its hind feet while eating fruit with both hands.
Instead of having anal scent glands like skunks or ferrets, kinkajous mark their canopy highways using specialized scent glands located on their throats, chests, and the corners of their mouths.
Strictly nocturnal, a kinkajou avoids sunlight so religiously that it spends every single day curled up deep inside dark tree hollows with its hands pressed tightly over its giant eyes.

mammals.name: Snowshoe hare
mammals.summary: The snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus), also called the varying hare or snowshoe rabbit, is a species of hare found in North America. The "snowshoe" moniker refers to the hare's large hind feet, which prevent it from sinking into soft snow, much like snowshoes.
facts: Twice a year, the snowshoe hare undergoes a dramatic 'photoperiodic' color molt triggered by the changing length of daylight: as autumn days shorten, receptor cells in its eyes signal the brain to shut off pigment production, turning its rusty-brown summer coat pure snow-white in just 10 weeks.
It gets its name from its oversized hind feet, which sprout thick mats of stiff winter bristles between the toes that spread its weight across powdery drifts like a pair of natural snowshoes.

Every 8 to 11 years across the boreal forests of Canada and Alaska, snowshoe hare populations explode and crash tenfold in lockstep with their main predator, the Canada lynx, a textbook ecological cycle tracked for over 200 years in Hudson's Bay Company fur-trapping ledgers.

Biologists discovered that during peak lynx years, female snowshoe hares don't just die from being eaten; chronic stress hormones from hearing and smelling lynx everywhere actually lower the hares' fertility and cause them to have smaller litters!

Unlike baby rabbits (kits), which are born blind, naked, and helpless in underground burrows, baby snowshoe hares ('leverets') are born above ground fully furred, with their eyes wide open, and can hop around within hours of birth.
Even the tips of a snowshoe hare's ears stay permanently jet-black in winter because the dark melanin protein actually strengthens the delicate ear cartilage against frostbite and tearing.

mammals.name: Siamang
mammals.summary: The siamang (, also UK: ; Symphalangus syndactylus) is an endangered arboreal, black-furred gibbon native to the tropical rainforests of Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. The largest of the gibbons, the siamang can be twice the size of other gibbons, reaching 1 m (3.3 ft) in height, and weighing up to 14 kg (31 lb).
facts: Beneath a siamang's chin sits a hairless, gray throat sac ('gular sac') that can inflate to the size of a grapefruit, and as big as the ape's entire head, acting as a booming acoustic resonating chamber that amplifies its morning calls for two miles through the Sumatran rainforest.

Look closely at a siamang's feet and you'll spot its signature anatomical quirk: the second and third toes are fused together by a web of skin almost to the top knuckle, which gives the species its scientific name *Symphalangus syndactylus* ('fused fingers').

As the largest of all gibbon species, a siamang has an arm span reaching five feet across, nearly 1.5 times its standing height, allowing it to swing through the treetops hand-over-hand with effortless grace.

Unlike almost all other primates, where the mother does nearly 100 percent of infant care, a father siamang takes over carrying, grooming, and sleeping with his baby all day once the infant reaches eight months old.

Mated siamang pairs are so inseparable that they eat, travel, and sleep within 30 feet of each other every day of their 30-year lives, performing synchronized 20-minute vocal duets each morning to keep rival pairs out of their fruit trees.
When carrying fruit across the canopy so its hands stay free for swinging, a siamang grips snacks using a specialized thumb-like big toe on its hind feet.

mammals.name: Indri
mammals.summary: The indri ( ; Indri indri), also called the babakoto, is one of the largest living lemurs, with a head-body length of about 64–72 cm (25–28+1⁄2 in) and a weight of between 6 and 9.5 kg (13 and 21 lb). It has a black and white coat and maintains an upright posture when climbing or clinging.
facts: In the Malagasy language of Madagascar, the word *'indri'* doesn't actually mean 'lemur'; it literally translates to *'There it is!'* or *'Look at that!'*; when French naturalist Pierre Sonnerat visited in 1780 and his local guide pointed into the trees shouting *'Indri!'*, Sonnerat mistakenly wrote it down as the animal's name.

The local Malagasy people actually call the indri *'Babakoto'*, meaning 'Ancestor of Man' or 'Father of Little Koto,' and revere it with a sacred cultural taboo (*fady*) against hunting or harming it because legend says an indri once rescued a lost boy from the forest.

While every other living lemur has a long, prominent tail, the indri is the largest living lemur and has only a tiny, two-inch vestigial stump, yet it can still leap 33 feet horizontally from tree trunk to tree trunk.

Instead of chattering or grunting like ring-tailed lemurs, indri families sing haunting, whale-like harmonic songs that carry for over two miles across the rainforest canopy, and a 2021 study proved indri songs are the only known mammal vocalizations besides human music that follow strict 'categorical rhythms' (like 1:1 and 1:2 beat ratios).
To neutralize the alkaloids and toxins in the young rainforest leaves they eat, indris regularly descend to the forest floor to swallow handfuls of mineral-rich red soil as an antacid.

Despite countless attempts over the last two centuries, not a single indri has ever survived more than a year or bred in captivity outside Madagascar because it requires a hyper-specific diet of dozens of native rainforest tree leaves.

mammals.name: Vampire bat
mammals.summary: The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) is a small, leaf-nosed bat native to the Americas. It is one of three extant species of vampire bats, the other two being the hairy-legged and the white-winged vampire bats.
facts: Packed inside the skin around a vampire bat's flattened nose are specialized infrared heat sensors ('TRPV1 ion channels') that work like thermal night-vision goggles, pinpointing the exact spot within eight inches where warm blood vessels flow closest to a sleeping cow's skin.

Contrary to horror movies, a vampire bat does not suck blood through hollow fangs; it makes a tiny, painless three-millimeter shaving nick with its razor-sharp upper incisors and laps up the pooling blood with grooves on the underside of its tongue.

To keep the wound bleeding freely for 20 minutes, a vampire bat's saliva contains a potent anti-clotting protein appropriately named 'draculin' by biochemists, which doctors have studied as a treatment for stroke patients.
Because blood is mostly water and very heavy, a vampire bat has to start peeing within two minutes of beginning its meal so it isn't too bloated to fly home!

Unlike almost all other bats, which can barely crawl on a flat surface, the vampire bat can walk, run, and bound forward at nearly five miles per hour by vaulting on its muscular folded thumbs like a four-legged sprinter.

If a bat fails to find a blood meal for three nights in a row, it will starve to death, so roost-mates practice reciprocal altruism, regurgitating mouthfuls of blood to feed hungry neighbors who previously shared with them.

mammals.name: Harbor porpoise
mammals.summary: The harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) is one of eight extant species of porpoise. It is one of the smallest species of  cetacean.
facts: Nicknamed the 'puffing pig' by fishermen in Atlantic Canada and Maine, the harbor porpoise makes a loud, sharp sneezing sound ('chuff!') every time it rolls smoothly to the surface to breathe.

Here is how marine biologists instantly distinguish a porpoise skull from a dolphin skull: dolphins have pointed, cone-shaped teeth, whereas a harbor porpoise has flat, spade-shaped teeth that look like miniature shovels.

Because it is one of the smallest cetaceans in cold northern oceans, weighing only about 130 pounds, a harbor porpoise loses body heat rapidly into the chilly water and must eat nearly 10 percent of its own body weight in herring and sand eels every single day just to stay warm.

Wait until you hear how it hunts: the harbor porpoise clicks in an ultra-high-frequency narrow acoustic beam around 130 kilohertz, a pitch completely inaudible to killer whales, allowing the tiny porpoise to echolocate for fish in stealth mode without alerting its #1 predator!
When attempting to woo a female, a male harbor porpoise swims up to her at full speed, performs an acrobatic aerial twist right over her back, and showers her with spray.
Female harbor porpoises pull off one of the most exhausting feats in the ocean, nursing a growing calf while simultaneously pregnant with next year's calf for almost their entire adult lives.

mammals.name: Lynx
mammals.summary: The Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) is one of the four extant species within the medium-sized wild cat genus Lynx. It is widely distributed from Northern, Central and Eastern Europe to Central Asia and Siberia, the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas.
facts: Why do lynxes have those two-inch black tufts of hair sprouting from the tips of their ears? Acoustic testing suggests the tufts act like furry hearing aids and wind vanes, funneling faint sound waves down into the ear canal while helping the cat sense wind direction.

A lynx's dinner-plate-sized paws are wider than a human hand or a mountain lion's track, spreading the cat's weight so effectively that it exerts less than half the downward pressure per square inch on deep snow as a coyote or bobcat.

Look at the lush ruff of long fur framing a lynx's cheeks like muttonchop sideburns: the cat can flare those cheek ruffs forward like parabolic reflectors to amplify the faint squeak of a vole tunneling beneath three feet of snow.

Notice how a lynx always looks like it is walking uphill even on flat ground? Its hind legs are roughly 20 percent longer than its front legs, turning its rear end into a coiled catapult for pouncing onto snowshoe hares.

The word 'lynx' comes from the Ancient Greek word *leukos* ('light' or 'brightness'), a tribute to the reflective 'tapetum lucidum' layer behind its retinas that makes its eyes glow like twin lanterns in the dark.

Medieval bestiaries claimed that a lynx's eyesight was so supernatural it could see straight through solid stone walls, and that its frozen urine hardened in the earth into a magical amber gemstone called 'lyncurium.'

mammals.name: Harp seal
mammals.summary: The harp seal (Pagophilus groenlandicus), also known as the saddleback seal or Greenland seal, is a species of earless seal, or true seal, native to the northernmost Atlantic Ocean and Arctic Ocean. Originally in the genus Phoca with a number of other species, it was reclassified into the monotypic genus Pagophilus in 1844.
facts: For the first 12 days of its life on the drifting Arctic pack ice, a newborn harp seal pup ('whitecoat') drinks milk containing an astonishing 48 percent butterfat, more than 12 times richer than cow's milk, allowing the pup to gain nearly five pounds of blubber every single day.

Before that whitecoat pup has enough blubber to stay warm, its hollow, translucent white hairs act like fiber-optic tubes, trapping sunlight and conducting solar heat directly down to the pup's dark skin!

Once the pup hits about 80 pounds at just 12 days old, its mother abruptly stops nursing, dives into the sea, and abandons it forever; the plump pup then fasts alone on the ice for up to six weeks while shedding its white fluff for a silvery, waterproof swimming coat.

Wait until you see how a harp seal got its name: adult males and females develop a striking, jet-black wishbone or saddle mark across their silvery backs that looks just like a classical concert harp.

To prevent its giant eyes from drying out or freezing solid in howling Arctic winds on the ice, a harp seal has zero tear ducts; instead, its eyes continuously secrete a thick, oily mucous film that coats the cornea like ski goggles.

During the underwater breeding season, harp seals gather under the pack ice and produce a cacophony of at least 19 distinct calls, including chirps, whistles, grunts, and trills that sound like a sci-fi laser battle.

mammals.name: Golden hamster
mammals.summary: The golden hamster or Syrian hamster (Mesocricetus auratus) is a rodent belonging to the hamster subfamily, Cricetinae. Their natural geographical range is in an arid region of northern Syria and southern Turkey.
facts: Almost every single domesticated golden (Syrian) hamster kept as a pet or lab animal in the world today is descended from a single wild mother and her 11 babies dug up from an eight-foot burrow in a wheat field near Aleppo, Syria, by zoologist Israel Aharoni in April 1930.

The word 'hamster' comes from the Middle High German word *hamustro* and the verb *hamstern*, which translates literally to 'to hoard', a nod to the animal's obsession with stockpiling up to 90 pounds of seeds in underground pantries.
A golden hamster's stretchy cheek pouches extend all the way from its mouth back to its hip bones, allowing it to stuff up to 20 percent of its entire body weight in dry food into its face at once.

Before taking a stuffed cheek pouch into the water or down a narrow burrow, a hamster uses its salivary glands carefully: the inside of its cheek pouches has zero saliva glands so stored seeds stay bone-dry and don't rot or sprout!
Given a running wheel in its cage, a single tiny golden hamster will voluntarily log up to 5.5 miles every single night; the human equivalent of running a full marathon before breakfast.

Researchers discovered that golden hamsters have a steel-clad liver capable of metabolizing massive doses of grain alcohol: in lab tests, hamsters happily chose 15-percent alcohol solutions over plain water without ever losing their balance or getting drunk.

mammals.name: Bactrian camel
mammals.summary: The Bactrian camel (Camelus bactrianus), also known as the Mongolian camel, domestic Bactrian camel, two-humped camel or double-humped camel, is a camel native to the steppes of Central Asia. It has two humps on its back, in contrast to the single-humped dromedary.
facts: Need an easy memory trick to tell the two camel species apart? Turn the first letter of each name on its side: **B**actrian has **two** humps (like the two loops of a capital 'B'), while **D**romedary has **one** hump (like the single curve of a capital 'D').

Contrary to desert legend, a Bactrian camel's two humps do not store liquid water; they store up to 80 pounds of solid fat; when food is scarce in the Gobi Desert, the humps shrink and flop over like empty deflated bags to the side of the animal's spine.

Critically endangered wild Bactrian camels (*Camelus ferus*) in China's Lop Nur desert are the only land mammals on Earth that can survive by drinking brackish saltwater with a higher salt concentration than the ocean!

Because a dehydrated camel's red blood cells are oval-shaped rather than round, they can keep flowing smoothly through capillaries even when the blood thickens like syrup, and then swell to 240 percent of their original size without bursting when the camel gulps down 30 gallons of water in 10 minutes.

During Gobi Desert sandstorms and -40°F winters, a Bactrian camel protects its face with double rows of interlocking eyelashes, hairy ear openings, and muscular slit nostrils that clamp shut like trapdoors.
To conserve every drop of moisture, a Bactrian camel lets its own body temperature swing wildly from 93°F at dawn to 105°F at midday before it even begins to sweat.

mammals.name: Bighorn sheep
mammals.summary: The bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) or bighorn is a species of sheep native to North America. It is named for its large horns, a pair of them may weigh up to 14 kg (30 lb); the sheep altogether typically weigh up to 143 kg (315 lb).
facts: During the autumn rut, two rival bighorn rams rear up on their hind legs and charge into each other at a combined closure speed of 40 miles per hour, clashing horns with up to 3,400 newtons of force (roughly 60 times the force needed to fracture a human skull) in battles that can last for 24 hours.

Why don't bighorn rams suffer concussions? Along with a double-layered skull filled with shock-absorbing struts of bone, a ram slows down venous blood leaving its brain right before impact to slightly inflate the blood vessels around its brain like biological bubble wrap, just like a woodpecker!
A single pair of curl-shaped horns on a mature ram can weigh up to 30 pounds, more than the combined weight of all the other bones in the ram's entire skeleton.

You can read a bighorn ram's biography right off its horns: because horn growth slows down every autumn during the exhausting mating rut, dark annual 'growth rings' form around the horn that reveal the sheep's exact age just like tree rings.

A bighorn sheep's split hooves have a hard, sharp outer rim for biting into tiny 2-inch rock ledges and a soft, spongy, concave rubbery pad in the center that grips sheer granite like a climbing shoe.

Because bighorn sheep never evolved immunity to European livestock germs, a single stray domestic sheep touching noses with a wild bighorn can pass along *Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae* bacteria that wipes out 80 percent of the wild mountain herd.

mammals.name: Vicuña
mammals.summary: The vicuña (Lama vicugna) or vicuna (both , very rarely spelled vicugna, its Latin specific name) is a wild South American camelid which lives in high alpine areas of the Andes. It is a relative of the llama, the domesticated descendant of the guanaco, the only other still wild South American camelid.
facts: Vicuña fleece is the finest, softest, and most expensive animal fiber on Earth, with individual hairs just 12 microns thick (one-sixth the thickness of a human hair); because the hairs have microscopic scales that lock air pockets in place, a single authentic vicuña overcoat sells for $20,000 to $50,000.
Under the law of the ancient Inca Empire, it was a capital crime punishable by death for anyone except Inca royalty to wear vicuña cloth.

Instead of hunting vicuñas, the Incas organized a sacred royal roundup called the *Chaccu* every four years, where 20,000 people linked hands in a human chain miles wide to gently herd wild vicuñas into stone corrals, shear them, and release them unharmed, a tradition revived by Peruvian communities today!

Because a vicuña grows its ultra-fine fleece so slowly in the freezing Andes, an individual animal can only be sheared once every two to three years and yields barely half a pound (250 grams) of usable wool.

Unlike all other camelids (llamas, alpacas, and camels), a vicuña possesses lower incisor teeth that never stop growing for its entire life, just like a rodent's, with thick enamel on the front face so they stay chisel-sharp while clipping tough mountain bunchgrass off rocky soil.

To honor the animal that rescued Peru's mountain economy after rebounding from just 6,000 individuals in the 1960s to over 350,000 today, the vicuña stands proudly in the top-left corner of Peru's national coat of arms and flag.

mammals.name: Aye-aye
mammals.summary:
The aye-aye (, Daubentonia madagascariensis) is a long-fingered lemur, a strepsirrhine primate native to Madagascar with rodent-like teeth that perpetually grow and a special thin middle finger that they can use to catch grubs and larvae out of tree trunks.
It is the world's largest nocturnal primate.
facts: The aye-aye's skeletal middle finger looks like a dry twig, three times thinner than its other fingers and mounted on a ball-and-socket joint that swivels 360 degrees, which it uses to tap on hollow tree trunks up to eight times per second to echolocate wood-boring grubs tunneling inside.

It is the only primate on Earth known to use percussive echolocation: as it taps on bark, its giant, leathery, bat-like ears focus on the hollow acoustic reflections beneath the wood, and then it gnaws open the bark with beaver-like teeth and hooks the grub out with that skinny middle finger.

When not in use for tapping or picking its nose, that delicate middle finger runs four degrees cooler than the rest of its hand; only when the aye-aye starts foraging does it pump warm blood and extra nerve sensitivity into the finger.

In 2022, high-speed night-vision footage from the Duke Lemur Center went viral when scientists discovered the aye-aye slides the entire three-inch length of its skinny middle finger all the way down its nasal passages into its throat to pick its nose and lick it clean.

When European naturalists first examined the aye-aye in 1780, its continuously growing, chisel-like front incisor teeth fooled them into classifying it as a giant tree squirrel for nearly 70 years before realizing it is actually the world's largest nocturnal primate!
Female aye-ayes are the only primates known to have their nipples located down near their groin rather than on their chest.

mammals.name: Guanaco
mammals.summary: The guanaco ( gwah-NAH-koh; Lama guanicoe) is a camelid native to South America, closely related to the domesticated llama. Guanacos are one of two wild South American camelids; the other species is the vicuña, which lives at higher elevations.
facts: The wild guanaco is the direct evolutionary ancestor of the domesticated llama, having been bred by indigenous Andean shepherds starting around 6,500 years ago.

When a pack of guanacos spots a stalking puma in Patagonia, they don't immediately scatter; instead, the herd stands ground, stares directly at the big cat, and lets out a high-pitched, staccato alarm laugh that sounds like a horse whinnying, telling the ambush predator *'We see you, don't bother running!'*
To shield their throats from each other's razor-sharp fighting fangs during brutal territorial battles, adult male guanacos grow a thickened leather-like collar of skin around their necks.

Because they roam from the salt flats of the Atacama Desert, the driest place on Earth, up to 13,000-foot glaciers, guanacos can lick moisture directly off fog-drenched cacti and drink salty ocean water without getting sick.
Their thick, double-layered eyelashes are so lush that howling Patagonian dust storms with 70-mph winds can't scratch their corneas.
Wait until a guanaco crosses a Patagonian fjord or glacier river: despite being a desert camelid, it is a strong swimmer that can paddle across icy channels at nearly four miles per hour.

mammals.name: Fennec fox
mammals.summary: The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) is a small fox native to the deserts of North Africa, ranging from Western Sahara and Mauritania to the Sinai Peninsula. Its most distinctive feature is its unusually large ears, which serve to dissipate heat and listen for underground prey.
facts: Measuring a full six inches long, up to a third of its entire body length, the fennec fox's enormous ears act as twin radiators packed with blood vessels near the skin that dump excess body heat into the cool desert night air.
At only two to three pounds when fully grown, the fennec fox is the smallest of all canine species in the world, weighing less than a standard six-pack of soda or a Chihuahua.

Those gigantic ears are also sensitive enough to hear a beetle, scorpion, or lizard crawling underneath a foot of dry Sahara sand, which the fox then excavates by digging up to 20 feet of sand in a single night.

A fennec fox's kidneys are so hyper-efficient at concentrating urine and preventing water loss that the animal can live its entire life in the Sahara without ever drinking free-standing water, getting 100 percent of its moisture from insects, roots, and desert berries.
The soles of its tiny paws are completely covered in thick, silky fur that works both as insulated desert boots on 150°F sand and as wide snowshoes to keep it from sinking into loose dunes.
Unlike most solitary foxes, fennec foxes live in cozy underground family clans of up to 10 individuals and actually purr just like a domestic housecat when happy and relaxed!

mammals.name: Coati
mammals.summary: The South American coati (Nasua nasua), also known as the ring-tailed coati or brown-nosed coati, is a coati species and a member of the raccoon family (Procyonidae), found in the tropical and subtropical parts of South America. An adult generally weighs from 2–7.2 kg (4.4–15.9 lb) and is 85–113 cm (33–44 in) long, with half of that being its tail.
facts: Ever seen a video of tiny 'miniature brachiosaurus dinosaurs' marching backward through a tropical meadow? If you play footage of a troop of coatis running through tall grass with their long, ringed tails held straight up in the air in reverse, their swaying tails look uncanny, like a herd of long-necked sauropods!

Why do coatis hold their two-foot-long ringed tails straight up like radio antennas? It isn't for balance on the ground; the vertical striped tails act as high-visibility periscopes so the whole family troop of 30 females and juveniles can keep track of each other in chest-high jungle ferns.

A coati's long, pig-like snout contains a flexible bone tip ('rostral cartilage') that allows the nose to bend 60 degrees in any direction to poke under rotting logs and sniff out tarantulas, crabs, and lizards.

Adult male coatis are kicked out of the female family troop as soon as they reach two years old and forced to live completely solitary lives, earning adult males the local name *'coatimundi'* (from the Tupí language for 'lone coati').

When a coati catches a hairy tarantula or a toxic millipede, it places the bug between its front paws and rapidly rolls it back and forth like someone rolling dough into a cylinder until every irritating hair and leg is rubbed neatly off before swallowing.
Thanks to double-jointed ankles that rotate more than 180 degrees, a coati can sprint down vertical tree trunks headfirst faster than almost any predator can follow.

mammals.name: Minke whale
mammals.summary:
The common minke whale or northern minke whale (Balaenoptera acutorostrata) is a species of minke whale within the suborder of baleen whales.
It is the smallest species of the rorquals and the second smallest species of baleen whale.
facts: In the 1960s, Cold War submarines patrolling the Southern Ocean kept picking up a mysterious, rhythmic underwater 'boing-boing' and 'quack-quack' sound that baffled naval intelligence for nearly four decades; submarine crews nicknamed the phantom caller the 'Bio-Duck' until acoustic tags in 2014 proved it was the winter song of the Antarctic minke whale!

Wait until you hear the Northern minke whale's call: off Australia's Great Barrier Reef, dwarf minke whales produce a mechanical, metallic laser-blaster twang officially known to marine biologists as the 'Star Wars vocalization.'

How did the smallest of the rorqual baleen whales get the funny name 'minke'? It is named in mockery of an 18th-century Norwegian whaling rookie named Meincke, who famously mistook a puny 25-foot minke whale for a gargantuan 90-foot blue whale and harpooned it, prompting whalers everywhere to call any undersized whale a 'Meincke's whale.'
Among whalers and whale-watchers, the minke carries the grim nickname 'Stinky Minke' because when it exhales at the surface, its warm spout smells overwhelmingly of rotting fish and digested krill.

Northern Atlantic and Pacific minke whales wear permanent white 'armbands', a bold white stripe across each pectoral flipper, which they flash underwater to startle schools of herring into tight bait balls.
Unlike larger whales that veer away from boats, dwarf minke whales are famously 'boat-positive,' frequently approaching snorkelers and drifting vessels to circle them curiosity-first for hours.

mammals.name: Wallaby
mammals.summary: The red-necked wallaby or Bennett's wallaby (Notamacropus rufogriseus) is a medium-sized macropod marsupial (wallaby), common in the more temperate and fertile parts of eastern Australia, including Tasmania. Red-necked wallabies have been introduced to several other countries, including New Zealand, the United Kingdom (in England and Scotland), Ireland, the Isle of Man, France and Germany.
facts: In 2009, Tasmania's Attorney General told a parliamentary committee that wild Bennett's wallabies were breaking into high-security medical opium poppy fields at night, eating the poppy heads until they were 'high as a kite,' and hopping in frantic circles until they flattened the crops into mysterious 'crop circles' before crashing!

Wallabies are masters of energy recycling: with every hop, their giant Achilles tendons stretch like heavy industrial rubber bands when their feet hit the ground and snap back on takeoff, returning up to 65 percent of the energy of each bound for free.

Even wilder, when a wallaby hops at full speed, the bouncing of its heavy internal guts slams forward and backward against its diaphragm like a piston, automatically pumping air in and out of its lungs without the animal spending muscle energy to breathe.

A female swamp wallaby holds a reproductive record unique among all mammals: because she has two separate uteri and ovulates *before* giving birth to her current baby, she is literally pregnant for her entire adult life without a single day off!

What is the official difference between a wallaby and a kangaroo? Scientists actually classify them in the exact same family (*Macropodidae*, meaning 'big foot'); 'wallaby' (from the Dharug Aboriginal word *walabi*) is simply the traditional name given to small-to-medium species under about 45 pounds with more colorful coats and flatter grinding teeth for forest leaves.
Rock-wallabies have rubbery, textured foot pads edged with stiff fringe hairs that let them bound up near-vertical cliff faces and leap 13 feet across rocky chasms.

mammals.name: Mongolian gerbil
mammals.summary: The Mongolian gerbil, also referred to as the Mongolian jird (Meriones unguiculatus), is a rodent belonging to the subfamily Gerbillinae. Their body size is typically 110–135 mm (4+1⁄4–5+1⁄4 in), with a 95–120 mm (3+3⁄4–4+3⁄4 in) tail, and body weight 60–130 g (2–4+1⁄2 oz), with adult males larger than females.
facts: Known affectionately by early explorers as the 'gentle desert rat,' the Mongolian gerbil evolved in the bone-dry Gobi Desert where water is so precious that a gerbil produces only two or three drops of highly concentrated, nearly odorless urine per day, and recycles water internally by storing fat in its cell layers.

When a Mongolian gerbil spots a hawk or snake overhead, it stands on its hind legs and drums both oversized hind feet against the tunnel floor at super-speed, sending a seismic warning vibration thumping through the ground to every burrow mate.

Why should you never pick up a gerbil by the tip of its furry tail? As a defense against desert birds of prey, a gerbil can instantly shed the outer skin sleeve of its tail ('degloving') to slip free while the predator is left holding a hollow piece of fur, after which the exposed tail bone dries up and drops off.

On the middle of a gerbil's belly sits a narrow, yellowish hairless strip: that is its ventral sebaceous scent gland, which both mothers and fathers rub across rocks, tunnels, and their own babies so the whole family shares one group badge.

Because Mongolian gerbils lack the typical 'Circle of Willis' artery loop at the base of the brain that most mammals have, they played a major historical role in 20th-century stroke research before becoming beloved classroom pets.

Unlike hamsters, which are strictly nocturnal and grumpy if woken at noon, Mongolian gerbils are 'polyphasic', alternating between three hours of frantic digging and three hours of napping right around the clock, day and night.

mammals.name: Margay
mammals.summary: The margay (Leopardus wiedii) is a small wild cat native to Mexico, Central and South America. A solitary and nocturnal felid, it lives mainly in primary evergreen and deciduous forests.
facts: In 2005, researchers in the Brazilian Amazon caught a wild margay doing something no other cat had ever been proved to do: hiding in tangled vines and perfectly mimicking the distress cries of a baby pied tamarin monkey to lure adult monkeys down from the treetops into an ambush!

Alongside the clouded leopard, the margay is the most acrobatic cat on Earth: its hind ankles can rotate a full 180 degrees inward, allowing it to run straight down smooth vertical tree trunks headfirst like a squirrel.

Even more impressively, if a margay misses a branch while leaping 12 feet through the rainforest canopy in the dark, it can grab a passing vine or twig mid-fall with a single front or hind paw and swing itself right back up onto the branch.
A margay is the only cat known that can hang upside down beneath a branch suspended solely by its two hind feet while using both front paws to peel and eat prey.

Because a female margay spends her entire life high in the treetops, she is the only small wild cat that possesses just a single pair of nipples and almost always gives birth to a single kitten at a time.
Its huge, bulging dark brown eyes are proportionally larger than those of any other neotropical cat, gathering the faintest starlight filtering through the dense jungle canopy.

mammals.name: Chipmunk
mammals.summary: Chipmunks are small, striped burrowing squirrels of subtribe Tamiina. Chipmunks are found in North America, with the exception of the Siberian chipmunk, which is found primarily in Asia.
facts: Using two expandable cheek pouches inside its mouth, a single tiny eastern chipmunk can carry up to 12 whole acorns or 70 sunflower seeds at once, expanding its cheeks until its head is literally three times wider than its shoulders, and stockpile up to 165 acorns in a single day!

Unlike groundhogs and bears, which pack on thick body fat and sleep straight through the winter without eating, a chipmunk enters winter 'torpor' with almost zero body fat; instead, it sleeps directly on top of a massive underground bed of thousands of nuts and wakes up every few days to snack in bed.

During deep winter torpor, a chipmunk cools its body temperature from 99°F all the way down to 40°F (the temperature of a kitchen refrigerator) and slows its heart rate from 350 beats per minute down to just 4 beats per minute.

Despite living in dense neighborhoods, chipmunks are fiercely solitary and build secret, hidden burrow entrances under rocks or roots; to make sure no predator spots freshly dug dirt outside their front door, they carry every mouthful of excavated soil away in their cheek pouches and dump it yards away!

The word 'chipmunk' comes from the Odawa (Ojibwe) word *ajidamoo*, which translates poetically to 'one who descends trees headlong', combined with the sharp *'chip!'* alarm call it makes when a hawk flies over.

When a snake approaches rather than a hawk, a chipmunk switches from its high bird-like *'chip!'* to a low-pitched, resonant *'chuck-chuck'* call to tell neighboring chipmunks whether danger is coming from the sky or the ground.

mammals.name: Chinchilla
mammals.summary: Chinchilla is a genus consisting of two species (Chinchilla chinchilla and Chinchilla lanigera) of crepuscular rodents of the parvorder Caviomorpha, native to the Andes Mountains in South America. They live in colonies called "herds" at high elevations up to 4,270 m (14,000 ft).
facts: The chinchilla boasts the densest fur of any land mammal on Earth: whereas a human grows just one hair per skin follicle, a chinchilla sprouts a mind-blowing 50 to 80 ultra-fine hairs from every single follicle, packing more than 20,000 hairs into every square centimeter!
That plush coat is so impossibly dense that fleas, ticks, and lice cannot even breathe in it; parasites literally suffocate before they can reach the chinchilla's skin.

Never give a chinchilla a water bath! Because their fur is so dense, water trapped inside the undercoat will never air-dry and will quickly grow fungus and rot; instead, chinchillas roll and flip wildly in fine volcanic ash and pumice dust ('dust baths') that absorbs skin oils like dry shampoo.

Wait until you hear how a wild chinchilla escapes an Andean fox or owl: along with leaping six feet into the air off rocky ledges, it can involuntarily release big clumps of its own fur ('fur slip') right into the predator's mouth while the naked chinchilla bolts into a rock crack.

Just like the golden hamster, almost every domestic pet chinchilla in North America and Europe traces its ancestry back to just 11 wild chinchillas brought down carefully from the high Andes to California in 1923 by mining engineer Mathias F. Chapman; who took three years descending the mountain so the animals could acclimate to lower altitudes!
A chinchilla's orange front incisor teeth grow up to 12 inches per year, requiring it to chew constantly on volcanic pumice stones and tough sticks to wear them down.

mammals.name: Star-nosed mole
mammals.summary: The star-nosed mole (Condylura cristata) is a small semiaquatic mole found in moist, low elevation areas in the northeastern parts of North America. It is the only extant member of the tribe Condylurini and genus Condylura.
facts: The star-nosed mole is officially the fastest-eating mammal on Earth, as certified by *Guinness World Records* and high-speed cameras in *Nature*, identifying whether a tiny worm or insect larva is edible and swallowing it in as little as 120 milliseconds (nearly a tenth of a second)!

Look at the bizarre pink firework on its snout: those 22 fleshy, wriggling nasal tentacles are not used for smelling; they are covered in 25,000 microscopic touch domes called 'Eimer's organs' packed with over 100,000 nerve fibers (five times more touch fibers than the entire human hand), allowing the nearly blind mole to 'see' in 3D by touch while touching up to 13 spots per second.

Even wilder, the star-nosed mole is one of only two mammals known to science (along with the water shrew) that can *smell underwater*: while swimming along muddy stream bottoms, it blows tiny air bubbles out of its nostrils onto sunken worms and immediately inhales the bubbles back in to sniff the trapped odor molecules!

The two lowest central tentacles right above its mouth (the 11th pair) function just like the high-resolution fovea in the center of a human eye: whenever the outer 20 tentacles brush something interesting, the mole snaps its head so those two central 'fovea tentacles' inspect it before taking a bite.

A map of the star-nosed mole's brain reveals that more than half of its entire sensory cortex is wired strictly to those 22 nose rays, organized into 22 neat stripes that match the tentacles on its face.

During freezing northern winters, this amphibious mole dives straight beneath frozen pond ice and uses its broad, shovel-like front paws and water-repellent fur to hunt aquatic insects in pitch darkness.

mammals.name: Elephant seal
mammals.summary: The southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) is one of two species of elephant seals. It is the largest member of the clade Pinnipedia and the order Carnivora, as well as the largest extant marine mammal that is not a cetacean.
facts: Elephant seals are the deepest-diving pinnipeds on Earth and spend 90 percent of their time at sea completely submerged: they have been recorded diving nearly 1.5 miles deep (over 7,800 feet) and holding their breath for two full hours while hunting giant squid in pitch-black ocean trenches!

Because an elephant seal spends up to eight months at sea diving continuously with only two-minute breathing breaks at the surface, when does it sleep? In 2023, researchers using brainwave-recording caps discovered that elephant seals take 10-minute REM naps *while spiraling slowly downward like falling leaves* at depths of 1,000 feet where sharks and killer whales rarely go!

A dominant adult bull northern or southern elephant seal can weigh up to 8,800 pounds (4 tons), making it the largest member of the order Carnivora, heavier than eight polar bears combined, and outweighs his own female mates by up to eight times, the most extreme size difference of any mammal.

During the winter breeding season on onshore beaches, alpha 'beachmaster' bulls inflate their two-foot, trunk-like noses into resonant echo chambers to produce rhythmic, metallic, drum-like roars that carry for miles while fasting on beach sand for three straight months without eating or drinking.

To survive crushing deep-sea pressures without nitrogen sickness, an elephant seal exhales before diving, stores oxygen directly inside oxygen-binding blood and muscle proteins (its blood volume is over 20 percent of its body weight), and squeezes extra red blood cells out of a giant spleen that works like a scuba tank.

By 1892, commercial sealers hunting blubber oil had slaughtered northern elephant seals until biologists believed they were extinct, only for a single surviving colony of fewer than 20 individuals to be found hiding on Mexico's remote Guadalupe Island, from which all 200,000+ northern elephant seals alive today descend!

mammals.name: Gazelle
mammals.summary: Thomson's gazelle (Eudorcas thomsonii) is one of the best known species of gazelles. It is named after explorer Joseph Thomson and is sometimes referred to as a "tommie".
facts: When spotted by a predator, they perform 'stotting', leaping up to 10 feet straight into the air with all four legs stiff, as an honest signal that they are too fit to be worth chasing.

Grant's gazelles can go their entire lives without drinking a single drop of standing water, extracting all the moisture they need from dew-soaked plants and by letting their body temperature rise to prevent sweating.
Their liver and heart can literally shrink by up to 50 percent during prolonged droughts so the organs consume less oxygen and require less water to operate.
The word 'gazelle' comes from the Arabic word 'ghazal,' which is also the name of a traditional form of love poetry inspired by the animal's graceful eyes and tragic beauty.
Newborn fawns spend their first few weeks completely odorless and flattened in tall grass, with mothers deliberately grazing far away so they don't give away the baby's hiding spot.

mammals.name: Pygmy hippopotamus
mammals.summary: The pygmy hippopotamus or pygmy hippo (Choeropsis liberiensis) is a small hippopotamid which is native to the forests and swamps of West Africa, primarily in Liberia, with small populations in Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Ivory Coast. It has been extirpated from Nigeria and possibly Guinea-Bissau.
facts: Like their giant cousins, they secrete a thick, pinkish 'blood sweat' called hipposudoric acid that acts as both a natural broad-spectrum antibiotic and a waterproof sunscreen.
When they dive underwater, muscular valves automatically snap their nostrils and ears shut like submarine hatches.
Males mark their territory via 'muck-spreading,' spinning their tails like high-speed helicopter blades while defecating to fling dung as far into the surrounding bushes as possible.
In 1927, tire mogul Harvey Firestone gifted a pygmy hippo named Billy to President Calvin Coolidge, and Billy became the genetic ancestor of almost every pygmy hippo in American zoos.

Unlike common hippos whose eyes and nostrils sit on top of their heads for floating, pygmy hippos have eyes on the sides of their skulls and sloped backs made for ducking through dense forest undergrowth.

mammals.name: Bat-eared fox
mammals.summary: The bat-eared fox (Otocyon megalotis) is a species of fox found on the African savanna. It is the only extant species of the genus Otocyon, and is the sister species to all other members of the tribe Vulpini, not genetically being a true fox.
facts: They possess up to 50 teeth, more than almost any other land mammal, with tiny, specialized molars built to pulverize tough insect exoskeletons.
Their five-inch-tall ears are packed with a dense network of blood vessels that shed excess body heat while amplifying the faint crunch of subterranean beetle larvae chewing roots a foot underground.
A special muscle attachment in their lower jaw lets them open and snap their mouths shut five times per second like a rapid-fire staple gun.
A single bat-eared fox consumes over 1.15 million harvester termites a year, getting nearly all of its daily water directly from the body fluids of its prey.
Among bat-eared foxes, fathers do the majority of the parenting, guarding the den, grooming the pups, and taking them on their very first foraging trips while the mother rests.

mammals.name: Weasel
mammals.summary: The least weasel (Mustela nivalis), little weasel, common weasel, or simply weasel is the smallest member of the genus Mustela, family Mustelidae and order Carnivora. It is native to Eurasia, North America and North Africa, and has been introduced to New Zealand, Malta, Crete, the Azores, and São Tomé.
facts: To confuse and hypnotize rabbits, they perform a frantic 'weasel war dance' of erratic flips, sideways hops, and somersaults before delivering a lightning-fast bite to the neck.
Because their long, tubular bodies lose body heat rapidly, they have a furnace-like metabolism and must eat up to half their own body weight every single day just to stay alive.
In snowy regions, their brown summer coat molts into pure white 'ermine' fur; except for a jet-black tail tip designed to trick diving hawks into striking at the tail instead of the head.
A least weasel can squeeze through a hole no wider than a wedding ring and routinely raids underground mouse tunnels that are completely inaccessible to larger predators.
Despite weighing less than a candy bar, the least weasel routinely takes down prey up to ten times its own size, including full-grown hares.

mammals.name: Jerboa
mammals.summary: Jerboas ( ) are the members of the family Dipodidae. They are nocturnal hopping desert rodents found throughout North Africa and Asia.
facts: Their hind feet have fused cannon bones, three separate foot bones melted into one solid rod, acting as shock-absorbing pogo sticks that let them leap up to ten feet in a single bound.
The tufts of stiff hair on the bottoms of their feet work just like snowshoes, preventing them from sinking into loose desert sand and kicking dust into predators' faces.
Wait-time in pregnancy is flexible for some jerboas, which enter deep winter hibernation and emerge to mate using an internal biological clock triggered by soil temperature.
The long-eared jerboa boasts ears that are up to two-thirds the length of its entire body, making its ears proportionally larger than an African elephant's.
During World War II, the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa adopted the jerboa as their emblem and became famously known as the 'Desert Rats.'

mammals.name: Harbor seal
mammals.summary: The harbor (or harbour) seal (Phoca vitulina), also known as the common seal, is a true seal found along temperate and Arctic marine coastlines of the Northern Hemisphere. The most widely distributed species of pinniped (walruses, eared seals, and true seals), they are found in coastal waters of the northern Atlantic and Pacific oceans, Baltic and North seas.
facts: While lounging on rocky shores, they hold their heads and hind flippers high in the air in a curved 'banana pose' to regulate body temperature and keep dry until the tide rises.
Before diving up to 1,500 feet deep, a harbor seal actually exhales to empty its lungs, preventing decompression sickness ('the bends') and storing oxygen directly in its thick, dark blood instead.

Their beaded, wavy whiskers, called vibrissae, are so sensitive to hydrodynamic water trails that a blindfolded harbor seal can track the exact size and direction of a fish that swam past 30 seconds earlier.
Unlike almost all other mammals, harbor seal pups shed their fluffy white lanugo coat inside their mother's womb before birth, enabling them to swim within minutes of being born.

In the 1970s and 80s, an orphaned harbor seal in Maine named Hoover learned to mimic human speech in a thick New England fisherman's accent, shouting 'Hey! How are ya?' and 'Get outta there!' at aquarium visitors.

mammals.name: Galago
mammals.summary: Galagos , also known as bush babies or nagapies (meaning "night monkeys" in Afrikaans), are small nocturnal primates native to continental, sub-Sahara Africa, and make up the family Galagidae (also sometimes called Galagonidae). They are considered a sister group of the Lorisidae.
facts: Also known as bushbabies because their eerie nighttime cries sound just like a wailing human infant, they can jump over six feet straight up in the air powered by elastic tendons in their ankles.
Their enormous eyes are so large and tubular that they are locked completely in place within their sockets; to look around, a galago must swivel its entire head like an owl.
They practice 'urine washing,' deliberately peeing onto their hands and rubbing the urine onto the soles of their feet to improve their grip on slick branches and leave a scent trail with every leap.
A galago possesses a second, spiky 'sub-tongue' hidden underneath its main tongue, which works with comb-like lower front teeth to scrape sticky tree gum and clean matted fur.
While flying through pitch-black branches in mid-air, they fold their delicate, bat-like ears completely flat against their heads to shield them from twigs and thorns.

mammals.name: American badger
mammals.summary: The American badger (Taxidea taxus) is a North American badger  similar in appearance to the European badger, although not closely related. It is found in the western, central, and northeastern United States, northern Mexico, and south-central Canada to certain areas of southwestern British Columbia.
facts: American badgers and coyotes have been filmed teaming up as hunting partners; the badger digs into squirrel burrows from below while the coyote waits at the escape holes above.

Armed with two-inch curved front claws and loose neck skin that lets them twist around and bite even while pinned in a predator's jaws, they can dig themselves completely underground in less than a minute.
Female badgers use 'delayed implantation,' mating in mid-summer but pausing the fertilized egg's development until the dead of winter so their cubs are born in the warmth of spring.
To preserve food in the summer heat, a badger will bury a slain ground squirrel or prairie dog completely underground in a cool, custom-dug pantry tunnel.
Wisconsin got its nickname 'The Badger State' not from the animal itself, but from 1820s lead miners who dug cave-like shelters into hillsides instead of building houses.

mammals.name: Marmoset
mammals.summary: The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), also called white-tufted marmoset or white-tufted-ear marmoset, is a New World monkey. It originally lived on the northeastern coast of Brazil, in the states of Piauí, Paraíba, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco, Alagoas, and Bahia.
facts: Nearly every marmoset pregnancy produces fraternal twins that share a fused placenta in the womb, swapping stem cells so that each sibling carries the other's DNA in its blood and organs for life.

Fathers and older brothers carry the newborn twins on their backs almost continuously, experiencing spikes in prolactin, the hormone associated with nursing, and losing up to 10 percent of their body weight from the effort.
Pygmy marmosets can weigh less than a single AA battery, clinging vertically to tree trunks and chiseling rows of tiny holes into the bark so they can return the next day to lap up the sap.
Young marmosets go through a babbling phase just like human babies, stringing together random chirps, trills, and whistles until their parents respond and shape their vocalizations into adult calls.
Instead of flat fingernails like most primates, marmosets have sharp, claw-like nails called tegulae on every digit except their big toes, allowing them to scamper up smooth tree bark like squirrels.

mammals.name: American pika
mammals.summary: The American pika (Ochotona princeps) is a small, herbivorous mammal of the family Ochotonidae, closely related to rabbits and hares (order Lagomorpha). It is native to the mountainous regions of western North America, typically inhabiting rocky slopes and talus fields at or above the tree line.
facts: Because they do not hibernate, pikas spend the entire summer building giant 'haypiles' of up to 60 pounds of wildflowers and grasses under rocks to sustain them under the winter snowpack.

They are savvy organic chemists: they intentionally harvest toxic alpine plants filled with natural preservatives that won't rot, storing them until the poison breaks down in late winter and the plants become safe to eat.

A pika's resting body temperature is dangerously close to its lethal limit, around 104°F, meaning that just a few hours trapped in temperatures above 78°F without cool shade can cause fatal heatstroke.
Like rabbits, pikas produce two distinct types of droppings, immediately eating the soft, shiny green 'cecotropes' straight from their bodies to extract B vitamins and protein a second time.
Even the soles of a pika's feet are covered in dense fur, giving them both insulation on freezing snow and traction when leaping across slick granite boulders.

mammals.name: Gemsbok
mammals.summary: The gemsbok (Oryx gazella) is a large antelope in the genus Oryx. It is endemic to the dry and barren regions of Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and (parts of) Zimbabwe, mainly inhabiting the Kalahari and Namib Deserts, areas in which it is supremely adapted for survival.
facts: Despite standing under scorching Kalahari sun where their body temperature climbs past 113°F, a specialized network of blood vessels called the carotid rete cools blood flowing to their brain by several degrees so they don't suffer brain damage.
Both males and females wield rapier-straight, ringed horns up to nearly four feet long, and females actually have longer, thinner horns that are even deadlier for skewering attacking lions.

When viewed in profile from a distance, a standing gemsbok's two horns align so perfectly that they look like a single horn, a visual illusion widely believed to have inspired early traveler myths of the unicorn.
They can sniff out buried desert melons and water-storing tubers deeply hidden beneath dry sand, digging them up with their hooves to survive months without surface water.
Striking black-and-white Kabuki-style facial markings help herd members communicate gaze direction and head posture across shimmering desert heat mirages.

mammals.name: Striped skunk
mammals.summary: The striped skunk (Mephitis mephitis) is a skunk of the genus Mephitis that occurs across much of North America, including southern Canada, the United States, and northern Mexico. It is currently listed as least concern by the IUCN on account of its wide range and ability to adapt to human-modified environments.
facts: Before firing its notorious spray, a striped skunk always gives a three-step polite warning: it stomps its front paws loudly, hisses while raising its tail, and sometimes pops up into a handstand.
Their dual anal scent glands act like twin squirt guns with directional nozzles that can accurately hit a target between the eyes from up to 15 feet away.

Skunk spray contains sulfur compounds called thiols that are so flammable and pungent the human nose can detect them at concentrations of just 10 parts per billion, and it takes up to 10 days for a skunk to fully recharge its empty glands.
Striped skunks are functionally immune to rattlesnake and copperhead venom, allowing them to casually hunt and eat venomous pit vipers without getting sick.
Great horned owls are the striped skunk's top natural predator simply because the owls have almost no sense of smell and aren't bothered in the slightest by being sprayed.

mammals.name: South American tapir
mammals.summary: The South American tapir (Tapirus terrestris), also commonly called the Brazilian tapir (from the Tupi tapi'ira), the Amazonian tapir, the maned tapir, the lowland tapir, anta (Brazilian Portuguese), and sachavaca (literally "bushcow", in mixed Quechua and Spanish), is one of the four recognized species in the tapir family (of the order Perissodactyla, with the mountain tapir, the Malayan tapir, and the Baird's tapir). It is the largest surviving native terrestrial mammal in the Amazon.
facts: Their flexible snout is actually a fusion of the nose and upper lip that works as a prehensile snorkel, grabbing high leaves on land and breathing above the surface while the tapir walks along riverbeds underwater.
Born looking like walking watermelons, baby tapirs sport a dark coat covered in white stripes and spots that mimic dappled forest sunlight until the camouflage fades at around six months of age.
With four toes on their front feet and three on their back feet, their splayed hooves work like mud-shoes on soft riverbanks.

Known as the 'gardeners of the forest,' a single tapir swallows thousands of large fruit seeds whole and deposits them in nutrient-rich dung piles inside rivers and clearings across miles of territory.

Male South American tapirs boast one of the largest penises relative to body size of any land mammal, which actually features flared, gripping lobes at the tip to ensure successful mating in the water.

mammals.name: Flying squirrel
aliases: red and white giant flying squirrel
mammals.summary: Flying squirrels (scientifically known  as Pteromyini or Petauristini) are a tribe of 50 species of squirrels in the family Sciuridae. Despite their name, they are not in fact capable of full flight in the same way as birds or bats, but they are able to glide from one tree to another with the aid of a patagium, a furred skin membrane that stretches from wrist to ankle.
facts: Under ultraviolet blacklight, flying squirrels glow a vibrant neon bubble-gum pink due to porphyrin compounds in their fur, a secret visual signal visible to nocturnal owls and fellow squirrels.

They possess a special wrist spur of cartilage called the styliform cartilage that pops out like a switchblade when they leap, stretching their furry gliding membrane tight and acting as a winglet to reduce air drag.

Though they never truly flap to fly, a flying squirrel can glide over the length of a football field from a single tall tree, using its flat, feathery tail as a rudder to make mid-air 90-degree turns.
In freezing winter weather, up to 20 otherwise solitary flying squirrels will pack tightly into a single woodpecker cavity to share body heat, raising the nest's temperature by more than 50°F.
Right before slamming into a tree trunk at the end of a glide, the squirrel flips its body upward to stall like a parachute and lands softly on all four shock-absorbing paws.

mammals.name: Red kangaroo
mammals.summary: The red kangaroo (Osphranter rufus) is the largest of all kangaroos, the largest terrestrial mammal native to Australia, and the largest extant marsupial. It is found across mainland Australia, except for the more fertile areas, such as southern Western Australia, the eastern and southeastern coasts, and the rainforests along the northern coast.
