facts: At high speeds, a red kangaroo actually uses *less* energy the faster it hops because its giant Achilles tendons stretch and snap back like rubber bands, while the bouncing of its internal organs pumps air in and out of its lungs like a piston.

A female red kangaroo can be perpetually pregnant, simultaneously nursing an older joey outside the pouch, a tiny hairless joey attached to a teat inside the pouch, and holding a third fertilized embryo in suspended animation.

Even more remarkably, the mother can produce two completely different formulas of milk at the exact same time from two separate teats; one high-fat milk for the older joey and one high-carbohydrate milk for the newborn.

During heatwaves, red kangaroos lick their own forearms until they are soaking wet; a dense patch of superficial blood vessels right beneath the skin cools their entire bloodstream as the saliva evaporates.
When moving slowly while grazing, a kangaroo uses its muscular tail as a 'fifth leg,' planting it on the ground to support its entire body weight while swinging both hind legs forward together.

mammals.name: Tiger quoll
mammals.summary: The tiger quoll (Dasyurus maculatus), also known as the spotted-tailed quoll, spotted quoll, spotted-tailed dasyure, or tiger cat, is a carnivorous marsupial of the quoll genus Dasyurus native to Australia. With males and females weighing around 3.5 and 1.8 kg (7.7 and 4.0 lb), respectively, it is the world's second-largest extant carnivorous marsupial, behind the Tasmanian devil.
facts: Despite being the size of a housecat, the tiger quoll possesses the second-strongest bite force relative to body size of any living mammal on Earth, trailing only its cousin, the Tasmanian devil.

A mother tiger quoll gives birth to up to 30 rice-grain-sized joeys at once, even though her backward-facing pouch only has six teats, creating a ruthless race where only the first six babies to latch on survive.
Unlike almost all other marsupials, tiger quolls establish communal 'latrine sites' on flat rocky ledges where every quoll in the area deposits its droppings to leave social updates for neighbors.

Ridged, fleshy pads on the bottoms of their paws and a fully opposable hallux (thumb-toe) on their hind feet allow them to climb smooth eucalyptus trunks and ambush sleeping possums and gliders in the canopy.
During the brief mid-winter mating season, female tiger quolls develop swollen necks to survive the famously rough courtship bites of males that clamp onto their shoulders for hours.

mammals.name: Chamois
mammals.summary: The chamois (; French: [ʃamwa] ; Rupicapra rupicapra), or Alpine chamois, is a species of goat-antelope native to mountainous parts of Europe and Western Asia, from the Pyrenees and the Cantabrian Mountain Range, the Alps, the Apennines, the Dinarides, the Tatra to the Carpathian Mountains, the Balkan Mountains, the Rila–Rhodope massif, Pindus, the northeastern mountains of Turkey, and the Caucasus. It has also been introduced to the South Island of New Zealand.
facts: Before synthetic microfiber was invented, 'shammy' leather cloths used for polishing cars without scratching paint were genuinely made from the oil-tanned hide of the alpine chamois.
Their hooves have a hard, sharp outer rim surrounding a soft, spongy inner pad that acts like a suction cup on wet, icy limestone cliffs.
A chamois can leap nearly 20 feet horizontally across mountain chasms and bound up near-vertical rock faces at speeds topping 30 miles per hour.
In winter, males grow a prized tuft of eight-inch-long hair along their spine called the 'Gamsbart' (chamois beard), which traditional Alpine hunters wear as an expensive plume on their hats.
Both sexes carry backward-curved, fishhook-shaped black horns that they use not just for headbutting rivals, but for hooking an opponent's legs or belly from underneath on steep ledges.

mammals.name: Vervet monkey
mammals.summary: The vervet monkey (Chlorocebus pygerythrus), or simply vervet, is an Old World monkey of the family Cercopithecidae native to Africa. The term "vervet" is also used to refer to all the members of the genus Chlorocebus.
facts: Vervet monkeys use distinct vocabulary words for different predators: a 'leopard' alarm sends the troop scrambling into the highest thin tree branches, an 'eagle' call makes them dive into low bushes, and a 'snake' call makes everyone stand on their hind legs and peer into the grass.

Adult males display a bright turquoise-blue scrotum framed by a vivid scarlet-red penis and brilliant white belly fur, and the shade of blue actually fades if a dominant male loses social status in the troop.

On the Caribbean island of St. Kitts, where escaped vervets have lived since the 1600s, scientists studying them discovered the monkeys voluntarily raid beach bars to drink leftover cocktails in exact proportion to human drinking patterns (some teetotalers, most social drinkers, and a few heavy binge drinkers).
High-ranking mothers get preferential babysitting from lower-ranking females eager to curry favor and gain grooming privileges within the troop's strict matriarchal hierarchy.
When crossing open ground between patches of trees, vervets often walk upright on two legs so they can carry stolen farm crops in both hands while keeping watch over tall grass.

mammals.name: Babirusa
mammals.summary: Babirusas, also called deer-pigs (Malay: babi rusa), are a genus, Babyrousa, in the swine family found in the Indonesian islands of Sulawesi, Togian, Sula and Buru. Previously all members of this genus were considered part of a single species, B. babyrussa, but in 2002 they were split into several species.
facts: In male babirusas, the upper canine teeth never enter the mouth at all; instead, they grow upside-down straight through the flesh and bone of the top of the snout, curving backward toward the eyes.

If a male babirusa does not wear down or snap off his ever-growing upper tusks by rubbing them against trees, the tusks can eventually curl all the way back and pierce right through his own skull and brain.
Because their curving upper tusks are actually quite brittle, battling males don't slash each other; instead, they rear up on their hind legs and box like kangaroos with their front hooves.

Unlike every other wild pig species, which have tough rostral bones in their snouts for rooting up hard earth, the babirusa has a soft nose and can only forage in loose mud, rotting logs, and fallen fruit.

Their digestive tract features an enlarged fore-stomach more like a sheep's or hippo's than a typical pig's, leading local Indonesian folklore to view them as half-pig, half-deer (the name literally translates to 'pig-deer').

mammals.name: Ibex
mammals.summary: The Alpine ibex (Capra ibex), also known as the steinbock, is a European species of goat which lives in the Alps. It is one of ten species in the genus Capra, and its closest living relative is the Iberian ibex.
facts: In Northern Italy, Alpine ibexes regularly scale the near-vertical 160-foot stone wall of the Cingino Dam on hooves the width of a human thumb just to lick mineral salts seeping from the masonry.

Male ibexes carry scimitar-shaped, heavily ridged horns that can reach nearly five feet in length and weigh over 30 pounds, and during fights, they rear up on their hind legs to slam those horns down with a crack audible a mile away.

In the Middle Ages, powdered ibex horn and 'bezoar stones' from an ibex's stomach were worth their weight in gold as supposed cure-alls for poison, driving the species to the brink of extinction until a single Italian king protected the last 100 survivors in 1821.
Their split hooves operate independently like pincers, gripping tiny rock seams less than an inch wide while soft, rubbery heel pads conform to uneven granite.
Every single living Alpine ibex today is descended from that tiny royal herd kept in Italy's Gran Paradiso mountains in the 19th century.

mammals.name: Elephant shrew
mammals.summary: Sengis, also called elephant shrews or jumping shrews, are small insectivorous mammals native to Africa, belonging to the family Macroscelididae, in the order Macroscelidea. Their traditional common English name "elephant shrew" comes from a perceived resemblance between their long noses and the trunk of an elephant, and their superficial similarity with shrews (family Soricidae) in the order Eulipotyphla.
facts: Despite looking like a mouse with a miniature anteater snout, DNA studies revealed they are not rodents or shrews at all; their closest living relatives include elephants, manatees, and aardvarks.

They spend hours every day maintaining a meticulous network of tiny, swept 'highways' through the leaf litter, clearing away every twig and pebble so they can sprint away from predators at nearly 18 miles per hour without tripping.
A giant elephant shrew's tongue is so long it extends past the tip of its flexible trunk-like nose, allowing it to flick ants and termites into its mouth while keeping its snout in constant motion.

Monogamous pairs share the exact same territory for life, yet they rarely hang out together; each partner patrols the shared highway network solo and only meets up briefly to mate or defend the border.

When startled, they drum their long hind feet rapidly against dry leaves to broadcast a seismic and acoustic vibration that tells snakes and lizards, 'I've already spotted you, don't bother chasing me.'

mammals.name: Muntjac
mammals.summary: Muntjacs (  MUNT-jak), also known as the barking deer or rib-faced deer, are small deer of the genus Muntiacus native to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Muntjacs are thought to have begun appearing 15–35 million years ago, with remains found in Miocene deposits in France, Germany and Poland.
facts: Known as the 'barking deer,' an alarmed muntjac can bark continuously for over an hour with a sharp, hoarse yip that sounds almost indistinguishable from a medium-sized dog.

They can open their face like a transformer: four large scent glands on their forehead and beneath their eyes literally turn inside out and inflate into fleshy pockets when the deer marks branches or courts a mate.
Male muntjacs are armed with both small branched antlers *and* razor-sharp, downward-pointing upper canine tusks, using their antlers to parry a rival's head and then slashing with their fangs.
The Indian muntjac holds the record for the lowest chromosome count of any mammal on Earth; females have just six chromosomes and males have seven, compared to 46 in humans.
After a handful of Reeves's muntjacs escaped from Woburn Abbey in 1925, they quietly colonized the British countryside and are now one of the most widespread wild mammals in England.

mammals.name: Proboscis monkey
mammals.summary: The proboscis monkey or long-nosed monkey (Nasalis larvatus) is an arboreal Old World monkey with an unusually large nose (or proboscis), a reddish-brown skin color and a long tail. It is endemic to the Southeast Asian island of Borneo and is found mostly in mangrove forests and on the coastal areas of the island.
facts: An adult male's pendulous, eggplant-shaped nose can grow past four inches long, hanging down over his mouth so that he physically has to push it aside with his hand to eat certain foods.
That oversized nose acts as a natural echo chamber, amplifying the male's honks and roars across dense mangrove swamps to intimidate rivals and attract females.

They have partially webbed hands and feet and are the most aquatic of all primates, frequently belly-flopping off branches 50 feet high into crocodile-infested rivers and swimming up to 65 feet completely underwater.

Their permanent 'pot belly' isn't fat; it's a massive, four-chambered cow-like stomach packed with symbiotic bacteria that ferment toxic mangrove leaves and unripe fruit, making up a quarter of the monkey's entire body weight.
Eating sweet, ripe fruit can actually kill a proboscis monkey; the sugars ferment so rapidly inside their specialized stomachs that they cause fatal, balloon-like bloating.

mammals.name: Spinner dolphin
mammals.summary: The spinner dolphin (Stenella longirostris) is a small dolphin found in off-shore tropical waters around the world. It is famous for its acrobatic displays in which it rotates around its longitudinal axis as it leaps through the air.
facts: They are the only cetaceans that can spin like a drill bit in mid-air, launching ten feet above the waves and completing up to seven full body rotations in a single leap before splashing back down.

Scientists found that their spinning leaps aren't just for fun; the torque of spinning in the air followed by a loud belly-flop strips off parasitic remora suckerfish and broadcasts an acoustic ping to keep the pod together at night.
Like other dolphins, they sleep with only half their brain at a time, swimming slowly in tight, synchronized formations with one eye open to watch for sharks and remember to surface for air.

In Hawaiian waters, spinner dolphins hunt deep-water squid and lanternfish all night long, then spend their mornings resting over bright white sand flats so the pale seafloor makes dark shark silhouettes instantly visible.
An adult spinner dolphin can pack up to 260 tiny, needle-sharp interlocking teeth into its long, slender beak; more teeth than almost any other dolphin species.

mammals.name: Agouti
mammals.summary: The agouti ( , ə-GOO-tee) or common agouti is any of several rodent species of the genus Dasyprocta, from Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús), meaning "hair", and πρωκτός (prōktós), meaning "anus". They are native to Central America, northern and central South America, and the southern Lesser Antilles.
facts: The agouti is virtually the only animal in the Amazon rainforest with chisel-like front teeth strong enough to gnaw open the rock-hard, cannonball-sized seed pods of the Brazil nut tree.
Because they bury surplus Brazil nuts one by one across the forest floor and forget where they hid many of them, huge commercial Brazil nut trees cannot reproduce in the wild without wild agoutis.
When eating, an agouti sits upright on its haunches and holds fruit or nuts between its front paws just like an oversized squirrel, peeling away the tough rind before eating the flesh.
If threatened, the agouti erects a dramatic fan of long, coarse hairs on its rump and leaps up to six feet straight into the air while letting out a piercing alarm bark.

Although monogamous pairs stay together until one partner dies, the male isn't allowed near the burrow when babies are born; the fiercely protective mother chases him off until the precocial pups are ready to forage.

mammals.name: Kudu
mammals.summary: The greater kudu  (Tragelaphus strepsiceros) is a large woodland antelope, found throughout eastern and southern Africa. Despite occupying such widespread territory, they are sparsely populated in most areas due to declining habitat, deforestation, and poaching.
facts: A male greater kudu's corkscrew horns take six full years to complete their two-and-a-half twists, and if straightened out, a single horn could reach nearly six feet in length.
Sometimes two sparring male kudus lock their spiraling horns together so tightly that neither animal can pull free, resulting in both rivals dying together of exhaustion.
Despite standing five feet tall at the shoulder and weighing up to 700 pounds, a kudu can effortlessly clear an eight-foot-high ranch fence from a nearly standing start.
Traditional African sportsmen and scouts have long blown hollowed-out kudu horns as deep, resonant 'vuvuzelas' and ceremonial trumpets whose low notes carry for miles across the bushveld.

When hiding in dry woodland, a kudu freezes completely motionless; the vertical white stripes down its flanks break up its outline so effectively that predators can walk within yards without seeing it.

mammals.name: Honduran white bat
mammals.summary: The Honduran white bat (Ectophylla alba), also called the Caribbean white tent-making bat, is a species of bat in the family Phyllostomidae. It is the only member of the genus Ectophylla.
facts: Measuring less than two inches long, they are tiny snow-white puffballs that chew the side veins of giant Heliconia leaves until the leaf collapses into a waterproof, V-shaped tent.

As sunlight filters through the green leaf tent from above, the bats' pure white fur reflects the green glow, rendering the huddled colony nearly invisible to predators looking up from the forest floor.
They are one of the only mammals on Earth able to accumulate bright yellow carotenoid pigments (lutein) in their skin, giving their noses, ears, and wings a vivid marigold-orange color.

Up to a dozen bats, usually one adult male and a harem of females, roost pressed tightly in a single line along the leaf's central rib, ready to burst out into flight the instant a snake vibrates the stem.
Unlike almost all other small bats that hunt insects, Honduran white bats are strict fruit specialists that feed almost exclusively on a single species of wild fig.

mammals.name: Warthog
mammals.summary: The common warthog (Phacochoerus africanus) is a wild member of the pig family (Suidae) found in grassland, savanna, and woodland in sub-Saharan Africa. In the past, it was commonly treated as a subspecies of P. aethiopicus, but today that scientific name is restricted to the desert warthog of northern Kenya, Somalia, and eastern Ethiopia.
facts: Despite their fierce tusks, a warthog's facial 'warts' aren't blemishes or skin growths at all; they are thick, cartilaginous crash pads that protect the eyes and jawbones during high-speed tusk battles.

When retreating into an abandoned aardvark burrow for the night, a warthog always backs in rear-end first so its razor-sharp lower tusks are facing the doorway ready to gore any leopard or hyena that tries to follow.
To reach short, sweet grass shoots without bending their short necks, warthogs drop down onto calloused, padded wrists and shuffle across the savanna on their knees.

At the crack of dawn, warthogs explode out of their burrows at full sprint in case a predator is waiting outside to ambush them, a behavior that occasionally sends waiting lions flying through the air.
While fleeing danger, the entire family runs in single file with their tufted tails held straight up in the air like radio antennas so the piglets can follow the herd through tall grass.

mammals.name: Squirrel monkey
mammals.summary: Squirrel monkeys are New World monkeys of the genus Saimiri. Saimiri is the only genus in the subfamily Saimiriinae.
facts: The squirrel monkey holds the highest brain-to-body mass ratio of any primate, about 1:17, which is roughly twice the brain-to-body ratio of a human being.

In 1959, a Peruvian squirrel monkey named Miss Baker rode a Jupiter rocket 300 miles into space and returned safely, going on to live for another 25 years on a diet of bananas, cottage cheese, and strawberry gelatin.

During the annual two-month breeding season, adult males transform into 'fatted males,' rapidly gaining up to 25 percent of their body weight in water and fat around their shoulders and arms to look more impressive to females.
Because they cannot sweat through their body skin, squirrel monkeys keep cool in the humid canopy by urinating on their hands and feet and letting the moisture evaporate as they climb.

Unlike larger South American monkeys that use their tails to hang from branches, adult squirrel monkeys use their long, black-tipped tails strictly as a balancing pole, though infants curl their tails around their mother's back like a seatbelt.

mammals.name: Tree-kangaroo
mammals.summary: Tree-kangaroos are marsupials of the genus Dendrolagus, adapted for arboreal locomotion. They inhabit the tropical rainforests of New Guinea and far northeastern  Queensland, Australia, along with some of the islands in the region.
facts: Unlike ground-dwelling kangaroos, tree-kangaroos can move their hind legs independently to walk and climb, and they always climb down tree trunks backward.
They can leap down from canopy branches as high as 60 feet to the forest floor without suffering a single injury, using their heavy, furry tails as a counterbalance.
Their sponge-like, rubbery paw pads and curved claws act like natural climbing cleats to grip slippery, moss-covered bark in cloud forests.
Because their diet of tough leaves is slow to digest, they have a multi-chambered stomach full of fermenting bacteria, much like a cow.
Matschie's tree-kangaroos stay completely dry in torrential rainforest downpours thanks to a whorl of hair on their backs that channels rainwater right off their coats.

mammals.name: Kangaroo rat
mammals.summary: Kangaroo rats, small mostly nocturnal rodents of genus Dipodomys, are native to arid areas of western North America. The common name derives from their bipedal form.
facts: A kangaroo rat can go its entire life without ever drinking a single drop of liquid water, manufacturing all the moisture it needs metabolically from dry seeds.
Its kidneys are roughly five times more efficient than a human's, producing urine so concentrated that it crystallizes almost immediately after hitting the ground.
To escape ambushing rattlesnakes in pitch darkness, it has oversized, hollow middle-ear chambers that can detect the low-frequency rustle of a snake's scales before the strike finishes.
Wait-time in midair is no problem for a kangaroo rat: it can flick its long tail mid-leap to change direction in flight and kick sand directly into a rattlesnake's eyes.
Inside its long nasal passages, cooler tissue condenses moisture from every exhaled breath so the animal reabsorbs water just by breathing.

mammals.name: Mountain goat
mammals.summary: The mountain goat (Oreamnos americanus), also known as the Rocky Mountain goat, is a cloven-footed mammal that is endemic to the remote and rugged mountainous areas of western North America. A subalpine to truly alpine species, it is a sure-footed climber commonly seen on sheer rock faces, near-vertical cliffs and icy passages.
facts: The mountain goat is not actually a true goat at all, but a member of the goat-antelope group more closely related to the European chamois and Asian takin.
Each of its hooves features a hard outer rim surrounding a soft, rubbery inner pad that conforms to tiny rock ledges like the sole of a high-friction climbing shoe.
With a single bound, a mountain goat can jump nearly 12 feet laterally across sheer cliff faces while pulling its body weight up with powerful shoulder muscles.
Their dense, double-layered white coats can withstand freezing winds of 100 miles per hour and temperatures plunging to minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit.
Dominant nannies are fiercely territorial over mineral licks and will even chase off subordinate billies to secure salt for themselves and their kids.

mammals.name: Pine marten
mammals.summary: The European pine marten (Martes martes), also known as the pine marten, is a mustelid native to and widespread in most of Europe, Asia Minor, the Caucasus, and parts of Iran, Iraq, and Syria. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
facts: Pine martens have semi-retractable claws and ultra-flexible ankle joints that can rotate 180 degrees, allowing them to run straight down vertical tree trunks headfirst.

In parts of Ireland and Scotland, resurgent pine marten populations have naturally restored native red squirrels because heavier, less agile invasive gray squirrels are much easier for martens to catch.
A female pine marten can delay the implantation of fertilized eggs for nearly seven months, mating in mid-summer so her kits are born safely the following spring.
Instead of digging their own burrows, pine martens keep up to a dozen different hollow-tree and rock-crevice dens across their territory and rotate between them nightly.
Despite being fierce woodland hunters, pine martens develop a serious sweet tooth in late summer and will gorge on bilberries, rowan berries, and stolen honey.

mammals.name: Malayan tapir
mammals.summary: The Malayan tapir (Tapirus indicus), also called Asian tapir, Asiatic tapir, oriental tapir, Indian tapir, piebald tapir, or black-and-white tapir, is the only living tapir species outside of the Americas. It is native to Southeast Asia from the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra.
facts: Although an adult Malayan tapir looks stark and unmistakable with its two-tone black-and-white 'saddle' coat, that bold pattern actually acts as disruptive camouflage by breaking up its outline in moonlit forests.
Baby Malayan tapirs look nothing like their parents, arriving covered in chocolate-brown fur patterned with white stripes and spots like a furry watermelon.
A tapir's flexible snout is a true prehensile proboscis made of muscle and soft tissue that it uses both to pluck leaves and as a snorkel while walking underwater along riverbeds.
When startled, a Malayan tapir can defend itself by spraying a powerful, foul-smelling jet of urine backward up to several feet.
Often called living fossils, tapirs have kept almost the exact same body plan for over 30 million years and are most closely related to horses and rhinoceroses.

mammals.name: Bongo
mammals.summary: The bongo (Tragelaphus eurycerus) is a large, mostly nocturnal, forest-dwelling antelope, native to sub-Saharan Africa. Bongos are characterised by a striking reddish-brown coat, black-and-white markings, white-yellow stripes, and long, slightly spiraled horns.
facts: Unlike almost all other spiral-horned antelopes, both male and female bongos grow long, lyre-shaped horns that twist in a full spiral.
When running through dense tangles of jungle vines, a bongo tilts its chin up so its long horns lie flat along its back, preventing them from snagging on branches.
After lightning storms in the forest, bongos purposefully seek out burned trees and chew on the charred wood and ash to get vital salts and minerals.
The white vertical stripes along a bongo's rich chestnut coat mimic shafts of sunlight filtering through dense forest foliage, making a standing bongo nearly invisible.
Local folklore in parts of Central Africa once held the bongo in such awe that villagers believed touching one or eating its meat would cause neurological spasms.

mammals.name: Pocket gopher
mammals.summary: Pocket gophers, commonly referred to simply as gophers, are burrowing rodents of the family Geomyidae. The roughly 41 species are all endemic to North and Central America.
facts: A pocket gopher's fur-lined cheek pouches are actually on the outside of its cheeks and can be turned completely inside out like pant pockets to shake out dirt.
Because its lips close tightly *behind* its four large front incisor teeth, a pocket gopher can chew straight through hard roots and packed soil without getting a mouthful of dirt.
Its front teeth grow up to 14 inches a year to compensate for the relentless wear of chiseling through rocky underground soil.
To navigate backward through pitch-dark tunnels just as fast as it moves forward, the pocket gopher uses its nearly hairless, touch-sensitive tail like a blind person's cane.

After the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, researchers airlifted pocket gophers onto the barren pumice slopes for just one day, and their digging churned up buried soil spores that jump-started plant recovery.

mammals.name: Fossa
mammals.summary: The fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox;  FOSS-ə or  FOO-sə; Malagasy: [ˈfusə̥]) is a slender, long-tailed, cat-like mammal that is endemic to Madagascar. It is a member of the carnivoran family Eupleridae.
facts: Despite looking like a cross between a sleek cougar and a dachshund, the fossa is neither cat nor dog, but a giant, specialized cousin of the mongoose.

Female fossas go through a unique phase as juveniles called 'transient masculinization,' temporarily developing male-like physical traits and secreting an orange, musky chest substance until they mature.
During mating season, a female fossa claims a high branch in a single 'mating tree' for up to a week, often returning to the exact same branch year after year while males compete below.
Equipped with flexible ankles that rotate backward and a tail nearly as long as its body, the fossa is the only predator capable of chasing lemurs at full speed through the treetops.
Fossa pups are born blind and toothless, and do not leave their hidden den until they are over four months old.
The fossa is the largest mammalian carnivore native to the island of Madagascar and the top predator of lemurs.
Although it looks like a cross between a cougar and a mongoose, the fossa belongs to the endemic Malagasy family Eupleridae.
Flexible ankle joints allow a fossa to run down vertical tree trunks headfirst just like a squirrel.

mammals.name: Alpine marmot
mammals.summary: The alpine marmot (Marmota marmota) is a large ground-dwelling squirrel, from the genus of marmots. It is found in high numbers in mountainous areas of central and southern Europe, at heights between 800 and 3,200 m (2,600–10,500 ft) in the Alps, Carpathians, Tatras and Northern Apennines.
facts: Alpine marmots hibernate in tightly huddled family piles of up to 20 individuals for up to eight months a year, dropping their heartbeats to just three to five beats per minute.
During communal hibernation, older brothers and parents literally sacrifice their own fat reserves by periodically warming up to keep the youngest pups from freezing to death.
Their winter burrows are sealed from the inside with a plug of mixed grass, earth, and dung that can be several feet thick to lock out freezing alpine air.
Before diving underground for the winter, an alpine marmot purges its digestive tract completely and shrinks its stomach and intestines by roughly half.
Lookout marmots emit piercing, bird-like whistles that vary in pitch and cadence depending on whether danger is approaching from the sky, like a golden eagle, or across the rocks, like a fox.

mammals.name: Fur seal
mammals.summary: The northern fur seal (Callorhinus ursinus) is an eared seal found along the north Pacific Ocean, the Bering Sea, Sea of Japan and the Sea of Okhotsk. It is the largest member of the fur seal subfamily (Arctocephalinae) and the only living species in the genus Callorhinus.
facts: A fur seal's coat is so astonishingly dense, packing up to 300,000 hairs into a single square inch, that cold seawater never actually touches its skin when it dives.
Unlike true seals that wriggle on their bellies, fur seals have rotating hip bones and long flippers that let them gallop across rocky beaches as fast as a running human.

While sleeping at sea, northern fur seals float on their sides in a posture called the 'jug handle,' holding one front flipper tucked neatly into their hind flippers above the waves to conserve body heat.
Wait-listed mothers returning from week-long fishing trips can locate their single pup among thousands of noisy youngsters on a crowded rookery solely by the unique voice and scent of their baby.
When sleeping in the open ocean, a fur seal can engage unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, keeping half of its brain awake and one eye open looking into the water to watch for sharks and orcas.

mammals.name: Eland
mammals.summary: The common eland (Tragelaphus oryx), also known as the southern eland or eland antelope, is a large savannah and plains antelope found in East and Southern Africa. An adult male is around 1.6 m (5.2 ft) tall at the shoulder and can weigh up to 942 kg (2,077 lb) with a typical range of 500–600 kg (1,100–1,300 lb).
facts: Despite weighing as much as a small car, an adult male eland can leap straight over a six-foot-high fence from a standstill.
As bull elands walk, their knees make a loud, rhythmic clicking sound audible from a hundred yards away, which broadcasts their exact size and strength to rivals without a fight.
Milk from female elands contains roughly three times the butterfat and double the protein of domestic cow's milk, and resists spoiling in hot temperatures for much longer.

To survive scorching droughts without drinking water, an eland allows its core body temperature to rise by up to seven degrees Celsius during the day and releases the stored heat into the cool night air.
Both sexes sport tightly spiraled horns that they use like garden hooks to twist and snap high tree branches down to mouth level for the rest of the herd.

mammals.name: Fallow deer
mammals.summary: Fallow deer is the common name for species of deer in the genus Dama of subfamily Cervinae. The two living species are the European fallow deer (Dama dama), native to Europe and Anatolia, and the Persian fallow deer (Dama mesopotamica), native to the Middle East.
facts: Rather than growing pointed tines like most deer, mature male fallow deer grow wide, flattened, shovel-shaped antlers called 'palms.'
During the autumn rut, fallow bucks develop a massively enlarged Adam's apple and vocal tract, allowing them to emit deep, rhythmic, pig-like groans up to 3,000 times an hour.
When startled, fallow deer perform a stiff-legged bouncing gait called 'pronking' or 'stotting,' springing into the air with all four hooves leaving and hitting the ground simultaneously.
Ancient Romans and later Normans loved fallow deer so much as status symbols and game animals that they transported them by boat from the eastern Mediterranean across Europe and Britain.
A single herd of fallow deer can display four completely different coat colors at once: classic white-spotted chestnut, dark chocolate-black, pale sandy menil, and ghostly pure white.

mammals.name: Bumblebee bat
mammals.summary: Kitti's hog-nosed bat (Craseonycteris thonglongyai), also known as the bumblebee bat or hog-nosed bat, is a near-threatened species of bat and the only extant member of the family Craseonycteridae. It occurs in western Thailand and southeast Myanmar, where it occupies limestone caves along rivers.
facts: Also known as Kitti's hog-nosed bat, it holds the title for the smallest skull of any mammal on Earth, with a body no bigger than a human thumb and a weight lighter than a single U.S. penny.
Its upturned, pig-like snout and lack of a true tail membrane help it hover like a hummingbird while plucking tiny spiders directly off limestone cave ceilings.
Every evening, these minuscule bats limit their hunting trips to just 30 minutes at dusk and 20 minutes at dawn, spending the rest of their lives roosting deep inside limestone caverns.
Even though they roost in large caves, individuals never huddle together in clusters like other bats, preferring to hang spaced evenly apart along the rock walls.
Because their wings flap so rapidly and silently, local villagers along Thailand's Kwai River knew them simply as 'flying bumblebees' until scientists formally described them in 1974.
Also called Kitti's hog-nosed bat, the bumblebee bat weighs just two grams, making it the smallest mammal by skull size and tied for lightest on Earth.
Its wingspan is barely six inches across, and its body is no larger than a large bumblebee.
Discovered in 1973, it roosts exclusively in limestone caves along rivers in western Thailand and southeastern Myanmar.

mammals.name: Patagonian mara
mammals.summary: The Patagonian mara (Dolichotis patagonum) is a rodent in the mara genus Dolichotis. It is also known as the Patagonian cavy or Patagonian hare.
facts: Looking like a jackrabbit on the front half and a miniature deer on the back half, the Patagonian mara is actually a giant rodent closely related to the household guinea pig.
Patagonian maras form strictly monogamous pairs for life, with the male constantly shadowing his mate and marking the ground around her to ward off bachelor rivals.
Even though pairs stay fiercely loyal to each other in the open, up to 20 different mara couples will share a single communal underground nursery burrow for their pups.
Mothers never enter the communal nursery burrow; instead, she sits outside and calls out until only her own biological pups run out to nurse, briskly chasing away any freeloaders.
When fleeing across windswept scrublands, a mara can switch between a rabbit-like hop, a horse-like gallop, and a four-footed spring called stotting at speeds up to 28 miles per hour.

mammals.name: Crested porcupine
mammals.summary: The crested porcupine (Hystrix cristata), also known as the African crested porcupine, is a species of rodent in the family Hystricidae native to Italy, North Africa, West Africa, Central Africa and East Africa. Alongside the Cape porcupine, it is one of the largest porcupine species in the world.
facts: Before launching an attack, a crested porcupine shakes a group of hollow, open-ended quills on its short tail that rattle together like a maraca to warn predators away.
Despite the enduring cartoon myth, porcupines cannot shoot their quills; instead, they charge *backward* or sideways at high speed to slam their barbed spines into an attacker's face.

Each detached quill is coated in natural fatty acids that act as a mild antibiotic, evolved not to help predators, but so the porcupine doesn't get fatal infections when it accidentally pokes itself falling out of rocks.
Crested porcupines are obsessive bone collectors, dragging sun-bleached skeletons, antlers, and even ivory tusks back to their underground burrows to gnaw on for calcium and to sharpen their teeth.
Their quills are modified hairs filled with a spongy, foam-like core that makes them buoyant enough to help the porcupine float effortlessly when swimming.

mammals.name: Dik-dik
mammals.summary: Kirk's dik-dik (Madoqua kirkii) is a species of small dik-dik antelope native to Eastern and Southern Africa. It is believed to have six subspecies and possibly a seventh existing in southwest Africa.
facts: This miniature antelope gets its name from the high-pitched 'zik-zik' or 'dik-dik' alarm whistle that females blow through their noses when running in a zigzag pattern from predators.
When overheated, a dik-dik elongates its flexible nose and pants rapidly to cool venous blood inside its nasal passages before that blood circulates to its brain.
Monogamous dik-dik pairs mark the borders of their territory by poking twigs directly into a dark, sticky tear-like paste secreted from large pits right below the inside corners of their eyes.
Even at full adult size, a dik-dik stands barely 12 to 16 inches tall at the shoulder and can easily hide behind a single clump of tall grass.
Look closely at a male dik-dik's forehead and you'll often see his spiky horns almost completely swallowed by an unruly tuft of fluffy crown hair.

mammals.name: Raccoon dog
mammals.summary:
Nyctereutes (Ancient Greek: νύξ, νυκτ- [nýx, nykt-] 'night' + ἐρέυτης [eréutēs] 'wanderer') is a genus of Asian canid with two extant species, the raccoon dogs: the common raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and the Japanese raccoon dog (Nyctereutes viverrinus).
Nyctereutes entered the fossil record 5.5 million years ago (Mya) in northern China.
facts: Despite looking almost identical to a North American raccoon, complete with a bandit mask, the raccoon dog is a true wild canid most closely related to foxes.
It is the only member of the entire dog family (Canidae) on Earth that truly hibernates during the harsh winter months, packing on up to 50 percent more body weight in autumn.
Unlike almost all other dogs, the raccoon dog has curved claws and short legs adapted for climbing straight up tree trunks to forage for persimmons, berries, and bird eggs.
Raccoon dogs do not bark like domestic dogs; instead, they communicate with high-pitched whines, growls, and a soft, cat-like mewing sound.
In Japanese folklore, the raccoon dog is celebrated as the *tanuki*, a cheerful, shape-shifting trickster spirit famous for using magic leaves to disguise itself and drumming on its own belly.

mammals.name: River otter
mammals.summary: The North American river otter (Lontra canadensis), also known as the northern river otter and river otter, is a semiaquatic mammal that is endemic to the North American continent throughout most of Canada and along the coasts of the United States and its inland waterways. An adult North American river otter can weigh between 5 and 14 kilograms (11–31 lb).
facts: River otters are famous for building slick 'slides' on mudbanks and snowdrifts, plunging down on their bellies repeatedly not just to travel fast, but purely for play.
To stay dry in icy rivers, an otter constantly rubs and rolls on grassy banks to work natural oils from its skin into a double coat so thick that air bubbles get trapped like a wetsuit.
The long, stiff whiskers (vibrissae) on a river otter's muzzle are so sensitive to underwater vibrations that it can track the wake of a darting fish in pitch-black, muddy water.
When a river otter dives, its nostrils and ears automatically snap shut with watertight muscular valves, and its heart rate slows down to stretch its oxygen supply.
River otters create communal bathroom spots along shorelines called 'sprainting sites,' where they perform an energetic, tail-lifting 'poop dance' to leave scent messages for neighbors.

mammals.name: Gray squirrel
mammals.summary: The eastern gray squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis), spelled as grey squirrel outside of the United States, is a species of tree squirrel in the genus Sciurus. It is native to eastern North America, where it is the most prodigious and ecologically essential natural forest regenerator.
facts: Gray squirrels are unwitting forest builders: because they bury thousands of individual nuts every autumn using spatial memory and forget roughly a quarter of them, they plant countless oak trees.

When a gray squirrel suspects another squirrel or a blue jay is watching, it performs 'deceptive caching', digging a hole, pretending to pat a nut inside with its nose, and covering the empty hole while hiding the real nut in its mouth.
When descending a tree trunk headfirst, a gray squirrel rotates its hind ankles a full 180 degrees so its rear claws point backward and hook securely into the bark like crampons.

The Latin species name *carolinensis* sits alongside *Sciurus*, which comes from ancient Greek words meaning 'shadow-tail,' a nod to the way squirrels hold their bushy tails over their backs like a parasol.
By twitching its tail and pumping hot blood into it on sweltering days, or wrapping it tightly around its nose in blizzards, a gray squirrel uses its tail as a built-in thermostat.

mammals.name: North Pacific right whale
facts: In the 19th century, commercial whalers named them 'right whales' because they swam slowly near shore, yielded massive amounts of oil and baleen, and conveniently floated rather than sinking when killed.

Recently, bioacousticians discovered that eastern North Pacific right whales sing complex, patterned songs featuring repeating rhythms of 'gunshot' sounds and low moans; the first time singing was ever recorded in a right whale species.

Each individual has a unique constellation of rough, calcified skin patches on its head called callosities, which appear white not because of the skin itself, but because millions of tiny whale lice live on them.
Its arched upper jaw holds up to 250 plates of feathery baleen per side, each growing over eight feet long to strain microscopic copepods from the water.
Because their heads make up nearly a third of their total body length and they lack a dorsal fin on their wide backs, they can push right through thin sea ice to breathe.

mammals.name: Goa
facts: The goa gets its scientific name, *picticaudata* ('painted tail'), from the crisp, heart-shaped white patch on its rump that flashes brightly when it sprints across the high plateau.
Living comfortably at altitudes up to 18,000 feet where oxygen is half that of sea level, the goa has a remarkably oversized heart and extra-dense red blood cells.
Instead of barking or bleating loudly when a wolf approaches, a goa relies almost entirely on ultrasonic-like silent visual flashes of its white rump patch and short nasal snorts.
Only male goas carry horns, which curve gracefully backward like slender black scimitars with finely ridged rings along their length.
During the dead of winter when temperatures plummet below minus 30 degrees Fahrenheit, the goa's hollow guard hairs trap warm air around its skin like thousands of miniature thermoses.

mammals.name: Southern right whale
facts: Southern right whales practice a remarkable behavior called 'sailing,' sticking their massive tail flukes straight up into the air to catch the wind and glide effortlessly across the water's surface.
Males do not fight brutally with teeth or horns for mates; instead, they compete via 'sperm competition,' possessing the largest testes of any animal on Earth, weighing nearly a ton per pair.
Instead of a normal V-shaped blowhole spout, a right whale has two widely separated blowholes that shoot out two distinct plumes of mist in a signature V-shape up to 16 feet high.
Curious southern right whales along the coast of Argentina frequently swim right up to beaches and gently poke surfers, kayaks, and paddleboards with their rostrums.
Around five percent of southern right whale calves are born almost completely white, a condition called grey-morphism, before gradually darkening into a slate-grey or black coat as they grow up.

mammals.name: North Atlantic right whale
facts: Before a female North Atlantic right whale chooses a mate, she often rolls onto her back at the surface to keep her belly out of reach while up to 30 suitors jostle around her in a frothy 'surface active group.'

When mothers and newborn calves travel through busy waters, they switch to 'acoustic crypsis,' dropping their calls to whisper-quiet grunts barely louder than the crashing waves so killer whales cannot eavesdrop.

Scientists have tracked individual North Atlantic right whales for over 40 years using aerial photographs of the distinctive white callosity patches on their heads, which remain unchanged like fingerprints for life.
To feed, a North Atlantic right whale swims open-mouthed through dense underwater clouds of rice-sized copepods, filtering thousands of gallons of water per minute through its frayed baleen.
Because its blubber layer can be well over a foot thick, a right whale struggles to shed excess body heat if it swims into warm tropical waters.

mammals.name: Red wolf
facts: Red wolves are so secretive and nocturnal that biologists tracking them with radio collars have walked within yards of a resting pack in dense brush without ever seeing or hearing a single wolf.

When greeting packmates or alerting the family to intruders, red wolves communicate with a rich repertoire of body language and a unique vocalization that blends a wolf howl with a high-pitched coyote yip.
Both parents, along with older brothers and sisters from previous years' litters, take turns regurgitating food for new pups and babysitting them while the rest of the pack hunts.
During the warmer summer months, a red wolf sheds its thick winter coat to reveal oversized, radar-like ears that help dissipate body heat and pinpoint rustling rodents in tall marsh grass.

After being declared extinct in the wild in 1980 after the last survivors were brought into captivity, the red wolf became the first large carnivore ever reintroduced from a captive-breeding program into its native landscape.

mammals.name: Hartebeest
facts: The hartebeest's name comes from the Dutch settlers' word *hertebeest* ('stag-ox'), inspired by its long, narrow face and bizarrely twisted horns that rise from a single bony pedestal on top of its skull.
Because its eyes sit so high up at the very top of its elongated skull, a hartebeest can graze with its nose buried deep in tall savanna grass while still scanning the horizon for lions.
Rather than hiding when a predator is spotted, a sentinel hartebeest often climbs on top of a tall termite mound to stand like a statue and keep watch over the herd.

When a calf is born, its sandy coat matches the dry grass so closely that its mother leaves it hidden alone in the brush for weeks, visiting only briefly to nurse so her scent doesn't give its spot away.
Although they look stiff and awkward with their steeply sloping backs, hartebeests can bolt at 45 miles per hour and weave through acacia scrub with sudden sideways dodges.

mammals.name: Sumatran rhinoceros
facts: Covered in patches of coarse, reddish-brown bristles, especially when young, the Sumatran rhino is known as the 'hairy rhino' and is the closest living relative to the extinct Ice Age woolly rhinoceros.
Unlike its quieter cousins, the Sumatran rhino is extraordinarily vocal, constantly conversing through the rainforest with melodic 'eeps,' whale-like whistles, and low, humming 'whale-blows.'
As the smallest of all living rhinos, it spends hours every day wallowing in deep mud pits; if deprived of mud, its surprisingly sensitive skin quickly cracks and becomes inflamed.
Using its hooked upper lip and stubby horns, a Sumatran rhino pushes over saplings up to three inches thick just to munch on the tender leaves at the crown.
They are skilled mountain climbers that carve well-worn, tunnel-like highways through dense bamboo and thorny vines up steep volcanic ridges.

mammals.name: Marsh rice rat
facts: Unlike almost all other rats, the marsh rice rat is semi-aquatic and can dive underwater and swim over 30 feet beneath the surface in a single breath to escape hawks and owls.
Its dense coat traps a shimmering silver layer of microscopic air bubbles underwater, keeping the rat warm and naturally buoyant even in chilly tidal marshes.
During high tides that flood the salt marshes, the marsh rice rat weaves a waterproof, grapefruit-sized ball of cordgrass suspended high in the reeds, complete with a hidden bottom entrance.
Rather than sticking to seeds and plants, the marsh rice rat is an aggressive nocturnal hunter that raids fiddler crab burrows, cracks open marsh snails, and even snatches baby marsh wrens.
On the Florida Keys, isolated populations evolved a unique silver coat color, earning them the nickname 'silver rice rat.'

mammals.name: Sei whale
facts: The sei whale is one of the fastest cetaceans in the ocean, capable of surging through the water at bursts of over 30 miles per hour.

Unlike other baleen whales that either gulp huge mouthfuls of water *or* skim the surface, the sei whale is a versatile 'switch-hitter' that can do both depending on whether it's chasing fish or copepods.

Rather than arching its back and lifting its tail flukes high into the air when diving like a humpback, a sei whale simply sinks straight beneath the waves, leaving behind a series of swirling 'fluke prints' on the glassy surface.
Its name comes from the Norwegian word for pollock (*seje*), because the whales used to arrive off the coast of Norway at the exact same time each year as massive schools of those fish.
A sei whale's baleen plates are uniquely fringed with ultra-fine, silky white hairs that look and feel remarkably like sheep's wool.

mammals.name: Nilgai
facts: Despite its popular nickname 'blue bull,' the nilgai is not a bull at all, but a massive antelope with a striking slate-blue coat in adult males and a sandy-brown coat in females.
In India, the nilgai's name literally translates to 'blue cow,' which for centuries granted it cultural protection among Hindus who associated it with sacred cattle.
To reach high acacia leaves and blossoms, a heavy nilgai can rear up and balance stably on its hind legs like a goat.

An entire herd of nilgai uses the exact same communal dung pile day after day, sometimes building a mound up to ten feet wide, which serves as a neighborhood bulletin board and reduces parasite spread across pastures.
Unlike their long-horned cousins the eland and kudu, male nilgai sport short, lethal, dagger-sharp conical horns and fight rivals by dropping to their front knees and wrestling neck-to-neck.

mammals.name: Banteng
facts: Adult males develop a thick, hairless, horny shield of skin across their forehead between their horns that acts as a helmet during head-butting matches.
Calves and females are a bright chestnut-red, while mature bulls undergo a dramatic color change, turning dark bluish-black or chocolate brown as they age.
All individuals sport immaculate white 'stockings' on their lower legs and a stark white rump patch that flashes like a beacon when the herd flees into dark forest cover.
A domesticated form known as Bali cattle has been used as a draft animal in Indonesia for centuries and makes up roughly a quarter of the country's cattle population.
In 2003, scientists successfully cloned a wild individual from frozen skin cells saved at the San Diego Zoo, using a domestic beef cow as the surrogate mother.

mammals.name: Baiji
facts: Known in Chinese folklore as the 'Goddess of the Yangtze,' legend held that the dolphin was the reincarnation of a princess who leaped into the river to escape a greedy stepfather.
Because the muddy waters of the Yangtze River made vision nearly useless, its eyes were reduced to tiny, pinhole-sized organs placed high on its head.
A resident male named Qiqi lived in a Wuhan dolphinarium for over 22 years, providing nearly everything scientists ever learned about the species' acoustics and physiology.
Unlike oceanic dolphins that travel in large, noisy pods, this river dweller had an unusually quiet echolocation click and rested for hours in calm eddy currents behind sandbars.
Its long, narrow beak curved slightly upward at the tip like a pair of tweezers, allowing it to probe muddy river bottoms for bottom-dwelling catfish.

mammals.name: Gray mouse lemur
facts: Despite being a primate, it sings ultrasonic courtship songs completely above the range of human hearing, punctuated by high-pitched whistles.
Before the dry season begins, it binges on sugary insect secretions and stores almost all the excess fat inside its tail, which swells up like a plump sausage.
Its brain weighs less than two grams, making it the smallest brain of any known primate, yet it excels at complex spatial memory tests to relocate fruiting trees.
To survive chilly, food-scarce winters, it can enter daily torpor or even weeks-long hibernation inside tree hollows, dropping its body temperature to match the outside air.
During the brief breeding window, a male's testes swell to roughly 5% of his entire body weight to outcompete rivals in sperm competition.

mammals.name: Striped polecat
facts: Also called the zorilla, its anal glands spray a foul-smelling liquid that not only reeks like a skunk's but causes temporary blindness and a fierce burning sensation if it hits an attacker's eyes.
Before firing its chemical weapon, it performs a dramatic warning handstand, fluffing its long tail hair and arching its back to display its high-contrast black-and-white stripes.
If cornered by a pack of predators after exhausting its spray, it can play dead so convincingly that lions and hyenas will sniff the limp body and walk away.
It is remarkably immune to snake venom and will happily hunt puff adders and spitting cobras, dodging strikes with lightning-fast footwork.
Poor swimmers that avoid deep water, they have occasionally been observed paddling awkwardly across small streams with their bushy tails held high to stay dry.

mammals.name: Vaquita
facts: Its Spanish name translates to 'little cow,' while dark rings around its eyes and curved black lip patches give it the permanent appearance of wearing mascara and smiling.
Unlike almost any other marine cetacean, it thrives in shallow, sun-baked lagoon waters where temperatures swing wildly from 14°C in winter to 36°C in summer.
Its dorsal fin is proportionally taller and wider than those of other porpoises, acting as a biological radiator to dump excess body heat in warm coastal shallows.
Wait times between sightings are so long because it surfaces with an almost imperceptible, slow forward roll that barely disturbs the water's surface and produces no visible blow.
Western science had no idea the animal existed until 1958, when three weather-bleached skulls washed up on a beach in Baja California.

mammals.name: Lamia
facts: Rather than curling downward like a monkey's tail, the tip of its prehensile tail is hairless and grips branches by wrapping upward over the top.
The scales along its tail aren't arranged in neat rings like a sewer rat's, but overlap like roof shingles in spiral rows with three tiny hairs poking out from under each scale.
Instead of excavating dirt burrows, it chews circular entrance holes into hollow tree limbs and weaves cozy spherical nests out of shredded palm fibers.
Its skull has a noticeably domed, broad forehead and heavy brow ridges that give its face a surprisingly blunt, pug-like profile compared to typical field mice.
Females have only four nipples located near the groin, and their nursing pups cling so tightly to them that the mother can drag the entire litter along if startled from her nest.

mammals.name: Wildcat
facts: Unlike domestic tabbies whose tails taper to a sharp point, this felid sports a thick, blunt-ended tail banded with black rings that looks like a furry club.
Even when hand-raised from birth with bottle-feeding and constant affection, kittens retain a fierce, untamable streak and will hiss and spit at humans as adults.
An Near Eastern cousin buried alongside a human on the island of Cyprus 9,500 years ago provided the earliest archaeological evidence of cats living beside people.
In the Scottish Highlands, centuries of interbreeding with feral domestic cats have created a 'hybrid swarm' so extensive that genetically pure individuals are nearly impossible to find in the wild.
The soles of its paws are jet-black and heavily furred between the pads to muffle footsteps when stalking rodents across crisp winter snow or dry leaves.

mammals.name: European polecat
facts: Around 2,500 years ago, people bred and domesticated this feisty hunter to create the modern pet ferret, originally used to flush rabbits out of underground warrens.

When it catches more frogs and toads than it can eat in autumn, it bites them at the base of the skull to paralyze them without killing them, keeping fresh live rations stacked in its burrow all winter.
Unlike solitary stoats or weasels, it has a remarkably low metabolic rate for a mustelid and can survive weeks of bitter frost curled tightly inside an abandoned rabbit hole.
In medieval England, its habit of raiding henhouses earned it the Old French nickname 'poul-chat' (chicken-cat), which gradually morphed into its modern English name.
To neutralize the poisonous skin secretions of common toads, it frantically rolls the amphibian through damp grass and soil like a baker kneading dough before taking a bite.

mammals.name: Rice's whale
facts: For decades it was mistaken for a local subpopulation of another whale until a skull washed into the Everglades in 2019, revealing unique bone structures around the blowhole that proved it was an entirely distinct species.
Unlike almost all other baleen whales that embark on epic pole-to-equator migrations, it spends its entire life year-round in a single narrow depth belt in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico.
During the day it dives deeply to hover just above the sea floor at 200 meters to gulp schools of lanternfish, then spends nearly 90% of the night resting within 15 meters of the surface.
Instead of displaying three symmetrical ridges along the top of its snout like its closest relatives, its lateral ridges are tucked inside shallow grooves.
Its low-frequency moans include a distinctive 'long-moan' call lasting over twenty seconds that pulses like a slow heartbeat through the deep gulf waters.

mammals.name: Indiana bat
facts: Despite its name, the first specimen ever described by science was actually discovered inside Wyandotte Cave in southern Indiana in 1904, where millions once wintered.
During winter hibernation, they pack onto cave ceilings so tightly, up to 4,800 individuals per square meter, that the rock surface looks like a single thick pelt of brown fur.
Females mate in autumn before hibernating, store the live sperm inside their reproductive tracts all winter long, and only fertilize the egg once they wake up in spring.
In summer, up to a hundred pregnant females squeeze underneath the peeling, sun-warmed bark of dead shagbark hickory trees, which act as natural solar incubators for their pups.
A single nursing female can catch and devour up to half her own body weight in moths, caddisflies, and beetles in a single night.

mammals.name: Blackbuck
facts: A male's horns twist in tight corkscrew spirals up to four full turns and are ringed with prominent ridges from base to tip.
Wait until monsoon season ends and dominant males can change coat color back and forth, fading from jet-black to light tan when hormone levels drop, then darkening again before the next rut.
When startled on open plains, the entire herd erupts into 'pronking', leaping two meters straight into the air with stiff legs before breaking into a 80-kilometer-per-hour sprint.
During courtship displays, a buck tilts his nose straight up toward the sky, lays his long spiral horns flat along his back, and struts with short, mincing steps while flipping his white tail.
Under Emperor Akbar in 16th-century Mughal India, royal trainers kept stables of tame cheetahs specifically to course these fleet-footed antelopes across the plains.

mammals.name: Alcathoe whiskered bat
facts: Named after Alcathoe, a princess in Greek mythology whom Dionysus transformed into a bat for refusing to join his revels and choosing to weave indoors instead.

It went completely unrecognized by science until 2001 because it looks almost identical to two cousin species, until researchers noticed its echolocation clicks pitched up to a sizzling 120 kilohertz.
As Europe's smallest whiskered bat, it weighs roughly the same as a single penny (about 3.5 to 5 grams) and can comfortably curl up inside a walnut shell.
Instead of roosting in caves or church attics like many bats, it prefers tiny lightning cracks and woodpecker holes high in the canopy of old-growth oak and sycamore trees.
You can tell an adult apart from its lookalike cousins by its pinkish-brown snout, short ears with a notch on the outer edge, and miniature feet.

mammals.name: African forest elephant
facts: Unlike its savanna cousin which has four toenails on the front foot and three on the back, this forest dweller has five rounded toenails on the front and four on the back.
Its tusks don't curve outward and upward, but grow straight down toward the ground so they won't snag on thick jungle vines as it pushes through dense undergrowth.
The ivory of its tusks has a subtle pinkish tint and is much harder and denser than savanna ivory, helping it crack open rock-hard seeds of forest trees like *Panda oleosa*.
So many rain forest tree species rely exclusively on this giant to swallow their seeds and deposit them miles away in nutrient-rich dung piles that botanists call them 'megagardener' trees.
Groups gather in muddy forest clearings called *bais*, where they kneel down to dig up mineral-rich clay and socialize through ground-shaking, infrasonic rumbles.

mammals.name: Irrawaddy dolphin
facts: Completely lacking a sleek dolphin beak, it has a high, rounded forehead and highly mobile lips that allow it to make comical, expressive faces underwater.
It can spit cohesive jets of water up to 1.5 meters into the air from its mouth, a trick it uses both during social play and to herd panicked schools of fish into tight balls.
Along the Ayeyarwady River in Myanmar, wild pods cooperate with traditional fishermen; slapping their flukes to signal when fish are near the boat and driving the catch directly into cast nets.
Unlike almost all other dolphins, its neck vertebrae are not fused together, allowing it to turn its head side-to-side and nod like a human.
Despite living in muddy freshwater rivers a thousand kilometers inland, DNA reveals its closest living relative is actually the killer whale.

mammals.name: Gaur
facts: Standing up to 2.2 meters at the shoulder and weighing well over a metric ton, it is the heaviest and most muscular wild bovine on Earth.
Adult bulls secrete an oily, aromatic sweat called 'seladang oil' that gives their dark coats a musky scent and is believed to act as a natural insect repellent in steamy jungles.
Rather than charging straight into an opponent head-on, rival bulls circle each other sideways with their heads lowered to show off the towering muscular ridge along their shoulders.
Its massive, upward-curving horns grow from a bulging pale-yellow boss across the forehead and are always tipped with glossy black points.
Tigers are the only predators bold enough to ambush an adult, and even then, a herd will sometimes form a defensive phalanx and trample a stalking big cat to death.

mammals.name: Silky sifaka
facts: Nicknamed the 'angel of the forest' for its long, snow-white fur, it is one of the rarest primates on Earth and has never survived for long in captivity outside its native rainforest.
Although its coat is pure white, the skin on its face, ears, and palms starts out jet-black in youth and gradually loses pigment with age, turning mottled pink in older adults.
Males use a dark, bare scent gland right in the center of their chest to rub a pungent musky mark onto tree trunks, often gouging the bark with their teeth first.
It moves through the canopy by vertical clinging and leaping, launching itself sideways across 10-meter gaps between vertical trunks without ever touching the ground.
Even newborn infants have a shockingly strong grip, locking their fingers into the long silky fur on their mother's belly while she bounds effortlessly through the treetops.

mammals.name: Cotton-top tamarin
facts: Its wild shock of flowing white hair puffs straight up like a punk-rock mohawk whenever it is startled or angry, making its tiny head look twice its actual size.
Fathers and older brothers do almost all the heavy lifting of childcare, carrying twin babies on their backs all day and only handing them back to the mother to nurse.
While carrying heavy infants, caring fathers actually lose up to 10% of their body weight due to the energy spent hauling the twins through the branches and sharing food with them.
Its vocal repertoire of 38 distinct chirps, whistles, and trills is arranged using syntax-like rules, combining warning calls with food calls in specific sequences.
Within a family troop, only the dominant female ovulates; she releases pheromones in her scent marks that chemically suppress pregnancy in all her subordinate daughters.

mammals.name: Ethiopian wolf
facts: Despite its name and coyote-like build, it ignores large hoofed prey and is a specialist rodent hunter, subsisting almost entirely on giant mole-rats and grass rats.

Researchers stunned the scientific world when they photographed these wolves lapping sugary nectar from red-hot poker flowers, dusting their muzzles in yellow pollen and acting as the first known large carnivore pollinator.
To catch a giant mole-rat weighing nearly two pounds, it stalks in slow motion around a burrow entrance and waits motionless for up to an hour before lunging face-first into the dirt.

Rather than avoiding local herds of gelada monkeys, it calmly walks right through the middle of grazing baboon troops, using the monkeys as living camouflage so nearby rodents don't spot the wolf approaching.
Packs patrol freezing Afro-alpine plateaus above 4,000 meters in elevation, greeting each other at dawn and dusk with high-pitched, chorus-like yips and howls.

mammals.name: Diademed sifaka
facts: Named for the bright crown-like ring of white fur framing its black face, its hindquarters and legs glow in brilliant shades of golden-orange and silver-gray.
To fuel its explosive leaps between tree trunks, it seeks out high-energy seeds and parasitic mistletoe flowers, trekking over a mile each day through steep cloud forests.
Females sit firmly at the top of the troop's social ladder, getting first pick of the ripest fruit and cuffing adult males on the nose if they try to eat out of turn.

Its alarm call for aerial predators like the Madagascar harrier-hawk is a roaring bark, whereas ground predators trigger a sneezing sound that sounds distinctly like 'tzisk-tzisk-tzisk'; the origin of the word *sifaka*.
Because its hind legs are so much longer than its arms, if forced onto flat ground it cannot walk on all fours, instead hopping sideways like a miniature ballet dancer with its arms held overhead.

mammals.name: Grey seal
facts: Its Latin name, *Halichoerus grypus*, translates directly to 'hook-nosed sea-pig', a nod to the adult bull's huge, arched Roman nose and noisy snorting.
To communicate territory boundaries underwater without opening their mouths, bulls clap their front flippers together so forcefully that the crack sounds like a gunshot.
Pups are born wrapped in creamy white lanugo fur and drink milk that is nearly 60% pure fat, allowing them to gain over three pounds of blubber every single day.

After only three weeks of nursing, the mother abruptly abandons her beachball-round pup on the shore, where the youngster fasts for up to a month while molting its baby coat before ever touching the ocean.
In Celtic folklore throughout Orkney and the Hebrides, the soulful, human-like eyes of these seals inspired legends of the Selkies; magical beings who shed their seal skins to walk on land as humans.

mammals.name: Saola
facts: Often called the 'Asian Unicorn,' it remained completely unknown to science until 1992, when surveyors found a pair of strange, spindle-horned skulls hanging in a hunter's house in Vietnam.
Its face is dotted with remarkably huge scent glands along the muzzle that are covered by movable fleshy flaps; when lifted, they secrete a thick greenish-white paste used to mark rocks.
Both males and females carry a pair of razor-sharp, nearly straight horns up to half a meter long that slant backward at the exact same angle as a traditional Vietnamese weaving spindle.
Though it looks like a cross between an Arabian oryx and an antelope, DNA analyses proved it is actually a primitive relative of wild cattle and buffaloes.
No biologist has ever directly observed one living in the wild; every piece of footage from its mountain forest home has come from automated motion-triggered camera traps.

mammals.name: European hare
facts: The famous phrase 'mad as a March hare' comes not from fighting males, but from annoyed females rising onto their hind legs and boxing persistent suitors right in the nose with their front paws.

Through an extraordinary reproductive quirk called superfetation, a pregnant female can conceive a brand-new second litter of embryos inside her womb before she has even given birth to the first litter.
Unlike rabbits that give birth to blind, naked kits deep underground, hares drop their babies right in the open grass; fully furred, wide-eyed, and ready to hop within minutes of birth.
To evade greyhounds and foxes, it can hit speeds of 70 kilometers per hour while executing sudden 90-degree zigzags and doubling back over its own scent trail.
A mother visits her scattered leverets only once a day for less than five minutes right after sunset, nursing them with super-rich milk so her scent doesn't draw predators to their hiding spots.

mammals.name: Javan rhinoceros
facts: Its thick gray skin folds into dramatic, overlapping plates across its shoulders, back, and rump, giving it the unmistakable look of wearing medieval plate armor.

Unlike African rhinos that carry two formidable horns, only the males of this species grow a single modest horn, usually shorter than 20 centimeters, while females often have only a small bump or no horn at all.
Instead of using its horn to fight predators or rivals, it uses it primarily to scrape mud in wallows and pull down high saplings so its prehensile upper lip can strip the leaves.
Once found from eastern India all the way across Southeast Asia, the entire global population now lives inside a single peninsula at Ujung Kulon National Park on the western tip of Java.
Because it spends hours soaking in deep mud holes to prevent sunburn and biting flies, its skin often dries with a reddish or blackish crust depending on the local soil.

mammals.name: Bryde's whale
facts: It is the only baleen whale you can identify at a glance from above by the three parallel ridges running from the tip of its snout back to its blowholes.

Rather than skimming quietly through plankton, it often lunges straight up out of the water with its jaws wide open, gulping a swimming-pool-sized mouthful of anchovies before clamping its baleen shut.

In the Gulf of Thailand, individuals have perfected a lazy 'tread-water' feeding technique: they poke their open jaws vertically above the waves and wait as panicked fish leap directly into their mouths to escape seabirds.
Named after Johan Bryde, the Norwegian consul who built the first modern whaling stations in South Africa in the early 1900s, its name is actually pronounced 'BROO-duhz.'
Unlike humpbacks or blues that fast for months while migrating to icy polar waters, this warm-water whale stays in tropical and temperate seas above 16°C all year round.

mammals.name: Mule deer
facts: Instead of running at a normal gallop like a white-tailed deer, it escapes up rocky canyon slopes using a four-footed bounce called 'stotting,' where all four hooves strike the ground and push off simultaneously like a pogo stick.
Its oversized ears, nearly a foot long and independent like radar dishes, inspired Lewis and Clark to give the animal its barnyard nickname during their 1804 expedition.
You can tell its antlers apart from a white-tail's because the beams fork into two equal branches that each fork again, rather than growing single tines off one main beam.

A buck residing in southwestern Wyoming named '255' was tracked by GPS collar making the longest documented land-mammal migration in the lower 48 states: a 390-kilometer trek across mountain passes and highways twice a year.
When threatened by a coyote, a doe won't always flee; mothers frequently team up to rush the canine and pummel it with razor-sharp front hooves.

mammals.name: Waterbuck
facts: Skin glands across its coat secrete a thick, musky oil when the animal is excited or wet, which waterproofs its hair as it wades through rivers.
That oily secretion smells and tastes so potent that it seeps into the meat if the animal isn't skinned carefully, earning a reputation among even hungry lions as a last-resort meal.
One widely spread subspecies sports a stark white ring painted squarely around its rump, Looking exactly as if it had just sat down on a freshly painted white toilet seat.
According to an old East African folktale, the waterbuck got that white ring because it was the very first creature to test out the newly built ark's freshly painted latrine.
When chased by wild dogs or leopards, it dives straight into deep crocodile-infested pools and stands submerged with only its nostrils and backward-swept horns poking above the surface.

mammals.name: Barbary macaque
facts: The famous troop living atop the Rock of Gibraltar is the only wild monkey population in Europe; British legend claims that if the monkeys ever leave the Rock, Britain will lose Gibraltar, prompting Winston Churchill to airlift reinforcements from Morocco during World War II.
Despite sometimes being called the 'Barbary ape,' it is a true monkey whose external tail has shrunk to a barely visible, boneless vestigial nub.

Adult males use babies as 'social passports', picking up an infant (even one that isn't theirs), carrying it over to a rival male, and chattering their teeth together over the baby to diffuse tension and build alliances.
Living high in the cedar forests of the Atlas Mountains, they grow thick winter coats and spend snowy days foraging under pine needles and huddling in tight, multi-monkey balls for warmth.
Females mate with virtually every adult male in the troop during estrus, purposely obscuring paternity so that every male in the group treats all infants with protective care.

mammals.name: Drill
facts: Although its face is glossy jet-black rather than blue and red like its cousin the mandrill, a dominant male's chin is framed by a hot-pink lower lip and a snow-white beard.

What a dominant male lacks in facial color, he makes up for on his backside: his rump glows in vivid shades of violet, lilac, and magenta that brighten further the higher he climbs in the social hierarchy.
When greeting a troop member peacefully, it pulls the corners of its mouth back and shakes its head side-to-side in what looks exactly like a friendly human grin.
Males weigh over three times as much as females, one of the most extreme size differences between sexes of any living primate on the planet.
Equipped with cheek pouches the size of baseballs, it can stuff an entire handful of oil-palm nuts into its face while foraging on the forest floor and climb safely into a tree to chew them later.

mammals.name: Omura's whale
facts: Like its cousin the fin whale, its head is strikingly asymmetrical: the lower jaw is pure creamy white on the right side, while the left side is dark slate-gray.

Because it is small, shy, and stays in remote tropical waters, science didn't recognize it as a valid species until DNA tests in 2003, and no one ever filmed a live one in the wild until 2015 off the coast of Madagascar.
It lacks the lateral snout ridges of Bryde's whale, displaying only a single prominent ridge running down the center of its flat, V-shaped head.
Even though it grows up to 11 meters long, its blows are so low and faint that researchers often spot the bright white flash of its right jaw underwater before they ever see a spout.
Groups gathering in shallow waters off northwestern Madagascar sing repetitive, low-frequency songs that sound like rhythmic, pulsing bass notes echoing across the coral shelves.

mammals.name: Black rat
facts: Also called the 'ship rat' or 'roof rat,' this agile climber prefers living in rafters, attics, and palm tree crowns rather than underground sewers, using its extra-long tail as a tightrope-walker's counterbalance.

Long blamed solely for the 14th-century Black Death, modern epidemiological studies suggest that human body lice and fleas, and even central Asian gerbils, likely shared the blame for spreading the plague so rapidly.

Different island populations of black rats have distinct chromosome counts: Asian populations typically have 42 chromosomes, while European and Oceanian populations fused four pairs together and carry only 38.

With a vertical leap of over three feet and the ability to tread water for up to three days straight, they hitchhiked on ancient Roman and Polynesian vessels to become one of the most widespread mammals on Earth.
Unlike their larger, ground-dwelling brown rat cousins, black rats are surprisingly picky eaters that strongly prefer fresh fruit, nuts, and seeds over garbage.

mammals.name: Nyala
facts: Male and female nyalas look so drastically different, a charcoal-gray, maned giant with spiraled horns versus a petite, hornless chestnut doe with bright white stripes, that early naturalists initially classified them as two separate species.

When rival males square off, they avoid lethal goring by performing a slow-motion, stiff-legged 'parallel walk,' raising a crest of long white hair along their backs like a giant mohawk to make themselves look massive.
