Nyalas have formed a mutualistic alliance with red-billed oxpeckers, which ride on their backs to pluck blood-sucking ticks and sound a hissing alarm whenever a leopard creeps near.
Young male nyalas retain the bright reddish coat of females until puberty, allowing them to blend in with the herd and avoid being driven off by jealous dominant bulls.
Watchful nyalas often shadow troop movements of baboons and vervet monkeys, waiting beneath the canopy to feast on figs and seed pods accidentally dropped by the primates above.

mammals.name: Tamaraw
facts: Found exclusively on the Philippine island of Mindoro, the dwarf tamaraw is a fiery, pint-sized water buffalo whose V-shaped horns grow backward at a sharp angle specifically suited for crashing through dense bamboo thickets.
Though often confused with the domestic carabao, the wild tamaraw is notoriously untamable and fiercely territorial, shaking its head to warn intruders before charging with lethal speed.
In 1936, the Commonwealth of the Philippines honored the endangered buffalo by stamping its likeness onto the one-centavo coin, turning the elusive island beast into an everyday national icon.
Tamaraws are clever mud-bathers that coat their hides in thick wallows not just to cool off, but to create a dried clay armor against biting tropical flies.
Originally diurnal grazers, surviving tamaraws shifted to an almost entirely nocturnal lifestyle over the last century to avoid human hunters and loggers.

mammals.name: Jungle cat
facts: Despite its name, the jungle cat rarely sets foot in rainforests; instead, it prowls reed swamps, marshes, and tall grasslands, earning the much more accurate nickname 'reed cat.'
Ancient Egyptians occasionally mummified and trained jungle cats alongside African wildcats to flush waterfowl out of papyrus marshes along the Nile.
Unlike almost all other small cats, the jungle cat is an enthusiastic swimmer that dives completely underwater to catch fish and frogs.
With long, stilt-like legs and lynx-like black tufts atop its ears, it can leap nearly six feet straight into the air to snatch pheasants and francolins mid-takeoff.
During the breeding season, male jungle cats abandon feline purrs and meows for a deep, hoarse barking roar that sounds remarkably like a large dog.

mammals.name: Red squirrel
facts: Before winter sets in, Eurasian red squirrels hang fresh mushrooms in the forks of tree branches to air-dry like jerky before stashing them in hollow trunks so they won't rot.
They are champion swimmers that cross wide rivers with a choppy 'doggy paddle,' holding their bushy tails high out of the water like a dry furry sail.
Because a red squirrel cannot digest cellulose, it avoids leaves and grass, instead stripping the scales off up to 100 spruce cones a day to extract the oil-rich seeds inside.
In autumn, red squirrels grow long, theatrical tufts of hair called 'ear-pencils' on the tips of their ears, which shed away completely by mid-summer.
Red squirrels on the British Isles carry an ancient strain of Mycobacterium leprae, the exact bacterium responsible for medieval human leprosy, though they rarely transmit it to people today.

mammals.name: Big brown bat
facts: When temperatures plunge below freezing inside their winter caves, big brown bats can survive having their body temperatures drop below the freezing point of water without suffering tissue damage.

Equipped with extra-thick jawbones and specialized molars, they specialize in crunching right through the hard, armor-plated exoskeletons of agricultural pest beetles like stink bugs and cucumber beetles.
A single maternity colony of 150 big brown bats can devour over a million crop-destroying insects in a single summer season.

While emitting ultrasonic echolocation clicks during flight, tiny muscles in the bat's middle ear contract just before each call to prevent the bat from deafening itself, then relax microseconds later to hear the faint echo.
One banded wild big brown bat in Ontario was documented living for 19 years, an astonishing lifespan for a mammal that weighs barely half an ounce.

mammals.name: Japanese serow
facts: Known in Japan as the 'Kamoshika,' this shaggy mountain goat-antelope looks like a creature lifted straight out of a Studio Ghibli film, and in fact inspired the forest spirit appearances in 'Princess Mononoke.'
In 1955, the Japanese government declared the serow a 'Special Natural Monument,' rescuing it from near-extinction caused by poachers who prized its waterproof winter pelt.

Both males and females possess large, musky scent glands just below their eyes that make them look as if they are constantly weeping; they rub this jelly-like secretion on rocks and saplings to stake out solitary territories.
In rural Japanese slang, a woman with slender, graceful legs was traditionally complimented as having 'kamoshika legs.'
Nimble-footed serows escape predators by bounding straight up near-vertical, ice-crusted mountain cliffs where wolves and bears cannot follow.

mammals.name: Saharan striped polecat
facts: Also called the Libyan striped weasel, this bold desert carnivore wears the exact black-and-white warning livery of a North American skunk despite living thousands of miles away in North Africa.
When cornered by a jackal or eagle, it arches its back, fluffs its tail into a bottle-brush, and blasts a blinding, nauseating musk from its anal glands that can be smelled half a mile away.
To survive in hyper-arid sand dunes without standing water, it extracts nearly 100 percent of its moisture from the blood and organs of the jerboas, lizards, and beetles it hunts at night.
Using long, curved front claws like miniature backhoes, it excavates deep daytime burrows in stabilized sand dunes to escape the blistering Saharan sun.
Though fiercely solitary, mothers lead their kits across the desert at dusk in a tight 'caravan' formation, nose-to-tail, so the youngsters look like a single undulating serpent.

mammals.name: White-fronted capuchin
facts: To fend off biting mosquitoes and ticks during the rainy season, white-fronted capuchins crush toxic millipedes and citrus leaves into a paste and rub the pungent ointment all over their fur.
They are among the few non-human animals observed using sticks as weapons, repeatedly clubbing venomous pit vipers on the forest floor to protect their troop.
Because their thumbs are only pseudo-opposable, these clever monkeys make up for it with extraordinary problem-solving brainpower and a muscular prehensile tail that acts as a fifth hand.
Members of a troop reaffirm lifelong alliances through bizarre trust rituals, including gently sticking their fingers into a partner's nostrils or mouth while swaying back and forth.

When foraging for palm nuts, they carefully tap each fruit with their knuckles and sniff it to test whether the kernel inside is ripe before spending energy cracking the hard shell against a tree branch.

mammals.name: Sitatunga
facts: As the world's most aquatic antelope, the sitatunga has elongated, banana-shaped hooves that splay out widely like snowshoes, keeping it from sinking into bottomless papyrus swamps.
When pursued by leopards or wild dogs, a sitatunga submerges its entire body in deep marsh water, leaving only the tip of its nostrils poking above the surface like a periscope for hours.
Its shaggy coat is coated in natural water-repellent oils so thick that water rolls right off its back the moment it steps out of a lagoon.

Because they spend their lives trampling through dense reedbeds, sitatunga herds create labyrinthine underwater tunnels and floating mats of crushed vegetation where they sleep safely out of reach of land predators.
Unlike almost all other antelopes, the sitatunga is a clumsy runner on hard, dry ground because its long, flexible pasterns and splayed hooves are built for mud rather than sprinting.

mammals.name: Golden-crowned sifaka
facts: Despite being a large, brightly colored primate with a gleaming gold cap, the golden-crowned sifaka remained completely unknown to Western science until primatologist Elwyn Simons spotted one in northeastern Madagascar in 1988.

Because its arms are much shorter than its spring-loaded hind legs, it cannot walk on all fours on the ground; instead, it crosses open clearings by hopping sideways like a joyful ballet dancer with its arms held high.
This lemur lives in a rare ecological stronghold framed by two rivers and the Indian Ocean, where dry deciduous forests stand side-by-side with humid rainforests within a few miles.
Females sit at the absolute top of the social hierarchy, claiming first rights to the best fruiting trees and casually cuffing males who try to eat out of turn.
Every morning, family groups climb to the highest exposed branches of the canopy and sit with their arms spread wide to sunbathe and warm up their digestive tracts.

mammals.name: Black-backed jackal
facts: Fossil evidence from South Africa shows that the black-backed jackal has remained virtually unchanged for over two million years, making it the oldest surviving member of the dog family.
Unlike many mammals, black-backed jackals form lifelong monogamous pairs; if one partner dies, the survivor rarely finds a new mate and often loses its territory.
Older siblings from the previous year's litter frequently stay behind as 'helper' babysitters, regurgitating food for the new pups and standing guard against eagles and hyenas.
Along Namibia's Skeleton Coast, jackals patrol the beaches in the fog to raid Cape fur seal rookeries and scavenge stranded whales alongside brown hyenas.
Southern African Khoikhoi folklore casts the clever black-backed jackal as the ultimate trickster who repeatedly outwits the mighty, arrogant lion.

mammals.name: Egyptian fruit bat
facts: While almost all other old-world fruit bats navigate exclusively by eyesight and smell, the Egyptian fruit bat is a rare exception that clicks its tongue from side to side to echolocate in pitch-black caves.

Researchers studying giant colonies in Israel discovered that their noisy roost-side squabbles aren't random screeches; each bat call encodes who is speaking, who they are yelling at, and whether the argument is over food, sleeping space, or unwanted mating attempts.

Using miniature GPS trackers, scientists found that an Egyptian fruit bat keeps a mental map of specific fig and loquat trees up to 30 miles away, flying straight as an arrow to a single favored tree night after night.
Mother Egyptian fruit bats speak 'motherese' to their pups, slowing down and changing the pitch of their vocalizations so the babies can learn the local colony's dialect.
Every evening after waking up, it eats up to twice its own body weight in fruit pulp, spitting out dry pellets of indigestible fiber and scattering seeds across arid river valleys.

mammals.name: Hector's dolphin
facts: Recognizable by its rounded dorsal fin that looks just like a single Mickey Mouse ear, New Zealand's Hector's dolphin is one of the smallest marine cetaceans on the planet.
A critically endangered North Island subspecies known as the Maui dolphin numbers fewer than 60 surviving adults, making it the rarest marine dolphin in the world.
Rather than clicking in lower ultrasonic ranges that killer whales can eavesdrop on, Hector's dolphins hunt using ultra-high-frequency acoustic pulses that remain completely silent to prowling orcas.
Their skulls and foreheads are adorned with striking black facial masks that contrast against pale gray flanks and pure white bellies.
Playful pods often surf in the breaking waves just yards from South Island beaches and chase floating pieces of bull kelp like toys.

mammals.name: White-throated woodrat
facts: True to its nickname 'packrat,' the white-throated woodrat builds fortresses out of thousands of prickly pear cactus pads, mesquite thorns, and cow dung; along with stolen shiny bottle caps, keys, and coins.

Because their urine crystallizes into an amber-like resin that cements their nest piles together in dry desert caves, preserved woodrat middens up to 40,000 years old serve as time capsules of Ice Age plant life and pollen for paleobotanists.
By eating succulent cholla and prickly pear cactus pads, this desert rodent gets all the water it needs for its entire life without ever taking a sip from a stream or puddle.
To neutralize the kidney-stone-causing oxalic acid packed inside cactus flesh, its gut is colonized by specialized bacteria that break down the toxins harmlessly.
Inside its thorny cactus dome, the temperature remains up to 30 degrees cooler than the baking Sonoran Desert floor outside, attracting rattlesnakes and lizards looking for shade.

mammals.name: Klipspringer
facts: The klipspringer walks on the very tips of its cylindrical, rubbery hooves like a ballerina en pointe; an adult can balance all four feet on a rock ledge no wider than a silver dollar.

Its coat is made of thick, hollow, brittle hairs that trap tiny pockets of air, acting simultaneously as thermal insulation against chilly mountain winds and as a built-in airbag cushion if the antelope slips against jagged granite.
Monogamous klipspringer pairs stay within a few body lengths of each other for life, taking turns standing like statues on high boulders as lookouts while their partner feeds below.
To mark the boundaries of their rocky territories, pairs carefully deposit tiny bead-like pellets of black scent-gland secretion onto thin twigs at exact nose height.
Its Afrikaans name literally translates to 'rock jumper,' a nod to its ability to bound 15 feet vertically up a sheer cliff face from a standstill.

mammals.name: Greater bamboo lemur
facts: Every single day, a greater bamboo lemur consumes enough cyanide-laced giant bamboo shoots to kill a human twelve times over, yet suffers zero ill effects thanks to an evolutionary superpower we still don't fully understand.
Feared extinct for decades, the species was dramatically rediscovered by primatologist Patricia Wright in 1986, leading directly to the creation of Madagascar's famous Ranomafana National Park.
It possesses powerful, bulldog-like jaws and specialized premolars capable of shearing through woody culms of giant bamboo as thick as a baseball bat.
Unlike smaller bamboo lemurs that stick to tender leaves, the greater bamboo lemur strips away the tough outer bark during the dry season to feast on the fibrous inner pith.
In Malagasy folklore, this gray, tufted-eared primate is revered as a sacred ancestor, which historically protected it from hunting in several remote highland villages.

mammals.name: Short-beaked common dolphin
facts: Distinguished by a striking 'hourglass' pattern of tan and pale gray crossing its flanks, this dolphin was the revered sacred dolphin painted on ancient Minoan frescoes in Crete over 3,500 years ago.
In open ocean waters, individual pods merge into 'super-pods' numbering up to 10,000 dolphins that churn the sea into white foam for miles as they herd baitballs of sardines.
Each dolphin uses a unique 'signature whistle', essentially its spoken first name, to call out to family members in murky water or crowded super-pods.
When a member of the pod is injured or sick, companions swim underneath their stricken friend and use their backs to buoy the dolphin to the surface so it can breathe.
Powered by streamlined bodies and high-speed tail flukes, they can rocket through the waves at speeds exceeding 35 miles per hour while riding the bow waves of passing ships.

mammals.name: Talamancan rice rat
facts: Living high in the cloud forests of Costa Rica and western Panama, this mountain rodent remained lumped together with lowland cousins until geneticists recognized it as a distinct species in 1998.
As mist rolls through the Talamanca Mountains at night, it scurries over moss-draped fallen logs and tangles of epiphyte roots searching for fallen highland acorns, berries, and beetles.
Its exceptionally long, two-toned tail, dark on top and pale underneath, helps it balance while scrambling up wet bamboo stalks in steep montane ravines.
To survive the chilly, damp nights at elevations above 8,000 feet, it weaves globular nests of dried moss and fern fronds tucked inside hollow tree roots.
By caching oak seeds and cloud-forest fruits under leaf litter and forgetting some of its stashes, it serves as an unsung gardener of Central America's sky-island forests.

mammals.name: Markhor
facts: The national animal of Pakistan, the markhor sports spectacular corkscrew horns that can twist upward for more than five feet, resembling giant wrought-iron drills.
Its Persian name 'Mar-khor' literally translates to 'snake-eater,' stemming from ancient mountain legends claiming the goat kills cobras with its hooves and chews them up.

According to local folklore, chewing the cud makes a markhor spit a foamy substance onto the ground that dries into a mystical gemstone called a 'zahrmohra,' once believed to draw snake venom out of wounds.
Male markhors wear an extravagant flowing beard and chest mane that sweeps down to their knees in winter, blowing majestically in the Himalayan wind as they scale limestone crags.
They regularly climb up into the crooked branches of evergreen oak trees, standing twenty feet off the ground to browse on leaves during deep winter snows.

mammals.name: Onager
facts: Before horses were introduced to Mesopotamia, ancient Sumerians harnessed onagers (or onager-donkey hybrids called 'kungas') to pull four-wheeled battle wagons into war around 2600 BCE.
One of the fastest land mammals on Earth, the Asian wild ass can sustain speeds of 30 miles per hour across rocky desert flats and sprint at up to 43 miles per hour when startled.
Despite countless attempts by ancient kings and modern zookeepers, the wild onager has proven practically impossible to domesticate, retaining a fierce, kicking streak in captivity.
During blistering summer droughts in the Iranian and Indian deserts, onagers use their front hooves to dig two-foot-deep wells in dry riverbeds to reach hidden subterranean water.
Their pale sandy coats reflect scorching desert sunlight in summer, then grow twice as thick and turn reddish-brown to brave freezing continental winds in winter.

mammals.name: Olympic marmot
facts: Found exclusively in the high alpine meadows of Washington's Olympic Peninsula, the Olympic marmot is the official endemic mammal of Washington State.
Before greeting each other, family members touch noses and sniff cheeks, and friendly colony mates wrap their paws around each other in what looks like a playful wrestling match.
Because snow buries their mountain meadows for most of the year, Olympic marmots spend up to eight months hibernating underground, losing half their body weight before emerging in late May.

They are the only marmot species whose coat changes color twice a year: emerging in spring in blondish-brown fur, molting to nearly jet-black by late autumn, and lightening again underground during hibernation.

Lookout marmots use four distinct, ear-piercing whistles, varying in pitch and length, to tell their colony whether danger is approaching from the sky (golden eagles) or the ground (coyotes and cougars).

mammals.name: Mantled guereza
facts: Born completely snow-white with a pink face, baby mantled guerezas are passed around and babysat by every female in the troop in a practice primatologists call 'allomothering.'

Their scientific genus name, Colobus, comes from the Greek word for 'mutilated' or 'docked,' because their thumbs have shrunk down to tiny, vestigial nubs, turning their remaining four long fingers into effortless grappling hooks for swinging through treetops.
When leaping between high forest canopies, the long, silky white curtain of fur draping their flanks billows out like a parachute to slow their descent.
Like cows of the treetops, they possess a massive, multi-chambered stomach filled with fermenting bacteria that breaks down tough, toxic mature leaves that would poison other monkeys.
At dawn, males across the forest boom out a resonant, frog-like 'roar-chorus' that echoes for over a mile to warn neighboring troops away from their favorite fig and ironwood trees.

mammals.name: Kultarr
facts: Though it looks exactly like an oversized desert jerboa or kangaroo rat, the kultarr is actually a carnivorous marsupial cousin of the Tasmanian devil.
Unlike true hopping rodents or kangaroos that bounce on two hind legs, the kultarr runs using a unique four-footed 'bound' in which its long hind feet land ahead of its tiny front paws.
During cold desert nights or food shortages in the Australian Outback, it enters daily torpor, dropping its body temperature and metabolic rate by 70 percent to conserve energy.
Instead of an enclosed pouch like a kangaroo's, a mother kultarr develops a temporary fold of skin around her teats during breeding season where her grain-of-rice-sized joeys cling tight.
Despite weighing less than an ounce, this miniature hunter fearlessly pounces on wolf spiders, scorpions, and centipedes nearly half its own size.

mammals.name: Rakali
facts: Long dismissed as the 'common water rat,' the Australian government officially promoted its Indigenous Ngarrindjeri name, Rakali, in 1995 to help the public appreciate this gorgeous native otter-like rodent.

After invasive cane toads poisoned almost every native predator in northern Australia, clever rakali figured out how to flip the giant toads onto their backs and perform surgical incisions with their incisors to eat only the non-toxic hearts and livers.
Built like a miniature otter, the rakali boasts partially webbed hind feet, waterproof fur that traps an insulating layer of air, and a thick rudder-tail tipped in bright white.
Before eating hard-shelled freshwater mussels, a rakali carries them onto a favorite lakeside 'dining table' rock and leaves them sitting in the hot sun until the shells pop open on their own.
Unlike almost all other Australian native mammals, the rakali thrives right in the middle of major cities, hunting crayfish and carp along the Sydney Harbour foreshore and Melbourne's Yarra River.

mammals.name: Melon-headed whale
facts: Despite its name, the melon-headed whale is actually a sleek, torpedo-shaped oceanic dolphin named after its rounded, cantaloupe-like forehead.
By day, pods of up to 1,000 individuals rest lazily near the surface in tight, synchronized formations around tropical volcanic islands, waiting for nightfall to hunt deep-water squid.
Around the island of Hawaii, a unique resident population remains year-round in deep offshore trenches rather than roaming the open Pacific like their pelagic cousins.
Their dark charcoal bodies feature a distinctive 'cape' dip below the dorsal fin and bright white lips that glow faintly in deep, dim waters, earning them the nickname 'many-toothed blackfish.'
Highly sensitive to high-powered naval sonar, melon-headed whales have occasionally fled in mass panic into shallow coral lagoons during military exercises.

mammals.name: Addax
facts: Also called the 'screwhorn antelope,' the addax is so supremely adapted to the hyper-arid Sahara that it can live its entire life without ever drinking liquid water, extracting all moisture from desert grasses and morning dew.
Its coat acts as a natural thermostat: in winter it is grayish-brown to absorb solar warmth, and in summer it turns dazzling chalk-white to reflect the relentless desert sun.
Wide, flat hooves with low fetlocks act like sand-shoes, allowing the heavy antelope to stride effortlessly across soft, shifting sand dunes where horses and camels sink.
Even its nostrils are air-conditioned, specialized nasal passages cool arterial blood headed to the brain before it can overheat, even when the animal's body temperature hits 105°F.
Once depicted in ancient Egyptian tombs as a prized possession of noblemen, fewer than 100 wild addax survive today in remote corners of Niger and Chad.

mammals.name: Leopard cat
facts: About the size of a slender house cat, the wild Asian leopard cat was crossbred with domestic cats in the 1960s and 1970s to create the wildly popular, rosetted Bengal cat breed.
Unlike most felines, leopard cats have partially webbed toes that help them paddle through flooded rice paddies and walk smoothly across slick mudbanks while hunting frogs and eels.

An ancient leopard cat skeleton excavated from a 5,300-year-old Neolithic village in Shaanxi, China, revealed that leopard cats were independently tamed alongside early Chinese grain farmers to control rodents; millennia before Western domestic cats arrived via the Silk Road.

Depending on where it lives, a leopard cat can look like two different animals: tropical Indonesian individuals are tiny and bright ochre-yellow, while northern Amur individuals are twice as heavy with thick silver-gray coats.
They are agile nocturnal climbers that rest in high tree hollows by day and drop silently onto tree squirrels and roosting birds after dark.

mammals.name: American marten
facts: Instead of hibernating through sub-zero boreal winters, the American marten dives headfirst into deep snowdrifts to hunt voles and mice in the 'subnivean zone', a hidden network of air pockets between the ground and the snowpack.
During winter, the soles of its oversized paws sprout thick pads of coarse fur, turning its feet into natural insulated snowshoes that distribute its weight over powdery snow.
Female martens mate in mid-summer but use 'delayed implantation,' holding the fertilized embryos in suspended animation for seven months so the kits are born in the warmth of spring.
Prized by Hudson's Bay fur trappers as 'American sable,' its luxurious, glossy pelt drove much of the early European exploration of northern Canada.
With ankle joints that can rotate nearly 180 degrees, a marten can sprint headfirst down a vertical pine trunk while chasing an agile red squirrel.

mammals.name: Tenrec
mammals.summary: The tailless tenrec (Tenrec ecaudatus), also known as the common tenrec, is a species of mammal in the family Tenrecidae. It is the only member of the genus Tenrec.
facts: Having arrived on Madagascar on floating vegetation rafts millions of years ago, tenrecs evolved via convergent evolution to look like hedgehogs, shrews, otters, and mice, despite being more closely related to elephants and aardvarks than to any of them.

The streaked tenrec is the only mammal on Earth known to use 'stridulation', rubbing specialized quills on its back together like a cricket's wings to broadcast high-pitched ultrasonic clicks to family members.
Common tailless tenrecs hold the record for the largest litter size of any mammal, giving birth to up to 32 tiny babies at once and nursing them with up to 29 teats.
Instead of having separate openings for waste and reproduction, tenrecs retain a single primitive opening called a 'cloaca', a trait shared with reptiles, birds, and the platypus.
During Madagascar's dry winter, some tenrecs can hibernate for up to nine months without waking up to eat, drink, or urinate, letting their body temperature match the surrounding soil.

mammals.name: Hirola
facts: Nicknamed the 'four-eyed antelope' by Somali pastoralists, the hirola possesses huge, dark preorbital scent glands below its eyes that look exactly like a second pair of eyes.
A conspicuous white chevron stripe bridging its forehead gives the antelope the appearance of wearing a pair of reading spectacles.
The hirola is a 'living fossil' and the sole surviving member of an entire evolutionary genus (Beatragus) that once roamed across Africa alongside early hominids millions of years ago.
With fewer than 500 individuals surviving along the Kenya-Somalia border, it is the world's most endangered antelope, and the only critically endangered mammalian genus on mainland Africa.

Ironically, its crisis deepened in the 1980s when poaching wiped out local elephants; without elephants knocking down thorny scrub trees, open grasslands turned into dense thickets where hirolas cannot spot ambushing lions.

mammals.name: Culpeo
facts: Also called the Andean fox, the culpeo isn't a true fox at all; genetic studies show it is much more closely related to wolves, coyotes, and jackals.

Around 1,000 years ago, the indigenous Selk'nam and Yaghan peoples of Tierra del Fuego domesticated the culpeo into the 'Fuegian dog,' a loyal hunting companion that sadly went extinct in the early 20th century.
Adapted to hunt from coastal deserts all the way up to 15,000-foot Andean mountain passes, it is the second-largest native canid in South America after the maned wolf.
In Patagonia, bold culpeos have recently begun diving into coastal kelp beds and sneaking into Magellanic penguin colonies to snatch seabirds and penguin eggs.
When hunting introduced European hares in the high pampas, culpeos stalk silently upwind using bunchgrass for cover before launching a blistering short-distance ambush.

mammals.name: Argali
facts: Standing up to four feet tall at the shoulder and weighing over 350 pounds, the Central Asian argali is the largest wild sheep species on the planet.
A mature ram's massive, corkscrewing horns can measure over six feet along the curve and weigh up to 50 pounds, accounting for more than 13 percent of the animal's entire body weight.
One legendary Pamir subspecies, the Marco Polo sheep, was first described to Western readers by the Venetian explorer himself while crossing the Roof of the World in 1271.
When rival rams clash during the autumn rut, the crack of their hollow horns slamming together at 20 miles per hour echoes across mountain valleys like a rifle shot.
Unlike mountain goats and ibex that escape predators by climbing jagged cliffs, long-legged argali rely on sheer open-ground speed across high, rolling alpine plateaus.

mammals.name: Black wildebeest
facts: Known in South Africa as the 'white-tailed gnu,' this eccentric antelope is famous for its bizarre 'clowning' displays, spinning in circles, bucking wildly, and tossing its head while snorting loudly for no apparent reason.
Its heavy horns curve forward and downward before hooking sharply up like twin meat hooks, protected at the base by a thick boss that shields its skull during head-butting duels.

Unlike the famous blue wildebeest that migrates over a thousand miles across the Serengeti, the black wildebeest is a homebody of the South African highveld that migrates only up and down mountain slopes.

By the 1890s, relentless hide hunters had reduced the entire species to fewer than 600 animals surviving on just two private farms in the Orange Free State; every one of the 18,000 alive today descends from those few survivors.
Its cream-colored, horse-like tail was historically prized by Zulu warriors and traditional healers as a ceremonial fly-whisk called an 'ishoba.'

mammals.name: Boodie
facts: Also known as the burrowing bettong, the boodie is the only member of the entire kangaroo superfamily (Macropodoidea) that excavates and lives inside deep underground burrow warrens.
A large boodie warren can have over a hundred separate entrances and stretch across an entire hillside, housing a noisy, polygynous clan of a male and several females.
When foraging at night, this pint-sized kangaroo relative uses its muscular, semi-prehensile tail like a shopping basket, curling it around bundles of dried grass to hop them back down into its nest.

Once one of the most common marsupials across mainland Australia, invasive red foxes and feral cats wiped out every single mainland population by the 1960s, leaving survivors only on four predator-free offshore islands.
As 'ecosystem engineers,' their relentless digging turns over tons of hard desert soil each year, creating tiny water-catching pits where native desert seeds can sprout.

mammals.name: Brush mouse
facts: Named for the tiny tuft of hair at the tip of its long tail, the brush mouse is a semi-arboreal acrobat that scrambles up rough oak bark and chaparral branches with ease.
During dry California summers, it enters short bouts of daily torpor to save energy and water while sleeping inside hollow logs or abandoned woodrat middens.
By stashing thousands of coast live oak and valley oak acorns in shallow underground caches, and forgetting to dig many of them back up, it is one of the primary planters of western oak woodlands.
After wildfires scorch chaparral hillsides, brush mice are among the very first mammals to move back into the ash, feasting on heat-opened seeds and scorched insects.
Even when food is abundant, a brush mouse is fiercely fastidious, spending hours grooming its bicolored tail and velvety oversized ears.

mammals.name: Leadbeater's possum
facts: Nicknamed the 'woodland fairy' because it darts through misty eucalyptus canopies like a phantom, Leadbeater's possum was declared completely extinct for over 50 years until a young naturalist spotted one near Marysville, Victoria, in 1961.
Unlike sugar gliders, it has no gliding membrane at all; instead, it hurls itself across three-foot gaps between branches in the dark, using its club-shaped tail as a rudder.
At night, it uses its chisel-like lower incisors to gouge V-shaped notches into smooth acacia bark, returning the next evening to lap up the sweet, protein-rich gum that oozes from the wounds.
Colonies sleep huddled together inside hollow mountain ash trees that are at least 150 years old, guarded by a single alpha female who aggressively drives away any strange females.
Despite weighing no more than a deck of cards, it serves alongside the helmeted honeyeater as the official faunal emblem of the Australian state of Victoria.

mammals.name: Oribi
facts: When startled in tall savanna grass, an oribi performs a spectacular 'stotting' leap, springing straight up into the air with all four legs held stiffly vertical and flashing its white underside to tell predators, 'I've already seen you, don't bother chasing me.'
Simultaneously with its stiff-legged jump, the tiny antelope emits a piercing, high-pitched alarm whistle through its nostrils that alerts every grazer within half a mile.
Look closely below its ears and you'll spot a round, bare black patch of skin, one of six different pairs of scent glands distributed across its face, knees, groin, and hooves.
Oribi pairs and small family groups share communal 'dung middens,' backing up together in a polite ceremony to deposit their droppings in the exact same spot to mark their turf.
Instead of fleeing when a predator approaches, a fawn will drop flat in the grass with its ears folded back and remain motionless even if a human walks within inches of it.

mammals.name: Darwin's fox
facts: In December 1834, a young Charles Darwin was so engrossed in watching a curious little fox on Chiloé Island, Chile, that a crewman walked right up behind the distracted animal and dispatched it with a geological hammer for the Beagle's specimen collection.
Darwin immediately recognized it as a unique island species, famously writing in his journal that this solitary fox was distinct from anything known on the South American mainland.

For over a century after Darwin's voyage, biologists thought the fox lived only on Chiloé Island, until 1975, when a tiny, isolated ghost population was discovered 350 miles away in the high coastal mountains of Nahuelbuta National Park.
With stubby legs, a stocky body, and dark grizzled fur, it navigates dense Valdivian temperate rainforests where larger mainland foxes cannot maneuver.
Because fewer than 1,000 individuals survive in the wild today, unvaccinated domestic dogs wandering into national parks pose the single greatest threat to the species via canine distemper virus.

mammals.name: Colocolo
facts: Also known as the Pampas cat, the colocolo wears such wildly different coats across South America, from rosetted cinnamon in the Andes to solid silvery-brown in the Argentine grasslands, that taxonomists still debate whether it is one species or five.
When threatened, a colocolo erects a long crest of four-inch hairs running from the top of its head all the way down its spine, instantly making itself look twice as large.
High in the treeless altiplano at 16,000 feet, this tough little cat stalks mountain chinchillas and viscachas across freezing boulder fields where few other predators can breathe.
Its name honors Colo Colo, a legendary 16th-century Mapuche chieftain whose wisdom and stealth helped unite Indigenous Chilean tribes against Spanish conquistadors.

In northern Chile and Peru, rural Andean communities traditionally revered the cat, decorating preserved pelts with colorful wool ribbons during harvest fertility ceremonies to protect crops from rodents.

mammals.name: Arctic ground squirrel
facts: This tough rodent is the only mammal known to survive 'supercooling', during its eight-month hibernation in permafrost burrows, its core body temperature drops to 26.8°F (-2.9°C), nearly five degrees below the freezing point of water, without its blood turning to ice.

While supercooled, its heart beats just once every minute and its brain loses a massive fraction of its synaptic connections; yet every three weeks it shivers violently to warm up for 12 hours and rebuild every single brain synapse from scratch.
Indigenous Iñupiat and Yup'ik peoples of Alaska call the squirrel 'sik-sik' after its sharp, metallic two-note alarm chirp, and historically sewed its soft pelts into lightweight summer parkas.
Arctic ground squirrels are among the very few tundra animals whose burrows must stay above the rock-hard permafrost layer, just three feet below the surface.

Before curling up for winter in late summer, males hoard massive underground pantries of willow twigs, seeds, and mushrooms so they can wake up a full month before females and bulk up in snow-covered burrows.

mammals.name: Gilbert's potoroo
facts: Declared completely extinct after 1879, Gilbert's potoroo pulled off one of conservation history's greatest Lazarus acts when researcher Elizabeth Sinclair accidentally caught one in a cage trap set for quokkas at Two Peoples Bay in 1994.
With roughly 100 individuals alive today across a single peninsula and three safe-haven islands, this rabbit-sized marsupial is officially Australia's most critically endangered mammal.
Over 90 percent of its diet consists of underground truffle-like fungi, which it sniffs out beneath dense coastal heath using its long, curved snout and digs up with long front claws.

The potoroo and the eucalyptus trees of southwestern Australia need each other to survive: the marsupial's droppings are packed with undigested fungal spores that trees need around their roots to absorb nutrients from poor sandy soils.

When a devastating lightning bushfire incinerated 90 percent of its only mainland habitat in 2015, a tiny insurance colony that scientists had moved to Bald Island a decade earlier saved the species from vanishing a second time.

mammals.name: Cuvier's beaked whale
facts: This elusive cetacean is the undisputed champion of mammalian diving: in 2020, researchers tracked a Cuvier's beaked whale diving nearly two miles down (9,816 feet) and holding its breath for an astonishing 3 hours and 42 minutes.

To survive crushing deep-sea pressures that would flatten a submarine, its ribcage folds down flat, its lungs collapse completely to prevent the bends, and its muscles store massive reserves of oxygen-binding myoglobin.
Despite its name, French anatomist Georges Cuvier originally thought the first skull handed to him in 1823 belonged to an extinct fossil whale until live specimens washed ashore decades later.

Only adult males grow two visible tusk-like teeth that jut out from the tip of their lower jaw even when their mouths are shut; they use these tusks like sabers, leaving older bulls covered from head to tail in white battle scars.

Because they have almost no functional teeth for chewing, they capture deep-sea squid at 6,000 feet by dropping their lower jaw and tongue like a piston, sucking prey whole into their mouths like an underwater vacuum cleaner.

mammals.name: Mexican free-tailed bat
facts: Forget the peregrine falcon's gravity-assisted dive, in level, powered flight, the Mexican free-tailed bat is the fastest flyer in the animal kingdom, clocked by researchers at an astonishing 99 miles per hour.
Every summer, Bracken Cave outside San Antonio, Texas, hosts around 20 million Mexican free-tailed bats, the largest known concentration of mammals anywhere on Earth.
When the Bracken Cave colony spirals out into the evening sky to hunt, the cloud of bats is so dense and vast that it shows up on National Weather Service Doppler radar as a giant rainstorm.
Each night, that single Texas super-colony devours roughly 100 tons of corn earworm and cotton bollworm moths, saving Southwestern farmers billions of dollars in crop damage and pesticides.

To keep other bats from stealing their insect targets in crowded airspace, hunting free-tailed bats emit a rapidly warbling ultrasonic 'jamming signal' that scrambles a rival bat's sonar at the exact moment it closes in on a moth.

mammals.name: Himalayan tahr
facts: Built for life on razor-thin vertical ledges up to 16,000 feet high, the Himalayan tahr has hooves with a hard, sharp outer rim that grips microscopic rock crevices and a flexible, rubbery inner pad that acts like a suction cup.
Introduced to New Zealand's Southern Alps in 1904 as a gift from the Duke of Bedford, six escaped tahrs found a predator-free paradise and multiplied into tens of thousands.
A smaller runaway population even colonized Table Mountain right above Cape Town, South Africa, after a pair escaped from Groote Schuur Zoo in 1936.
During winter in the Himalayas, adult males grow a magnificent, lion-like ruff of coarse reddish-gold hair around their necks and shoulders that sheds waterfall-like snow and icy sleet.

Unlike bighorn sheep that charge headfirst from a distance, rival male tahrs prefer to wrestle side-by-side, trying to hook their short, curved horns under an opponent's flank to throw him off balance.

mammals.name: Dormouse
mammals.summary: The hazel dormouse or common dormouse (Muscardinus avellanarius) is a small dormouse species native to Europe and the only living species in the genus Muscardinus. Its habitat include mainly the woodland as well as hedgerows and scrub.
facts: In 1993, Slovenian biologists discovered that the edible dormouse has a real-life superpower straight out of 'X-Men': when it wakes up from hibernation, its chromosomes automatically re-lengthen their telomeres, essentially reversing cellular aging.

Ancient Romans considered the fat dormouse ('glis') the ultimate luxury appetizer; they fattened them up on walnuts and chestnuts inside specialized terra-cotta jars called 'gliraria' before roasting them and dipping them in honey and poppy seeds.
True to the sleepy Dormouse at the Mad Hatter's tea party in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' these rodents can hibernate for up to 11 months in a single year when beech mast crops fail.

If an owl or weasel grabs a dormouse by its fluffy tail, the outer sheath of skin and fur slips right off like a loose glove so the dormouse can escape, though unlike a lizard's tail, it never grows back and the rodent chews off the bare bone.
Unlike almost every other mammal on Earth, the dormouse completely lacks a cecum in its digestive tract, forcing it to avoid fibrous grass and leaves in favor of pure nuts, berries, and insects.

mammals.name: Hispid cotton rat
facts: Because early 20th-century scientists discovered that the hispid cotton rat was the first non-primate mammal susceptible to human poliovirus, this humble field rodent played a heroic role in testing the first polio vaccines.
Female cotton rats live life in the fast lane: they can become pregnant before they are even six weeks old, carry a litter for just 27 days, and mate again within hours of giving birth.

As they scurry through tall broomsedge and bluestem fields, they clip stems at the base to build covered 'runways'; miniature green tunnels that hide them from the eyes of red-tailed hawks and barn owls.
Even newborn cotton rats are remarkably precocious: born with a coat of hair and metabolisms already running hot, their eyes pop open within 24 hours and they can sprint away from danger on day two.
Their name comes from two traits: 'hispid' refers to their bristly, grizzled guard hairs, while 'cotton' nods to their habit of shredding cotton bolls to line their soft spherical nests.

mammals.name: Sika deer
facts: In the ancient city of Nara, Japan, over 1,200 wild sika deer roam the streets as sacred messengers of the Shinto gods, and have learned to politely bow their heads to tourists in exchange for special rice-bran crackers called 'shika-senbei.'
Unlike almost all other deer species whose fawns lose their spots by autumn, sika deer keep their dappled white summer spots for their entire lives.
During the autumn rut, stags don't bellow like red deer; instead, they let out an eerie, three-part high-pitched whistle that ends in a guttural groan, sounding like a banshee in the woods.

In 1916, Boy Scouts released five Japanese sika deer onto James Island in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay; those five animals swam to the mainland and grew into a thriving population of over 15,000 across the Delmarva Peninsula.
When alarmed, the pure white hairs on a sika deer's rump flare outward into a bright heart-shaped puff, flashing a visual warning to the rest of the herd.

mammals.name: Sable
facts: For centuries, the silky, smoky-brown winter pelt of the Siberian sable, prized as 'soft gold', was so valuable that Imperial Russian czars demanded tribute from Siberian tribes paid exclusively in sable skins, reserving the finest pelts for royal crowns.
To survive -50°F Siberian winters, the sable grows fur so dense and plush that snow doesn't melt when the animal curls up on top of a snowbank, keeping its coat bone-dry.
Remarkably, the hair on a sable's back has no fixed 'grain'; you can stroke a sable pelt forward, backward, or sideways and it lies perfectly smooth in any direction.
Although it is a fierce carnivore that hunts chipmunks, mice, and musk deer fawns, the sable has a surprising sweet tooth in autumn, gorging on Siberian pine nuts and wild blueberries.
Like its North American marten cousin, the sable uses 'delayed implantation,' mating in the summer sun while pausing embryo development for nearly eight months until the spring thaw.

mammals.name: Kouprey
facts: Towering six feet at the shoulder in the remote dry forests of Cambodia, the enigmatic kouprey was the last large land mammal discovered by science in the 20th century, formally described by a French veterinarian in 1937.
Adult bulls sport unique, lyre-shaped horns that fray near the tips into jagged, fibrous brushes, a result of the bulls habitually digging their horn tips into soil and tree trunks.
Hanging from an older bull's throat is a massive dewlap of loose skin up to 16 inches long that drags through tall savanna grass like a pendulum to radiate away excess body heat.

Because no confirmed photograph or sighting of a wild kouprey has been recorded since 1988, biologists fear this forest giant may already be extinct, or reduced to a tiny ghost herd in war-scarred borderlands.
In 1960, Prince Norodom Sihanouk declared the kouprey the national mammal of Cambodia, and today the country's national football team proudly calls itself the 'Koupreys.'

mammals.name: Kiang
facts: Roaming the roof of the world at elevations up to 18,000 feet, the kiang is the largest of all wild asses, and so unfazed by freezing glacial torrents that herds swim across icy Tibetan rivers for fun.

When threatened by packs of Tibetan wolves, a herd of kiangs doesn't always scatter; instead, they sometimes wheel into a tight defensive circle with their heads facing inward, lashing out with bone-crushing hind hooves.
During the brief two-month Tibetan summer when protein-rich needlegrass blooms across the plateau, an adult kiang packs on nearly 100 pounds of insulating body fat to survive the coming blizzards.
Their oversized nasal cavities warm and humidify the thin, freezing Himalayan air before it reaches their lungs, allowing them to gallop at 35 miles per hour where humans gasp for breath.
With a rich chestnut coat that contrasts sharply against pure white legs and underbellies, herds of up to 400 kiangs look from a distance like red-and-white ribbons streaming across the steppes.

mammals.name: Bushpig
facts: Despite its fearsome reputation for charging leopards and hunting dogs with razor-sharp lower tusks, the African bushpig is a devoted family animal led by a monogamous alpha boar and sow who groom each other daily.

When foraging through pitch-black forest undergrowth at night, sounders stay together by exchanging soft, musical grunts and squeaks, while the dominant boar raises a long white dorsal mane to act as a visual beacon.
Using its tough, muscular snout disc like a steel plow, a bushpig can roll aside heavy boulders and rotting logs weighing over 100 pounds to unearth roots, bulbs, and earthworms.

Before giving birth, a pregnant sow chops up hundreds of tall grass stems with her teeth and piles them into a three-foot-tall 'haystack' nest that keeps her striped piglets warm and dry like an incubator.

In Madagascar, an introduced population of bushpigs has lived wild in the forests for at least 1,000 years, serving as a vital disperser of large rainforest tree seeds since the island's giant lemurs went extinct.

mammals.name: Island fox
facts: No bigger than a house cat, the Channel Islands fox evolved via 'insular dwarfism' from mainland gray foxes that washed out to California's offshore islands on storm debris or Chumash canoes roughly 9,000 years ago.

In the 1990s, the island fox nearly vanished after DDT wiped out local bald eagles (which eat fish) and golden eagles moved in from the mainland (which ate the foxes); relocating the golden eagles and restoring bald eagles pulled off the fastest mammal recovery in U.S. Endangered Species Act history.
Having lived for millennia without coyotes, wolves, or bears on their islands, these little foxes show almost zero fear of humans and hunt boldly under the midday sun.
Like their mainland gray fox ancestors, island foxes have semi-retractable claws and flexible forelegs that let them scramble straight up the twisted trunks of toyon and island oak trees.
Six of the eight Channel Islands have their own genetically distinct subspecies of island fox, each adapted to the specific plants and seabirds of its home island.

mammals.name: Golden snub-nosed monkey
facts: Why does this snow-dwelling Chinese primate have no protruding nose at all? Primatologists believe its flat, upturned nostrils evolved specifically so its nose wouldn't succumb to frostbite during -20°F mountain winters.

To survive bitter blizzards in the Qinling and Hengduan mountains at 10,000 feet, troops of up to 400 monkeys huddle together in massive, rotating furry balls where outer members take turns cycling into the warm center.
It is one of the very few primates on Earth that regularly walks upright on two legs across deep snowdrifts while carrying food in both hands.

During winter when leaves and fruit vanish, golden snub-nosed monkeys survive almost entirely by peeling beard lichens off frozen fir branches and digesting them in their cow-like multi-chambered stomachs.
With its fiery golden cape and pale electric-blue face, this alpine monkey is widely considered the real-life inspiration for Sun Wukong, the legendary Monkey King of classic Chinese literature.

mammals.name: South Asian river dolphin
facts: Swimming through the mud-choked, chocolate-brown waters of the Ganges and Indus rivers, this freshwater dolphin is functionally blind; its tiny eyes lack crystalline lenses entirely and can only sense whether it is day or night.
To navigate murky currents and avoid tangled tree roots along the riverbed, it swims on its side, trailing one broad, paddle-like flipper in the mud to feel for bottom-dwelling shrimp and catfish.
Because it must surface every 30 to 120 seconds and lets out a loud, sneezing 'susu!' exhale through its blowhole, villagers across India, Nepal, and Bangladesh simply call the animal the 'Susu.'

Unlike ocean dolphins that click only when hunting, the blind river dolphin clicks nonstop for 24 hours a day; stopping its sonar in a fast-moving river would be like driving down a highway with your eyes shut.
Its long, forceps-like snout is armed with up to 120 needle-sharp teeth that interlock visibly outside its mouth even when its jaws are closed, growing longer and more curved near the front.

mammals.name: Gray fox
facts: The gray fox is one of only two members of the entire dog family (alongside Asia's raccoon dog) that can climb straight up vertical, branchless tree trunks, hugging the bark with its forelegs and pushing upward with its hind feet like a lumberjack.
Once thirty feet up in the canopy, it leaps from branch to branch like a cat and even naps inside high hollow tree cavities or abandoned hawk nests.

Fossil genetics reveal that the gray fox isn't closely related to red or arctic foxes at all; instead, it sits at the very base of the entire family tree of all living dogs, wolves, and foxes, tracing its lineage back 10 million years.
How does a gray fox get back down a tree? It can either back down slowly tail-first like a house cat or rotate its flexible wrists and ankles to run down headfirst like a squirrel.
Unlike the meat-heavy diet of red foxes, the gray fox is a true omnivore that switches largely to wild persimmons, grapes, acorns, and corn during the autumn harvest.

mammals.name: Lemming
mammals.summary: The Norway lemming, also known as the Norwegian lemming (Lemmus lemmus), is a common species of lemming found in northern Fennoscandia, where it is the only vertebrate species endemic to the region. The Norway lemming dwells in tundra and fells, and prefers to live near water.
facts: The famous myth that lemmings commit mass suicide by leaping off cliffs is completely fake; it was staged by filmmakers for the 1958 Disney documentary 'White Wilderness,' who bought dozens of lemmings in Manitoba, shipped them to Alberta, and flung them off a turntable into the Bow River.

What is real is the lemming's explosive four-year population boom: under ideal conditions, a female can give birth just 20 days after mating and produce up to eight litters a year, sending millions of lemmings marching across the tundra in search of food.
Rather than hibernating during freezing Arctic winters, lemmings grow forked, shovel-like claws on their middle front toes to dig miles of warm tunnels beneath the snowpack.

Despite weighing less than a lemon, a cornered Norway lemming has zero chill; instead of running away, it rears up on its hind legs, bares its bright orange incisors, and shrieks while lunging at dogs, foxes, or hikers.
The entire breeding success of snowy owls, Arctic foxes, and jaegers rises and falls with lemming cycles; in 'crash' years with few lemmings, snowy owls often skip nesting altogether.

mammals.name: Dibatag
facts: When a dibatag sprints across the Somali scrubland, it holds its long neck arched backward and flips its black-and-white tail straight up over its back until the tip nearly touches its head.
Like its famous cousin the gerenuk, the pencil-thin dibatag routinely stands upright on its hind legs, balancing like a biped to pluck tender buds from high, thorny Commiphora bushes.
Its name comes from two Somali words, 'dabu' (tail) and 'tag' (erect), describing its signature upright-tail salute when fleeing danger.

With its slate-gray coat and stilt-like cinnamon legs, a motionless dibatag standing behind a dry bush is so practically invisible that hunters and biologists call it one of the hardest antelopes in Africa to spot.
Even today, not a single dibatag exists in any zoo on Earth, making this secretive Horn of Africa browser one of the least-studied hoofed mammals alive.

mammals.name: Mountain cottontail
facts: Also called Nuttall's cottontail after naturalist Thomas Nuttall, this high-altitude rabbit has furry soles on its hind feet that give it sure-footed traction on icy sagebrush slopes and rimrock ledges.
Unlike European rabbits that live in crowded communal warrens, the mountain cottontail is a solitary mountaineer that shelters inside rocky crevices or borrows abandoned marmot and badger holes.

When pursued by a bobcat or golden eagle, it dashes in a frantic zigzag pattern before freezing dead still beside a clump of sagebrush, tucking its fluffy white tail down so its gray back blends into the stones.
During deep winter snows in the Rockies and Cascades when green grass is buried, it survives by stripping the bitter bark and buds off juniper and big sagebrush bushes.
To extract every drop of nutrition from tough woody plants, it practices 'coprophagy', eating its own soft, vitamin-rich green night pellets straight from its rear to digest the food a second time.

mammals.name: Barasingha
facts: In Hindi, 'Barasingha' literally means 'twelve-tined,' yet mature stags of this magnificent Indian swamp deer regularly grow up to 20 points on a single crown of antlers.
During the winter rut, lovesick stags wade into marshy reedbeds and toss clumps of waterweeds into the air until their antlers are draped in trailing green crowns to impress watching hinds.

The rare central Indian subspecies ('hard-ground barasingha') was down to just 66 survivors in Kanha National Park in 1970 before intense conservation efforts rebuilt the herd to over a thousand, and inspired Kanha's official mascot, 'Bhoorsingh the Barasingha.'
Because Kanha National Park is the real-life setting that inspired Rudyard Kipling's 'The Jungle Book,' the barasingha shared those exact sal forests and meadows with Shere Khan and Baloo.

The northern subspecies living in the flooded Terai marshes has widely splayed, spongy hooves that keep it from sinking into deep mud, while the central Indian subspecies evolved hard, compact hooves for running on sun-baked clay.

mammals.name: Columbian ground squirrel
facts: First described by explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark while crossing the Bitterroot Mountains in 1805, this sociable rodent spends nearly eight months of every year fast asleep underground.

Each squirrel excavates a special 'hibernaculum' chamber lined with shredded dry grass and plugs the entrance tunnel tightly with packed dirt from the inside to lock out both freezing air and hungry badgers.
When friends or family members meet outside their burrows in spring, they press their mouths together in an affectionate greeting that looks remarkably like a French kiss.
During the frantic 90-day alpine summer, an adult Columbian ground squirrel must double its body weight in fat before retreating back underground by mid-August.

A female's entire reproductive window lasts just five hours on a single afternoon in spring, during which she mates with up to four different males, resulting in a single litter where almost every pup has a different father.

mammals.name: Bilby
mammals.summary: The greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) or often simply bilby, is a long-eared, rabbit-like marsupial found in Australia. It lives in burrows and is active at night, feeding on insects, fruit, or fungi.
facts: In Australia, chocolate makers and conservationists launched the 'Easter Bilby' campaign in the 1990s, replacing invasive European Easter Bunnies with chocolate bilbies whose sales fund predator-proof desert sanctuaries.
Because a bilby burrows headfirst into sandy soil like a living torpedo, a mother's pouch opens backward toward her hind legs so it won't scoop up a pouchful of dirt onto her joey.
Its huge, hairless rabbit-like ears aren't just for hearing termites chewing underground; they are threaded with a dense network of blood vessels that radiate away excess body heat in the Outback.
The bilby has one of the shortest gestation periods of any mammal on Earth: just 12 to 14 days after mating, a joey the size of a baked bean crawls blindly into the backward pouch.

A single bilby keeps up to a dozen spiral burrows scattered across its territory, each spiraling down up to ten feet below the desert floor with no exit door; instead, if a predator digs in, the bilby furiously tunnels deeper into the sand faster than the hunter can dig.

mammals.name: Tufted capuchin
facts: In Brazil's Serra da Capivara, tufted capuchins have been filmed using heavy quartzite cobblestones as hammers and flat tree roots as anvils to smash open rock-hard palm nuts, a Stone Age tool culture that archaeologists discovered goes back at least 3,000 years.
Before selecting a hammer stone, a capuchin actually lifts and taps several rocks to test their weight and density, often carrying a favorite three-pound boulder to the same anvil tree for years.
Named for the two dark tufts of hair on its crown that can be raised like devil horns when the monkey is excited or angry, it was the classic 'organ grinder' monkey of 19th-century street performers.
Female tufted capuchins court the alpha male with a hilarious flirting display: raising their eyebrows, grinning, whistling softly, and throwing sticks or pebbles at him until he pays attention.

Because of their uncanny manual dexterity, trained tufted capuchins have served as 'Helping Hands' service animals for quadriplegic humans, flipping light switches, turning book pages, and fetching water bottles.

mammals.name: Bharal
facts: Popularly known as the 'blue sheep' for the slate-blue sheen of its dense winter coat, the Himalayan bharal is so perfectly camouflaged against blue-gray shale cliffs that it vanishes the moment it stops moving.

Look closely at its anatomy and you'll see why taxonomists were baffled for a century: although called a sheep, DNA proves the bharal is actually much closer to a goat, lacking a sheep's facial glands while missing a goat's chin beard and strong billy smell.
The bharal is the single most important prey item for the endangered snow leopard, often luring the big cats onto near-vertical precipices above 15,000 feet.
Unlike true wild sheep whose horns curl in tight loops beside their cheeks, a male bharal's thick, smooth horns grow outward sideways before curving backward like an upside-down handlebar mustache.

Living comfortably above the treeline up to 18,000 feet, herds graze on open grassy slopes but never stray more than 200 yards from a vertical cliff face where they can bolt at the first sign of danger.

mammals.name: Black-tailed jackrabbit
facts: Despite its name, the black-tailed jackrabbit isn't a rabbit at all; it is a true hare whose babies ('leverets') are born wide-eyed, fully furred, and ready to hop within minutes of birth.
Early American pioneers originally called it the 'jackass rabbit' because its enormous, seven-inch ears looked just like a donkey's ears poking above the desert brush.

Those giant ears act as desert radiators: when the shade temperature is cooler than the hare's body, it dilates the blood vessels in its ears to dump heat, and when the desert air exceeds 105°F, it constricts them so the boiling wind won't heat its blood.
When flushed by a coyote, a jackrabbit rockets away at up to 40 miles per hour, throwing in an occasional five-foot-high 'spy hop' mid-stride to check where its pursuer is.
With eyes set high on the sides of its head, a resting jackrabbit enjoys a nearly 360-degree panoramic field of view, allowing it to spot a hawk behind its back without ever turning its head.

mammals.name: Gerenuk
facts: Whose Somali name literally translates to 'giraffe-necked,' the gerenuk has modified wedge-shaped lumbar vertebrae and specialized hip joints that allow it to stand bolt upright on its hind legs to browse high acacia leaves no other antelope can reach.
While standing on two legs like a furry mannequin, it uses one front hoof to hook down thorny branches while stripping leaves with its tough, pointed lips and long tongue.
A gerenuk never needs to visit a watering hole, which are dangerous ambush hotspots for lions and crocodiles, because it gets 100 percent of its water from succulent desert leaves and fruit.
Even newborn gerenuk fawns practice standing on their hind legs within two weeks of birth, steadying themselves against their mother's flank while learning to balance.
Among several East African pastoral tribes, folklore holds that gerenuks are magical relatives of camels; killing or eating one is strictly taboo lest a family's actual camel herd fall ill.

mammals.name: Brazilian false rice rat
facts: Native to the misty Atlantic Forest and Restinga coastal scrublands of southeastern Brazil, this secretive nocturnal rodent looks so much like a true rice rat that only skull and dental details give away its separate evolutionary branch.
Equipped with long, sensitive whiskers and grasping hind feet, it scrambles through low bromeliads and tangled vines just a few feet above the damp forest floor.
During the rainy summer months, it feasts on fallen palm fruits, fern spores, and forest beetles, tucking extra seeds beneath rotting bark.
By day, it curls up inside spherical nests woven from shredded palm fibers and dry leaves hidden deep inside hollow logs or terrestrial bromeliad rosettes.
Because it thrives only in undisturbed, humid forest fragments with thick leaf litter, conservationists use its presence as a living bio-indicator of Atlantic Forest health.

mammals.name: Moustached guenon
facts: Looking like a dapper Victorian gentleman who fell into a paintbox, this Central African monkey wears a crisp white handlebar mustache beneath a bright turquoise-blue mask and fluffy yellow ear tufts.

Despite spending their lives in noisy, colorful troops high in the rainforest canopies of Gabon and the Congo, these monkeys never groom their own colorful faces; instead relying on troopmates to pick through their facial fur.

Moustached guenons regularly form permanent, multi-species 'super-troops' with crowned guenons and greater spot-nosed monkeys, combining three sets of eyes and ears to spot ambushing crowned eagles and leopards.

Inside its cheeks are stretchy pouches that can hold almost as much fruit as its actual stomach, letting the monkey stuff its face in exposed fruit trees and dash back to dense cover to chew in peace.

Adult males possess a resonant vocal sac in their throat that lets them boom out a deep 'pyow' alarm call that warns both their own family and neighboring monkey species which type of predator is nearby.

mammals.name: Ringed seal
facts: As the smallest and most abundant seal in the Arctic, the ringed seal uses the stout, 2.5-inch-thick claws on its front flippers like ice picks to carve and maintain up to half a dozen breathing holes through sea ice six feet thick.

In early spring, pregnant females haul out through a breathing hole and dig an igloo-like snow cave ('birth lair') inside a drift atop the pack ice, hiding their fluffy white pups from the eyes of polar bears and Arctic foxes.

During the spring mating season, adult male ringed seals undergo a dramatic transformation called 'tiggak' by Inuit hunters: their faces turn jet-black from oily sebaceous secretions and they emit a pungent smell like gasoline that can be detected through the snow by polar bears half a mile away.

In Finland and Russia, two isolated landlocked subspecies, the Saimaa and Ladoga ringed seals, were trapped in freshwater lakes when glaciers retreated 9,500 years ago and have lived in fresh water ever since.
Each seal is named for the pale gray rings scattered like smoke circles across its dark back, and no two ringed seals have the exact same ring pattern.

mammals.name: Hispaniolan solenodon
facts: Looking like an oversized shrew with a long, flexible trunk, the Hispaniolan solenodon is one of the very few venomous mammals on Earth, injecting paralyzing venom through deep grooves in its lower second incisors just like a viper's fangs.

Even stranger, its long cartilaginous snout is attached to the skull by a literal 'ball-and-socket' joint, giving its nose incredible 360-degree flexibility to probe into narrow rock cracks and rotting logs for insects.

This living fossil split off from all other living placental mammals around 78 million years ago, meaning its ancestors were already sniffing around Caribbean ferns while Tyrannosaurus rex walked North America.

Because it evolved on an island with zero land mammal predators, its only defense mechanism when startled is to freeze or run in a clumsy, erratic zigzag that sometimes causes it to trip over its own long toes.
Like bats and shrews, it navigates the pitch-black forest floor at night by emitting high-frequency tongue clicks that bounce off obstacles.

mammals.name: European mink
facts: Distinguished from the invasive American mink by having a pure white upper lip as well as a white chin patch, the native European mink is now one of the most critically endangered carnivores in Europe.
When hunting in icy streams, its coat traps a silvery sheen of microscopic air bubbles that keep its skin completely dry while it dives for crayfish, frogs, and water voles.

Even if an aggressive male American mink doesn't kill a European mink over territory, the larger American males bully native European females into mating during early spring, triggering sterile hybrid pregnancies that get reabsorbed and ruin the female's entire breeding season.

To save the species from vanishing, Estonian conservationists eradicated invasive American mink from the Baltic island of Hiiumaa and established a thriving, predator-safe sanctuary for native European mink.
Equipped with webs between all five toes on both its front and hind paws, it can hold its breath underwater for up to two minutes while probing beneath undercut riverbanks.

mammals.name: Spectral bat
facts: Boasting a wingspan of over three feet, the spectral bat (or false vampire bat) is the largest bat in the Americas and the largest carnivorous bat anywhere in the world.

Early European naturalists saw this giant, fang-toothed predator in South American caves and assumed it drank blood, giving it the scientific name Vampyrum spectrum, before realizing it actually hunts parakeets, doves, rodents, and even other bats.

Unlike almost all other bats, spectral bats form devoted, lifelong monogamous pairs; while the female stays inside their hollow-tree roost nursing their single pup, the male hunts all night and carries whole birds back in his jaws to feed his partner.
When wrapping up to sleep by day, the mated pair and their offspring fold their huge leathery wings around one another in a tight family embrace.

Rather than relying purely on loud sonar clicks when stalking sleeping cuckoos or wrens in the canopy, the spectral bat tracks the musky odor of bird feathers in the dark and hovers silently before striking.

mammals.name: Kob
facts: Each year, up to a million white-eared kobs march nearly 1,000 miles across the swamps and floodplains of South Sudan and Ethiopia, forming the second-largest land mammal migration in Africa, rivaled only by the Serengeti wildebeest.

During the breeding season, male kobs abandon normal territories and pack into tiny 'leks', trampled arenas no bigger than a tennis court where up to 40 bulls stand shoulder-to-shoulder, strutting and whistling to win over visiting females.

Hold onto a prime center circle on a busy lek and a champion bull may mate with a dozen females in a single day, though exhaustion forces him to surrender his spot within a week to a fresh challenger.
So iconic is the Uganda kob in East Africa that a golden buck rearing up on its hind legs stands prominently on the official national coat of arms of Uganda.
White rings around its eyes and a white throat patch act as visual bullseyes during ritualized head-bobbing displays, allowing bulls to size up rivals without fatal horn fights.

mammals.name: Olinguito
facts: In 2013, the teddy-bear-faced olinguito made global headlines as the first new carnivorous mammal species identified in the Americas in 35 years.

For a full century, museum skins and even a live individual named 'Ringerl' kept at several U.S. zoos in the 1960s were misidentified as standard olingos; zookeepers couldn't figure out why Ringerl refused to mate with any male olingo they put in her enclosure!
Although it belongs to the taxonomic order Carnivora alongside bears, wolves, and raccoons, the olinguito is almost a complete vegetarian that feasts on cloud-forest figs, nectar, and berries.
Living high in the misty Andean cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador, which locals call 'neblina', it wears a thick, woolly auburn coat that keeps it warm in chilly, dripping mountain fog.
Strictly nocturnal and solitary, this two-pound tree-dweller leaps effortlessly across canopy gaps at night and gives birth to just a single baby at a time.

mammals.name: Common brushtail possum
facts: While protected as a beloved native marsupial across Australia, the common brushtail possum became Public Enemy #1 in New Zealand after fur trappers introduced it in 1837; with no predators, the population exploded to 30 million, devouring native forests and eating kiwi eggs.

In New Zealand today, blended possum fur and merino wool ('possum merino') is spun into luxury sweaters because each possum hair is hollow like a polar bear's, making it 55 percent warmer than sheep's wool and completely pill-free.

In Australian suburbs, bold brushtails are infamous for squeezing under roof tiles to nest inside house ceilings, where their nocturnal thumping and blood-curdling territorial screeches sound like a poltergeist.

During the breeding season, adult males secrete a reddish, musky oil from a large scent gland in the middle of their chests, staining their fur bright rust-red and rubbing their chests against tree branches.
Armed with opposable, clawless 'thumbs' on its hind feet and a naked, grippy underside on its bushy tail, it can hang upside down by its tail tip to pluck eucalyptus blossoms.

mammals.name: Fox squirrel
facts: Every fox squirrel has a rare genetic condition called congenital erythropoietic porphyria, which causes porphyrin pigments to build up in its body so its bones and teeth glow bright fluorescent pink under ultraviolet blacklight!

Look across the United States and you'll see three dramatically different wardrobe styles: Midwestern fox squirrels are rusty orange, Mid-Atlantic Delmarva individuals are silver-gray, and southeastern fox squirrels wear striking jet-black Zorro masks with white noses and ears.

Instead of piling all its winter acorns into a single hollow tree, a fox squirrel practices 'scatter-hoarding', burying up to 10,000 individual nuts in separate one-nut holes and relocating over 80 percent of them by smell and spatial memory.
Before burying an acorn, a clever fox squirrel shakes it in its teeth to judge its weight and even chews out the tiny embryo bud at the tip of white oak acorns so the nut won't sprout before spring.
As the largest tree squirrel native to North America, it spends far more time foraging on open ground and prairie edges than its skittish gray squirrel cousins.

mammals.name: Meadow vole
facts: As meadow voles scurry along their grass-clipping 'highways,' they leave behind tiny drops of urine that reflect ultraviolet light; unfortunately for the voles, hunting American kestrels and rough-legged hawks can see UV light and follow the glowing yellow trails right to dinner.
Female meadow voles hold the mammalian record for earliest puberty: a young female can ovulate and become pregnant at just 21 days old, before she is even fully weaned from her mother.

In summer, meadow voles are fiercely territorial loners that fight any neighbor on sight; yet when autumn days shorten, a surge of oxytocin rewires their brains so they happily cuddle together in communal winter nests of up to ten voles for warmth.
Every few hours around the clock, a meadow vole must wake up and eat nearly its own body weight in grass and sedge stems just to keep its furnace-like metabolism from starving.
Whenever a meadow vole population booms in an old field, the local populations of foxes, coyotes, bobcats, hawks, and owls surge right alongside them.

mammals.name: Bolivar rice rat
facts: Living in the super-wet Chocó and premontane rainforests from eastern Panama down through Colombia and Ecuador, the Bolivar rice rat is crowned with long, dark vibrissae (whiskers) that extend well past its shoulders.
Those extra-long whiskers act like radar antennae in pitch-black, rain-drenched undergrowth, allowing the rat to map wet roots and mossy boulders without bumping its nose.
Its large hind feet are uniquely elongated for wading through shallow forest streams and scrambling over slick, mud-coated fallen logs.
Rather than digging burrows that would instantly flood in tropical downpours, it constructs tight, waterproof nests beneath tangled tree buttresses and rotting palm trunks.
By eating fallen rainforest seeds and fungi at night, it plays a quiet role in recycling nutrients across one of the rainiest biodiversity hotspots on Earth.

mammals.name: Hammer-headed bat
facts: Adult male hammer-headed bats look like flying gargoyles or winged moose: their skulls and muzzles are hugely inflated to house a gigantic larynx and resonating chambers that fill more than half their body cavity, crowding their heart, lungs, and intestines backward into their abdomen!

Twice a year along riverbank trees in Central Africa, up to 130 males gather in noisy 'lek' arenas where they flap their wings at double speed and blast a deafening, metallic 'kwoink-kwoink' honk like a chorus of car horns to attract picky females.
Nearly 80 percent of all matings at a hammer-headed bat lek are won by just the top 6 percent of males holding the prime central branches.
With a three-foot wingspan, it is the largest bat on the entire African continent, yet despite its terrifying face, it eats almost nothing but sweet figs and banana juice.
Females have normal, fox-like faces and weigh barely half as much as the giant-headed males, creating the most extreme sexual dimorphism of any bat species in the world.

mammals.name: Weddell seal
facts: Living farther south than any other mammal on Earth, the Weddell seal thrives along the frozen edge of Antarctica in McMurdo Sound, barely 800 miles from the South Pole.

To keep breathing holes open through seven feet of rock-hard Antarctic fast ice, it opens its jaws 180 degrees wide and uses its protruding upper canines and incisors like an ice saw, rasping away at the freezing ice until its teeth wear down to stubs in old age.

Underwater, male Weddell seals sing an eerie, sci-fi repertoire of laser-like trills, whistles, and deep booming chirps so loud that explorers sleeping inside tents on top of the ice can feel the vibrations through their sleeping bags.
Before diving up to 2,000 feet deep for over an hour, a Weddell seal actually exhales most of the air from its lungs, relying instead on massive oxygen reserves stored in its spleen and muscles.
Because they evolved on Antarctic ice sheets where polar bears and land predators have never existed, Weddell seals on the ice have zero fear of walking humans.

mammals.name: Hoffmann's two-toed sloth
