Today, fewer than one percent of its original South American grassland habitat remains untouched, yet isolated populations still thrive inside Brazil's vast flooded Pantanal wetlands.

When a mother spots a maned wolf or puma stalking her fawn, she performs a 'broken-leg dance,' limping noisily away in full view to lure the predator after her while her spotted baby freezes flat in the grass.
Inquisitive rather than skittish, a pampas deer will often stand up on its hind legs like a kangaroo to peer over tall pampas grass plumes at passing riders.
Every fawn is born with rows of creamy white spots that vanish completely by three months of age, replaced by a sleek reddish-tan coat.

mammals.name: Djungarian hamster
facts: Commonly known as the 'winter white dwarf hamster,' its brown-and-black summer fur transforms into a snowy-white camouflage coat as autumn daylight shrinks across the Siberian steppes.

Rather than sleeping through the entire winter in deep hibernation, it practices 'daily torpor', dropping its body temperature to sixty degrees for a few hours each morning to save calories before waking up to snack on cached seeds.
Even the soles of its tiny paws and the inside of its ears are covered in dense white fur to prevent frostbite while tunneling under snowdrifts at minus-forty degrees.
Both parents share nursery duty in the wild: the father helps clean newborn pups, keeps the nest warm while the mother forages, and even assists during birth.
Along its spine runs a sharp, dark racing stripe that stays visible even when the rest of its body turns winter-white.

mammals.name: Mountain degu
facts: Unlike almost all small rodents, which are creatures of the night, the mountain degu is strictly diurnal and has retinas tuned to see ultraviolet light.

Why does an Andean rodent need UV vision? Fresh degu urine reflects ultraviolet rays like neon paint, allowing colonies to read each other's scent trails and territorial borders at a glance across sun-bleached rocks!
If a hawk or fox grabs a mountain degu by the tail, the outer skin and fur slip right off like a glove, a trick called 'degloving', while the degu escapes and chews off the bare vertebrae later.
Wait, does the tail grow back? Unlike a lizard's tail, a degu's tail never regenerates once lost, so a stub-tailed degu has used up its one get-out-of-jail-free card.
Its figure-eight-shaped molar teeth give its whole family (Octodontidae) its name, partnered with bright orange front incisors colored by iron-hard enamel.

mammals.name: Bornean ferret-badger
facts: Found only on the misty, 10,000-foot slopes of Mount Kinabalu and neighboring peaks in Borneo, this masked mustelid looks like a miniature badger stretched out onto a ferret's body.
When cornered by a clouded leopard or dog, it combines a vicious bite with a skunk-like secret weapon, firing a pungent, foul-smelling liquid from its anal glands.
Its rubbery, pig-like snout projects well past its lower jaw, acting as a built-in trowel for rooting through mossy mountain leaf litter after earthworms and beetles.
Long, non-retractable white claws on its front paws are curved like garden picks to rip open rotting logs and dig sleeping burrows beneath rhododendron roots.
Despite living in cold, wet cloud forests high above the tropical lowlands, it never hibernates, foraging through freezing midnight downpours under a starkly contrasted black-and-white face mask.

mammals.name: Roloway monkey
facts: Distinguished by a magnificent, pointed white wizard's beard up to four inches long and a matching crown fringe shaped like a tiara, this West African canopy dweller is one of the most regal primates on Earth.
A master of interspecies teamwork, it regularly forms mixed-species patrols with Diana monkeys and red colobus monkeys to double the number of eyes watching for crowned eagles.
To avoid competing with their travel partners in the same tree, Roloway monkeys specialize in peeling bark to hunt insects and eating mature seeds while neighboring monkeys take the ripe fruit.
Inside its mouth are expandable cheek pouches that can hold an entire fistful of forest berries, allowing it to grab food in dangerous open branches and chew later in hidden foliage.
Today, fewer than a few hundred individuals survive in the wild forests of Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, making a sighting of its white beard in the high canopy one of conservation's rarest prizes.

mammals.name: Manchurian hare
facts: Unlike its snowy northern cousins that turn pure white in winter, this woodland hare keeps its dappled brown-and-black camouflage coat all year long to blend into oak leaf litter.
A rare entirely jet-black morph was once so distinctive in the Primorsky forests of the Russian Far East that 19th-century naturalists mistakenly classified it as a separate species.
Rather than digging burrows like a rabbit, it rests inside a shallow depression scratched into the forest floor or hides inside hollow fallen larch trunks.
When pursued by a Siberian leopard cat or sable, it weaves through dense hazel thickets and bangs its hind feet against the frozen ground to warn neighboring hares.
Its ears and hind legs are noticeably shorter than those of open-steppe hares, trading top-end straight-line speed for razor-sharp cornering among tightly packed forest trees.

mammals.name: Banded palm civet
facts: Across its reddish-buff back run four to five bold, coal-black transverse saddles that break up its silhouette under moonlit ferns like the stripes of a miniature Tasmanian tiger.

Unlike tree-dwelling palm civets, it spends most of its nights prowling along rainforest stream banks, using sensitive front paws to feel under wet stones for earthworms, crickets, and freshwater snails.
The hairs along the back of its neck grow pointing forward toward its head rather than backward, creating a plush, reversed-nap collar.
When startled on the forest floor, it arches its striped back like a Halloween cat, puffs its tail to twice its normal thickness, and hisses while stamping its front paws.
Wait until it climbs: equipped with fully retractable claws like a feline's, it keeps its weapons razor-sharp for scrambling up vertical lianas and sleeping in high tree holes.

mammals.name: Six-banded armadillo
facts: Unlike almost all other armadillos, which cannot digest fat easily and stick to ants, the six-banded armadillo stores a thick layer of subcutaneous yellow fat beneath its shell to survive lean Brazilian dry seasons.
Because its eyes contain only rod cells and zero cone cells, it is completely colorblind and nearly blind in bright midday sun, navigating instead by a bloodhound-grade sense of smell.
When digging out a subterranean wasp or fire-ant nest, it can hold its breath for six full minutes so it never inhales choking dust or angry insects, even while furiously shoveling dirt!
After tearing into a rotting log or carrion pile, it stands up on its hind legs and balances against its stiff, armored tail like a tripod to sniff the wind for jaguars.
Though solitary for most of the year, half a dozen individuals will suddenly gather around a single fallen palm tree or carcass to feast side by side before wandering off.

mammals.name: Suni
facts: Weighing less than a gallon of milk, often just eight to ten pounds, this pint-sized East African antelope vanishes completely inside ankle-high leaf litter on the coastal forest floor.
Beneath each eye sits a massive preorbital gland nearly as large as the eyeball itself, which oozes a dark, musky paste rubbed onto the tips of low twigs to mark territory.
When a crowned eagle or python approaches, the suni freezes completely motionless until the predator is within arm's reach, then explodes away in a frantic series of erratic zigzags.
Even though it lives in hot, humid coastal thickets from Kenya to South Africa, it requires zero standing water, getting every drop of moisture from freshly fallen leaves and fungi.
To warn its lifelong mate without giving away its exact location in the dark brush, it vents a faint, wheezing whistle through its nostrils that sounds like a windblown reed.

mammals.name: Tonkin snub-nosed monkey
facts: Looking like an elfin cartoon character, it has no protruding nose bridge at all, just two upturned nostrils set flat into its face accompanied by puffy, sky-blue eye rings and thick, bright-pink lips.

According to local Vietnamese folklore in the limestone karst mountains of Ha Giang, when torrential monsoon rains fall, these monkeys sit in the trees with their heads tucked between their knees so rainwater doesn't drip straight into their upturned nostrils and make them sneeze!

For nearly forty years after World War II, scientists feared this flamboyant primate had gone completely extinct until a surviving population was rediscovered on steep limestone cliffs in northern Vietnam in 1989.
When swinging through vertical jungle canopies above razor-sharp karst pinnacles, its cream-and-black tail, longer than its entire body, acts as a fifth limb for balance.

Unlike noisy macaques, troops of Tonkin snub-nosed monkeys communicate with soft, ventriloquist-like 'hiccup' calls that echo off limestone cave walls without revealing which tree they are sitting in.
